entries.text: The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection and prevent the RCS pressure exceeding design limits to protect the integrity of the RCPB and vacuum breakers on the outlet piping.
Control RCS pressure and accommodate volume changes
The pressurizer design controls pressure and accommodates coolant volume changes to ensure operational limits are not exceeded. The pressurizer

The RPVis a thick-walled cylindrical pressure vessel with an integrally welded bottom head and a removable flanged top head. The RCS leg piping is welded directly to the RPV. The control rod drive mechanisms are mounted on the RPV upper hemispherical head. The RPV head vent discharges to the Passive Core Make-up Water Tanks (PCMWT), which is part of the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCM). The RCS design has provisions for venting non-condensable gases from the RPV head and RCPs. Venting from the pressurizer is accomplished via connections to other systems.

The steam generator is a vertical shell and tube Once-Through Steam Generator (OTSG). The steam generator is designed to utilize reactor coolant on the tube side and feedwater on the shell side. The hot legs connect the OTSG upper channel to the RPV outlet nozzles. The hot reactor coolant from the RPV flows down through the OTSG tubes to the lower head and into the cold leg shells back to the RPV. The primary coolant transfers heat to the feedwater flowing up the shell side of the OTSG to produce superheated steam.

The pressurizer has a thick cylindrical shell with a top hemispherical head and is laterally restrained by supports. The pressurizer is sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure during operational maneuvers and transients, thus eliminating the need for fast-acting power operated relief valves (PORVs) in the SMR-300 design.

The RCP is a vertical, centrifugal type pump. The pump is designed to use traditional seals designed to allow continued operation of the pump for a period of at least one week after failure of one of the several stages in order to permit an orderly plant shutdown, without excessive loss of reactor coolant, in the event of the degradation of a second seal stage. The RCP has provisions to prevent motor damage due to overheating by the use of an onboard heat exchanger that is supplied with component cooling water.

Two 50 percent capacity pumps are provided, one on each cold leg. There are two safety related characteristics of the RCP. First, in the event of a reactor trip or loss of power, the pumps maintain flow to the core during pump coast down using a flywheel. Second, the RCPs serve as part of the RCS pressure boundary. The pumps are not required to perform any active safety functions and will be de-energized during LOCA or operation of the primary or secondary decay heat removal systems. The SMR-300 design does not include provisions to operate with a single pump running during power operations (Mode 1).

Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure and Vessel Code Section III [13]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT. The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients.
Figure 8-1 depicts the RCS overpressure protection subsystem as modeled in the SMR-300 PSA.

entries.text: Flag events can be provided in the system level fault tree model to allow for sensitivity studies to be performed, and the use of flag events also allows the model to be customized for various initiating events. In addition, flag events can be used to represent split fraction events as needed to condition model logic. The use of flag / split fraction events was determined to not be applicable for the RCS system model. The flag / split fraction events developed for the system level RCS model, including its description, is presented in Table 8-5.

A system level quantification was performed to identify any cut sets that are nonsensical because they contain two failures of the same component, they contain conditional probability events that cannot occur simultaneously, they contain test and maintenance events on two trains simultaneously that is not allowed by operating procedures or technical specifications, or they contain other nonsensical combinations of events. No nonsensical combinations of events were identified for the RCS. The mutually exclusive list developed for the system level RCS model, including its description, is presented in Table 8-6.

Analysis of the RCS shows that there is no credible way to divert the system flow within the RCS for the functions modeled in the RCS model. RCS interfaces with other fluid systems are evaluated as part of the ISLOCA analysis [25].

Uncertainties with RCP tripping (Assumption 1 in Section 4.0) represent realistic expectations of the SMR-300 plant operation and are expected to represent negligible uncertainty within the model. The RCPs are designed to trip upon the actuation of the DHR function since the RCPs add head load to the RCS and their continued operation would require additional heat removal by the DHR function. Should the RCPs not trip as expected, the overpressure protection function would not be impacted in any manner. The uncertainty introduced is judged to be negligible based on the very low probability of occurrence of the RCP trip failure, as discussed below.

The information provided in this report provides the foundation from which the system level fault tree will be developed. This information is based on the SMR-300 plant design as available in HIDOC as of December 19, 2024. When supporting references are revised, the changes need to be reviewed to determine if they impact any of the information used in this report, and this report and the fault tree developed based on it will need to be revised if the supporting information changes any of the modeling assumptions or bases [27].

[1] American Society of Mechanical Engineers/American Nuclear Society, "Addenda to ASME/ANS RA-S-2008 Standard for Level 1/Large Early Release Frequency Probabilistic Risk Assessment for Nuclear Power Plant Applications", ASME/ANS RA-Sa- 2009.

[2] American Society of Mechanical Engineers/American Nuclear Society, "Standard for Level 1/Large Early Release Frequency Probabilistic Risk Assessment for Nuclear Power Plant Applications", ASME/ANS RA-S-1.1-2022, May 31, 2022.

[3] U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, "An Approach for Determining the Technical Adequacy of Probabilistic Risk Assessment Results for Risk-Informed Activities", Regulatory Guide 1.200, Revision 2, March 2009.
[4] Holtec International, "SMR-300 PSA Modeling Groundrules and Assumptions", HI- 2240197, Rev.0.
[5] Holtec International, "PSA System Model and Supporting Notebook Development", HPP- 8002-3103, Rev.0.

entries.text: This section discusses the common cause failure events that can affect the RCS, including their causes, effects, and mitigation strategies. It provides a detailed analysis of the events that can lead to simultaneous failures in multiple components or systems.

This section describes the model flags and split fractions used in the PSA analysis for the RCS. It explains how these parameters are used to model the behavior of the system under different conditions and events.
This section identifies and discusses the mutually exclusive events that can occur within the RCS. It explains the conditions under which these events can occur and their impact on system safety.

This section analyzes the flow diversion events that can affect the RCS, including their causes, effects, and mitigation strategies. It provides a detailed overview of the events that can lead to abnormal flow conditions within the system.

This section discusses the uncertainties associated with the PSA analysis for the RCS. It identifies the sources of uncertainty, their potential impact on the analysis results, and the methods used to address these uncertainties.

This section presents the results of the PSA analysis for the RCS, including the system success criteria, fault tree top gate and event, and the overall conclusions drawn from the analysis. It provides a summary of the key findings and their implications for system safety.

This section lists the references used in the PSA analysis for the RCS. It includes the sources of data, models, and methodologies used in the analysis, providing a comprehensive bibliography for further reading.

This section provides a list of the appendices included in the document, detailing the additional information and data that support the PSA analysis for the RCS. It includes descriptions of the content and purpose of each appendix.
This notebook details the functions of the RCS that are credited in the SMR-300 PSA and provides the basis and description of the RCS system level fault tree that models the credited function(s).

The SMR-300 PSA is quantified by integrating top logic, intermediate logic, and system level fault trees that have been developed in accordance with standard PSA modeling techniques and following the rules and assumptions detailed in HPP-8002-3103 [5] and HI-2240197 [4]. The development of the SMR-300 PSA system level fault tree models and supporting system notebooks are based on the requirements of the ANS/ASME PSA Standard 111[2], Regulatory Guide 1.200 [3] and best PSA practices in use as of December 2024. This report provides the rationale behind the system level modeling decisions, and provides the documentation that details how the requirements of the ANS/ASME PSA Standard [2] and Regulatory Guide 1.200 [3] have been met. The RCS system information is primarily contained in its System Design Description report [6].

This report documents the system functions as credited in the PSA, and provides the details required to understand the specific components and actions necessary to support the system functions being successfully performed. Simplified piping and instrumentation drawings (P&IDs) are provided that show the system boundaries as defined for the PSA and show the components whose failure(s) would result in a failure of the system to be able to perform its modeled function.
In addition, this report identifies the following fault tree model information:

The system level top gates and associated success criteria that need to be modeled to support the overall SMR-300 integrated PSA model. A system level top gate must be developed for each function required to be modeled in the SMR-300 PSA. A top gate is any gate required to support linking of the fault trees and does not need to be an actual "top" in the fault tree model being developed but must be identified as a top gate to ensure the correct gate name is used in the system model that requires the support system logic for linking.

The basis for common cause component groupings (CCCGs) and component failure modes that are included in the system level fault tree model, including the CCCG names that are used in the fault tree model, if any are required to be modeled for the system.

The basis for test and maintenance activities that are included in the system level fault tree model, including the test and maintenance names that are used in the fault tree model, if any are required to be modeled for the system.
The basis for any pre-initiator and/or post-initiator system level operator actions that are included in the system level fault tree model, including the human failure event (HFE)

entries.text: The pressurizer has a thick cylindrical shell with a top hemispherical head and is laterally restrained by supports. The pressurizer is sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure during operational maneuvers and transients, thus eliminating the need for fast-acting power operated relief valves (PORVs) in the SMR-300 design.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The RCP is a vertical, centrifugal type pump. The pump is designed to use traditional seals designed to allow continued operation of the pump for a period of at least one week after failure of one of the several stages in order to permit an orderly plant shutdown, without excessive loss of reactor coolant, in the event of the degradation of a second seal stage.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The RCP has provisions to prevent motor damage due to overheating by the use of an onboard heat exchanger that is supplied with component cooling water. Two 50 percent capacity pumps are provided, one on each cold leg.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: There are two safety related characteristics of the RCP. First, in the event of a reactor trip or loss of power, the pumps maintain flow to the core during pump coast down using a flywheel. Second, the RCPs serve as part of the RCS pressure boundary.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The pumps are not required to perform any active safety functions and will be de-energized during LOCA or operation of the primary or secondary decay heat removal systems. The SMR-300 design does not include provisions to operate with a single pump running during power operations (Mode 1).

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure and Vessel Code Section III [13]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients. Figure 8-1 depicts the RCS overpressure protection subsystem as modeled in the SMR-300 PSA.

entries.section_title: 8.7.2 Latent Human Error (Maintenance Related Operator Errors) Review
entries.text: A review of the RCS was performed to identify potential latent human errors that should be included in the SMR-300 PSA model. Any errors in calibrating the spring-loaded PSVs would be detected in post-maintenance testing. No errors were identified for inclusion in the RCS model.
There are no required operator interactions with the RCS during normal power operations.

There are potentially required operator interactions with the RCS during low power and shutdown operations for RCS coolant/inventory level changes, securing RCPs, and RHR actuation. These potential actions will be clarified as part of the SMR-300 low power and shutdown PSA. These low power and shutdown functions are not a required part of and are not included in the normal power operation model.
There are no required operator interactions with the RCS during abnormal operations.

Reference [6] notes the reactor vessel head vent valves are opened from the main control room to allow venting from the RPV head vent and RCS if non-condensable gases accumulate following an accident. The RPV head vent is not credited to be venting as a safety function or a safety-related core cooling function. The PSVs operate the same way in post-core damage scenarios where the RCS is intact. The PSVs are not designed for mitigating severe accident phenomena. Note that the ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident. These Level 2 functions are not part of and are not included in the normal power operation model.

The Holtec SMR-300 is comprised of a number of systems that work together to produce electrical energy. When the safe operation of the SMR-300 is challenged, the plant is designed to shut down and enter a long term safe stable condition. The SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Analysis (PSA) is associated with evaluating the very small possibility that the plant is not able to reach a safe stable condition, and that core damage and potentially a radioactive release occurs. Since not all systems are required to safely shut down the plant, the PSA is focused on those systems that play a role in shutting down the plant and ensuring it reaches a safe stable condition.

The SMR-300 PSA models the front-line systems that are relied upon to shut down the reactor and maintaining it in a safe, stable state and the supporting systems that are needed to support the front-line systems. The Reactor Coolant System (RCS) has been identified as one of the systems required to ensure the plant safely shuts down and reaches a safe stable condition. The RCS, as modeled in the SMR-300 Internal Events At-Power PSA, is detailed in this report.

Flag events can be provided in the system level fault tree model to allow for sensitivity studies to be performed, and the use of flag events also allows the model to be customized for various initiating events. In addition, flag events can be used to represent split fraction events as needed to condition model logic. The use of flag / split fraction events was determined to not be applicable for the RCS system model. The flag / split fraction events developed for the system level RCS model, including its description, is presented in Table 8-5.

A system level quantification was performed to identify any cut sets that are nonsensical because they contain two failures of the same component, they contain conditional probability events that cannot occur simultaneously, they contain test and maintenance events on two trains simultaneously that is not allowed by operating procedures or technical specifications, or they contain other nonsensical combinations of events. No nonsensical combinations of events were identified for the RCS. The mutually exclusive list developed for the system level RCS model, including its description, is presented in Table 8-6.

Analysis of the RCS shows that there is no credible way to divert the system flow within the RCS for the functions modeled in the RCS model. RCS interfaces with other fluid systems are evaluated as part of the ISLOCA analysis [25].

Uncertainties with RCP tripping (Assumption 1 in Section 4.0) represent realistic expectations of the SMR-300 plant operation and are expected to represent negligible uncertainty within the model. The RCPs are designed to trip upon the actuation of the DHR function since the RCPs add head load to the RCS and their continued operation would require additional heat removal by the DHR function. Should the RCPs not trip as expected, the overpressure protection function would not be impacted in any manner. The uncertainty introduced is judged to be negligible based on the very low probability of occurrence of the RCP trip failure, as discussed below.

entries.text: Modeling assumptions are used when information is not known, when multiple potential options are available, or to ensure model simplification measures are realistic or conservative. Since the SMR-300 is still in the design phase, several modeling assumptions have been made to allow the PSA model to be completed for sensitivity analysis and to provide insights into proposed system designs.

Modeling notes are used to help the PSA analyst understand the basis for the modeling included in the system level fault tree. These modeling notes may be associated with decisions on what is modeled or what is not modeled (e.g., flow diversion pathways) or may provide clarification as to why the modeling technique used was determined to be appropriate.

The overall SMR-300 PSA modeling groundrules and assumptions are documented in HI-2240197 [4]. The modeling assumptions and modeling notes specific to the RCS are detailed below. Unverified assumptions may impact the system analysis significantly and require validation. Modeling notes are intended for general notes and clarifications only.
System specific assumptions list:

1. The Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCPs) are designed to trip (stop running) in response to a SMR-300 plant trip that actuates the Decay Heat Removal (DHR) function or involves a loss of offsite power which powers the RCPs [8]. Failure of the RCP tripping for DHR actuation is not explicitly modeled in the RCS fault tree analysis since this failure potential (failure to trip automatically represented as a relay failure or RCP breaker failure on two series channels which would be ANDed with each other, which would in turn be ANDed with Operator failing to trip the RCPs) would be orders of magnitude below the PSV failure probability and is screened from consideration. It is also assumed that the initial RCP breaker failure to trip does not prevent the backup operator action to trip the RCPs. This is a reasonable assumption and typical treatment for RCP design and modeling.

1. In the RCS model, all sensors mounted on the RCS components/piping are considered elements of the RCS pressure boundary only, and failure of these sensors do not fail the Pressurizer Safety Valves (PSVs) from performing their design function. Therefore, sensors are not included in the RCS over-pressurization fault tree model. This is a reasonable assumption and typical treatment for passive components such as the PSVs.

2. Major passive mechanical components of the RCS (such as Reactor Pressure Vessel, Steam Generator, Pressurizers and piping) are not explicitly included into the fault tree model. Instead, they are considered implicitly as part of the Loss of Coolant Accident (LOCA) Initiating Event identification and frequency estimation [8].

3. Although the Automatic Depressurization System (ADS) (Stage 1 and 2) valves and piping are considered within the RCS pressure boundary, the ADS is considered to be part of the Passive Core Cooling System, and is modeled separately in the SMR-300 PSA.

4. Although the main design safety function of the PSVs is to protect the RCS from RCS over-pressurization, the PSVs must also successfully re-close after relieving the pressure to maintain the pressure boundary. A PSV that opens as designed but fails to re-close results in a steam space LOCA.

5. The success criteria for the PSVs to re-close is two of two PSVs. A single failure is sufficient to fail this function, therefore, a common cause fails to close event for the two PSVs is not required or included in the model.

The information in this report is based on the system level design as of December 19, 2024. Approved HIDOC reports and drawings are referenced with the Revision number of the report or drawing included in the reference call out. Reports and drawings that are still in formal development, but that are of sufficient quality to be used in support of this analysis are identified as "Draft" in the reference call out.

The CAFTA computer code [10] is an approved Class A computer program on the Holtec Approved Computer Program List (ACPL). This software is used in the development of the system level fault tree associated with this report.

entries.text: The purpose of this document is to provide a detailed analysis of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) as part of the SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Analysis (PSA). The RCS is a critical system in ensuring the safe shutdown and stable condition of the SMR-300 reactor. This report focuses on the modeling and analysis of the RCS within the context of the PSA, highlighting its role in maintaining the reactor's safety during normal and abnormal operations.

The methodology employed in this report involves a comprehensive review of the RCS design, operational procedures, and failure modes. The analysis is based on the PSA framework, which includes event tree and fault tree analyses. The document outlines the assumptions, modeling notes, and acceptance criteria used in the PSA to evaluate the RCS performance.

The acceptance criteria for the RCS within the PSA are defined to ensure that the system meets the required safety standards. These criteria include the probability of core damage and the likelihood of a radioactive release. The document specifies the thresholds and benchmarks used to assess the RCS performance against these criteria.

Several assumptions and modeling notes are provided to clarify the approach taken in the PSA. These include assumptions about system interactions, failure rates, and human actions. The modeling notes detail the specific methods and tools used to construct the event trees and fault trees for the RCS.

The input data for the PSA includes system parameters, failure probabilities, and operational data. This section provides a comprehensive list of the data sources and the rationale behind the selection of specific data points. The data is critical for the accuracy and reliability of the PSA results.

The computer codes used in the PSA are described in this section. These codes are essential for simulating the RCS behavior under various scenarios. The document outlines the software tools, their capabilities, and the specific algorithms employed in the analysis.

This section details the computer files generated during the PSA. These files include input data files, simulation results, and output reports. The document provides a guide on how to access and interpret these files for further analysis and validation.

The analysis section presents the results of the PSA for the RCS. This includes the event tree and fault tree analyses, the calculation of failure probabilities, and the assessment of system performance against the acceptance criteria. The document discusses the key findings and their implications for reactor safety.

The system function of the RCS is described in detail, outlining its role in maintaining the reactor's safety during normal and abnormal operations. This section provides a technical overview of the RCS components and their interactions.

A comprehensive description of the RCS is provided, including its design, components, and operational procedures. This section serves as a reference for understanding the system's functionality and its integration within the SMR-300 reactor.
The system boundaries for the RCS within the PSA are defined, specifying the scope of the analysis. This includes the interfaces with other systems and the external conditions considered in the PSA.
This section details the interfaces and dependencies of the RCS with other systems within the SMR-300 reactor. It highlights the critical interactions that influence the RCS performance and safety.

The instrumentation and control systems associated with the RCS are described, including sensors, actuators, and control algorithms. This section explains how these systems monitor and regulate the RCS to ensure safe operation.

A detailed description of the instrumentation used in the RCS is provided, including the types of sensors, their locations, and their functions. This section emphasizes the importance of accurate monitoring for system safety.

The control systems for the RCS are outlined, detailing the algorithms and procedures used to regulate the system. This includes automatic and manual control mechanisms designed to maintain the RCS within safe operating parameters.

This section describes the operational procedures for the RCS, including normal, low power, shutdown, and abnormal operations. It provides a step-by-step guide to ensure the system operates safely and effectively.

The procedures for normal plant operations involving the RCS are detailed, ensuring that the system functions correctly under standard conditions. This includes routine monitoring and maintenance activities.
The operational procedures for low power and shutdown conditions are described, highlighting the specific actions required to transition the RCS safely from normal to shutdown mode.

This section outlines the procedures for handling abnormal operations involving the RCS, including emergency shutdowns and fault management. It emphasizes the importance of quick and effective responses to maintain safety.

The procedures for Level 2 operations, which involve more severe conditions and potential core damage, are detailed. This includes the actions required to mitigate the effects of such events and ensure the reactor remains in a safe condition.
The test and maintenance procedures for the RCS are described, ensuring that the system remains in optimal condition. This includes routine inspections, calibrations, and repairs.

This section reviews the maintenance unavailability of the RCS, assessing the impact of maintenance activities on system availability and safety. It provides recommendations for minimizing downtime while ensuring system integrity.

This section describes the model flags and split fractions used in the PSA analysis for the RCS. It explains how these parameters are used to model the behavior of the system under different conditions and events.

entries.text: The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during normal plant operation.
The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during normal plant operation.

Reference [6] notes that the RCS could be in standby or operating during low power and shutdown operations, depending on the exact plant state. The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during low power and shutdown operations, with a closed primary circuit.
The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is not used during refueling operations.
The RCS is not used during refueling operations though water is present within the system for refueling activities.

During accident conditions the RCPs are not required to remain functional [6]. The only safety functions of the RCPs are to provide adequate pump coast down to ensure reactor coolant continues to flow for a short time after pump trip and to maintain the RCPB.

The PSVs would remain closed during accident conditions unless RCS pressure exceeds their opening setpoint. In that case, the PSVs would be expected to open to lower RCS pressure and subsequently reclose when RCS pressure is again below the PSV opening setpoint to maintain the RCPB.

Reference [6] notes the reactor vessel head vent valves are opened from the main control room to allow venting from the RPV head vent and RCS if non-condensable gases accumulate following an accident. The RPV head vent is not credited to be venting as a safety function or a safety-related core cooling function. The PSVs operate the same way in post-core damage scenarios where the RCS is intact. The PSVs are not designed for mitigating severe accident phenomena. Note that the ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident. These Level 2 functions are not part of the Level 1 PSA model.

Since the RCS is always operating during normal plant operation, online testing of the system is not performed. Any testing is expected to occur during plant shutdown and refueling operations. Both PSVs are spring-loaded safety valves [6] that are located inside the Containment. Since the valves are spring-loaded, remote testing or operation of the valves is not possible. Since Containment is not accessible when the SMR-300 is at-power, local operation or maintenance of the valves is not possible.
There are no test or maintenance activities for the RCS during normal power operation as discussed above.

entries.text: A review of the RCS was performed to identify potential latent human errors that should be included in the SMR-300 PSA model. Any errors in calibrating the spring-loaded PSVs would be detected in post-maintenance testing. No errors were identified for inclusion in the RCS model.
There are no required operator interactions with the RCS during normal power operations.

There are potentially required operator interactions with the RCS during low power and shutdown operations for RCS coolant/inventory level changes, securing RCPs, and RHR actuation. These potential actions will be clarified as part of the SMR-300 low power and shutdown PSA. These low power and shutdown functions are not a required part of and are not included in the normal power operation model.
There are no required operator interactions with the RCS during abnormal operations.

entries.text: 1. In the RCS model, all sensors mounted on the RCS components/piping are considered elements of the RCS pressure boundary only, and failure of these sensors do not fail the Pressurizer Safety Valves (PSVs) from performing their design function. Therefore, sensors are not included in the RCS over-pressurization fault tree model. This is a reasonable assumption and typical treatment for passive components such as the PSVs.

2. Major passive mechanical components of the RCS (such as Reactor Pressure Vessel, Steam Generator, Pressurizers and piping) are not explicitly included into the fault tree model. Instead, they are considered implicitly as part of the Loss of Coolant Accident (LOCA) Initiating Event identification and frequency estimation [8].

3. Although the Automatic Depressurization System (ADS) (Stage 1 and 2) valves and piping are considered within the RCS pressure boundary, the ADS is considered to be part of the Passive Core Cooling System, and is modeled separately in the SMR-300 PSA.

4. Although the main design safety function of the PSVs is to protect the RCS from RCS over-pressurization, the PSVs must also successfully re-close after relieving the pressure to maintain the pressure boundary. A PSV that opens as designed but fails to re-close results in a steam space LOCA.

5. The success criteria for the PSVs to re-close is two of two PSVs. A single failure is sufficient to fail this function, therefore, a common cause fails to close event for the two PSVs is not required or included in the model.

entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is comprised of a number of systems that work together to produce electrical energy. When the safe operation of the SMR-300 is challenged, the plant is designed to shut down and enter a long term safe stable condition. The SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Analysis (PSA) is associated with evaluating the very small possibility that the plant is not able to reach a safe stable condition, and that core damage and potentially a radioactive release occurs. Since not all systems are required to safely shut down the plant, the PSA is focused on those systems that play a role in shutting down the plant and ensuring it reaches a safe stable condition.

The SMR-300 PSA models the front-line systems that are relied upon to shut down the reactor and maintaining it in a safe, stable state and the supporting systems that are needed to support the front-line systems. The Reactor Coolant System (RCS) has been identified as one of the systems required to ensure the plant safely shuts down and reaches a safe stable condition. The RCS, as modeled in the SMR-300 Internal Events At-Power PSA, is detailed in this report.

The purpose of this document is to provide a detailed analysis of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) as part of the SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Analysis (PSA). The RCS is a critical system in ensuring the safe shutdown and stable condition of the SMR-300 reactor. This report focuses on the modeling and analysis of the RCS within the context of the PSA, highlighting its role in maintaining the reactor's safety during normal and abnormal operations.

The methodology employed in this report involves a comprehensive review of the RCS design, operational procedures, and failure modes. The analysis is based on the PSA framework, which includes event tree and fault tree analyses. The document outlines the assumptions, modeling notes, and acceptance criteria used in the PSA to evaluate the RCS performance.

The acceptance criteria for the RCS within the PSA are defined to ensure that the system meets the required safety standards. These criteria include the probability of core damage and the likelihood of a radioactive release. The document specifies the thresholds and benchmarks used to assess the RCS performance against these criteria.

Several assumptions and modeling notes are provided to clarify the approach taken in the PSA. These include assumptions about system interactions, failure rates, and human actions. The modeling notes detail the specific methods and tools used to construct the event trees and fault trees for the RCS.

The input data for the PSA includes system parameters, failure probabilities, and operational data. This section provides a comprehensive list of the data sources and the rationale behind the selection of specific data points. The data is critical for the accuracy and reliability of the PSA results.

The computer codes used in the PSA are described in this section. These codes are essential for simulating the RCS behavior under various scenarios. The document outlines the software tools, their capabilities, and the specific algorithms employed in the analysis.

This section details the computer files generated during the PSA. These files include input data files, simulation results, and output reports. The document provides a guide on how to access and interpret these files for further analysis and validation.

The analysis section presents the results of the PSA for the RCS. This includes the event tree and fault tree analyses, the calculation of failure probabilities, and the assessment of system performance against the acceptance criteria. The document discusses the key findings and their implications for reactor safety.

The system function of the RCS is described in detail, outlining its role in maintaining the reactor's safety during normal and abnormal operations. This section provides a technical overview of the RCS components and their interactions.

A comprehensive description of the RCS is provided, including its design, components, and operational procedures. This section serves as a reference for understanding the system's functionality and its integration within the SMR-300 reactor.
The system boundaries for the RCS within the PSA are defined, specifying the scope of the analysis. This includes the interfaces with other systems and the external conditions considered in the PSA.
This section details the interfaces and dependencies of the RCS with other systems within the SMR-300 reactor. It highlights the critical interactions that influence the RCS performance and safety.

The instrumentation and control systems associated with the RCS are described, including sensors, actuators, and control algorithms. This section explains how these systems monitor and regulate the RCS to ensure safe operation.

A detailed description of the instrumentation used in the RCS is provided, including the types of sensors, their locations, and their functions. This section emphasizes the importance of accurate monitoring for system safety.

The control systems for the RCS are outlined, detailing the algorithms and procedures used to regulate the system. This includes automatic and manual control mechanisms designed to maintain the RCS within safe operating parameters.

This section describes the operational procedures for the RCS, including normal, low power, shutdown, and abnormal operations. It provides a step-by-step guide to ensure the system operates safely and effectively.

The procedures for normal plant operations involving the RCS are detailed, ensuring that the system functions correctly under standard conditions. This includes routine monitoring and maintenance activities.
The operational procedures for low power and shutdown conditions are described, highlighting the specific actions required to transition the RCS safely from normal to shutdown mode.

This section outlines the procedures for handling abnormal operations involving the RCS, including emergency shutdowns and fault management. It emphasizes the importance of quick and effective responses to maintain safety.

The procedures for Level 2 operations, which involve more severe conditions and potential core damage, are detailed. This includes the actions required to mitigate the effects of such events and ensure the reactor remains in a safe condition.
The test and maintenance procedures for the RCS are described, ensuring that the system remains in optimal condition. This includes routine inspections, calibrations, and repairs.

This section reviews the maintenance unavailability of the RCS, assessing the impact of maintenance activities on system availability and safety. It provides recommendations for minimizing downtime while ensuring system integrity.

entries.text: The review of latent human errors related to maintenance activities is detailed, identifying potential operator errors and their impact on the RCS. This section provides strategies for mitigating human error and enhancing safety.

The system success criteria for the RCS within the PSA are defined, specifying the conditions under which the system is considered to have performed successfully. This includes the criteria for avoiding core damage and radioactive release.

entries.text: The following subsections discuss the instrumentation and control logic as related to the RCS.
The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during normal plant operation.
The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during normal plant operation.

Reference [6] notes that the RCS could be in standby or operating during low power and shutdown operations, depending on the exact plant state. The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is in standby during low power and shutdown operations, with a closed primary circuit.
The RCS overpressure protection subsystem is not used during refueling operations.
The RCS is not used during refueling operations though water is present within the system for refueling activities.

During accident conditions the RCPs are not required to remain functional [6]. The only safety functions of the RCPs are to provide adequate pump coast down to ensure reactor coolant continues to flow for a short time after pump trip and to maintain the RCPB.

The PSVs would remain closed during accident conditions unless RCS pressure exceeds their opening setpoint. In that case, the PSVs would be expected to open to lower RCS pressure and subsequently reclose when RCS pressure is again below the PSV opening setpoint to maintain the RCPB.

Reference [6] notes the reactor vessel head vent valves are opened from the main control room to allow venting from the RPV head vent and RCS if non-condensable gases accumulate following an accident. The RPV head vent is not credited to be venting as a safety function or a safety-related core cooling function. The PSVs operate the same way in post-core damage scenarios where the RCS is intact. The PSVs are not designed for mitigating severe accident phenomena. Note that the ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident. These Level 2 functions are not part of the Level 1 PSA model.

Since the RCS is always operating during normal plant operation, online testing of the system is not performed. Any testing is expected to occur during plant shutdown and refueling operations. Both PSVs are spring-loaded safety valves [6] that are located inside the Containment. Since the valves are spring-loaded, remote testing or operation of the valves is not possible. Since Containment is not accessible when the SMR-300 is at-power, local operation or maintenance of the valves is not possible.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The pressurizer has a thick cylindrical shell with a top hemispherical head and is laterally restrained by supports. The pressurizer is sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure during operational maneuvers and transients, thus eliminating the need for fast-acting power operated relief valves (PORVs) in the SMR-300 design.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The RCP is a vertical, centrifugal type pump. The pump is designed to use traditional seals designed to allow continued operation of the pump for a period of at least one week after failure of one of the several stages in order to permit an orderly plant shutdown, without excessive loss of reactor coolant, in the event of the degradation of a second seal stage.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The RCP has provisions to prevent motor damage due to overheating by the use of an onboard heat exchanger that is supplied with component cooling water. Two 50 percent capacity pumps are provided, one on each cold leg.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: There are two safety related characteristics of the RCP. First, in the event of a reactor trip or loss of power, the pumps maintain flow to the core during pump coast down using a flywheel. Second, the RCPs serve as part of the RCS pressure boundary.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The pumps are not required to perform any active safety functions and will be de-energized during LOCA or operation of the primary or secondary decay heat removal systems. The SMR-300 design does not include provisions to operate with a single pump running during power operations (Mode 1).

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure and Vessel Code Section III [13]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT.

entries.section_title: Pressurizer and Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) Description
entries.text: The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients. Figure 8-1 depicts the RCS overpressure protection subsystem as modeled in the SMR-300 PSA.
The RCS system boundaries are defined as shown on Figure 8-1.

Some components or failure modes within the mechanical equipment boundary of the system may not be included in the system level fault tree if the failure does not impact the ability of the system to perform its credited function, or the failure mode has been determined to not be applicable based on the assumptions and modeling notes in Section 4.0, or the groundrules in Reference [4].
The following systems either provide support to, or influence the operation of, the RCS system [6]. Those systems and their functions are briefly described below:

Besides the function of maintaining the RCP boundary, none of the support systems identified above are necessary for successful RCS overpressure protection. Support system models include specific top gates that provide a direct link from the support system model to the RCS system model. These are developed in the associated system notebook and fault tree appendix.

entries.text: A1. INTERPRET DRAWING IN ACCORDANCE WITH THE COMPANY'S DRAWING STANDARDIZATION PROCEDURE HP-160-3002.
A2. DRAWING SHOWS A SINGLE DIVISION AND (A) THE SAME LOGIC IS APPLIED FOR DIVISION B. (B) REFER TO DWG-15333 (LOGIC LEGEND AND SYMBOLS FOR LOGIC DIAGRAM) FOR FUNCTIONAL BLOCK INFORMATION.
G1. THE LP OUTPUT LATCHED WHEN 1SL INPUT IS TRUE. IF THE RESET INPUT IS TRUE, THE OUTPUT IS RESET UNTIL THE ACTUATION SIGNAL GOES FALSE AND THEN BACK TO TRUE.
G2. SPLITTING THE MANUAL AND AUTOMATIC LATCHES ALLOW THE OPERATOR TO INITIATE A ESF AFTER IT'S BEEN RESET EVEN IF THE AUTOMATIC INITIATION HAS NOT BEEN RESET YET.

G3. EACH ESF FUNCTION OF A DIVISION HAS ITS OWN RESET PERMISSIVE, WHICH BECOMES TRUE WHEN THE CORRESPONDING ESF COMPONENTS IN THAT DIVISION HAVE BEEN PLACED IN THE DESIGNATED ESF STATE. THIS PREVENTS ITS APPLIED TO THE PCS FROM INADVERTENTLY RESETTING THE ACTUATION FUNCTION. (REFER TO APPENDIX B OF HI-224049-R1.0)
G4. MANUAL INITIATION AT THE DIVISION LEVEL, WHERE ACTUATION FORM EITHER DIVISION OR THE PCS WILL CAUSE ACTUATION OF THE FUNCTION.
G5. MANUAL INITIATION AT A CHANNEL LEVEL, WHERE ACTUATION REQUIRES TWO TOUCHES FROM A SINGLE DIVISION OR TWO INITIATIONS FROM THE PCS TO ACTUATE THE FUNCTION.

G6. THE REACTOR TRIP (RT) FUNCTION HAS A PHYSICAL RT SWITCH IN ADDITION TO THE INITIATION SCREEN CONTROLS. THE TWO CONTACTS OF THE PHYSICAL SWITCH ARE INPUT TO A HARDWIRED AND/OR SOFTWARE INITIATOR. THE PHYSICAL RT SWITCH IS APPLIED TO THE DIVISION, THE MANUAL RT SIGNAL GENERATES A LOGICAL RT SIGNAL THROUGH AN OR GATE, COMBINED WITH THE RT SIGNAL FROM OTHER DIVISION VIA DATALINK. THEREFORE, EACH MANUAL RT INITIATES BOTH DIVISIONS.

G7. THE FLEX DOUBLER FUNCTION TAKES INPUT OF A COUNT RATE FROM ONE OF THE SOURCE RANGE CHANNELS. THE CALCULATION CALCULATES A RUNNING AVERAGE OF THE PREVIOUS MINUTE, AS WELL AS THE PREVIOUS NINE MINUTE INTERVAL. IF THE MOST RECENT INTERVAL IS GREATER THAN TWO TIMES ANY OF THE PREVIOUS NINE ONE MINUTE INTERVALS, THE OUTPUT IS TRUE.
G8. THE ONE SHOT TIME PARAMETER IS SET TO BE ONE 'OPERATION CYCLE'.
G9. THE 2H BYPASS LOGIC USED FOR INSTRUMENT BISTABLE VOTING IS DEFINED IN MELCO DOCUMENT JEXX-0135-004.

3.1 US NRC Regulatory Requirements
The following US regulatory requirements apply to the design of the RAB.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 1 [24]: GDC 1 requires the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of its safety function, a quality assurance program be established and implemented, and that sufficient and appropriate records be maintained.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 2 [24] and 10CFR50 Appendix S [25]: GDC 2 [24] and Appendix S [25] require the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 3 [24]: GDC 3 requires the RAB to be designed and located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 4 [24]: GDC 4 requires the RAB to be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 60 [26]: GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.

entries.text: RAB shall provide sufficient number of sumps for the collection of equipment and floor drains.

The materials used shall meet the applicable requirements of American Concrete Institute (ACI) 349 [13] for concrete structures and American Institute of Steel Construction (AISC) N690 [14] for steel structures, including any standards referenced therein.
The interior finish and decorative materials used for the RAB shall meet the applicable requirements of IBC [15] or relevant specification produced by Holtec International.
The following requirements are based on good fabrication/construction practices.

The RAB structural design and systems shall be standardized to the extent possible. This includes structural details and support for piping, electrical raceway, and HVAC ductwork, as well as for purchased equipment.

The RAB design shall accommodate and facilitate the selected construction schedule. System completion, pre-operational and startup testing must be considered in the formulation of the construction schedule.
The RAB design shall permit preassembly and installation of large modules. The selection of scope and design of modules must be evaluated in conjunction with the construction sequence.

In the RAB, space must be allocated adjacent to the structures for installation of temporary elevators to handle peak manpower requirements during construction. Permanent plant elevators should be designed and installed early and should be capable of heavy-duty operation during the construction phase, EPRI URD, Chapter 6, Section 4.12.2.1 [47].
Site construction requirements shall be developed during the detailed design.

Structural members shall be designed with provisions like anchor bolts, embedment plates etc. for supporting components. The design and analysis of anchors (steel embedment) used for components and structural supports on concrete structures shall be in accordance with applicable guidelines in Appendix D to ACI 349 [3], as supplemented by RG 1.199 [30].

Design in concrete attachments shall be avoided as a design basis but may be used as design alternatives to embedment plates for supports that require relocation during construction after the concrete is cast.
The local effect of the attachment loads as well as the effect on the gross structure must be considered in the design.
8.13.4. Structural steel columns shall be used for building designs in lieu of free-standing concrete columns, where technically feasible.

8.13.5. The steel and CFSS structural members shall be designed per applicable guidelines in AISC N690 [4] and ASME Section III Subsection NF [37]. The concrete members shall be designed per applicable guidelines in ACI 349 [3] and ACI 318 [34].
8.13.6. Concrete floors on structural steel beams can be used. The use of metal floor decking is acceptable.
8.13.7. Concrete walls shall be sized to facilitate the use of embedded plates to relieve rebar congestion.
8.13.8. Concrete walls shall line up with one another between floor levels, where possible.
8.14.1. The RAB shall provide access to the containment equipment hatch (with appropriate layout space for equipment movement in and out of the containment during shutdown).
8.14.2. The RAB shall provide access to the personnel access hatch (personnel access to the containment during shutdown).
8.14.3. The RAB shall provide access to all containment penetrations and associated isolation valves.

8.14.4. The RAB shall provide overhead door access for HI-TRAC movement from roadways. The overhead door shall be designed to minimize the contamination from the radiologically controlled area to outside.
8.14.5. The RAB design shall conform to system interfacing requirements between the RAB area and neighboring areas as defined within individual system requirements.
8.14.6. The RAB design shall accommodate leakage detection systems for AR and PCMWT, as applicable.
8.15.1. Inspection and testing of concrete structures shall be guided by those in ACI 349 [13].
8.15.2. Inspection and testing of steel structures shall be guided by those in AISC N690 [14].
8.15.3. The RAB design shall meet the inspection and testing requirements of the structures, systems, and components housed within the RAB.

8.15.4. The control room design during emergencies in the main controlling area of the MCR, etc.) shall support operation during emergencies in the main controlling area of the MCR by a maximum crew complement consisting of the following: • Two individuals with SRO licenses; • Three individuals with RO licenses; • One STA; • Two equipment operators. Provision shall also be made for three active observers and assistants in the main controlling area of the MCR: • One from the NRC; • One to the Plant Owner's management; • One to handle communications.

entries.text: The RAB shall include the requirements of Chapter 11 of NUREG-0800 [51], as applicable.
The RAB shall provide separation between safety and non-safety related areas.
Grouping and separation of SSC shall follow the SMR-300 Design Standard for Grouping and Separation [52].
The RAB overhead crane shall be designed to support equipment lifts through the main RAB floor hatch.

RAB shall be designed to allow removal and replacement of SFC and RHR heat exchangers. If need arises. The beam on the +45' EL roof above will be used to attach a monorail on that in future if need arises. This monorail shall be used to access the aforementioned heat exchangers and move them to the main crane area on 0' for replacement. So, that the monorail will be used to lift the heat exchangers and move them to the main crane area on 0' for replacement. So, that beam on +45' EL shall be over-designed for that potential load in future.

In-plant noise levels must not exceed 90 dBA for an 8-h exposure. Plant perimeter noise levels must not exceed 65 dBA during the day and 55 dBA during the night, EPRI URD, Chapter 1, Appendix C, Annex A [47].

All control stations which are continuously manned on a routine basis, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall have an ambient noise level no greater than 60 dBA from installed equipment in the immediate neighborhood of the control station and plant equipment which may operate for long periods. This limit shall be met for all normal or emergency HVAC system lineups in all areas of those control stations where communication between operators is necessary.

All control stations which may be continuously manned for substantial periods of time, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall be provided with carpeting and sound absorbing walls and ceilings. These materials shall be selected for fire resistance, ease of upkeep, durability, freedom from generation of static electricity, and appearance in addition to their sound absorption.

The MCR shall have at least two independent exits which can be used in case the MCR must be evacuated. The remote shutdown station(s) shall be accessible to the operators from either exit without the use of security devices such as keys or key cards and without electric power.

A restroom adequate for both men and women shall be provided. Kitchen facilities with provisions for food preparation shall be provided (e.g., an oven, hot water, drinking water, and refrigeration). These facilities shall not be shared with areas outside the MCR.
The arrangement of the workstations in the MCR shall facilitate direct communication between the operators at the workstations. This includes the ability for direct conversation and visual contact.
Radiation protection as applicable to RAB for plant, personnel, public and environment shall comply with the requirements established in the SMR-160 Design Standard for Radiation Protection [3].

The RAB design shall include provisions for handling and processing personnel to control contamination and radiation exposure (minimize or eliminate the need for plant personnel to enter areas greater than 100 mrem/hr for routine operation). Additionally, radiation monitoring will be placed in all discharge lines with an interlock/permissive to automatically isolate any permitted liquid or gaseous release should the release allowance criteria be exceeded.
Security and radiological control points shall be sized to accommodate personnel with minimum delay and shall be sized based on major maintenance operations or normal operations, whichever controls.

The MCR wall, ceiling, and floor materials and thickness shall be designed such that operators as well as other plant personnel are protected from radiation sources associated with normal plant operation and postulated initiating events (PIE).
Structures designed to manage radioactive waste shall comply with the guidance provided in Regulatory Guide 1.143 [27].

Following the guidance of Regulatory Guide 4.21 [53], the design features shall be provided to minimize contamination of the facility and environment, facilitate decommissioning and minimize the generation of radioactive material to comply with the 10 CFR 20.1406 [39]. Design features to reduce accumulation of radioactive material in components of systems used to process resin and sludges should reflect specific considerations given in Section C.2.(h) of RG 8.8 [54].
Concrete radiation shields shall be designed in accordance with Regulatory Guide 1.69 [3].

Shielding design features include permanent shielding and separation of components that constitute substantial radiation sources, the use of shielded cubicles, labyrinths, and shielded entrances to minimize dose. The selection of shielding materials should consider the ambient environment and potential degradation mechanisms. Temporary shielding is considered where it is impractical to provide permanent shielding for substantial radiation sources.

Streaming of radiation into accessible areas through penetrations for pipes, ducts, and other shield discontinuities is reduced by using layouts that prevent alignment with the radiation source, placing penetrations above head height to reduce personnel exposures, and using shadow shields to attenuate radiation streaming. Shield wall penetrations shall be sufficiently compensated to comply with the associated radiation zone map dose rates for normally accessible areas.

entries.text: 8.1 Safety Requirements
8.1.2. The RAB shall be designed to provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long-term concrete degradation.

8.1.3. The RAB shall be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena such as wind, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes according to HI-2240117 [45] and the appropriate combination of all loads.

8.1.4. The RAB shall be designed to protect components essential for the safe operation of the plant against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids from the postulated pipe break events.

8.1.5. The RAB has been evaluated for the potential effects of a postulated aircraft impact in accordance with NEI-07-13, and a below-grade backup has been provided for safety-related SSCs located above grade that could exhibit vulnerability to the postulated impact.

8.1.6. The RAB layout shall have 3 reinforced concrete walls (two 24" and one 18" thick) to preclude any direct strike on the Equipment Hatch and therefore preclude any damage to the containment structure. This requirement will ensure the containment boundary remains intact.
8.1.7. The RAB shall accommodate a RSF from which actions can be taken to maintain the nuclear power unit in a safe condition after an accident, including loss-of-coolant accidents.
8.1.8. The RAB shall be designed to limit the amount of radionuclide released to the environment.
8.1.9. The fuel handling, radwaste and other systems containing radioactivity in RAB shall be designed to the following requirements:
a. Capability to permit appropriate periodic inspection and testing of components important to safety
b. Suitable shielding for radiation protection
c. Provide appropriate containment, confinement, and filtering systems
8.1.10. The RAB shall be designed to provide physical divisional separation between division A and division B.

8.1.11. The RAB shall be designed to provide physical separation between Class 1E and non-Class 1E. The design of the plant electric power distribution systems shall be such that non-Class 1E circuits are not connected to safety circuits or power sources.
8.2 Functional Requirements
8.2.2. The RAB shall be designed to incorporate physical security protection measures in accordance with the HPP-160-3012 [4].

3. International Building Code (IBC), International Code Council, 2018 [15]

7. NFPA 90A, "Standard for the Installation of Air-Conditioning and Ventilating Systems", 2024 [19]

3.1 US NRC Regulatory Requirements
The following US regulatory requirements apply to the design of the RAB.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 1 [24]: GDC 1 requires the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed, fabricated, erected, and tested to quality standards commensurate with the importance of its safety function, a quality assurance program be established and implemented, and that sufficient and appropriate records be maintained.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 2 [24] and 10CFR50 Appendix S [25]: GDC 2 [24] and Appendix S [25] require the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 3 [24]: GDC 3 requires the RAB to be designed and located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 4 [24]: GDC 4 requires the RAB to be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 60 [26]: GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.
Regulatory Guide 1.143 [27]: provides design guidance in assigning seismic, safety, and quality group classifications for natural phenomena and man-induced hazards as defined

entries.text: The RAB is designed to perform the following safety functions: Provide protection and separation for the Seismic Category I structures, and mechanical and electrical equipment located outside the Containment Structure (CS); Class 1E Battery Rooms and associated equipment Containment Penetrations/Accessways Safety-related Instrumentation and Control (I&C) Provide control room with provisions for plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal conditions and safely shutdown the plant following a design basis accident.

The RAB is designed to perform the following non-safety functions: House systems, components, and structures critical for the normal operation/shutdown of the plant such as RHR, CVC, SFC, radwaste systems and CCW. Provide provisions to support spent fuel removal to interim dry storage. Provide provisions to support new fuel receipt and storage. Provide HVAC for all the components and structures of the RAB and containment purging. Provide radiation protection for plant personnel from radioactive components and minimization of contamination and radioactive waste generation, by incorporating the following design features to ensure compliance with applicable regulations such as 10 CFR 20.1101 [38] and 10 CFR 20.1406 [39] correspondingly: Radiation zoning and access control, Remotely operated Process Instrumentation and Controls, Isolation and decontamination of substantial radiation sources, Minimization of accumulation of radioactive materials in Resin and Sludge Treatment Systems etc. Provide suitable environments for personnel and equipment during all phases of plant operation. Provide adequate laydown space to facilitate inspection, testing, and maintenance of structures, systems, and components located within the RAB. Provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long- term concrete degradation. Control, collect, process, handle, store, segregate and dispose of radwaste. Process and dispose of steam generator blowdown if significant radioactivity is detected. Degas reactor coolant in conjunction with the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC). Transport processed gases to the monitored release point.

The RAB structure is partially embedded into the ground. The RAB houses mechanical and electrical equipment used for normal plant operation and safe shutdown of the reactor. The SMR-300 RAB combines the functions of an auxiliary building, control building, traditional fuel handling building and radioactive waste building into a single structure. The RAB is designed as a Seismic Category-I (SC-I) structure that interfaces with the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES).
The major structures, equipment, and systems contained within the RAB are:
Containment equipment hatch entrance and containment personnel access
Class 1E and non-Class 1E electrical equipment and rooms
Instrumentation and control equipment and rooms
Mechanical equipment rooms
Containment mechanical piping penetration areas
Containment electrical penetration areas

The RAB is constructed mostly from modular concrete filled steel structure (CFSS) similar to the CES. The external walls of the RAB are exclusively designed as CFSS while the internals will be a combination of reinforced concrete, structural steel or CFSS. The CFSS type of construction is anticipated to be comparable or superior to the structural properties of reinforced concrete structures by the US NRC (see NUREG-1793 [40]). The CFSS type of construction enables the RAB steel parts to be shop manufactured as modular sections and field assembled. This significantly reduces construction time compared to reinforced concrete. See Section 8.11 for material requirements of the RAB.

The RAB is a 5-story building with 3 stories located above grade and 2 stories located below grade. The lowest level is located at -42'-0" [-12.80m] (basemat level) and the highest level at +61'-6" [18.74 m] above ground1. The main entrance is from the north side. From there, one can access the non-RCA, i.e. electrical and control area. There is one entrance from the non-RCA side, marked as R4015 in the drawing. This is the control point, to have controlled access to the RCA side. At EL -21'-0" there is a common door between RCA and non-RCA which provides two-way access meant only for emergency egress. The RAB provides two access ways into the CS. The containment equipment hatch allows equipment movement, and the personnel access hatch allows for personnel access independent of the containment equipment hatch (see [41] for details).
The fuel handling area is located at ground elevation to facilitate easy new and spent fuel operations to the RAB (since the equipment access to the containment is also at ground elevation).

entries.text: Provide the means for receiving, inspecting and storing the new fuel assemblies.
Provide the means for transferring new fuel assemblies (from the RAB) into the transfer cask which is then transported into the CS for loading into the reactor core.
Provide a dry storage preparation area where spent fuel (in the transfer cask) is prepared for loading into dry storage casks outside the RAB.
Protect spent fuel assemblies (in the transfer cask), the new fuel assemblies, and radioactive systems from external events such as tornadoes and tornado generated missiles.
Prevent the release of airborne radioactivity following any postulated design basis accident (DBA) from exceeding site boundary radiation levels.
Provide a Hot Equipment Storage Area to house equipment used to perform access operations in the CS via the equipment hatch through the RAB.

The SMR-300 plant includes a remote shutdown facility (RSF) located outside (physically separate) the Control Room Emergency Zone (CREZ) in case of emergency and the main control room (MCR) needs to be evacuated (see [43] for more details). The RSF provides operators full access to the Plant Safety System (PSS) and Plant Control System (PCS), if the MCR is unavailable.

The MCR area accommodates plant control interfaces and plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal condition and maintain the plant in a safe condition following a design basis accident. The CREZ contains the main control room area. The requirements related to the main control room have been included in Section 8.0.

The RAB houses equipment and systems for processing radioactive gaseous, liquid, and solid waste and for preparing waste for off-site shipment. The building houses equipment to prepare low-level radioactive waste for compaction to reduce volume and provides temporary storage for radioactive waste. The building is designed to maintain radiation exposures to operators and maintenance personnel as low as reasonably achievable. Radwaste generated from the operation of the SMR-300 will be classified, processed, and kept for varying periods of time:
To allow for the decay of short-lived radionuclides to a level at which the radioactive waste can be released from regulatory control (clearance) or authorized for discharge, or recycling and reuse.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its transfer to another facility.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its disposal.
To reduce the heat generation rate of high-level radioactive waste prior to its disposal and, in some cases, prior to steps in its predispositial management.
To provide long-term storage of radioactive waste when a suitable disposal facility is lacking.
The major equipment pertaining to radioactive waste management are:
Waste monitoring tank for LRW
Waste hold-up tank for LRW
Hot Equipment Storage Room
LRW Active Carbon Filter and Ion Exchangers
LRW pumps and GRW compressor
Gaseous Radwaste Tank
Solid Radwaste Storage tank and transportation equipment
Low Level radwaste storage areas
Liquid Radioactive Waste Release Radiation Monitor
Gaseous Radioactive Waste Release Radiation Monitor
The RAB is classified as Seismic Category I (SC-I) structure and SMR Class C based on the guidance provided in SMR-160 Systems, Structures, and Components Classification Standard [9].
The extent and boundaries of the RAB are shown in drawing 15299 [41].
The RAB interfaces with the CES.
The RAB interfaces with the CS through a personnel access hatch and containment equipment hatch.
Containment Enclosure Structure
The RAB accommodates majority of the containment penetrations required for normal operation of the plant. The RAB is otherwise structurally isolated from the CES.
Containment Structure

The RAB provides two access ways into the CS. The personnel access equipment hatch allows for equipment movement, and the personnel access hatch allows for personnel access independent of the containment equipment hatch.

entries.text: Design Specification for Reactor Auxiliary Building Report No. HI-2240311 Rev. 1

Concrete surfaces with the potential for radioactive contamination shall be protected with a smooth surface epoxy coating as necessary. These surfaces include operating floor surfaces and surfaces in rooms which have the potential for leaks or flooding.

8.6.1. The RAB shall be designed to house equipment and components of the Radiologically Controlled Area HVAC System (RCV), Control Room Normal Ventilation System (CRV) and Non-Radiologically Controlled Area HVAC System (NRV) [References - TBD].
8.6.2. The Radiologically Controlled Area (RCA) HVAC shall maintain a negative design pressure to prevent release of radioactivity.

8.6.3. The Battery Rooms division A and division B shall be equipped with forced air cooling to maintain low operating temperatures and to avoid rapid thermal aging of the components. [Reference - TBD]
8.6.4. The electrical equipment rooms shall be equipped with HVAC to maintain temperature limits as defined in HI-2188464, Section 8.1 [55].

8.6.5. The MCR shall be designed to reject heat passively during design basis events for a minimum duration of 72 hours without exceeding the ambient temperature requirements required for operator habitability.

8.6.6. The normal control room ventilation system shall be designed to prevent it becoming the path for transfer of radionuclides from other parts of the facility containment during normal and design basis accidents.

8.6.7. (a) For LRW, the waste holdup tanks are vented to the Radiologically Controlled Area (RCV). (b) For LRW, the effluent holdup tanks are normally vented to the Gaseous Radioactive Waste system where they are periodically sampled for oxygen, hydrogen, and radio-gas content.

8.6.8. For GRW, the processed gaseous effluents will be vented to the atmosphere through the HVAC System (RCV). A radiation monitor will be placed at the discharge vent with an interlock/permissive to automatically close the discharge isolation valve in the GRW. Also, the RCV is required which provides continuous ventilation to remove potentially flammable and/or radioactive gases from the spaces containing GRW equipment.

8.6.9. For SRW, the spent resin tanks are normally vented to the waste gas system where they are periodically sampled for oxygen, hydrogen, and radio-gas content. When spent resin tanks are emptied, they shall be purged and sampled multiple times to ensure radio gases and/or hydrogen is no longer present prior to sluicing their contents to mobile equipment for resin removal. The mobile processing equipment and containers will be vented to the RAB atmosphere.
8.7.1. Fire protection as applicable to the RAB structures shall comply with the requirements of SMR-160 Design Standard for Fire Protection [5].
8.7.2. The stairwell design shall be in conformance to NFPA Standard 804 [56].
