The RAB is classified as Seismic Category I (SC-I) structure and SMR Class C based on the guidance provided in SMR-160 Systems, Structures, and Components Classification Standard [9].
The extent and boundaries of the RAB are shown in drawing 15299 [41].
The RAB interfaces with the CES.
The RAB interfaces with the CS through a personnel access hatch and containment equipment hatch.
Containment Enclosure Structure
The RAB accommodates majority of the containment penetrations required for normal operation of the plant. The RAB is otherwise structurally isolated from the CES.
Containment Structure

The RAB provides two access ways into the CS. The personnel access equipment hatch allows for equipment movement, and the personnel access hatch allows for personnel access independent of the containment equipment hatch.
8.1 Safety Requirements
8.1.2. The RAB shall be designed to provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long-term concrete degradation.

8.1.3. The RAB shall be designed to withstand the most severe natural phenomena such as wind, tornadoes, hurricanes, floods, and earthquakes according to HI-2240117 [45] and the appropriate combination of all loads.

8.1.4. The RAB shall be designed to protect components essential for the safe operation of the plant against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids from the postulated pipe break events.

8.1.5. The RAB has been evaluated for the potential effects of a postulated aircraft impact in accordance with NEI-07-13, and a below-grade backup has been provided for safety-related SSCs located above grade that could exhibit vulnerability to the postulated impact.

8.1.6. The RAB layout shall have 3 reinforced concrete walls (two 24" and one 18" thick) to preclude any direct strike on the Equipment Hatch and therefore preclude any damage to the containment structure. This requirement will ensure the containment boundary remains intact.
8.1.7. The RAB shall accommodate a RSF from which actions can be taken to maintain the nuclear power unit in a safe condition after an accident, including loss-of-coolant accidents.
8.1.8. The RAB shall be designed to limit the amount of radionuclide released to the environment.
8.1.9. The fuel handling, radwaste and other systems containing radioactivity in RAB shall be designed to the following requirements:
a. Capability to permit appropriate periodic inspection and testing of components important to safety
b. Suitable shielding for radiation protection
c. Provide appropriate containment, confinement, and filtering systems
8.1.10. The RAB shall be designed to provide physical divisional separation between division A and division B.

8.1.11. The RAB shall be designed to provide physical separation between Class 1E and non-Class 1E. The design of the plant electric power distribution systems shall be such that non-Class 1E circuits are not connected to safety circuits or power sources.

The location, arrangement, and equipment in the MCR shall facilitate the necessary interaction between the operators in the MCR and other personnel, even though these contacts do not appear explicitly in the tasks assigned to the operators in the MCR. The MCR design shall identify all such interactions or contacts which have been considered in the design basis. Access by NRC inspectors and provisions for them to communicate with their headquarters, with the shift supervisor, or with the Plant Owner management without disrupting MCR activities;
Access by maintenance personnel related to operators actions and tagging needed to accomplish maintenance;

Access for maintenance of MCR equipment;

entries.text: Radiation protection as applicable to RAB for plant, personnel, public and environment shall comply with the requirements established in the SMR-160 Design Standard for Radiation Protection [3].

The RAB design shall include provisions for handling and processing personnel to control contamination and radiation exposure (minimize or eliminate the need for plant personnel to enter areas greater than 100 mrem/hr for routine operation). Additionally, radiation monitoring will be placed in all discharge lines with an interlock/permissive to automatically isolate any permitted liquid or gaseous release should the release allowance criteria be exceeded.
Security and radiological control points shall be sized to accommodate personnel with minimum delay and shall be sized based on major maintenance operations or normal operations, whichever controls.

The MCR wall, ceiling, and floor materials and thickness shall be designed such that operators as well as other plant personnel are protected from radiation sources associated with normal plant operation and postulated initiating events (PIE).
Structures designed to manage radioactive waste shall comply with the guidance provided in Regulatory Guide 1.143 [27].

Following the guidance of Regulatory Guide 4.21 [53], the design features shall be provided to minimize contamination of the facility and environment, facilitate decommissioning and minimize the generation of radioactive material to comply with the 10 CFR 20.1406 [39]. Design features to reduce accumulation of radioactive material in components of systems used to process resin and sludges should reflect specific considerations given in Section C.2.(h) of RG 8.8 [54].
Concrete radiation shields shall be designed in accordance with Regulatory Guide 1.69 [3].

Shielding design features include permanent shielding and separation of components that constitute substantial radiation sources, the use of shielded cubicles, labyrinths, and shielded entrances to minimize dose. The selection of shielding materials should consider the ambient environment and potential degradation mechanisms. Temporary shielding is considered where it is impractical to provide permanent shielding for substantial radiation sources.

Streaming of radiation into accessible areas through penetrations for pipes, ducts, and other shield discontinuities is reduced by using layouts that prevent alignment with the radiation source, placing penetrations above head height to reduce personnel exposures, and using shadow shields to attenuate radiation streaming. Shield wall penetrations shall be sufficiently compensated to comply with the associated radiation zone map dose rates for normally accessible areas.
The RAB arrangement shall provide for surfaces which have the following features to reduce the potential for spread of radioactive contamination and to facilitate cleanup:
Design Specification for Reactor Auxiliary Building Report No. HI-2240311 Rev. 1

Concrete surfaces with the potential for radioactive contamination shall be protected with a smooth surface epoxy coating as necessary. These surfaces include operating floor surfaces and surfaces in rooms which have the potential for leaks or flooding.

8.6.1. The RAB shall be designed to house equipment and components of the Radiologically Controlled Area HVAC System (RCV), Control Room Normal Ventilation System (CRV) and Non-Radiologically Controlled Area HVAC System (NRV) [References - TBD].
8.6.2. The Radiologically Controlled Area (RCA) HVAC shall maintain a negative design pressure to prevent release of radioactivity.

8.6.3. The Battery Rooms division A and division B shall be equipped with forced air cooling to maintain low operating temperatures and to avoid rapid thermal aging of the components. [Reference - TBD]
8.6.4. The electrical equipment rooms shall be equipped with HVAC to maintain temperature limits as defined in HI-2188464, Section 8.1 [55].

8.6.5. The MCR shall be designed to reject heat passively during design basis events for a minimum duration of 72 hours without exceeding the ambient temperature requirements required for operator habitability.

8.6.6. The normal control room ventilation system shall be designed to prevent it becoming the path for transfer of radionuclides from other parts of the facility containment during normal and design basis accidents.

8.6.7. (a) For LRW, the waste holdup tanks are vented to the Radiologically Controlled Area (RCV). (b) For LRW, the effluent holdup tanks are normally vented to the Gaseous Radioactive Waste system where they are periodically sampled for oxygen, hydrogen, and radio-gas content.

8.6.8. For GRW, the processed gaseous effluents will be vented to the atmosphere through the HVAC System (RCV). A radiation monitor will be placed at the discharge vent with an interlock/permissive to automatically close the discharge isolation valve in the GRW. Also, the RCV is required which provides continuous ventilation to remove potentially flammable and/or radioactive gases from the spaces containing GRW equipment.

8.6.9. For SRW, the spent resin tanks are normally vented to the waste gas system where they are periodically sampled for oxygen, hydrogen, and radio-gas content. When spent resin tanks are emptied, they shall be purged and sampled multiple times to ensure radio gases and/or hydrogen is no longer present prior to sluicing their contents to mobile equipment for resin removal. The mobile processing equipment and containers will be vented to the RAB atmosphere.
8.7.1. Fire protection as applicable to the RAB structures shall comply with the requirements of SMR-160 Design Standard for Fire Protection [5].
8.7.2. The stairwell design shall be in conformance to NFPA Standard 804 [56].

entries.text: The auxiliary systems area features auxiliary systems, structures and components (SSC) that are necessary for the normal operation/normal shutdown of the plant such as:
The auxiliary systems area also features SSC that are safety related and are required for the safe shutdown of the plant such as:

The RAB is designed to provide adequate shielding for components containing radioactivity and provides features for removal of radioactive fluids. The safety related equipment and components are protected from internal flooding due to postulated pipe break.

The fuel handling area features a Seismic Category I bridge crane (with a new fuel handling machine) to support new and spent fuel transfer activities and provisions to move the low-profile cask transporter (LPT) in and out of the CS through the containment equipment hatch. The fuel handling area is located at ground elevation. The RAB has a bay to receive new fuel from trailers or rail cars. The new fuel is stored in the New Fuel Storage Vault. No spent fuel is stored in the fuel handling area as all spent fuel is moved directly from the spent fuel pool in the CS to interim dry storage with the HI-STORM UMAX system [42] (located outside the RAB).

The primary function of the fuel handling area is to provide space for the handling and storage of new fuel and processing of spent fuel. The fuel handling area is designed to perform the following functions:
Provide the means for receiving, inspecting and storing the new fuel assemblies.
Provide the means for transferring new fuel assemblies (from the RAB) into the transfer cask which is then transported into the CS for loading into the reactor core.
Provide a dry storage preparation area where spent fuel (in the transfer cask) is prepared for loading into dry storage casks outside the RAB.
Protect spent fuel assemblies (in the transfer cask), the new fuel assemblies, and radioactive systems from external events such as tornadoes and tornado generated missiles.
Prevent the release of airborne radioactivity following any postulated design basis accident (DBA) from exceeding site boundary radiation levels.
Provide a Hot Equipment Storage Area to house equipment used to perform access operations in the CS via the equipment hatch through the RAB.

The SMR-300 plant includes a remote shutdown facility (RSF) located outside (physically separate) the Control Room Emergency Zone (CREZ) in case of emergency and the main control room (MCR) needs to be evacuated (see [43] for more details). The RSF provides operators full access to the Plant Safety System (PSS) and Plant Control System (PCS), if the MCR is unavailable.

The MCR area accommodates plant control interfaces and plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal condition and maintain the plant in a safe condition following a design basis accident. The CREZ contains the main control room area. The requirements related to the main control room have been included in Section 8.0.

The RAB houses equipment and systems for processing radioactive gaseous, liquid, and solid waste and for preparing waste for off-site shipment. The building houses equipment to prepare low-level radioactive waste for compaction to reduce volume and provides temporary storage for radioactive waste. The building is designed to maintain radiation exposures to operators and maintenance personnel as low as reasonably achievable. Radwaste generated from the operation of the SMR-300 will be classified, processed, and kept for varying periods of time:
To allow for the decay of short-lived radionuclides to a level at which the radioactive waste can be released from regulatory control (clearance) or authorized for discharge, or recycling and reuse.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its transfer to another facility.
To collect and accumulate a sufficient amount of radioactive waste prior to its disposal.

Section 1.2 - Added Radioactive Waste Management Area.

The Reactor Auxiliary Building is a multi-story structure which houses safety-related and non-safety-related systems, structures, and components for the SMR-300 plant. This design specification report provides information on codes and standards, regulatory requirements, general requirements, safety and non-safety related functions, design conditions, environmental conditions, and load combinations for the Reactor Auxiliary Building.

The current design conditions for the Reactor Auxiliary Building are unverified assumptions based on an exclusive analysis; these assumptions are reasonable and will be verified during preliminary design of the Reactor Auxiliary Building.
The assumptions in Section 1.4 are based on references to SMR-160 documents. These assumptions will be verified when the referenced documents are re-issued under the SMR-300 project.

entries.text: Such other areas or rooms as are needed for equipment, such as computers, to which function and task analyses show the operators need ready access.

The M-MIS design shall specifically identify the access paths to and from the MCR by the operators for specific tasks. In addition, the MCR shall provide for the following more general access requirements:
Access from various parts of the plant to the MCR by equipment operators so that they may consult directly with the MCR operators.
Access from the MCR to locations in the plant where local operator actions may be needed because of abnormal conditions.
This access shall not disrupt the actions of the operating team in the main controlling area of the MCR unless it is necessary for efficient communication.

Specifically, in addition to adequate space in the main controlling area for visiting plant staff, space for consultation shall be provided outside the main controlling area and access to that space shall not require passage through the main controlling area.

The location, arrangement, and equipment in the MCR shall facilitate the necessary interaction between the operators in the MCR and other personnel, even though these contacts do not appear explicitly in the tasks assigned to the operators in the MCR. The MCR design shall identify all such interactions or contacts which have been considered in the design basis. The objective of the MCR arrangement shall be to limit the contacts of these non-operating personnel so that normally they do not distract the operators at the controls in the main controlling area of the MCR. In particular, routine contacts with the shift supervisor, the shift supervisor's clerk, the RO assigned to switching and tagging, or the shift technical advisor shall not require personnel to pass through the main controlling area of the MCR. Some specific items which shall be included are the following:
Access by NRC inspectors and provisions for them to communicate with their headquarters, with the shift supervisor, or with the Plant Owner management without disrupting MCR activities;
Access by maintenance personnel related to operators actions and tagging needed to accomplish maintenance;

Access by plant staff such as engineering or radiological protection when the operators request assistance; enterprise intranet access points shall be provided for both operational and non-operational staff.
Access for maintenance of MCR equipment;
Access to the shift supervisor for administration functions;
Access by fire brigades;

The layout of the MCR shall include an area designated as an operator relief area. This area should be adjacent to the kitchen and restroom facilities as well as being immediately accessible to the main controlling area of the MCR. The relief area shall be of sufficient size to allow an operator to relax and engage in limited physical activity.

The layout of the MCR shall specifically provide for the operations involved in shift turnover. In particular, a location where the personnel for a shift may meet without disturbing the activities in the main part of the MCR shall be provided. This area may be combined with operators' relief area (see Section 4.9.1.4 of the URD [47]).

The RAB shall include the requirements of Chapter 11 of NUREG-0800 [51], as applicable.
The RAB shall provide separation between safety and non-safety related areas.
Grouping and separation of SSC shall follow the SMR-300 Design Standard for Grouping and Separation [52].
The RAB overhead crane shall be designed to support equipment lifts through the main RAB floor hatch.

So, that the monorail will be used to lift the heat exchangers and move them to the main crane area on 0' for replacement. So, that beam on +45' EL shall be over-designed for that potential load in future.

In-plant noise levels must not exceed 90 dBA for an 8-h exposure. Plant perimeter noise levels must not exceed 65 dBA during the day and 55 dBA during the night, EPRI URD, Chapter 1, Appendix C, Annex A [47].

All control stations which are continuously manned on a routine basis, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall have an ambient noise level no greater than 60 dBA from installed equipment in the immediate neighborhood of the control station and plant equipment which may operate for long periods. This limit shall be met for all normal or emergency HVAC system lineups in all areas of those control stations where communication between operators is necessary.

All control stations which may be continuously manned for substantial periods of time, e.g., the MCR, the technical support center, and the emergency operations facility, shall be provided with carpeting and sound absorbing walls and ceilings. These materials shall be selected for fire resistance, ease of upkeep, durability, freedom from generation of static electricity, and appearance in addition to their sound absorption.

The MCR shall have at least two independent exits which can be used in case the MCR must be evacuated. The remote shutdown station(s) shall be accessible to the operators from either exit without the use of security devices such as keys or key cards and without electric power.

A restroom adequate for both men and women shall be provided. Kitchen facilities with provisions for food preparation shall be provided (e.g., an oven, hot water, drinking water, and refrigeration). These facilities shall not be shared with areas outside the MCR.
The arrangement of the workstations in the MCR shall facilitate direct communication between the operators at the workstations. This includes the ability for direct conversation and visual contact.

entries.text: The RAB structure is partially embedded into the ground. The RAB houses mechanical and electrical equipment used for normal plant operation and safe shutdown of the reactor. The SMR-300 RAB combines the functions of an auxiliary building, control building, traditional fuel handling building and radioactive waste building into a single structure. The RAB is designed as a Seismic Category-I (SC-I) structure that interfaces with the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES).
The major structures, equipment, and systems contained within the RAB are:
Containment equipment hatch entrance and containment personnel access
Class 1E and non-Class 1E electrical equipment and rooms
Instrumentation and control equipment and rooms
Mechanical equipment rooms
Containment mechanical piping penetration areas
Containment electrical penetration areas

The RAB is constructed mostly from modular concrete filled steel structure (CFSS) similar to the CES. The external walls of the RAB are exclusively designed as CFSS while the internals will be a combination of reinforced concrete, structural steel or CFSS. The CFSS type of construction is anticipated to be comparable or superior to the structural properties of reinforced concrete structures by the US NRC (see NUREG-1793 [40]). The CFSS type of construction enables the RAB steel parts to be shop manufactured as modular sections and field assembled. This significantly reduces construction time compared to reinforced concrete. See Section 8.11 for material requirements of the RAB.

The RAB is a 5-story building with 3 stories located above grade and 2 stories located below grade. The lowest level is located at -42'-0" [-12.80m] (basemat level) and the highest level at +61'-6" [18.74 m] above ground1. The main entrance is from the north side. From there, one can access the non-RCA, i.e. electrical and control area. There is one entrance from the non-RCA side, marked as R4015 in the drawing. This is the control point, to have controlled access to the RCA side. At EL -21'-0" there is a common door between RCA and non-RCA which provides two-way access meant only for emergency egress. The RAB provides two access ways into the CS. The containment equipment hatch allows equipment movement, and the personnel access hatch allows for personnel access independent of the containment equipment hatch (see [41] for details).
The fuel handling area is located at ground elevation to facilitate easy new and spent fuel operations to the RAB (since the equipment access to the containment is also at ground elevation).

The RAB is designed to provide adequate shielding for components containing radioactivity and provides features for removal of radioactive fluids. The safety related equipment and components are protected from internal flooding due to postulated pipe break.

The fuel handling area features a Seismic Category I bridge crane (with a new fuel handling machine) to support new and spent fuel transfer activities and provisions to move the low-profile cask transporter (LPT) in and out of the CS through the containment equipment hatch. The fuel handling area is located at ground elevation. The RAB has a bay to receive new fuel from trailers or rail cars. The new fuel is stored in the New Fuel Storage Vault. No spent fuel is stored in the fuel handling area as all spent fuel is moved directly from the spent fuel pool in the CS to interim dry storage with the HI-STORM UMAX system [42] (located outside the RAB).

entries.section_title: 10CFR50 Appendix A GDC 2 [24] and 10CFR50 Appendix S [25]
entries.text: GDC 2 [24] and Appendix S [25] require the RAB, which is important to safety, to be designed to withstand the effects of natural phenomena, such as earthquakes, without loss of capability to perform their safety functions.
GDC 3 requires the RAB to be designed and located to minimize the probability and effect of fires and explosions.

GDC 4 requires the RAB to be appropriately protected against dynamic effects, including the effects of missiles, pipe whipping, and discharging fluids, that may result from equipment failures and from events and conditions outside the nuclear power unit.

GDC 60 requires that the nuclear power unit design include means to suitably control the release of radioactive materials in gaseous and liquid effluents and to handle radioactive solid waste produced during normal reactor operation, including anticipated operational occurrences.
provides design guidance in assigning seismic, safety, and quality group classifications for natural phenomena and man-induced hazards as defined

The RAB is designed to perform the following safety functions: Provide protection and separation for the Seismic Category I structures, and mechanical and electrical equipment located outside the Containment Structure (CS); Class 1E Battery Rooms and associated equipment Containment Penetrations/Accessways Safety-related Instrumentation and Control (I&C) Provide control room with provisions for plant operators to monitor and operate the plant during normal conditions and safely shutdown the plant following a design basis accident.

The RAB is designed to perform the following non-safety functions: House systems, components, and structures critical for the normal operation/shutdown of the plant such as RHR, CVC, SFC, radwaste systems and CCW. Provide provisions to support spent fuel removal to interim dry storage. Provide provisions to support new fuel receipt and storage. Provide HVAC for all the components and structures of the RAB and containment purging. Provide radiation protection for plant personnel from radioactive components and minimization of contamination and radioactive waste generation, by incorporating the following design features to ensure compliance with applicable regulations such as 10 CFR 20.1101 [38] and 10 CFR 20.1406 [39] correspondingly: Radiation zoning and access control, Remotely operated Process Instrumentation and Controls, Isolation and decontamination of substantial radiation sources, Minimization of accumulation of radioactive materials in Resin and Sludge Treatment Systems etc. Provide suitable environments for personnel and equipment during all phases of plant operation. Provide adequate laydown space to facilitate inspection, testing, and maintenance of structures, systems, and components located within the RAB. Provide cooling to all the penetrations into RAB in excess of 500°F to ensure no long- term concrete degradation. Control, collect, process, handle, store, segregate and dispose of radwaste. Process and dispose of steam generator blowdown if significant radioactivity is detected. Degas reactor coolant in conjunction with the Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC). Transport processed gases to the monitored release point.

entries.text: This CSD report documents the basis for control and alarm functions of the RCS. This report is used by Mitsubishi Electric (MELCO) for programming the protection and control systems. Additionally, the simulator development team uses this to implement the simulator. This report includes information consistent with the RCS P&ID [3] and RCS SDD [4] to describe the RCS control system and all automatic functions therein. Signal-related information including signal tags internal to the PCS are derived from the RCS Function Block Diagram (FBD) [5], and MELCO POL Numbering Rule [6].

Due to the simulator being in the beginning stages of development, setpoints and control logic determined in this report have not been tested and tuned as is intended. Refined values will be included in a future revision of the CSD.

Additionally, specific models for pumps and valves have not been determined and therefore vendor specifications are unavailable to corroborate the nominal component and process conditions presumed by this report in the development of the RCS control system. Once the data is available, it will be incorporated into the CSD where necessary and checked against existing control conditions in a future revision of the CSD.
Open items and tracked assumptions covering the application of these limitations are listed in their respective sections below.

entries.text: The RCS consists primarily of input instrumentation that is used by the PSS and PCS. Aspects of the reactor control systems including rod control and steam generator level control are described in the PCS Functional Diagram and Integrated Plant Control System Logic Basis. The primary control functions of the RCS are the reactor coolant pump (RCP) controls, PZR heater and spray controls, and manual valve controls for draining, filling, venting and sampling the RCS. Each of these is discussed in more detail below.
The RCS provides many inputs to various safety functions in other systems, but the RCS has no active or control safety functions.
7.2.1 Control RCS Pressure and Accommodate Volume Changes

RCS volume changes due to changes in temperature and mass. Changes in mass are controlled by CVC and described in the CVC SD [20]. The control setpoint for PZR level is sent to CVC from RCS and varies with Tave. Table 7-1 below shows the relationship of reactor power in percentage to the PZR level setpoints in feet. The relationship between adjacent points is linear.
The associated pressure changes from the changes in RCS volume are handled by four groups of heaters and two spray control valves.

Each heater group is equipped with a standard component control that will accommodate its operation as a steady state (always on during normal operation), a proportional (partially on proportional to how much pressurizer pressure has fallen below its setpoint) operation, or a backup (fully on only when pressurizer pressure is significantly below its setpoint) operation. This capability is described and defined in Appendix J. Heater mode selection is done via a screen at the operational visual display unit (O-VDU) using buttons and logic described visually by Figure 7-1. The controls depicted in Figure 7-1 for heater group A are the same for heater groups B, C and D.

A steady state heater is always on during normal operations and allows for constant spray flow while maintaining the PZR at normal operating pressure. This provides two benefits: chemical mixing of RCS water and decreasing the response time of the pressure controller during

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: transients. This heater bank is taken to manual direct control by the operators during startup and maintained on.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The proportional heater receives a setpoint from the operator based on normal operating pressure and proportional heater offset (see Figure 7-2). This is the default mode of operation when the heaters are in manual setpoint control. At normal operating pressure, the proportional heater has minimal voltage applied. As pressure falls below the setpoint, the proportional heater increases in power to a maximum at some margin below the setpoint. The applied voltage between these two points is linear. This allows for prolonged operating life of the proportional heater and backup heaters by minimizing heater power cycles from minor transients and losses to ambient. If a heater fails and a deviation alarm is issued, it additionally transfers its mode of operation to that of a backup heater.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The heater banks identified as backup heaters turn on when pressure falls to a manually set pressure significantly below the normal operating pressure. This will provide additional heater input to raise pressure back to normal operating pressure in case a transient exceeds the capacity of proportional and steady state heaters.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The spray control valves are pressure control valves which open to permit subcooled spray into the PZR steam space to lower pressure through condensation. The spray valve will operate to maintain normal operating pressure at the manual setpoint (see Figure 7-2), opening as pressure rises and shutting as it decreases. Further detail regarding the control of the spray valve is found in Appendix J.

entries.text: Open items and tracked assumptions covering the application of these limitations are listed in their respective sections below. This CSD report documents the basis for control and alarm functions of the RCS. This report is used by Mitsubishi Electric (MELCO) for programming the protection and control systems. Additionally, the simulator development team uses this to implement the simulator. This report includes information consistent with the RCS P&ID [3] and RCS SDD [4] to describe the RCS control system and all automatic functions therein. Signal-related information including signal tags internal to the PCS are derived from the RCS Function Block Diagram (FBD) [5], and MELCO POL Numbering Rule [6].

Due to the simulator being in the beginning stages of development, setpoints and control logic determined in this report have not been tested and tuned as is intended. Refined values will be included in a future revision of the CSD. Additionally, specific models for pumps and valves have not been determined and therefore vendor specifications are unavailable to corroborate the nominal component and process conditions presumed by this report in the development of the RCS control system. Once the data is available, it will be incorporated into the CSD where necessary and checked against existing control conditions in a future revision of the CSD.

entries.text: The RCS uses forced flow from startup to shut down to provide core cooling and is achieved by running two RCPs. The RCPs are controlled manually from the MCR and are prevented from starting without adequate system pressure to provide NPSH. They are automatically tripped from a DHR actuation signal. Appendix J contains further details regarding the control scheme for the RCPs.

The RPV vent valves are solenoid-operated valves that provide venting capability to the RCS. The vent valves are manually operated from the MCR and have a permissive that prevents their opening when the RCS is pressurized. The gaseous primary sampling isolation valve can be used to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS prior to startup or during post-accident scenarios so that pressure control can be executed using the PZR steam bubble. Venting also prevents drawing a vacuum in the primary during RCS drain for refueling and shutdown inspections. Vent paths are opened prior to draining and RPV vents are opened when water level drops below the top of the RPV.

The RPV seals are connected to lines that lead to a temperature sensor. In case the primary seal fails, the temperature sensor will detect the high-temperature leak off from the failed seal. This prompts the operators to shift to the secondary seal. By shutting the primary leak off isolation valve and opening the secondary. If further leakage is detected, the operator will assess for shutdown and repairs rather than allow seal leakage to spill over to the RPV exterior.

The primary sampling isolation valves are provided to allow for drawing samples from various locations in the RCS. One is provided on each cold leg, one in the PZR liquid space and one in the PZR steam space. These valves are manually controlled from the MCR.
The components in the RCS system with controllers outside of the PCS or PSS are described in Table 7-2. These indications will be available from the MCR.

entries.text: There are no HFE HITS items for the RCS

The RCS consists primarily of input instrumentation that is used by the PSS and PCS. Aspects of the reactor control systems including rod control and steam generator level control are described in the PCS Functional Diagram and Integrated Plant Control System Logic Basis. The primary control functions of the RCS are the reactor coolant pump (RCP) controls, PZR heater and spray controls, and manual valve controls for draining, filling, venting and sampling the RCS. Each of these is discussed in more detail below.
The RCS provides many inputs to various safety functions in other systems, but the RCS has no active or control safety functions.
7.2.1 Control RCS Pressure and Accommodate Volume Changes

RCS volume changes due to changes in temperature and mass. Changes in mass are controlled by CVC and described in the CVC SD [20]. The control setpoint for PZR level is sent to CVC from RCS and varies with Tave. Table 7-1 below shows the relationship of reactor power in percentage to the PZR level setpoints in feet. The relationship between adjacent points is linear.
The associated pressure changes from the changes in RCS volume are handled by four groups of heaters and two spray control valves.

Each heater group is equipped with a standard component control that will accommodate its operation as a steady state (always on during normal operation), a proportional (partially on proportional to how much pressurizer pressure has fallen below its setpoint) operation, or a backup (fully on only when pressurizer pressure is significantly below its setpoint) operation. This capability is described and defined in Appendix J. Heater mode selection is done via a screen at the operational visual display unit (O-VDU) using buttons and logic described visually by Figure 7-1. The controls depicted in Figure 7-1 for heater group A are the same for heater groups B, C and D.

A steady state heater is always on during normal operations and allows for constant spray flow while maintaining the PZR at normal operating pressure. This provides two benefits: chemical mixing of RCS water and decreasing the response time of the pressure controller during

These parameters are plotted against each other in real time to show margin to pressure and temperature limits, as described in section 8.1.1.3.

Purpose This CSD report documents the basis for control and alarm functions of the RCS. This report is used by Mitsubishi Electric (MELCO) for programming the protection and control systems. Additionally, the simulator development team uses this to implement the simulator.

Scope This report includes information consistent with the RCS P&ID [3] and RCS SDD [4] to describe the RCS control system and all automatic functions therein. Signal-related information including signal tags internal to the PCS are derived from the RCS Function Block Diagram (FBD) [5], and MELCO POL Numbering Rule [6].

Limitations Due to the simulator being in the beginning stages of development, setpoints and control logic determined in this report have not been tested and tuned as is intended. Once the data is available, it will be incorporated into the CSD where necessary and checked against existing control conditions in a future revision of the CSD. Open items and tracked assumptions covering the application of these limitations are listed in their respective sections below.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The proportional heater receives a setpoint from the operator based on normal operating pressure and proportional heater offset (see Figure 7-2). This is the default mode of operation when the heaters are in manual setpoint control. At normal operating pressure, the proportional heater has minimal voltage applied. As pressure falls below the setpoint, the proportional heater increases in power to a maximum at some margin below the setpoint. The applied voltage between these two points is linear. This allows for prolonged operating life of the proportional heater and backup heaters by minimizing heater power cycles from minor transients and losses to ambient. If a heater fails and a deviation alarm is issued, it additionally transfers its mode of operation to that of a backup heater.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The heater banks identified as backup heaters turn on when pressure falls to a manually set pressure significantly below the normal operating pressure. This will provide additional heater input to raise pressure back to normal operating pressure in case a transient exceeds the capacity of proportional and steady state heaters.

entries.section_title: Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The spray control valves are pressure control valves which open to permit subcooled spray into the PZR steam space to lower pressure through condensation. The spray valve will operate to maintain normal operating pressure at the manual setpoint (see Figure 7-2), opening as pressure rises and shutting as it decreases. Further detail regarding the control of the spray valve is found in Appendix J.

The RCS uses forced flow from startup to shut down to provide core cooling and is achieved by running two RCPs. The RCPs are controlled manually from the MCR and are prevented from starting without adequate system pressure to provide NPSH. They are automatically tripped from a DHR actuation signal. Appendix J contains further details regarding the control scheme for the RCPs.

The RPV vent valves are solenoid-operated valves that provide venting capability to the RCS. The vent valves are manually operated from the MCR and have a permissive that prevents their opening when the RCS is pressurized. The gaseous primary sampling isolation valve can be used to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS prior to startup or during post-accident scenarios so that pressure control can be executed using the PZR steam bubble. Venting also prevents drawing a vacuum in the primary during RCS drain for refueling and shutdown inspections. Vent paths are opened prior to draining and RPV vents are opened when water level drops below the top of the RPV.

The RPV seals are connected to lines that lead to a temperature sensor. In case the primary seal fails, the temperature sensor will detect the high-temperature leak off from the failed seal. This prompts the operators to shift to the secondary seal. By shutting the primary leak off isolation valve and opening the secondary. If further leakage is detected, the operator will assess for shutdown and repairs rather than allow seal leakage to spill over to the RPV exterior.

Basis for Control: Heater SCC is capable of both modulating and on/off control. This enables swapping heater group designation as proportional, backup or steady state from the MCR without shutting down. Proportional control selected will enable manual setpoint control. The backup control selection enables the pop and clamp commands to control the heater group based on the manually set backup setpoint. The manual control selection places the heater group in manual direct control and is used for turning heaters off, as for outages, and for steady-state operation. Each of these mode selections are done manually from the pressure control HFE screen. A clamp demand is provided to prevent heaters starting or operating with insufficient coverage.

The statement of limitations below and section 1.3 address any items that require further investigation or refinement.

Although the scope of the information in this CSD is complete, several factors affect the fidelity of the data provided. After component specifications have been determined, proper flow characteristics can be verified. Additionally, once simulator data is refined, tuning constants and setpoints can be verified or improved.
Once the above data is available, it will be incorporated into the CSD where necessary and checked against existing control conditions in a future revision of the CSD.

entries.text: Revision 0 Initial Issue. This is Revision 0 of the Control System Description (CSD) for the SMR-300 design. Previous versions of this CSD that are not applicable to the SMR-300 design are in HI-2188814.

Changed assumptions table to be IAW MEMO 8002-002 Deleted obsolete assumptions (4-5, 7-16, and 19) and added assumptions 21-26 Added database-generated tables as Appendices A-K Added RCS sampling valves to description of control and applicable appendices Revised MELCO and HITS open items to reflect most recent documentation

The Reactor Coolant System (RCS) Control System Description (CSD) is an internal design document that defines the component control methodology for the RCS. Any component with an automatic function, including alarms and backups to operator action, will have that function and the basis for actuation included.

The CSD is generated to provide a consolidated repository of a system's control basis. This is particularly useful in tuning system response and troubleshooting improper operation. It is an input to the simulator, Integrated Plant Control (IPC) Logic Basis [1] and IPC Logic Diagram [2].
The statement of limitations below and section 1.3 address any items that require further investigation or refinement.

Although the scope of the information in this CSD is complete, several factors affect the fidelity of the data provided. After component specifications have been determined, proper flow characteristics can be verified. Additionally, once simulator data is refined, tuning constants and setpoints can be verified or improved.
Once the above data is available, it will be incorporated into the CSD where necessary and checked against existing control conditions in a future revision of the CSD.
Open items and tracked assumptions about the design are listed in their respective sections below.

entries.text: 8.1 Task Oriented Screens

The heat up and cooldown screen provides control of the MSS and MFS as well as displays temperatures and pressures of the RCS when in a sub-procedure for heat up or cooldown without the RHR system. These parameters are plotted against each other in real time to show margin to pressure and temperature limits, as described in section 8.1.1.3.

The following parameters are monitored and displayed on the left side of the heat up and cooldown screen as below. Only one I/O per row is displayed at a time, but the operator may select from any of the associated I/Os to display.
This section lists the components that require control from the heat up and cool down screen:

entries.section_title: Table 8-2 Heat Up and Cooldown Task Screen Controls
entries.text:
| Component Name | Equipment Tag |
|-----------------|---------------|
| RCP A           | RCS-PMP001A-1 |
| RCP B           | RCS-PMP001B-1 |
| Turbine control valve | TCS-MOV-TBD |
| Turbine bypass valve | TCS-PCV-065A/B/C-N |
| Atmospheric dump isolation valve | MSS-MOV-009-2 |
| Atmospheric dump valve | MSS-PCV-003-2 |
| Main steam isolation valve | MSS-SMV-057-2 |
| Feed water pump A | MFS-PMP-002A-N |
| Feed water pump B | MFS-PMP-002B-N |
| Feed water pump C | MFS-PMP-002C-N |
| Condensate pump A | MFS-PMP-001A-N |
| Condensate pump B | MFS-PMP-001B-N |
| Condensate pump C | MFS-PMP-001C-N |
| Feed control valve A | MFS-022A-N |
| Feed control valve B | MFS-022B-N |
| Feed control valve C | MFS-022C-N |

The right side of the heat up and cooldown task screen displays a scatter plot of temperature and pressure as represented by a data point (a dot) on the screen every six seconds. The bounding pressure and temperature curves, including (but not limited to) fracture prevention curve and saturation curve, are represented on the screen to provide operator feedback and show margin to limiting core conditions.

The gap values for the Upper/Lower limit monitor are designed to protect from chattering alarms. These values are defined by verification with Holtec/MELCO.

Is the SCC for Heater control correct PCS MOTOR Starter or PCS MOV? The CVCS uses the PCS MOTOR Starter. The RCS uses PCS MOV. Response: This was due to heaters operating as modulating or on/off. Updated SCC type for PZR heaters in RCS CSD.

The components number of P-001A-1/P-001B-1 of Reactor Coolant Startup Pumps (RCP) are different. In SCC, P-001A-1/P-001B-1. However, in IO-list, P-001A-3/P-001B-3. Also, in the 6.0HSI design, P-001A-1/P-001B-1 is listed. In the FBD, P-001A-1/P-001B-1 is listed. Response: RCSPs (startup pumps) don't exist anymore. Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCP) are defined in RCS CSD IAW RCS P&ID.

Table-7-5 About PZR HPV Valve SCC, I/O list, and ALARM list are not consistent. In SCC, it is "PZR HPV Valve". In the IO list and the Alarm list, it is "PZR HPV Iso Valve". The SCC Type is "AOV", but the I/O list and ALARM list shows "SOV". Fail to State 1(2) Time is 25, but it is 5 in other SOV devices. In the FBD, the following notation is used. Component name is "PZR HPV Iso Valve".SCC Type is "SOV".Fail to State 1/2 Time is set to "5 seconds" Response: AOV/SOV are identical SCC. SOVs therefore take AOV SCC. Fail to demand time should be 5 seconds for both.

In Table 7-10(HTR-001B-N) and Table 7-11(HTR-001A-N), the SCC Type is PCS MOV.However, FBD was created with PSS Protection State 2 MOV because of the Protection State 2 condition. Also, there are no IO tags for HTR-001A-N and HTR-001B-N in the I/O list and ALARM list, they were added to the FBD. Response: Protection state 2 no longer at SCC. This signal will be actuated at the breakers, which are safety-related. Heaters are not.

entries.section_title: Spray Line B Downstream Isolation Valve

entries.text: A single fuel beam model was created and benchmarked to the target modal frequencies in air [7] (as per GAIA test data in [9] and [10]) and in operating conditions in water to a model elaborated in FRANC [4] according to the methodology of the topical report [1].
Using the stiffness at mid span elevation (grid 5) of the GAIA test fuel bundle, the adjusted cross-sectional area and density of the fuel beam model are determined.
The fuel beam elements have an adjusted cross-sectional area, but with the same inertial properties as the Holtec GAIA fuel assembly design.
The development and validation of this fuel beam model in ANSYS [2] is done in two main phases:

1. Benchmark to GAIA test data at room temperature: Using the same values of the rotational spring stiffnesses for the ISG and IGM grids as in the CASAC [3] lateral benchmark model [7], it was demonstrated that the ANSYS [2] beam model yields similar target frequencies for lateral modes 1 and 3 at both BOL and EOL. It should be noted that, the lateral model [7] was benchmarked to GAIA test results [9] and [10] performed at room temperature. This verification was done for both BOL and EOL.

2. Benchmark to operating conditions in water: the ANSYS [2] model was verified to yield similar frequencies as the model established in FRANC [4] according to the methodology of the topical report [1]. This verification was done for both BOL and EOL. In this phase, the rotational spring stiffnesses of the grids in the ANSYS [2] model were tuned to match the frequencies of the FRANC [4] model. This is because the modelling approach used to define hydrodynamic coupling effects in FRANC [4] differs from that used in ANSYS [2].

For the first phase, the error acceptability criteria according to the topical report [1] was verified. The limits of these criteria are respectively 2.5% and 10% for mode 1 and 3. There is no topical requirement for phase two, however, the results from this phase still respect the aforementioned criteria of the topical report [1].
Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model, the HDS was incorporated to simulates its axial (vertical) dynamic behavior.

entries.text: Nodes 1 and 14 represent respectively the top surface of the bottom nozzle, and the extremity of the HDS fixed respectively to the Lower Core Plate and the Upper Core Plate (UCP). Node 13 represent the bottom surface of the top nozzle (or the extremity of the HDS attached to the fuel assembly). Only the displacement along the Z-axis is allowed at this node. The masses of the BN and TN are added as point masses respectively at element 1 (defined between node 1 and node 2) and element 12 (defined between node 12 and node 13) to account for the total mass of the fuel assembly. These point masses and the total masses of the fuel assembly are defined in §7.1.4. The final fuel beam model with both vertical and lateral dynamic responses is presented in Figure 7-12.

entries.text: Similarly to §7.2.3, added and coupling masses in the vertical direction (along Z) are defined in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1]. Based on engineering judgement, a value of preload within the range 2000-2500N is considered. In this analysis, the average value of this range is used. This preload causes the deflection of the fuel assembly in addition to the deflection caused by the fuel weight. Therefore, the input preload is calculated to account for the initial deflection. The Holtec GAIA fuel assembly is very similar to the standard 17x17 GAIA assembly with minor adjustments at the top nozzle to support the SMR-300 plant interfaces and operating conditions [15]. It is comprised of the following components:

The Holtec GAIA fuel assembly is very similar to the standard 17x17 GAIA assembly with minor adjustments at the top nozzle to support the SMR-300 plant interfaces and operating conditions [15]. It is comprised of the following components:

The single fuel beam model is a three-dimensional model consisting of beam elements and rotational spring elements (see Figure 7-1). The effective modulus of the beam elements varies over the entire length of the assembly to account for the variation in the cross section of the guide tube. Hence, we have the dashpot region which depicts the thick section of the guide tube and the non-dashpot section which depicts the thin section of the guide tube.

The effective modulus of the beam elements coupled with the length of the beam and the axial stiffness from GAIA axial compression tests (BOL [9] and EOL [10]) are used to evaluate the corresponding cross section of the beam.

Four stiffness values are used for the lateral rotational springs to represent the lower end grid, intermediate grids (ISG and IGM), and upper end grid. One stiffness value for each of the end grids, one for the ISG grids and one for the IGM grids.

The spacer grid centerline elevations of the Holtec GAIA SMR-300 design are defined in [6] and presented in Table 7-1. Z-axis is the vertical orientation, and the elevations are set so that the zero elevation is at the bottom surface of the 0.0695 m tall bottom nozzle. The X and Y coordinates for Nodes 1 through 13 are (0, 0).

The presence of the reactor coolant modifies the vibrational response of the fuel assembly. The nonstationary interaction between reactor coolant and fuel assembly constitutes the hydrodynamic coupling, a non-dissipative phenomenon, which is distinct from damping. This hydrodynamic coupling is used to account for the added mass effect and buoyancy.
This linearized interaction between the fuel assembly and the reactor coolant is accounted for via the mass matrix concept by using MATRIX27 elements in ANSYS [2].
The added mass is evaluated in the following steps:
The displaced fluid volume due to the fully submerged fuel assembly is corrected with added mass coefficient defined in the topical report [1].
This displaced fluid volume is then scaled along the height of the fuel assembly using the fluid length at each span as defined in FRANC [4] to obtain the fluid added mass.
Inner fluid mass is also evaluated and scaled along the height of the fuel assembly using the inner fluid inner volume defined for each span.
The fluid added mass, and the inner fluid mass are then combined to yield the added mass.
The coupling mass is evaluated in a similar manner but using the coupling mass coefficient defined in the topical report [1].

The added mass and coupling masses defined in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1] at each structural node of the fuel beam model (except for the HDS node) are summarized in Table 7-8. Water density at operating core conditions (583.5°F and 2250 psia) is defined using SteamTab [5].

Similarly to §7.1.5, rotational springs are included in the model to act about the two horizontal axes (X, Y). The same value of rotational spring stiffness for a given grid is used in both horizontal axes so that the overall model remains symmetric in the horizontal plane.

entries.text: A finite element model of the Holtec SMR-300 fuel assembly design is needed to support the Reactor Pressure Vessel Internals (RPVI) dynamic analyses being performed by Holtec. This task is listed in §.1.2. of the Project Plan (15). The finite element model of the fuel assembly is created using ANSYS computer code [2]. The model represents the lateral and vertical dynamic responses of a single fuel assembly and incorporates the preloaded Hold Down Spring (HDS).

The properties of the fuel beam established in this document at cold (ambient) and hot (operating) should be adapted to the temperature at any state point of interest while taking into consideration the actual environment of the reactor as well as other physical phenomena present in the core at this state point. Some recommendations (but not limited to) of elements to account for while integrating the fuel beam model into the RPVI model are listed in section §.7.4.

Two configurations of the fuel beam model are studied, in air at ambient conditions and in water at the average operating conditions of temperature and pressure of the reactor core [12]. For both configurations, a Beginning Of Life (BOL) model and an End Of Life (EOL) model are analyzed. Consequently, the validation of the model is done in two steps:
The BOL and EOL models in air at ambient conditions are benchmarked to target frequencies of the GAIA lateral benchmark model presented in [7].
The BOL and EOL models at operating conditions in water are benchmarked to target frequencies of the FRANC [4] model. This model was elaborated according to the methodology of the topical report [1].
These steps are presented in detail in §.3.

Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model in air and in operating conditions in water, presented respectively in §.7.1 and §.7.2, the HDS with its preload is incorporated to the final model (see §.7.3) to verify its vertical dynamic response.
A summary of results obtained during the validation of the lateral and vertical dynamic responses is provided in §.8 for all configurations of the fuel beam model.
ANSYS 2021 R2 [2] is used for this analysis, which is the latest Framatome certified version at the time this report was released.

The properties of the fuel beam model presented in this document are consistent with the standard GAIA design. The changes incorporated in the GAIA-AFM design are listed in Table 1 of the Project Plan [15]. The main difference between the two designs that could impact the dynamic behavior of the fuel beam model is the difference in weight. However, this weight change accounts just for 1% difference, as such the impact is considered negligible.

The interfaces of the fuel beam model defined in §.7.3 do not reflect the exact environment of the fuel at operating conditions in the reactor and should be updated accordingly by referring to generic recommendations of §.7.4 and based on engineering judgments of the analyst performing the RPVI analysis.

The operating core conditions as designated in this document are used principally to verify the dynamic behavior of the beam model at hot conditions. The properties of the fuel beam model should be scaled to a specific temperature (of a state point of interest for example) if need be.

The characteristics of the fuel assembly are presented in [6]. The fuel assembly is modeled as a single beam representing the cross-sectional areas and moment of inertias of the Fuel Rods (FR), Guide Tubes (GT), and Instrumentation Tube (IT). Rotational springs are included at spacer grid elevations to represent the shear coupling of grids.
The analytical methodology follows three main steps listed in §3.1 through §3.3 below.
The fuel beam model is constructed using standard GAIA axial compression test data ([9] for BOL and [10] for EOL) as follows:

1. The stiffness at mid elevation of the fuel assembly (at grid 5 according to Figure 9 of [9] and [10] respectively for BOL and EOL) is used as the equivalent stiffness of the fuel beam model. As illustrated in Figure 10-1 of Appendix A, a fuel beam model defined using the axial stiffness at mid elevation behaves very similarly to a fuel beam model defined with varying axial stiffnesses.
2. The length of the beam model is assumed to be the distance between the upper surface of the Bottom Nozzle (BN) and the lower surface of the Top Nozzle (TN).

3. The guides tubes (GT) are made up of two main regions (Monobloc/Dashpot and Regular/Non-dashpot regions) with a transition zone of 85 mm [6]. This transition zone is not considered, the dashpot region is considered to extend from the Bottom Nozzle (BN) to the first Intermediate Spacer Grid (ISG1) and the non-dashpot region extends from ISG1 to the Top Nozzle (TN). Consequently, the beam is made up of two main sections namely: Monobloc/Dashpot and Regular/Non-dashpot sections.

4. The effective modulus at each elevation is evaluated by considering the moment of inertia of components (FR, GT, IT) present at that elevation, with their corresponding Young's Moduli. This evaluation is done for both hot and cold conditions.

5. The effective Young's Moduli are used to correct the standard GAIA test stiffness obtained at cold conditions to obtain the corresponding axial stiffness at operating conditions. This correction is done for the two sections of the fuel beam model by using the ratio of the Young's Moduli at hot to cold condition.

6. The equivalent cross sections of the fuel beam model for the dashpot and non-dashpot regions are evaluated using the equivalent stiffness, the effective Young's Moduli and the length of the beam model.
7. Using the mass of the fuel assembly1, the cross sections and the length of the beam model, the equivalent density of the dashpot and non-dashpot regions are evaluated.
The validation of the fuel assembly beam model is done in two main steps:

1. Benchmark to GAIA target frequencies at BOL and EOL conditions in air: The same values for the spacer grids rotational spring stiffnesses used in the GAIA lateral benchmark model [7] are used in this model since in the modeling approach used by CASAC [3] (according to the methodology of the topical report [1]) and ANSYS [2] are similar. The fuel beam model is benchmarked to the target frequencies of the GAIA lateral benchmark model presented in [7]. This validation step is presented explicitly in §7.1.

1 HDS, BN and TN are not considered in the model used to validate the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model. This assumption is in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1]. However, in the final model that mimics both the lateral and vertical responses, the total mass of the fuel assembly was considered.

entries.section_title: 7.4. RECOMMENDATIONS: INTEGRATING THE FUEL BEAM MODEL INTO THE RPVI MODEL
entries.text: Adjustments (but not limited to) that should be considered while integrating the fuel beam model presented in §7.3 into the RPVI model are listed in subsections §7.4.1 through §7.4.4. It is the responsibility of the preparer of the RPVI analysis to make the necessary modifications and engineering calls if need be.

entries.section_title: 7.4. RECOMMENDATIONS: INTEGRATING THE FUEL BEAM MODEL INTO THE RPVI MODEL
entries.text: The axial contact interfaces that exist at both ends of the fuel assembly namely between the: LCP and the BN of the fuel assembly, UCP and the TN of the fuel assembly, should be modelled with an appropriate gap-spring-damper element defined by its stiffness, damping and gap. The purpose of this gap spring is to enable impact capabilities between the fuel beam model and the core plates in the RPVI analysis. Figure 7-13 is an example of the fuel beam model with its vertical interfaces with the reactor core plates represented by gap springs.

entries.section_title: 7.4.2. LATERAL CONTACT: FUEL BEAM – FUEL BEAM OR CORE BAFFLE
entries.text: Based on how the fuel beam model would be integrated into the RPVI model (as multiple single fuel beams or as a lumped fuel beam), the lateral contact with neighboring fuel assemblies or the core baffles should be defined accordingly with a gap spring using benchmarked spacer grids external equivalent stiffness and damping values presented in Table 11 of [7]. An extract of this table with the benchmarked parameters established at cold conditions is presented in Table 7-20 below.

The hydraulic lift off loads evaluated from an appropriate lift off analysis at different state point of the reactor core should be accounted for and introduced into the fuel beam model upon its integration into the RPVI model. The total lift off load of the fuel assembly should be distributed along the fuel assembly’s height using the corresponding pressure loss coefficients of different components of the fuel assembly at each spacer grid elevation.
The preload of the HDS should be updated to the appropriate preload taken from a Hold Down Spring analysis at a state point of interest for which the RPVI analysis is being performed.
These properties can be assumed to be applicable to the TN – UCP gap spring.

The presence of the reactor coolant modifies the vibrational response of the fuel assembly. The nonstationary interaction between reactor coolant and fuel assembly constitutes the hydrodynamic coupling, a non-dissipative phenomenon, which is distinct from damping. This hydrodynamic coupling is used to account for the added mass effect and buoyancy.
This linearized interaction between the fuel assembly and the reactor coolant is accounted for via the mass matrix concept by using MATRIX27 elements in ANSYS [2].
The added mass is evaluated in the following steps:
The displaced fluid volume due to the fully submerged fuel assembly is corrected with added mass coefficient defined in the topical report [1].
This displaced fluid volume is then scaled along the height of the fuel assembly using the fluid length at each span as defined in FRANC [4] to obtain the fluid added mass.
Inner fluid mass is also evaluated and scaled along the height of the fuel assembly using the inner fluid inner volume defined for each span.
The fluid added mass, and the inner fluid mass are then combined to yield the added mass.
The coupling mass is evaluated in a similar manner but using the coupling mass coefficient defined in the topical report [1].

The added mass and coupling masses defined in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1] at each structural node of the fuel beam model (except for the HDS node) are summarized in Table 7-8. Water density at operating core conditions (583.5°F and 2250 psia) is defined using SteamTab [5].

entries.section_title: FUEL BEAM MODEL WITH HDS IN WATER AT OPERATING CORE CONDITIONS
entries.text: Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model in §7.1 and §7.2, the HDS is incorporated to simulate its vertical dynamic response. As such, the fuel beam model with HDS (in water at operating core conditions) is identical to the lateral fuel beam model in water at operating core conditions presented in §7.2 with the exception of an extra element added to represent the HDS and hydrodynamic couplings defined in the vertical direction.

entries.section_title: FUEL BEAM MODEL WITH HDS IN WATER AT OPERATING CORE CONDITIONS
entries.text: This final fuel beam model mimics both the lateral and vertical dynamic responses of the fuel assembly.

The spacer grid centerline elevations of the Holtec GAIA SMR-300 design are defined [6] and are listed in Table 7-13. The coordinate system considers Z as the vertical orientation, and the elevations are set so that the zero elevation is at the bottom surface of the 0.0695 m tall bottom nozzle. The X and Y coordinates for Nodes 1 through 14 are (0, 0).
Table 7-13: Node Elevations

entries.section_title: Fuel Beam Model for Holtec SMR-300 Reactor Vessel Analyses
entries.text: Nodes 1 and 14 represent respectively the top surface of the bottom nozzle, and the extremity of the HDS fixed respectively to the Lower Core Plate and the Upper Core Plate (UCP). Node 13 represent the bottom surface of the top nozzle (or the extremity of the HDS attached to the fuel assembly). Only the displacement along the Z-axis is allowed at this node. The masses of the BN and TN are added as point masses respectively at element 1 (defined between node 1 and node 2) and element 12 (defined between node 12 and node 13) to account for the total mass of the fuel assembly. These point masses and the total masses of the fuel assembly are defined in §7.1.4. The final fuel beam model with both vertical and lateral dynamic responses is presented in Figure 7-12.

A finite element model of the Holtec SMR-300 fuel assembly design is needed to support the Reactor Pressure Vessel Internals (RPVI) dynamic analyses being performed by Holtec. This task is listed in §.1.2. of the Project Plan (15). The finite element model of the fuel assembly is created using ANSYS computer code [2]. The model represents the lateral and vertical dynamic responses of a single fuel assembly and incorporates the preloaded Hold Down Spring (HDS).

The properties of the fuel beam established in this document at cold (ambient) and hot (operating) should be adapted to the temperature at any state point of interest while taking into consideration the actual environment of the reactor as well as other physical phenomena present in the core at this state point. Some recommendations (but not limited to) of elements to account for while integrating the fuel beam model into the RPVI model are listed in section §.7.4.

Two configurations of the fuel beam model are studied, in air at ambient conditions and in water at the average operating conditions of temperature and pressure of the reactor core [12]. For both configurations, a Beginning Of Life (BOL) model and an End Of Life (EOL) model are analyzed. Consequently, the validation of the model is done in two steps:
The BOL and EOL models in air at ambient conditions are benchmarked to target frequencies of the GAIA lateral benchmark model presented in [7].
The BOL and EOL models at operating conditions in water are benchmarked to target frequencies of the FRANC [4] model. This model was elaborated according to the methodology of the topical report [1].
These steps are presented in detail in §.3.

Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model in air and in operating conditions in water, presented respectively in §.7.1 and §.7.2, the HDS with its preload is incorporated to the final model (see §.7.3) to verify its vertical dynamic response.
A summary of results obtained during the validation of the lateral and vertical dynamic responses is provided in §.8 for all configurations of the fuel beam model.
ANSYS 2021 R2 [2] is used for this analysis, which is the latest Framatome certified version at the time this report was released.

The properties of the fuel beam model presented in this document are consistent with the standard GAIA design. The changes incorporated in the GAIA-AFM design are listed in Table 1 of the Project Plan [15]. The main difference between the two designs that could impact the dynamic behavior of the fuel beam model is the difference in weight. However, this weight change accounts just for 1% difference, as such the impact is considered negligible.

The interfaces of the fuel beam model defined in §.7.3 do not reflect the exact environment of the fuel at operating conditions in the reactor and should be updated accordingly by referring to generic recommendations of §.7.4 and based on engineering judgments of the analyst performing the RPVI analysis.

The operating core conditions as designated in this document are used principally to verify the dynamic behavior of the beam model at hot conditions. The properties of the fuel beam model should be scaled to a specific temperature (of a state point of interest for example) if need be.

The hydraulic lift off loads evaluated from an appropriate lift off analysis at different state point of the reactor core should be accounted for and introduced into the fuel beam model upon its integration into the RPVI model. The total lift off load of the fuel assembly should be distributed along the fuel assembly’s height using the corresponding pressure loss coefficients of different components of the fuel assembly at each spacer grid elevation.
The preload of the HDS should be updated to the appropriate preload taken from a Hold Down Spring analysis at a state point of interest for which the RPVI analysis is being performed.
These properties can be assumed to be applicable to the TN – UCP gap spring.

A single fuel beam model was created and benchmarked to the target modal frequencies in air [7] (as per GAIA test data in [9] and [10]) and in operating conditions in water to a model elaborated in FRANC [4] according to the methodology of the topical report [1].
Using the stiffness at mid span elevation (grid 5) of the GAIA test fuel bundle, the adjusted cross-sectional area and density of the fuel beam model are determined.
The fuel beam elements have an adjusted cross-sectional area, but with the same inertial properties as the Holtec GAIA fuel assembly design.
The development and validation of this fuel beam model in ANSYS [2] is done in two main phases:

1. Benchmark to GAIA test data at room temperature: Using the same values of the rotational spring stiffnesses for the ISG and IGM grids as in the CASAC [3] lateral benchmark model [7], it was demonstrated that the ANSYS [2] beam model yields similar target frequencies for lateral modes 1 and 3 at both BOL and EOL. It should be noted that, the lateral model [7] was benchmarked to GAIA test results [9] and [10] performed at room temperature. This verification was done for both BOL and EOL.

2. Benchmark to operating conditions in water: the ANSYS [2] model was verified to yield similar frequencies as the model established in FRANC [4] according to the methodology of the topical report [1]. This verification was done for both BOL and EOL. In this phase, the rotational spring stiffnesses of the grids in the ANSYS [2] model were tuned to match the frequencies of the FRANC [4] model. This is because the modelling approach used to define hydrodynamic coupling effects in FRANC [4] differs from that used in ANSYS [2].

For the first phase, the error acceptability criteria according to the topical report [1] was verified. The limits of these criteria are respectively 2.5% and 10% for mode 1 and 3. There is no topical requirement for phase two, however, the results from this phase still respect the aforementioned criteria of the topical report [1].
Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model, the HDS was incorporated to simulates its axial (vertical) dynamic behavior.
