entries.text: The characteristics of the fuel assembly are presented in [6]. The fuel assembly is modeled as a single beam representing the cross-sectional areas and moment of inertias of the Fuel Rods (FR), Guide Tubes (GT), and Instrumentation Tube (IT). Rotational springs are included at spacer grid elevations to represent the shear coupling of grids.
The analytical methodology follows three main steps listed in §3.1 through §3.3 below.
The fuel beam model is constructed using standard GAIA axial compression test data ([9] for BOL and [10] for EOL) as follows:

1. The stiffness at mid elevation of the fuel assembly (at grid 5 according to Figure 9 of [9] and [10] respectively for BOL and EOL) is used as the equivalent stiffness of the fuel beam model. As illustrated in Figure 10-1 of Appendix A, a fuel beam model defined using the axial stiffness at mid elevation behaves very similarly to a fuel beam model defined with varying axial stiffnesses.
2. The length of the beam model is assumed to be the distance between the upper surface of the Bottom Nozzle (BN) and the lower surface of the Top Nozzle (TN).

3. The guides tubes (GT) are made up of two main regions (Monobloc/Dashpot and Regular/Non-dashpot regions) with a transition zone of 85 mm [6]. This transition zone is not considered, the dashpot region is considered to extend from the Bottom Nozzle (BN) to the first Intermediate Spacer Grid (ISG1) and the non-dashpot region extends from ISG1 to the Top Nozzle (TN). Consequently, the beam is made up of two main sections namely: Monobloc/Dashpot and Regular/Non-dashpot sections.

4. The effective modulus at each elevation is evaluated by considering the moment of inertia of components (FR, GT, IT) present at that elevation, with their corresponding Young's Moduli. This evaluation is done for both hot and cold conditions.

5. The effective Young's Moduli are used to correct the standard GAIA test stiffness obtained at cold conditions to obtain the corresponding axial stiffness at operating conditions. This correction is done for the two sections of the fuel beam model by using the ratio of the Young's Moduli at hot to cold condition.

6. The equivalent cross sections of the fuel beam model for the dashpot and non-dashpot regions are evaluated using the equivalent stiffness, the effective Young's Moduli and the length of the beam model.
7. Using the mass of the fuel assembly1, the cross sections and the length of the beam model, the equivalent density of the dashpot and non-dashpot regions are evaluated.
The validation of the fuel assembly beam model is done in two main steps:

1. Benchmark to GAIA target frequencies at BOL and EOL conditions in air: The same values for the spacer grids rotational spring stiffnesses used in the GAIA lateral benchmark model [7] are used in this model since in the modeling approach used by CASAC [3] (according to the methodology of the topical report [1]) and ANSYS [2] are similar. The fuel beam model is benchmarked to the target frequencies of the GAIA lateral benchmark model presented in [7]. This validation step is presented explicitly in §7.1.

1 HDS, BN and TN are not considered in the model used to validate the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model. This assumption is in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1]. However, in the final model that mimics both the lateral and vertical responses, the total mass of the fuel assembly was considered.
The validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model in air, is based on the criteria presented in §6.0 of the topical report [1].

Benchmark to BOL and EOL conditions at operating conditions in water: The properties of the fuel beam model are scaled to hot operating conditions to account for the increase in temperature. Hydrodynamic coupling elements are also incorporated into the model to account for the added mass and buoyancy effects due to the fuel assembly being submerged in the reactor coolant. These effects are incorporated in the form of mass elements which have on the diagonal, the added mass effect and in the off-diagonal positions, the coupling mass effect. This is done using MATRIX27 elements of the ANSYS [2] element library. The evaluation of the added and coupling masses in both the lateral and vertical directions are done in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1].

Unlike the CASAC [3] and ANSYS [2] models in air for which a similarity exist (same grid rotational stiffnesses are used), in operating conditions in water, the spacer grids rotational spring stiffnesses of the ANSYS [2] fuel beam model are adjusted in order to reproduce similar frequencies as the reference FRANC [4] model2. This validation step is presented explicitly in §7.2.

CONSOLIDATION OF LATERAL AND VERTICAL DYNAMIC RESPONSES Following the validation of the lateral dynamic response of the fuel beam model, the HDS is incorporated into the model to reproduce its vertical dynamic response. The masses of the BN and TN are also incorporated into this model to account for the total mass of the fuel assembly. The final fuel beam model that mimics both the lateral and vertical dynamic responses of the fuel assembly is presented explicitly in §7.3.

Material properties used to define the fuel beam models are taken from [14]. Ambient condition is considered as cold conditions and operating (hot) conditions are defined in [12]. Intermediary calculations as well as the inputs used, and the verification of results are presented in the Excel spreadsheet Holtec Beam Model Analysis.xlsx listed in Table 9-1.

ASSUMPTIONS REQUIRING VERIFICATION There are no assumptions requiring verification. However, engineering judgments have been applied in the development of the numerical models and the adequate justification of modeling uncertainties is provided throughout the report.
MODELING SIMPLIFICATIONS

The fuel assembly is modeled as a single beam with nodes representing the elevation at the top surface of the bottom nozzle, bottom surface of the top nozzle and the mid-height of the intermediate grids. The cross section at each elevation represents the following components: a. 264 Fuel Rods
A reference model to serve for comparison is developed in FRANC [4] in accordance with the methodology presented in the topical report [1] using the finite element code CASAC [3].

entries.section_title: 7.3.2. HYDRODYNAMIC COUPLING – LATERAL AND VERTICAL DIRECTIONS
entries.text: Similarly to §7.2.3, added and coupling masses in the vertical direction (along Z) are defined in accordance with the methodology of the topical report [1]. These added masses and coupling masses in the vertical direction at each structural node of the fuel beam model (except for the HDS node) are listed in Table 7-14.
The hydrodynamic added and coupling masses in the lateral direction (as defined in §7.2.3) are also incorporated into the fuel beam model with HDS.

Based on engineering judgement, a value of preload within the range 2000-2500N is considered. In this analysis, the average value of this range is used. This preload causes the deflection of the fuel assembly in addition to the deflection caused by the fuel weight. Therefore, the input preload is calculated to account for the initial deflection. The BOL and EOL initial deflections are calculated, accounting for weight and spring preload, as follows:

Where:
Fpreload = 2000 + 2500 = 2250 N ≡ average preload based on engineering judgement
m = 682.203 kg ≡ Total Fuel Beam Mass defined in §7.1.4
g = 9.815 m/s2 ≡ acceleration due to gravity constant
KBOL,H and KEOL,H are defined in §7.2.1. These stiffnesses are assumed to correspond to those of the non-dashpot region of the fuel beam model since axially the cross-section is predominantly of non-dashpot

nature. Also, the axial stiffness values for both the dashpot and non-dashpot regions are closely identical hence, using either of the values would yield similar results. Hence: (KBOLH , KEOLH ) = (KBOLNon-dashpotH , KEOLNon-dashpotH ) = ( 4.9969E + 07 N/m , 1.0750E + 08 N/m ) The evaluated initial deflections become: ΔBOL,fuel = Fpreload + m g 2 KBOLNon-dashpotH , ΔEOL,fuel = Fpreload + m g 2 KEOLNon-dashpotH Yielding: ΔBOL,fuel = 1.1203E − 04 m ΔEOL,fuel = 5.2075E − 05 m Considering this initial deflection, we can evaluate the equivalent preload to be applied to the fuel beam model. FBOL,model = Fpreload + KHD S ∗ ΔBOL,fuel , FEOL,model = Fpreload + KHD S ∗ ΔEOL,fuel Where: Fpreload = 2250 N KHD S = 265977 N/m = Stiffness of the four hold down springs at operating temperature. The value of one hold down spring stiffness is given in [13] as 411.8lb f /in (7.2117E + 04 N/m) at ambient temperature. Hence for the four springs at operating conditions the value becomes: KHD S = 4 ∗ (7.2117E + 04 ) ∗ 0.922 = 265977 N/m Where 0.922 = the elastic modulus ratio for IN-718 at operating temperature to ambient temperature. Hence: FBOL,model = 2280 N , FEOL,model = 2264 N
The same benchmarked rotational spring stiffnesses of grids defined in §7.2.4 are used.
The first and third lateral frequencies with the first vertical frequency of the fuel beam model with HDS are listed in Table 7-15 and Table 7-16 respectively for BOL and EOL configurations.

entries.text: The Holtec GAIA fuel assembly is very similar to the standard 17x17 GAIA assembly with minor adjustments at the top nozzle to support the SMR-300 plant interfaces and operating conditions [15]. It is comprised of the following components:

The Holtec GAIA fuel assembly is very similar to the standard 17x17 GAIA assembly with minor adjustments at the top nozzle to support the SMR-300 plant interfaces and operating conditions [15]. It is comprised of the following components:

The single fuel beam model is a three-dimensional model consisting of beam elements and rotational spring elements (see Figure 7-1). The effective modulus of the beam elements varies over the entire length of the assembly to account for the variation in the cross section of the guide tube. Hence, we have the dashpot region which depicts the thick section of the guide tube and the non-dashpot section which depicts the thin section of the guide tube.

The effective modulus of the beam elements coupled with the length of the beam and the axial stiffness from GAIA axial compression tests (BOL [9] and EOL [10]) are used to evaluate the corresponding cross section of the beam.

Four stiffness values are used for the lateral rotational springs to represent the lower end grid, intermediate grids (ISG and IGM), and upper end grid. One stiffness value for each of the end grids, one for the ISG grids and one for the IGM grids.

The spacer grid centerline elevations of the Holtec GAIA SMR-300 design are defined in [6] and presented in Table 7-1. Z-axis is the vertical orientation, and the elevations are set so that the zero elevation is at the bottom surface of the 0.0695 m tall bottom nozzle. The X and Y coordinates for Nodes 1 through 13 are (0, 0).
N° FS1-0074617 Rev. 1.0 Fuel Beam Model for Holtec SMR-300 Reactor Vessel Analyses framatome Handling: Restricted Framatome Page 13/46

Node 14 is included in the model for the orientation of elements. This node has as coordinates: (X = 1 m, Y = 1 m, Z = 0 m). The length of the fuel beam model is the difference in the elevations at node 1 and node 13, hence 3.901 m. Nodes 1 and 13 represent respectively the top surface of the bottom nozzle, and the lower surface of the top nozzle. They are fixed in all degrees of freedom.

entries.text: In this document the core source term is modelled as a fixed source based on data extracted directly from the detailed core design models [5]. The data taken from the core design models consider the following factors:
Radially, each assembly is treated independently based on the relative power of each assembly.
A systemic radial bias is not applied; however, a sampling bias (MCNP's sb functionality) may be used for variance reduction in downstream analyses.

Two levels of detail are provided in the attachments to this document. In the assembly-level source, the pin relative powers are not used and the source distribution is smeared uniformly across each individual assembly.

In the pin-level source, the power profile across pins is explicitly modeled for the peripheral assemblies. Interior assemblies are modeled as having a flat pin power distribution. The source distribution is smeared within each fuel channel.
These two approaches are provided for downstream analyses to use as appropriate.

Within each assembly, the fission neutron energy spectrum is modeled as a combination of Watt Spectra for each fissionable isotope weighted by the burnup dependent-total fission rate for the assembly, and nuclide dependent neutrons per fission. The burnup dependent nuclide fission fractions are obtained from the ORIGEN runs associated with [8] and the nuclide dependent average neutrons per fission are obtained from [11].
The core is divided into two radial (interior and peripheral) and 24 axial regions. The temperature of the coolant in each region is extracted from the core design models [7].
Water channels in the reflector are modeled with an axially varied temperature across the height of the core.
Downcomer/Inlet Plenum
Both the downcomer and the inlet plenum are modeled at the core inlet temperature.

entries.text: To stochastically check the geometry for errors, a deck is created which floods the geometry with particles. A voided problem is used with an isotropic volume source covering the problem. This results in particles crossing every surface from every angle.

To check that the source distribution conforms to the intended distribution, MCNP 6's source tally, fmesh type source, is used to graphically plot the source distribution. Code 8-4 shows the used. The tally consists of a rectilinear grid over the core region sized so that in the x and y directions, the mesh spacing results in 17x17 meshes inside each assembly roughly corresponding to each pin location, and there being a single axial meshes.
The key parameters to be checked are that the relative powers of each assembly match expectations, and that the pin power distributions are consistent.
The stochastically calculated volumes are shown in Table 9-1. These results provide a means of verification by inspection, either by points comparison or by noting expected trends.
The volumes may also be used in downstream analyses which require volumes for input on the sd cards associated with f4 tallies.

The volumes may also be used in downstream analyses which require volumes for input on the sd cards associated with f4 tallies.
The completion of the geometry check run without lost particles provides confidence that the geometry does not contain geometry errors.

Figure 9-1 provides a cross sectional view of the axial averaged source distribution. In this figure, the expected power profile can be observed by inspection. Notably, the peripheral assemblies show a higher power near the core center, confirming that the pin profiles are consistent.

entries.text: As the purpose of this document is to establish the SMR-300 cavity MCNP model, there are no specific analyses that are required. However, to demonstrate the adequacy of the model and provide potentially useful information, a stochastic volume calculation is performed.

A stochastic volume calculation is a method of calculating cell volumes using MCNP. See Section 3.3.1.1 of [1] for a description of the process. To perform a stochastic volume calculation, the following general steps are used:
With respect to step 3, there are two common approaches to constructing this source:

The second approach is generally better at testing for geometry errors as the variety in particle directions means there are no surfaces always parallel to the direction of particle travel, whereas the planar approach is generally less invasive and requires fewer edits to the input file.

Given the purpose of this document is to automate the generation of variant input files from the base deck, the first approach is used, with geometry validation being provided by an alternative method.

Code 8-1 shows the planar source that has been constructed on the bottom surface of the cylindrical problem. It takes the form of a circular disk with a starting weight equal to the circle's area. Photons are arbitrarily chosen for this process.
Code 8-2 shows the volume tally used to calculate the cell volumes. A single tally with tally segmenting is used to simplify the input and output processes, every cell number is
provided-cells filled by another universe return a calculated volume of 0.0 because MCNP does not record particle tracks in the containing universe.

Code 8-3 shows the run option cards used for the volume calculation. The run options consist of including a few non-default tables; for geometry debugging purposes, the void card, the mode card, and the nps runtime option.

Regarding the nps selection, due to the way the source has been constructed, each particle history will consist of a particle being born on the bottom surface of the problem and following a straight vertical path through the problem. As a result, the uncertainty of the volume calculation for a specific cell will be proportional to the cross-sectional area of the cell, and more importantly it means that the smallest feature (horizontal cross-sectional area) that can be resolved will be on the same order as the starting particle areal density.

For example, with the starting surface area being 1E5 cm2 and a hypothetical nps of 1E4, the average particle density is 0.1 particles/cm2 or inversely 10 cm2/particle. What this means is that for each particle that scores in a cell, 10 cm2 times the cell height will be added to the cell’s volume tally, this means that the resolution of the cell volumes is limited to cells with a large cross section. For this reason, a large nps value of 1E9 is used. Resulting in a resolution of 1E-4 cm2/particle. Because the problem is a void problem (i.e., no scatter or other particle interactions), this does not result in an unacceptable runtime.

For this analysis, the nps has been chosen such that the resolution is on the order of: area = 3.04 × 105 cm2 = 3.04 × 10-4 cm2 nps = 109 particles = particle Where area is the cross sectional area of the model, and nps is the number of starting particles. The resolution is sufficiently small for the purposes of this model.

entries.text: This document presents an MCNP geometry model for the SMR-300 and an associated source definition to be used in future analyses in and near the reactor cavity.
The geometry model developed herein is applicable only to the SMR-300 design, the source definition developed herein is only applicable to the 18-month equilibrium cycle EOC.

The models presented in this document have been generated with generic material definitions considered suitable for transport applications. For non-transport applications the suitability may be different. Specifically for activation purposes the lack of minor impurities, such as cobalt, make the material definitions non-suitable.

entries.text: Radially, each assembly is treated independently based on the relative power of each assembly.
A systemic radial bias is not applied; however, a sampling bias (MCNP's sb functionality) may be used for variance reduction in downstream analyses.

Two levels of detail are provided in the attachments to this document. In the assembly-level source, the pin relative powers are not used and the source distribution is smeared uniformly across each individual assembly.

In the pin-level source, the power profile across pins is explicitly modeled for the peripheral assemblies. Interior assemblies are modeled as having a flat pin power distribution. The source distribution is smeared within each fuel channel.
These two approaches are provided for downstream analyses to use as appropriate.

Within each assembly, the fission neutron energy spectrum is modeled as a combination of Watt Spectra for each fissionable isotope weighted by the burnup dependent-total fission rate for the assembly, and nuclide dependent neutrons per fission. The burnup dependent nuclide fission fractions are obtained from the ORIGEN runs associated with [8] and the nuclide dependent average neutrons per fission are obtained from [11].
The core is divided into two radial (interior and peripheral) and 24 axial regions. The temperature of the coolant in each region is extracted from the core design models [7].
Water channels in the reflector are modeled with an axially varied temperature across the height of the core.
Downcomer/Inlet Plenum
Both the downcomer and the inlet plenum are modeled at the core inlet temperature.
The outlet is modeled as being at the core outlet temperature.

As this document does not establish results there are no specific acceptance criteria. However, for geometry validation, a stochastic volume calculation is performed. The completion of the stochastic volume calculation without lost particles provides assurance that the geometry does not contain geometry errors, for example, gaps, overlaps, etc.

Code 8-2 Tally for Stochastic Volume Calculation
entries.text: print 110 128 void mode p nps 1E+9

entries.section_title: Code 8-3 Run Options for Stochastic Volume Calculation
entries.text: provided-cells filled by another universe return a calculated volume of 0.0 because MCNP does not record particle tracks in the containing universe. Code 8-3 shows the run option cards used for the volume calculation. The run options consist of including a few non-default tables; for geometry debugging purposes, the void card, the mode card, and the nps runtime option. Regarding the nps selection, due to the way the source has been constructed, each particle history will consist of a particle being born on the bottom surface of the problem and following a straight vertical path through the problem. As a result, the uncertainty of the volume calculation for a specific cell will be proportional to the cross-sectional area of the cell, and more importantly it means that the smallest feature (horizontal cross-sectional area) that can be resolved will be on the same order as the starting particle areal density. For example, with the starting surface area being 1E5 cm2 and a hypothetical nps of 1E4, the average particle density is 0.1 particles/cm2 or inversely 10 cm2/particle. What this means is that for each particle that scores in a cell, 10 cm2 times the cell height will be added to the cell’s volume tally, this means that the resolution of the cell volumes is limited to cells with a large cross section. For this reason, a large nps value of 1E9 is used. Resulting in a resolution of 1E-4 cm2/particle. Because the problem is a void problem (i.e., no scatter or other particle interactions), this does not result in an unacceptable runtime. For this analysis, the nps has been chosen such that the resolution is on the order of: area = 3.04 × 105 cm2 = 3.04 × 10-4 cm2 nps = 109 particles = particle Where area is the cross sectional area of the model, and nps is the number of starting particles. The resolution is sufficiently small for the purposes of this model.

To stochastically check the geometry for errors, a deck is created which floods the geometry with particles. A voided problem is used with an isotropic volume source covering the problem. This results in particles crossing every surface from every angle.

To check that the source distribution conforms to the intended distribution, MCNP 6's source tally, fmesh type source, is used to graphically plot the source distribution. Code 8-4 shows the used. The tally consists of a rectilinear grid over the core region sized so that in the x and y directions, the mesh spacing results in 17x17 meshes inside each assembly roughly corresponding to each pin location, and there being a single axial meshes.
The key parameters to be checked are that the relative powers of each assembly match expectations, and that the pin power distributions are consistent.

The purpose of this analysis is to develop an MCNP base deck to be used in subsequent MCNP analyses of the SMR-300 in-cavity but ex-core region. The downstream analyses include but are not limited to: Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) Fluence analyses, ex-core detector analyses, cavity streaming characterization, cavity activation rates, etc. It is the responsibility of downstream analysts to ensure that the assumptions and modelling simplifications made within this document are applicable to their specific use.

The Monte Carlo N-Particle Transport (MCNP) code is a general-purpose, continuous-energy, generalized-geometry, time-dependent code designed to track multiple particle types over a broad range of energies. The MCNP code makes use of a constructive solid geometry (CSG) input format which allows for an exact representation of the reactor's three-dimensional geometry. [1]

The three-dimensional exposure and power distribution data for each fuel assembly have been calculated using SIMULATES. Information from this core simulator code has been used as input to the MCNP model.
Figure 2-1 shows a representative axial cross section view of the SMR-300 model while Figure 2-2 shows a horizontal cross section.

The SMR-300 MCNP model is representative of the standard design with the modeling simplifications detailed in Section 4.0. Additional details of the geometric model for specific components are discussed below.

Each fuel assembly is modeled as a constant volumetric mixture of fuel (UO2), metallic components, and water (see Appendix A. A temperature-based density adjustment is made to the components, and water components (see Assumption 4). Materials and volume fractions are discussed in more details in Appendix B. An adjustment is made to the water component of the material such that each assembly has 24 axial segments, and the periphery assemblies are adjusted separately from the interior assemblies (see Assumption 5).
The temperature profile used is taken from the detailed core design analyses [7].

entries.text: provided-cells filled by another universe return a calculated volume of 0.0 because MCNP does not record particle tracks in the containing universe.

Code 8-3 shows the run option cards used for the volume calculation. The run options consist of including a few non-default tables; for geometry debugging purposes, the void card, the mode card, and the nps runtime option.

Regarding the nps selection, due to the way the source has been constructed, each particle history will consist of a particle being born on the bottom surface of the problem and following a straight vertical path through the problem. As a result, the uncertainty of the volume calculation for a specific cell will be proportional to the cross-sectional area of the cell, and more importantly it means that the smallest feature (horizontal cross-sectional area) that can be resolved will be on the same order as the starting particle areal density.

For example, with the starting surface area being 1E5 cm2 and a hypothetical nps of 1E4, the average particle density is 0.1 particles/cm2 or inversely 10 cm2/particle. What this means is that for each particle that scores in a cell, 10 cm2 times the cell height will be added to the cell’s volume tally, this means that the resolution of the cell volumes is limited to cells with a large cross section. For this reason, a large nps value of 1E9 is used. Resulting in a resolution of 1E-4 cm2/particle. Because the problem is a void problem (i.e., no scatter or other particle interactions), this does not result in an unacceptable runtime.

For this analysis, the nps has been chosen such that the resolution is on the order of: area = 3.04 × 105 cm2 = 3.04 × 10-4 cm2 nps = 109 particles = particle Where area is the cross sectional area of the model, and nps is the number of starting particles. The resolution is sufficiently small for the purposes of this model.

The lower internals geometry is derived primarily from [5]. The radial, axial, and conical dimensions for the lower internals are summarized in Table A-4, Table A-5, and Table A-6 respectively.
The materials used in this analysis consist of either basic materials (e.g., concrete, steel, water) or mixtures of basic materials.
To account for the density-change of water, during the mixing process, the volume fraction of water is adjusted based on its local temperature so that the total volume fraction sums to less than one.

Section B-1 summarizes the basic materials used.

Section B-4 details the determination of water temperatures.

The inlet plenum is modeled as pure water. See Assumption 15.

The lower core plate (LCP) is modeled as a homogenous mixture of steel and the water in the penetrations through the LCP. The metallic portion of the LCP consists of metal disk with a mass defined in [5], the water portion consists of water at the inlet temperature.

To properly mix the constituent materials, it is necessary to determine the volume fractions. The overall volume of the LCP region is taken to be a disk with dimensions as discussed in Appendix A, giving a total volume as specified by V_LCP in Table B-3.
The effective volume of the metallic portion is calculated using the mass of the LCP and the density of 304 stainless steel [10] giving an effective metal volume as specified by V_metal in Table B-3.

The water volume fraction is taken to be the remainder, v_water in Table B-3.

The source definition makes use of MCNP's nested distribution feature.

At the top level, the particle type is sampled. While this particle sampling does not have an effect, it does allow the other source parameters to be sampled on an assembly-wise basis and allows for future revisions to include the photon source. Code C-1 shows the layout of the sdef card used, while Code C-2 shows the particle distribution.

Code C-3 shows the cel distribution. In sampling the cel parameter, distribution 2 is used to select a pin distribution (distributions 200-268) corresponding to a single assembly. Note that due to MCNP's use of column major data entry, the pin powers must be transposed from the row major ordering that the SIMULATE5 output and Python use.

Code C-4, Code C-5, and Code C-6 show the x, y, and z distributions respectively. Because MCNP will sample the position relative to the lowest level universe (i.e., the pin universe), both the x and y distributions are independent distributions over the pin pitch. The z distribution, however, is selected from either the average axial profile for the interior assemblies, or the axial profile for the peripheral assemblies.

Code C-7 shows the erg distribution. The energy is sampled from assembly dependent distributions that uses the fractional fission rates to select from a series of Watt Spectra (one per nuclide). The fractional fission rates are found by interpolating the ORIGEN outputs attached to [8].
The remaining sections of this appendix detail how the numerical values used within the distributions are determined.

entries.text: The basic materials used to create mixtures (see Section B-3) are taken from [10]. The base materials are summarized in Table B-2:
The inlet plenum is modeled as pure water. See Assumption 15.

The lower core plate (LCP) is modeled as a homogenous mixture of steel and the water in the penetrations through the LCP. The metallic portion of the LCP consists of metal disk with a mass defined in [5], the water portion consists of water at the inlet temperature.

To properly mix the constituent materials, it is necessary to determine the volume fractions. The overall volume of the LCP region is taken to be a disk with dimensions as discussed in Appendix A, giving a total volume as specified by V_LCP in Table B-3.
The effective volume of the metallic portion is calculated using the mass of the LCP and the density of 304 stainless steel [10] giving an effective metal volume as specified by V_metal in Table B-3.
From the metal volume and the total LCP region volume, the metallic volume fraction is taken to be v_metal in Table B-3.
The water volume fraction is taken to be the remainder, v_water in Table B-3.

The bottom nozzle is modeled as a mixture of steel and water based on the volumes determined in [7] for Bottom Zone 3. In [7] the bottom nozzle is modeled as consisting of four parts: the bottom nozzle, the moderator, the lower connection screw assembly, and

The bottom gap is a modeled as a mixture of zircaloy and water based on the volumes determined in [7] for Bottom Zone 2, V_Zr and V_water in Table B-5. Leading to the two volume fractions: v_Zr and v_water in Table B-5.

The bottom plugs are a modeled as a mixture of zircaloy, stainless steel and water based on the volumes determined in [7] for Bottom Zone 1, see V_Zr and V_water in Table B-6. Leading to the two volume fractions: v_Zr and v_water in Table B-6.

The fuel plenum is modeled as a mixture of zircaloy, stainless steel, helium, and water based on the volumes determined in [7] for "Top Zone 1", see V_Zr, V_Stainless Steel, V_He, and V_water in Table B-7. Leading to the volume fractions: v_Zr, v_Stainless Steel, v_He, and v_water in Table B-7.
The top plug region is symmetric with the bottom plug, and thus uses the same volume fractions but a different water density: See Table B-8.
The top gap is modeled as a mixture based on the volumes determined in [7] for "Top Zone 5": V_Zr and V_water in Table B-9. Leading to the volume fractions: v_Zr and v_water in Table B-9.

The top nozzle is modeled as a mixture based on the volumes determined in [7] for "Top Zone 6": V_Zr, V_Stainless Steel, and V_water in Table B-10. Leading to the volume fractions: v_Zr, v_Stainless Steel, and v_water in Table B-10.
The upper core plate is assumed to have the same volume fractions as the lower core plate. See Assumption 14.

The downstream analyses include but are not limited to: Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) Fluence analyses, ex-core detector analyses, cavity streaming characterization, cavity activation rates, etc. It is the responsibility of downstream analysts to ensure that the assumptions and modelling simplifications made within this document are applicable to their specific use.

The Monte Carlo N-Particle Transport (MCNP) code is a general-purpose, continuous-energy, generalized-geometry, time-dependent code designed to track multiple particle types over a broad range of energies. The MCNP code makes use of a constructive solid geometry (CSG) input format which allows for an exact representation of the reactor's three-dimensional geometry. [1]

The three-dimensional exposure and power distribution data for each fuel assembly have been calculated using SIMULATES. Information from this core simulator code has been used as input to the MCNP model.
Figure 2-1 shows a representative axial cross section view of the SMR-300 model while Figure 2-2 shows a horizontal cross section.

The SMR-300 MCNP model is representative of the standard design with the modeling simplifications detailed in Section 4.0. Additional details of the geometric model for specific components are discussed below.

Each fuel assembly is modeled as a constant volumetric mixture of fuel (UO2), metallic components, and water (see Appendix A. A temperature-based density adjustment is made to the components, and water components (see Assumption 4). Materials and volume fractions are discussed in more details in Appendix B. An adjustment is made to the water component of the material such that each assembly has 24 axial segments, and the periphery assemblies are adjusted separately from the interior assemblies (see Assumption 5).
The temperature profile used is taken from the detailed core design analyses [7].

entries.text: The source definition makes use of MCNP's nested distribution feature.

At the top level, the particle type is sampled. While this particle sampling does not have an effect, it does allow the other source parameters to be sampled on an assembly-wise basis and allows for future revisions to include the photon source. Code C-1 shows the layout of the sdef card used, while Code C-2 shows the particle distribution.

Code C-3 shows the cel distribution. In sampling the cel parameter, distribution 2 is used to select a pin distribution (distributions 200-268) corresponding to a single assembly. Note that due to MCNP's use of column major data entry, the pin powers must be transposed from the row major ordering that the SIMULATE5 output and Python use.

Code C-4, Code C-5, and Code C-6 show the x, y, and z distributions respectively. Because MCNP will sample the position relative to the lowest level universe (i.e., the pin universe), both the x and y distributions are independent distributions over the pin pitch. The z distribution, however, is selected from either the average axial profile for the interior assemblies, or the axial profile for the peripheral assemblies.

Code C-7 shows the erg distribution. The energy is sampled from assembly dependent distributions that uses the fractional fission rates to select from a series of Watt Spectra (one per nuclide). The fractional fission rates are found by interpolating the ORIGEN outputs attached to [8].
The remaining sections of this appendix detail how the numerical values used within the distributions are determined.

Hot Leg Temperature [F]

Pipe length and elevation

The following computer codes are used to develop this design report:

Computer files for this design report are located in HIDOC supporting files. Important files included in this directory: M:\SMR-300\12. Systems\Tasks By System\RCS\RCS Reports\[HI- 2251404] PipeFLO Model\RO\Computer Files

The physical characteristics of the model are based on the current system layout from the isometric. All node elevations are relative to the models’ reference 0ft elevation which is the centerline of the RPV nozzles. A draft isometric of the RCS is used to identify the distance between node locations for interfacing systems and component connections on a given pipe run. Where the isometric lengths include bends of the main loop piping, the chord length of the bend is calculated and removed to avoid double counting the resistance of that section. All RCS pipe bends are 1.5 F/D.

Piping in the RCS, other than the main loop piping, is commercial stainless steel pipe. The appropriate size and schedule are selected from pipe tables in Pipe-FLO, ASME B36.19M and B36.10M. The main loop piping is custom size pipe with stainless steel cladding and roughness specifications. A custom table is added to Pipe-FLO specifying the roughness and cladding inside diameter for these pipe segments as specified in [4]. Connections to interfacing piping are expected to be made using weldouts and of such a size difference that the resistance effects of the tee connections are considered negligible, thus no flow-through-run tee fittings are used in the main lines of the model. The K for all bends are fixed to the value calculated in [4].

Components in the RCS model are shown as pipe segments. The specification comes from custom tables to Pipe-FLO. Each component specification is given the same roughness as the main loop piping. Inside diameter is sized to produce the flow velocity used to calculate the component K value specified [4]. The velocity and K represent the physical construction of the component. Length of the component is maintained however the design factor of components is set to 1E-05. This is done to reduce the excess resistance that occurs by modeling the component as a pipe.

The Pressurizer space above the divider plate is modeled as a tank and serves as the pressure source to allow the model to function. At normal full power operation, this is a saturated system. The fluid state for the tank is set to just below the saturation temperature to maintain a liquid state. Elevation of the tank modeled in Pipe-FLO is the elevation of the divider plate in relation to the RPV nozzles. Elevation of piping connected to that tank is in relation to the bottom of the tank, i.e. the divider plate.

Spray line PCV and bypass valves are modeled as sizing control valves in Pipe-FLO operating in a fixed flow rate, such that total flow equals the steady-state flow calculated in [1]. PSV are included with preliminary sizing data for discharge coefficient and discharge area.

The heat transfer segments of the system, the core and SGE tubes, are broken down into smaller segments to more accurately model the temperature change that occurs. In this model it is assumed that both sections have a linear temperature gradient. No heat input is modeled across the RCPs.

There are two bypass flow paths with a flow rate assumed in [4]. A custom K is applied and adjusted until the flow rates achieved match the assumptions of [4] while the pumps operation is fixed at design flow [6] and heat transfer segments are set to average coolant temperature.

Pipe-FLO warnings "Pipe length < change in elevation between endpoints" are expected. The flow resistance of fittings are included in the K, therefore, fitting lengths are not included in the connected pipe segments. This may result in an elevation difference between connected nodes.

The purpose of this report is to document all design bases, assumptions, and system input data used to build the preliminary Pipe-FLO RCS model. This model may be used for non-safety calculations and hydraulic analysis of steady state conditions.

The design case model includes all piping, vessels, and flow paths identified in the P&ID [2] and RCP sizing calculation [4]. Pipe-FLO relief valves are nodes and do not allow for modeling this elevation change.

entries.text: The purpose of this report is to record the design bases, assumptions, and system input data used to generate the Pipe-Flo model of the RCS. This model can then be used in subsequent calculations and hydraulic analysis.
PIPE-FLO Professional was used, along with inputs from various technical documents to generate a model for the RCS. Where conflicts exist the order of precedence is as follows:

The model is based on the normal full power operating conditions of the RCS. Each loop of the RCS has an RCP that will be operating at fixed speed. These pumps are modeled with a user defined pump curve based on the current vendor data. The normal operating pressure is the surface pressure of the PZR. There are three main temperature conditions in the system: Hot Leg, Cold Leg, and PZR. Regions where heat transfer occurs, the core and SGE tubes, will be broken into smaller segments to facilitate modeling the temperature change that occurs. Spray flow is modeled using sizing control valves at a fixed flow rate. The total spray flow will equal the steady-state spray flow calculated in the heater sizing calculation [1].

The components and diagram in each of the flow paths above are identified using the RCS Piping and Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID) [2]. Length and relative elevations are derived from the Isometrics [3]. The resistance of pipe bends is accounted for in their resistance values, K. The bend length to be removed from each straight segment length is the found using the following equation:
Bend Length = R * tan θdegrees 2

Bypass flow paths as identified in the RCP sizing calculation [4] are included in the model and sized to match the flow assumptions of that calculation. If a piping components' specific model or type is not determined, a generic component available in Pipe-FLO is used, such as for valves, fittings, flow devices, etc. K values of components on each pipe segment are detailed in the model breakdown in Appendix A.

Piping connections to interfacing systems are included in this model. None of the interfacing system connections are required to be in operation for proper functioning of the model. Each of these lines will be identified and the interfacing node will be placed at the proper elevation allowing them to serve as a placeholder. These connections will be closed pipe and the specifications: material, size, length, etc. are not included in this model.

Fluid states included in this model are based on normal full power operation. When this model is used for calculations and hydraulic evaluations, it is expected that future models will change operating characteristics as necessary.
This report must contain all the necessary assumptions, design bases, and input data to fully recreate the Pipe-Flo Model in order for the report to be accepted.

The purpose of this report is to record the design bases, assumptions, and system input data used to generate the Pipe-Flo model of the RCS. This model can then be used in subsequent calculations and hydraulic analysis.
PIPE-FLO Professional was used, along with inputs from various technical documents to generate a model for the RCS. Where conflicts exist the order of precedence is as follows:

The model is based on the normal full power operating conditions of the RCS. Each loop of the RCS has an RCP that will be operating at fixed speed. These pumps are modeled with a user defined pump curve based on the current vendor data. The normal operating pressure is the surface pressure of the PZR. There are three main temperature conditions in the system: Hot Leg, Cold Leg, and PZR. Regions where heat transfer occurs, the core and SGE tubes, will be broken into smaller segments to facilitate modeling the temperature change that occurs. Spray flow is modeled using sizing control valves at a fixed flow rate. The total spray flow will equal the steady-state spray flow calculated in the heater sizing calculation [1].

The components and diagram in each of the flow paths above are identified using the RCS Piping and Instrumentation Diagram (P&ID) [2]. Length and relative elevations are derived from the Isometrics [3]. The resistance of pipe bends is accounted for in their resistance values, K. The bend length to be removed from each straight segment length is the found using the following equation:
Bend Length = R * tan θdegrees 2

Bypass flow paths as identified in the RCP sizing calculation [4] are included in the model and sized to match the flow assumptions of that calculation. If a piping components' specific model or type is not determined, a generic component available in Pipe-FLO is used, such as for valves, fittings, flow devices, etc. K values of components on each pipe segment are detailed in the model breakdown in Appendix A.

entries.text: The design case model includes all RCS piping, major vessels, and flow paths using fluid states for normal full power conditions
All interface points with connected systems are identified as nodes with piping connections at the appropriate locations

The purpose of this report is to document all design bases, assumptions, and system input data used to build the preliminary Pipe-FLO RCS model. This model may be used for non-safety calculations and hydraulic analysis of steady state conditions.

The design case model includes all piping, vessels, and flow paths identified in the P&ID [2] and RCP sizing calculation [4]. The differences in pump TDH between the model and RCP sizing calculation are acceptable; the Pipe-FLO model analyzes elevation changes and temperature gradients differently than the assumptions in the hand calculation.

This model includes the preliminary pump curve data from the RCP vendor. Normal operation of the RCS will include simultaneous operation and interaction with interfacing systems. These systems are identified but not modeled as operating. Integrated system/plant models will be developed separately. There is a deviation between the elevations of the PSV outlet piping in the model and the isometric. This is a result of the elevation difference between the PSV inlet and outlet elevation. Pipe-FLO relief valves are nodes and do not allow for modeling this elevation change.

entries.text: With these simplifications, the SMR-300 twin-reactor configuration with shared non-safety and BOP systems and structures is expected to provide a distinctly improve plant economics and resource utilization needed to make it cost competitive.

For the supply of SMRs, Holtec is in an exclusive global teaming relationship with Hyundai E&C (HDEC) which designates them as Holtec's EPC construction partner. With its EPC construction partner Hyundai E&C (HDEC), Holtec's first SMR-300 is planned to be constructed and operated by 2031 at Palisades, MI in the US, with a Limited Work Authorization request submitted to the USNRC in Q1.2026 to begin site excavation and underground works, followed by a 10 CFR 50 Construction Permit Application submitted not later than Q3.2027, for construction and operation with an initial 40-yr operating license. Holtec has affirmed its ability and commitment to fund the project with internal and partner equity and debt financing. The Palisades LLWR PPA off-taker has a right-of-first refusal and plan for the SMR-300 electricity output. The FOAK SMR-300 power plant will be located adjacent to the exiting Palisades Large Light Water reactor in Covert MI, owned, due to be restarted by the 2025 year end, and operated by Holtec. The Twin SMRs at the Palisades site will benefit from common services and resources across the Palisades Nuclear Energy Center.

Described in Section 4 of this report, the GEH BWRX-300 is a practical boiling water reactor (BWR) power plant from a control and operations perspective. It uses substantially developed and proven technologies and components, leveraging decades of BWR operating experience - and excepting its revolutionary use of Reactor Isolation Valves (RIV) with a Dry Containment - its design is otherwise very similar to conventional generation large BWRs. A 'natural circulation reactor' with 100% high-pressure pumped condensate reactor feedwater during power operations, the plant is relatively easy to refuel during an outage, but its radioactive condenser steam both limits the plants application flexibility and greatly complicates turbine island and balance of plant outage maintenance issues and costs as compared to PWR SMRs. Unique aspects of the reactor plant include the use of unproven first-of-a-kind integrated nuclear RIVs. In conjunction with a single isolation condenser safety system performing multiple crucial safety functions and a small dry containment, GEH's BWRX-300 will challenge US, Canadian and international regulators to change certain key regulatory acceptance criteria to be able to license the plant.

GEH has attempted to simplify the reactor's engineered safety systems by eliminating diverse means and systems to cool or shutdown the reactor in case of accidents. The reactor relies on fine motion control rod drives (FMCRDs) for startup, control and scram, and those rods can be passively scrammed by pressurized accumulators. The FMCRDS include a secondary means of insertion for that same shutdown function, albeit one relying on non-safety AC powered screw drives. Another independent means to shut down the reactor relies on a manually actuated enriched boron liquid injection system reliant on non-safety AC power in case of an Anticipated Transient Without Scram (ATWS). It's clear how the design is able to assure shutdown in the event of an ATWS concurrent with a Loss of Offsite Power (LOOP) without reliance on non-safety AC power. The experience of the Fukushima Daiichi accident is certain to elicit heightened scrutiny of this single safety system design, which includes no ability to provide makeup water to the reactor in case of an unanticipated accident. The design incorporates hybrid composite steel plates originally developed and tested by Modular Wall Systems (Scotland, UK), now modified with a derivative Diaphragm Plate Steel Composite (DP-SC) module that GEH is developing in-house. The BWRX-300 integrated reactor building is substantially below grade, and to be constructed entirely with these DP-SC modules (in lieu of conventional rebar-concrete construction) within a deep excavated shaft. Like Holtec's CSSM civil modules and construction approach for major nuclear island structures, DP-SC panels are expected to be fabricated in factories in sizes that can be shipped to construction sites to be further assembled before being lifted into final position for grouting.

Importantly, the RIV design features may may prove un-licensable in certain domains and markets, as these nuclear safety components fail to comport with the 10 CFR 50.46 Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS) prescription, which effectively mandates Loss of Coolant Accident (LOCA) breaks at both inbound and outboard terminal ends of such devices. According to the USNRC, from pre-application meetings and submittals associated with the BWRX-300, GEH has essentially described an "alternate licensing framework" as their (or more correctly, a future applicant's) intended approach to address US regulations and acceptance criteria, that will require significant exemptions to NRC regulations, alternatives to the NRC 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDCs), and deviations to NRC regulatory guidance including NUREG-0800. Furthermore, the NRC recently performed a readiness review of the TVA-Clinch River draft PSAR, which implements the BWRX-300 design (letter: ML24302A104). Therein, the NRC observed that "staff identified major gaps in the content of information in the areas of key risk insights and quantitative results for the design, dominant accident sequences, design features that are major risk contributors, and quantified risk metrics. If not addressed... these gaps have the potential to challenge an effective and efficient review of the CP application...".

While unto itself this does not indicate the design cannot be licensed in the US, it does speak to the extraordinary commercial and regulatory risk GEH and its clients can expect when ultimately applying to build a BWRX-300 in the US, or UK/EU markets with arguably more demanding acceptance criteria than the USNRC. The BWRX-300 is essentially a scaled, or 'smalled-down', ESBWR reactor that appears to retain much of the Nuclear and Turbine Island structural area and volumes of the larger plant, resulting in a design that appears inefficient in terms of material and land use per MWe produced. The design information available provides no indication of, or allowance for adoption of air cooling via ACCs, and BWR turbine performance is far more sensitive to changes in back pressure than the PWR turbine. As such the plant appears to be limited to wet site deployments. The standard plant is limited by a bounding peak ground acceleration earthquake of 0.3g.

GE Hitachi's BWRX-300 completed the first two phases of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC)'s vendor design review. In April 2024, the CNSC confirmed that the existing environmental assessment for the Darlington New Nuclear Project (DNN) remains valid and applicable to the BWRX-300 technology. OPG applied in October 2022 for a construction license for a single BWRX-300 reactor, and in April 2025, the Commission authorized OPG to construct the first BWRX-300 unit at DNN.

Since December 2019, the NRC has engaged in pre-application review of GEH's BWRX-300, including topical reports and design white papers. In April 2025, TVA officially submitted the first part of the CPA—the environmental report—to the NRC, with the preliminary safety analysis report submitted in May 2025. The NRC has docketed the application for review and anticipates completing its review in 17 months—targeting December 2026.

The NuScale VOYR, discussed in Section 5 of this report, is a so-called "integral reactor" design, whereby the reactor internals, steam generator, and pressurizer are housed inside a single pressure vessel. An extraordinary feature of this integral design configuration is that secondary water is boiled and converted into steam inside the tubes which are helical in shape to fit into the limited available space.

This and other highly novel and untried features render the NuScale VOYR plant into a package of first-of-a-kind embodiments that challenge the plant's viability for broad commercial investments and operations. Several unique and novel means of construction and operation compared to normative, known, safe and reliable nuclear power plant operations are its obvious drawbacks. entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: Heat is removed from the RCS by rejecting heat to the steam turbine and condenser during power operations, and through active system operating with pumps and heat exchangers during refueling. Several available active systems are cross tied to further improve reliability (such as the Residual Heat Removal and Spent Fuel Pool Cooling systems) but are not credited or depended upon for assured safety.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: For response to anticipated operational occurrences and postulated events, SMR-300 safety systems include the Passive Core Cooling System (PCCS) and the Passive Containment Heat Removal System (PCHR).

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The Passive Core Cooling System (PCCS) is comprised of four individual subsystems: the Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDRHR), the Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDRHR), the Automatic Depressurization System (ADS), and the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCMS).

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The PDRHR and SDRHR are designed to reject decay heat from the RCS during all initiating events with the reactor coolant pressure boundary intact, where the normal heat rejection path is assumed to be lost. The PDRHR system is individually capable of removing 100% of the plant's decay heat indefinitely. The PDRHR rejects its heat to the Passive Core Makeup Water Tank (PCMWT) inside containment, while the SDRHR rejects its heat to the AR outside containment.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The ADS and the PCMWS are designed to provide core cooling near-and long-term for the complete range of loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA) required to be considered by nuclear licensing regulations.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The safety level achieved by the above systems is superior to that of large reactors. All engineered safety systems have redundancy and meet the single-failure-proof criterion, relying solely on the automatic one-time actuation of valves that are powered by Class 1E (safety) DC power or check valves to perform their safety function.

The PCCS provides a robust pathway to reject the plant's decay heat using conventional passive heat exchangers that rely on water-to-water heat transfer (PDHR). The PCCS is comprised of four subsystems, each of which is described briefly and exhibited separately below. These systems are designed to ensure there are no adverse inter-system interactions.
Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDRHR)
Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDRHR)
Automatic Depressurization System (ADS)

The PDHR and SDHR are designed to remove decay heat from the RCS when normal cooling is not available. The ADS and the PCMWS are designed to provide core cooling for the complete range of loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA) required to be considered by nuclear regulations. The ADS is a staged energy relieving system for the primary circuit, separate from the ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code safety relief valves. All makeup water required for LOCA events is inside containment, such that the containment can be fully isolated to prevent release of radioactivity.

The PDHR provides diverse passive core cooling for non-LOCA accidents by removing core decay heat directly via closed-loop decay heat transfer directly from reactor coolant to PCMWT inside containment. The PDHR operates passively with liquid water via natural circulation. All system components are safely located and protected within the CES.

The SDHR provides diverse passive core cooling for non-LOCA accidents by removing core decay heat indirectly from the RCS via the steam generator shell side coolant and rejecting it to the annular reservoir via the SDHR heat exchanger located in the reservoir. The SDHR operates by condensing shell side steam and returning the condensate to the feedwater line of the steam generator much like the auxiliary steam systems of some current reactors but operating entirely passively. All system components are safely and securely located within the CES.

For a postulated loss of coolant accident (LOCA), the Automatic Depressurization System works in conjunction with the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCMWS) to depressurize the RCS to allow for passive safety injection from pressurized accumulators and atmospheric tanks. Decay heat is dissipated to the containment environment in the form of steam. The water that condenses on the inner metallic wall of the containment from a LOCA then returns to spent fuel pool where it can reenter the reactor primary loop via adjoining sump-strainers located in the PCMWS to support long-term cooling. The accumulators and PCMWS contain borated water for injection to the RPV as RCS pressure reduces, ensuring the reactor core is both cooled and rendered subcritical. All components are safely located and protected within the CES.

To do so, they include a novel concept of double isolation valves integrated to the reactor pressure vessel for all piping penetrations larger than 2".

To do so, the BWRX-300 incorporates a novel feature: isolating the reactor vessel to protect against LOCA by placing two integral RPV isolation valves on each major RPV connection, e.g., between the reactor vessel and each of the steam, feed, isolation condenser feed and return pipes inside containment. As the designer of these valves, GEH (with no apparent consideration or component construction or qualification experience to Holtec's knowledge), will need to describe and prove, verify, and validate (V&V) the control system, power supply and failure modes for these new components, since any common cause failure will essentially invalidate many claims and conclusions in the designer's safety case. Any leak, crack or break in valve casing in the inner most isolation valve for any of these numerous reactor-vessel-integrated valves would cause a break or leak that cannot be isolated by the BWRX-300 engineered safety systems. While details of the RPV vessel are not available for public scrutiny, it is not clear how GEH intends to develop, test, validate and license these FOAK safety components, demonstrating to the competent licensing authorities that, as a minimum, that the integrity of the valve bodies, welds, packings, stems, and seals will be of the same mechanical and operational reliability as the RPV vessel itself. No such valve can be dedicated from a commercial quality class than to one designed explicitly to ASME Section-III requirements for nuclear power reactors; these nuclear valves do not exist in the market for this type of application, and as such, the deployment and licensing claims made by the designer are very optimistic. For context, Holtec expects that a future applicant wishing to build the GEH BWRX-300 via 10CFR50 in the US (for example) will have a heavy lift satisfying the intent and acceptance criteria of the 10CFR 50.46 ECCS rule, even in the case GEH is able to construct these numerous and different sized valves in accord with the ASME code. GEH claims in public facing documents and presentations that this breakthrough innovation - these integral nuclear reactor vessel isolation valves - are patented and approved via a USNRC Licensing Topical Report. In fact, no such approval has been granted by the NRC for use of these isolation valves, lacking any proof, verification or prior nuclear OPEX.

The BWRX-300 includes three identical trains of an Isolation Condenser safety system to remove decay heat, protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from over pressurization, and to provide makeup water in case of AOOs and loss of coolant accidents. By lacking a second diverse engineered safety feature to ensure these safety functions for all anticipated or postulated accidents, the plant design may not be able to adequately address the intent and application of national regulations and normative standards.

entries.section_title: NuScale VOYGR (not updated in this revision (02))
entries.text: The NuScale VOYGR is essentially an SMR power plant comprised of modular factory-fabricated nuclear steam supply systems, assembled within a large, wet reactor building. At nearly 850 metric tons, each NPM is said to be shipped from a factory by rail, barge, or road to construction sites for rapid deployment. Having said this, NuScale provides no insight or proof that this is possible. It is inconceivable that the roads, bridges and transport infrastructure of most countries and Ukraine can handle such massive loads, undermining NuScale Power's claims regarding transportability, and further noting that few factories in the world have the capacity to turn these massive modules out. Astoundingly, each 77 MWe NuScale reactor module weighs nearly the same as a GEH ESBWR reactor vessel which is capable of 1600 MWe.

entries.section_title: NuScale VOYGR (not updated in this revision (02))
entries.text: Employing extraordinary unconventional operational and maintenance and refueling maneuvers and practices, the plant design eschews existing OPEX, and lessons learned from decades of operating light water reactors – a potential recipe for disaster. The plant incorporates a 1000mt single-failure proof NOG-1 crane, the largest of its kind in the world; any crane issue can threaten the ability to operate plant owing to its essentially continuous model refueling architecture and strategy. Individual 850t integrated power modules (RPV + CNV) require massive fabrication, transport and construction facilities, cranes, logistics. Disconnecting reactor power modules from steam and feed piping and transporting those modules past operating reactors in a common pool is a precarious and risky operation, conducted almost constantly to facilitate staggered module refueling. And with unproven and uncertified helical coil steam generators which cannot be replaced without replacing an entire reactor power module, this concept fails the commonsense test.

entries.text: The NuScale VOYGR has significant unproven and uncommon operational characteristics, and its cost is now estimated by its developer to dramatically exceed prior estimates. Using the metrics of merit approach, NuScale scores 75.4% of the maximum available score.

The Rolls Royce UK SMR is an unconventional forced circulation 3-loop PWR including both active and passive safety systems. The design relies on conventional PWR control rod assemblies (CRAs) for power control and scram, while lacking boron for shim and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the short (~9 feet) core comprising 121-fuel assemblies includes 89 control rods, nearly twice the control/fuel assembly ration as compared to typical PWRs (with FA/CRA ratios ~0.4), introducing a fuel cycle distinctly different, FOAK, to PWR OPEX and associated cycle and exposure dependent fuel mechanical limits of operation, a reactivity, power distribution, and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded power operation and attendant sequence exchanges, potentially with associated fuel conditioning safety or warranty requirements. The design includes an active low pressure boron injection for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of a transient or design basis earthquake.

On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation or design features that would lend the plant safer of more economical than a conventional large PWR. Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from others by claiming 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred in manufacturing factories, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with power plant 'assembly' at the site. While an ambitious goal, this appears practically unachievable when examining Ch09 of the Rolls Royce UK SMR Civil Construction Safety Case7, with its large conventional major underground and concrete structures, and an FOAK raft foundation and aseismic bearing, with no prior endorsed regulatory acceptance criteria or OPEX precedent, proof or practice. entries.text: The entire reactor coolant system sits under a 25-meter pool of borated water in a VOYGR plant. The RV is entirely inaccessible as is the steam generator. If they fail, there is no obvious means to fix or replace them. The power plant design includes numerous first of a kind components, instruments, valves, and electrical penetrations that are not environmentally qualified for use in the nuclear industry today.

In the NuScale power plant, the reactor building pool liner covers the entire extent of the football field-sized reactor building cavity which means numerous liner seams. The cavity liner is not accessible for repair only if a leak develops. Likewise, the NuScale helical coil steam generators are accessible for repair only by repair of underwater robotics, and the SGs are not replaceable – they are integral to the RV shell.

A NuScale power module containment operates under full vacuum, which makes its internal temperature rise to over 300 C. It is not apparent how the instrumentation and wiring in the containment will fare in a heavy radiation and hot temperature field. Furthermore, the NuScale power module containment must be designed to an accident condition pressure of over 10000 psi. Hydro-testing the CV for 10000 psi pressure at each outage is likely to be extremely arduous.

NuScale reactor refueling involves complex operations. A 12 module VOYGR reactor building must perform 6 refueling operations each year, meaning the plant will have virtually continuous outages. Performing refueling on a module while the adjacent ones are operating, may be viewed as inherently hazardous by experienced plant operators, and transporting a fueled reactor via heavy lift past operating reactors is likely to be disallowed in some regulatory regimes.
The NuScale plant must be located next to a river, lake, or sea. It cannot be deployed away from a natural source of water.
The approach to manage used fuel produced by VOYGR plants has not been articulated by NuScale Power at this time.

The Holtec SMR-300 plant incorporates numerous barriers for plant safety, including a thick enclosure constructed from steel plate and concrete, a large reservoir of water, and a composite steel and CSSM containment vessel. This layered approach provides substantial protection to the reactor and its safety systems, and allows the Holtec SMR-300 to guarantee a negligible predicted release of radioactivity with no relevant risk to health and safety of the public.

With all of its nuclear assets deeply embedded underground, the SMR-300 addresses common industry challenges associated with protection of a plant's spent nuclear fuel by locating the reactor's spent fuel pool inside containment with a small number of racked fuel assemblies. The design has eliminated the traditional LWR fuel transfer tunnel for vastly simplified fuel transfers into and out of the reactor building, and there is no need for future plant modifications to facilitate long term onsite interim spent fuel storage.

As a result of the in-containment spent fuel pool and integrated fuel management approach, the Holtec SMR-300 nuclear fuel assets are inherently self-protected, with no personnel access inside containment during operation.

Modularizing SMR-300 Nuclear Island civil structures (Figure 3.4-a) - beyond the ICS(CS + CES), including the Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) and Intermediate Buildings (steam tunnels) (IB) - is fundamental to developing a cost-efficient Standard SMR-300 power plant. Automated rebar reinforced concrete materials, methods, and manpower with factory fabricated-for-transport field welded and efficiently assembled CSSMs is expected to drastically improve craft (field and factory) productivity while dramatically reducing manpower labor hours constructing SMR-300 NI civil buildings, and CS internals. With a major portion of typical US NPP construction cost expended on inefficient craft and supervisory costs and expenses, Holtec expects to realize substantial cost reductions from the FOAK to NOAK NPPs.
modules to erect SMR-300 Standard plants by optimizing manufacture and assembly of CSSMs

These SMR-300 CSSMs (Figure 3.4-c) are inspired by Holtec's patented HI-STORM spent fuel storage cask - itself a concrete strengthend steel module, which is shipped to an NPP site to be installed - lifted, grouted, inspected for commissioning and use- before being loaded with spent nuclear fuel.

With decades of experience designing, licensing, fabricating, transporting, handling, installing, and loading HI-STORM CSSMs, and via regular improvements and repeat manufacture and installation, Holtec has benchmark actuals to validate the value of learning form to FOAK to NOAK. From early HI-STORMs, with attendant supply chain and manufacturing lead times, factory handling and labor hours, documentation production and management and QA practices, and field erection times to modern automated fabrication at AMD in Camden, NJ, with attendant savings, and improvements better than 10X in time and labor for site logistics, placement, grouting and loading - the benefits of practice are real. Leveraging that experience and learning, Holtec expects to speed the time and number of NNPs to realize FOAK to NOAK cost benefits through the significant and repeated use of SMR-300 CSSMs.
