entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH claims to achieve "dramatic design simplification, using a licensed and proven fuel design, and the incorporation of proven components and supply chain expertise, to allow the BWRX-300 to become the lowest-risk, most cost-competitive and quickest to market SMR in the market." In essence, GEH claims much, even all the technology and systems/components embodied in the BWRX-300 are already licensed, and as such, a BWRX-300 can effectively be deployed from a toolbox of licensing packages and IP, quickly and readily. These claims will be seriously challenged, and the tools and methods developed and used for licensed and operating BWR reactors and technologies will be shown to require significant extended qualification through testing and engineering analyses to be qualified as applicable to the BWRX-300. The reactor coolant pressure boundary and dry containment design are major departures from prior wet containment BWRs with diverse safety systems. GEH has gambled on a very stripped-down safety system nuclear power plant concept - incorporating RIVs with a dry containment into the DNA of the design - valves that are neither developed, qualified, or available in the marketplace. Their design may prove difficult to license without some fundamental design changes to incorporate added safety capacity, as it will challenge regulatory normative standards, regulations, and subjective acceptance criteria with respect to NRC and international regulatory intents and risk postures.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH and its partners are developing a design and a SAR to satisfy universal, and initially Canadian nuclear regulations, as needed to construct and license an FOAK reactor. The design includes certain basic features that will challenge regulations both in Canada, and in competent nuclear design regions around the world, given different cultures, experiences, insights and OPEX in those regions. Certain fundamental elements of the design introduce first-of-a-kind components, operations and technologies not previously developed, tested, or proven for use in nuclear reactor applications, and these elements introduce significant risks and challenges to the concept as currently envisioned. The design relies on a single Isolation Condenser System to perform numerous crucial safety functions, with no capability to ensure a safely cooled and shutdown reactor in case that ICS fails for any reason, foreseeable or not. The Fukushima accident is still fresh in the minds and memories of the world, where the unit-1 reactor core melted after the ICS did not perform as expected. GEH has promised that they have learned from this accident and improved the ICS - but have eliminated all other BWR safety systems in pursuit of cost reduction.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: Construction and Operations

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: While this BWRX-300 reactor and engineered safety system design is certainly revolutionary, GEH appears to have done little to address the complexity and severe operating environment and costs associated with commercial island of plant operations and costs, considering BWRs essentially contaminate most of the commercial island with radioactive steam. This not only adds to capital cost for shielding and separation of hot systems but dramatically limits the operations and maintenance work that can be performed while the reactor plant is in operating mode. Furthermore, the radioactive steam is not available for process heat applications and will require entirely separate systems and capital costs to facilitate such, as compared to PWRs and SMR-300. Ultimately the TI and associated systems yield a power block very difficult to scale, resulting in a plant very physically similar in size to the ESBWR, albeit with less than 20% of that plant's power output.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH claims to dramatically reduce the plant cost substantially through elimination of concrete as compared to prior BWRs, by replacing conventional concrete with DP-SC modules, but without eliminating the need for the associated BOP systems and structures. There is little or no evidence or FOAK to NOAK basis - GEH has no prior experience designing, fabricating or constructing such - to suggest that this will reduce plant capital cost, and in fact it may prove to dramatically increase constructed (vs estimated) cost when FOAK and early learnings are realized.
Substantial existing licensed technologies including supply chain control of fuel and FMCRds and reactor internals.
Substantial OPEX in design
Passive safety systems
Pedigree and Safety Evaluation Reports for existing nuclear and thermal hydraulic methods and models supporting decades of operating BWRs.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: GEH describes the BWRX-300 as requiring no core injection for LOCA mitigation, while noting the design includes high pressure injection via the fine motion control drive system. The BWRX-300 Emergency Core Cooling System relies entirely on the ICS to supply water and handle over pressure with fail safe (closed) double isolation valves integrated to reactor vessel for steam, feed, ICS exit and ICS return pipes.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: There is no additional water makeup other than active injection via the FMCRds. The containment is not sized to handle LOCA enthalpy if the ICS fails, or in case an RPV isolation valve were to break.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: The plant safety basis depends on the reliable integrity of the RPV double isolation valves. In accord with 10 CFR 50.46, an applicant can be expected to demonstrate the reactor fuel will survive a double-ended break of the most limiting valve. The design appears unable to withstand this postulated break, which would result in an unattenuated loss of cooling accident and potential core meltdown and associated radiological release.

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: The BWRX-300 control blades are used for power control, fuel reactivity management and power shaping, and for shutdown, startup, and scram. As such, the basic design does not include a second independent means to shut down the reactor, as expected and required by many competent regulators. While the design includes a Boron Injection System (BIS), this system will be credited to add negative reactivity but has no dedicated independent instrumentation or actuation logic and is not automated. Accordingly, it is not a credited shut down system according to today's interpreted regulations in the US, Canada, the UK, and other internationally regulated nuclear domains. Furthermore, it is not obvious how the plant can achieve assured safe shutdown for seven days without operator actions as the developer claims, as the BIS included in the plant design for an Anticipated Transient Without Scram (ATWS) is not automated and requires operator actions to actuate if or when needed. The FOIAK application in Canada will need to overcome the matter that Canadian regulations plainly require two independent shutdown systems.

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: There is a logical basis for Canadian regulations requiring independent shutdown systems, owing to the nature of CANDU reactors, and accordingly an expectation that GEH will be able to overcome this rule:

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: CANDU power plants have a positive void coefficient of reactivity. As a result, power can increase rapidly following postulated LOCA. This design characteristic is the primary driver for having two shutdown systems in current CANDUs. In addition, CANDU accident analysis for LOCA events defines performance requirements for key reactivity control measures (e.g., shutdown system speed and reactivity depth). Like most LWRs, the BWRX-300 has a negative void coefficient of reactivity, whereby void formations decrease reactivity and tend to shut LWRs down. For these LWRs, many of the traditional safety analysis issues in CANDU LOCA do not exhibit power excursions. However, for BWRs, the dominant reactivity phenomena that leads to a potential power increase is void reduction rather than void formation. Since anticipated operational

entries.text: The Local Ultimate Heatsink System comprises of three trains, each containing an LUHS tank and its associated ancillary equipment, including the provision of fill, drain and sampling functions. Each LUHS tank corresponds to a single PCC train. The LUHS tanks are arranged such that each tank (and most of the supporting equipment) is currently located outside containment in the interspace, adjacent to the Steam Generator (SG) with which it interfaces. Cross-connects are provided between each tank to enable the unused water in one tank to be gravity drained into a tank that is available to cool the plant. The final location and geometry of the LUHS tanks are still to be finalized. The PCC heat exchangers are cooled by water from the LUHS tank, which circulates water in a closed loop between the LUHS tank and PCC heat exchanger via natural circulation. It is noted that the LUHS cooling capability is shared between both the ECCS and Passive Decay Heat Sink (PDHS) protective safety measures, as well as the mitigative safety measure In-Vessel Retention (IVR). The ECCS and IVR share the in-containment PCC heat exchangers that are cooled by the LUHS water inventory, whereas the heat exchangers located inside the LUHS vessels are dedicated to PDHS.

The UK SMR fuel handling system covers the fuel route from initial receipt of new fuel to final disposal. The primary function of the system is to move fuel between the outside containment storage and the RPV, providing cooling and shielding of the fuel throughout. The key aspects of the fuel handling system are the fuel handling machine, the in-containment refueling pool, the spent fuel pool, and the long-term storage facility. During refueling operations, the RPV head, stud tensioner and RPV internals are lifted and moved away from the RPV body to facilitate the movement of fuel. Fuel assemblies are lifted in and out of the RPV using a fuel handling machine mounted on rails to and from the refueling pool. The refueling pool temporarily stores both new and spent fuel during a refueling outage. In the refueling pool, spent fuel is re-orientated using an upender and subsequently transported out of containment horizontally through an underwater transfer channel, directly into the spent fuel pool. The spent fuel pool is designed to store fuel assemblies for up to 5 years prior to transferring the fuel to dry storage casks. Transporting new fuel into the RPV is achieved using the reverse of the spent fuel route, following initial receipt and inspection. Both the refueling pool and spent fuel pool are supported by a dedicated chemistry control and heat removal system.

The UK SMR operates on an 18-24-month fuel cycle, with a three-core shuffle. Heat from the reactor is transferred from the primary circuit to the secondary circuit in the three SGs. Feedwater present in the SGs is converted to steam which is then routed by the Steam System through the one high pressure and two low pressure turbines. The turbines are coupled to and rotate a generator, thereby generating the plant's electrical output. The steam leaving the low-pressure turbines is condensed by heat exchange with the cooling water in the Main Cooling Water System (MCWS). The resulting condensate is then deaerated, pre-heated, and fed back into the SGs.

Rolls-Royce claims its UK SMR has been developed to deliver a market driven, affordable, low carbon, energy generation capability. Rolls Royce claims that rapid, certain, and repeatable build is enhanced through site layout optimization and maximizing modular build, standardization, and commoditization. The UK SMR is primarily intended to supply baseload electricity for both coastal and inland siting. The design can be configured to support other heat-requiring or cogeneration applications, as well as provide a primary, carbon free, power source to produce e-fuels.

The main nuclear structures are associated with the reactor island. These include the containment building, fuel and control building, radioactive waste building, access building and auxiliary building.

A hazard shield is included in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide protection against radioactivity release due to external hazards. The bounding case for the hazard shield is based on an aircraft impact hazard, aiming to ensure confinement of fuel, prevention of criticality, protection of reactor shutdown and cooling systems and protection of monitoring systems. The hazard shield is engineered to ensure all class 1 SSCs functions are protected from that bounding aircraft hazard ( e.g., post A1 fire and mechanical shock and LOLA).

The Hazard Shield is a large, reinforced concrete (RC) structure that protects critical SSCs from external hazards, including accidental and malicious aircraft impacts. It is approximately 91 m long, 61 m wide and extends 45 m above ground level. The Hazard Shield houses the Containment Internal Structures, Interspace, Fueling Block, Electrical, Control and Instrumentation (EC&I) Systems and Fluid Systems blocks.

entries.text: The Ultimate Heat Sink (UHS) is a pool of water located in the reactor building. The UHS consists of the reactor pool, the refueling pool, and the spent fuel pool. During normal plant operations, heat is removed from the pool with a pool cooling and cleanup system. In a design basis accident involving a sustained loss of AC power, decay heat is removed from the NPMs through passive heat transfer to the pool resulting in pool heat up and boiling. Water inventory in the reactor pool is adequate to cool the NPMs for at least 72 hours without adding water.

The functions of Containment Vessel (CNV) are to contain the release of radioactivity following postulated accidents, to protect the RPV from external hazards, and to provide heat rejection to the reactor pool following ECCS actuation. Each CNV consists of a steel cylinder with an outside diameter of 4.5 m and an overall height of 23.1 m. The CNV houses the RPV, control rod drive mechanisms, and associated piping and components of the NSSS. The CNV is immersed in the reactor pool of borated water, which is the plant's passive heat sink for containment heat removal under LOCA conditions. During normal power operation, the containment atmosphere is evacuated (less than 1psia) to provide an insulating vacuum to reduce heat loss from the reactor vessel.

The CNV is an evacuated pressure vessel fabricated with a combination of martensitic and austenitic stainless steel that houses, supports, and protects the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) from external hazards and provides a barrier to the release of fission products. The CNV is partially immersed in a below grade, borated water filled, stainless steel lined, reinforced concrete pool to facilitate heat removal. The CNV is an American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC) Class MC (steel) containment whose design, analysis, fabrication, inspection, testing, and stamping conform to ASME BPVC Class 1 pressure vessel requirements in accordance with Section III, Subsection NB.

A NuScale power plant in any power module configuration (6x, 12x, other) has two separate turbine buildings, each housing up to six turbines and air-cooled generators. The turbine buildings are above-grade structures that house the turbine-generators with their auxiliaries, the condensers, condensate systems, and the feedwater systems. Each turbine-generator is associated with a single NPM and has dedicated condensate and feedwater pumps. As such, a 6-module 462 MWe power plant includes nearly six times as much equipment to be procured, constructed, and maintained as a single reactor power plant producing the same output. This SMR design attempts to benefit by eliminating the single-shaft risk associated with large LWRs, with a novel small reactor (77 MWe) concept deployed in multiples, albeit one where individual small reactors weigh nearly 850 metric tons each.

The NuScale Power includes an extremely novel and untested sequence of refueling operations, with complex heavy lifts and first-of-a-kind tooling. Reactor/containment modules are refueled on a staggered 24-month cycle, by moving them via a 1000 metric ton overhead crane to a common refueling area adjacent to the spent fuel pool following module separation from all piping connections, and disassembly of the containment and reactor vessels.

Each module resides under a biological shield in a three-sided bay that is open to the common pool. Also included in the pool is the module assembly/disassembly facility, which is used for installation of new modules into the plant in conjunction with the building crane. The reactor building layout and equipment is designed for refueling to be completed for a single module while the other modules continue to generate power. This staggered refueling of individual modules is performed by a permanent team of plant personnel.

entries.text: Holtec International formed SMR LLC in 2011 with the mission to develop an inherently safe and economically viable small modular reactor to de-carbonize electric power generation around the world.

The result of the long development effort is the Holtec SMR-300 pressurized light-water small modular reactor which generates approximately 1050 MWt, with a minimum of 340 MWe net electric output. The Standard Plant design is a twin-reactor configuration with shared non-safety systems and structures, to optimize cost and power plant flexibility for a cost-effective SMR power plant producing 680 MWe net (minimum 640) electric output. All safety-related components in the reactor coolant system are passive. Specifically, the pumps used to boost thermal performance are not safety related. The power plant relies upon simple and passive systems to achieve its absolute safety goals and competitive economic performance. Among its key attributes summarized herein are unconditional safety, absence of reliance on a local water source, and a convenient long-term management solution of its spent used fuel. Progressive nuclear companies such as Mitsubishi Electric Corporation (Japan and US), Hyundai Engineers & Constructors (South Korea), and Framatome (France and US) play important roles in the Holtec SMR-300’s development, complementing the company’s R&D team as needed for expedited completion of the detailed design and licensing documents needed for plant construction and operation.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is an innovative pressurized water reactor (PWR) that has natural circulation as an integral feature of its performance which is central to its ability to cope with all conceivable accident conditions. The Holtec SMR-300 reactor is also characterized by supplemental recirculation pumps situated between the steam generator and the reactor vessel in each of its two cold legs. These pumps serve to boost the velocity and turbulence level in the core and the steam generator tubes leading to high coolant flow rates and heat transfer coefficients for a high-power density light water reactor coolant system. These pumps are a part of the reactor coolant system’s pressure boundary but are not safety-related system because their failure does not threaten the radiological, structural or criticality safety of the reactor.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The evolutionary features of the Holtec SMR-300 ensure a long service life by ameliorating life limiting causative factors such as stress corrosion cracking, erosion, wear, neutron embrittlement and flow induced vibration. The likelihood of core damage has been rendered negligible with improved operational reliability as compared to conventional reactors and is informed by lessons learned from over seven decades of light water reactor (LWR) operations.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 owes its unconditional assured safety to the thermosiphon-actuated circulation of its reactor coolant and engineered safety systems that remove heat from the reactor core and spent fuel pool by passive means in the event of postulated accidents. No operator action is required to mitigate events deemed to be credible for consideration in the safety analysis by regulatory agencies. The Holtec SMR-300 leverages gravity-driven convective and conductive heat transfer to provide for an unlimited post-accident coping period. The plant design provides redundant and diverse pathways to reject heat from the core and does so by incorporating only existing and proven materials and environmentally qualified components, penetrations, and instruments in the plant design.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: Each Holtec SMR-300 reactor and NSSS produces 1050MWt, with a conventional PWR connected to a once-through steam generator with integrated pressurizer, and using non-safety booster pumps. The booster pumps feature two speed motors which together, at maximum design basis flow increase the total primary natural circulation flow by approximately a factor of four, eliminating the risks of flow stagnation attendant to the purely thermosiphon flow regime The hot legs of the reactor coolant system are external to the steam generator facilitating convenient in-service inspection.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 plant has no penetrations in the lower 2/3rd of the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV). An Annular Reservoir (AR) containing over one million gallons of water surrounds the containment vessel which is enclosed by the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES). This reservoir can provide cooling to the containment for greater than 90 days in the event of a loss of cooling accident, followed by a transition to indefinite air cooling; no operator action is necessary to achieve this - the plant is walk-away safe. The above-grade steel Containment Structure (CS) serves as both a containment and a large passive heat exchanger to reject decay heat through the containment wall into the annular reservoir. The deeply embedded CS is protected from aircraft and missile impact by the thick CES, with the plant's nuclear commodities - reactor, core and spent fuel pool - located below grade. The CES, characterized by a deep below-ground foundation with a cylindrical cross section assembled from CSSM modules is configured expressly to withstand impulsive and impactive loads.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 design specification includes evaluation of the highest earthquake and most severe environmental phenomena loads, yielding an adaptable bounding standard plant design which will envelope most US and global sites. This approach fixes the plant's anatomy during the design phase, with enough additional margin embedded in each critical area to preclude the need for gross site-specific design changes. Site conditions and utility functional requirements may inform the electric power output, but not the standard plant design. The energy allocated to electric power and process-heat may be adjusted to suit local needs, lending SMR-300 plants to broad load-following capabilities. Coupled with an energy storage system, the Holtec SMR-300 can further enhance grid stability and energy efficiencies.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The CES and surrounding seismic category 1 structures (the most resilient type, required to assure nuclear safety in a worst case earthquake) are designed to prevent damage to any components of the nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) or any radiological release to the atmosphere in the event of a design basis earthquake, aircraft impact or any other external hazards. SMR-300 core components and reactor internals are readily removable for refueling, inspection, maintenance or change-out without disassembly of the reactor coolant system (RCS), or disconnection from its principal safety systems. The steam generator allows easy access for eddy current inspections as performed in the current US PWR fleet, and convenient in-service inspection.

entries.section_title: Figure 6-10 Rolls Royce UK SMR Reactor Island
entries.text: The Reactor Island includes major area or 'Process Blocks' including: Fuel Block - houses the Spent Fuel Storage and Cask Loading System, which comprises the Spent Fuel Pool, Underpin Pit and Cask Loading Pit. Electrical and I&C Block - surrounds the Containment and houses the main control room and safety-critical electrical and I&C systems with associated heating, ventilation and air conditioning system and back-up cooling system, within four separate trains. Fluids Blocks - The Fluids Blocks (2) house systems associated with the reactor plant and the cooling of the fuel temperature within the Reactor Island. Auxiliary Block - The Auxiliary Block houses the systems and functions required for the collection, storage, treatment, processing, and disposal of solid, liquid, and gaseous radioactive waste. Waste Processing Block - The Waste Processing Block houses functions for decontamination and processing and packing of low-level waste. Outage Block - The Outage Block houses the containment preparation and laydown area, which provides a space directly adjacent to the Containment Vessel and interspace to facilitate EMI and replacement activities. Access Block - The Access Block houses the primary personnel access point into the Reactor Island area, radiologically controlled areas and health physics. It also houses the site security control center, the outage control center, the emergency response center, and the technical support center.

Reactor Island structures are supported on a rectangular 2acre raft foundation 400ft long and 230ft wide, the top of which is 37ft below grade. The Containment Support Structure (45m (150ft) square on each side) supports the Containment Vessel and provides access into and out of Containment Vessel for construction and examination, maintenance, inspection, and testing activities. The Containment Vessel is 32m in diameter (105ft) and 37m high (121ft).

The Reactor Island is covered by a Hazard Shield (not shown), a large, reinforced concrete (RC) structure that protects safety critical SSCs from external hazards, including accidental and malicious aircraft impacts. This concrete roof over the top of the Reactor Island is 300ft long 200ft wide and extends 150ft above grade. The Hazard Shield covers and is credited in the plant's design and licensing basis with protecting the Reactor Island structures from external hazards, natural and man-made. Unlike typical reactor and SMR designs which incorporate a robust shield building or containment enclosure structure,

An RC Raft Foundation provides support to the Reactor Island structures which are themselves supported on a Basemat, separated by an Aseismic Bearing. A retaining wall is integral to the raft foundation at its base and retains the external ground and groundwater surrounding the Reactor Island. The retaining wall is physically separated from the Hazard Shield and Basemat.

The UK SMR fuel handling system covers the fuel route from initial receipt of new fuel to final disposal. The primary function of the system is to move fuel between the outside containment storage and the RPV, providing cooling and shielding of the fuel throughout. The key aspects of the fuel handling system are the fuel handling machine, the in-containment refueling pool, the spent fuel pool, and the long-term storage facility. During refueling operations, the RPV head, stud tensioner and RPV internals are lifted and moved away from the RPV body to facilitate the movement of fuel. Fuel assemblies are lifted in and out of the RPV using a fuel handling machine mounted on rails to and from the refueling pool. The refueling pool temporarily stores both new and spent fuel during a refueling outage. In the refueling pool, spent fuel is re-orientated using an upender and subsequently transported out of containment horizontally through an underwater transfer channel, directly into the spent fuel pool. The spent fuel pool is designed to store fuel assemblies for up to 5 years prior to transferring the fuel to dry storage casks. Transporting new fuel into the RPV is achieved using the reverse of the spent fuel route, following initial receipt and inspection. Both the refueling pool and spent fuel pool are supported by a dedicated chemistry control and heat removal system. The UK SMR operates on an 18-24-month fuel cycle, with a three-core shuffle.

Heat from the reactor is transferred from the primary circuit to the secondary circuit in the three SGs. Feedwater present in the SGs is converted to steam which is then routed by the Steam System through the one high pressure and two low pressure turbines. The turbines are coupled to and rotate a generator, thereby generating the plant's electrical output. The steam leaving the low-pressure turbines is condensed by heat exchange with the cooling water in the Main Cooling Water System (MCWS). The resulting condensate is then deaerated, pre-heated, and fed back into the SGs.

Parameter, Value Technology developer, GE-Hitachi Nuclear Energy, United country of origin, States and Hitachi-GE Nuclear Energy, Japan Reactor type, Boiling water reactor Coolant/moderator, Light-water / light-water Thermal/electrical capacity, 870 / 270 - 290 MW(t)/MW(e) Primary circulation, Natural circulation NSSS operating pressure (primary/secondary), MPa, 7.2 / Direct cycle Core inlet/outlet coolant temperature (°C), 270 / 288 Fuel type/assembly array, UO2 / 10x10 array Number of fuel assemblies in the core, 240 Fuel enrichment (%), 3.81 (avg) / 4.95 (max) Refuelling cycle (months), 12 - 24 Core discharge burnup (GWd/ton), 49.6 Reactivity control mechanism, Rods and solid burnable absorber (B4C, Hf, Gd2O3) Approach to safety systems, Fully passive Design life (years), 60 Plant footprint (m2), 9 800 RPV height/diameter (m), 26 / 4 RPV weight (metric ton), 485 Seismic design (SSE), 0.3g Fuel cycle, Open fuel cycle utilizing standard BWR requirements/approach Fuel cycle Distinguishing features, Natural circulation BWR, integral RPV isolation valves, isolation condenser Design status, Detailed design Note: Plant Footprint has been substantially increased since Rev02, with a Power Block (NI+TI) footprint of 11,550m2 within a 34-acre site.

NSSS Nuclear Boiler Components in the BWRX-300 NSSS include the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), with integrated RIVs and fine motion control rod drives (FMCRDs). The NSSS delivers steam from the RPV to the turbine via the main steam system, while the condensate and feedwater system delivers feedwater to the core as subcooled and provides overpressure protection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB).

Reactor Core The reactor core of the BWRX-300 is arranged as an upright cylinder containing 240 fuel assemblies located within a core shroud. During operation, the coolant/moderator enters the bottom of the core as subcooled water and exits the core as saturated steam. The BWRX-300 utilizes GNF2 fuel, typical of much of the BWR fleet today. The GNF2 fuel assembly comprises a 10x10 array of 78 full-length fuel rods, 14 part-length rods and two large central water rods.

Reactivity Control Reactivity control is provided by control rods loaded with either B4C or Hf neutron absorbers and burnable neutron absorbers loaded in the fuel rods. Cruciform control rods are moved using FMCRDs successfully deployed in the ABWRs in Japan. FMCRDs have two independent means of moving the control rods—motor driven fine control for reactivity control during normal operation and hydraulic rapid insertion during a scram.

Reactor Coolant System The reactor coolant system (RCS) is natural circulation driven and provides cooling of the reactor core in all operational states and all postulated off normal conditions. The BWRX-300 leverages natural circulation modelling and operational information from the ESBWR and the Downwind Nuclear Power Plant that operated in the Netherlands. That said, this natural circulation BWR's coolant is effectively propelled by high-pressure feedwater condensate pumped directly in the reactor vessel downcomer during power operations,

Reactor Pressure Vessel and Internals The BWRX-300's RPV assembly consists of a pressure vessel with removable head, internal components, and appurtenances. The reactor internals include the core, control rods and nuclear instrumentation, core support and alignment structures (shroud, shroud support, top guide, core plate, control rod guide tube and orifice fuel support), chimney (chimney head and steam separator assembly and steam dryer assembly).

Engineered Safety Systems The BWRX-300 is designed using IAEA guidelines countries. The basic BWRX-300 safety design philosophy is built on utilization of inherent margins (e.g., large structure volumes and water inventory) to eliminate system challenges to accommodate transients. Natural circulation safety-related systems mitigate design basis. The BWRX-300 defense in depth concept uses Fundamental Safety Functions (FSF) to define the interface between the defense lines and the physical barriers.

Decay Heat Removal System The normal, non-Safety Class 1, shutdown cooling (SDC) system for decay heat removal comprises two independent pumps and heat exchanger trains. These trains provide redundant decay heat cooling capacity. The major components of each train are a pump and an HX, along with valves, piping, instrumentation and controls, and power inputs.

entries.text: pumps and AC power. A significant departure from the most advanced light water reactors, likely made possible by the large number of RCCAs included in the design. Control rod drive mechanisms are expensive components, and the sheer number of RCCAs and RCCA adds substantially to the plant capital cost. While likely able to shut the reactor down, the absence of a second independent and passive shutdown system is very likely a fatal flaw in many international regulatory regimes.

Furthermore, Holtec suspects that the fundamental reactor physics and safety basis will be difficult to demonstrate for a boron-free PWR core lacking boron shim, heavy fuel Gd2O3 poison loadings, or RCCAs enriched in boron-10. Controlling power and criticality with RCCAs alone (no shim) is a complicated operation requiring constant control rod sequence exchanges to prevent a phenomenon known as control rod history effect, whereby controlled fuel rods in an unborated chemistry breed plutonium in fuel rods, which must be burned to prevent the rods from becoming too 'hot.' Typical of BWRs, it is a complex control scheme, and this feature is an extraordinary departure from PWR OPEX.

Rolls Royce can expect significant challenges satisfying regulatory expectations with respect to the design and construction of the plant's Reactor Island seismic isolation system over raft foundation. While novel in application to an NPP, Rolls Royce provides no information or insights to the maintenance, inspection, testing and serviceability of these complex nuclear structures, introducing substantial regulatory and commercial asset risk to the design and potential future projects.

Regarding modularity, Rolls Royce intends to use construction modules — or Process Clusters — 'conglomerations of 'system modules' manufactured into discrete structural framing systems, housing mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. Essentially, these clusters are site bolted and welded mechanical and process equipment frames containing spools and system sub-assemblies with signal and power cable, with associated mechanical/electrical/control interfaces connections prepped for site assembly — to be shipped and connected to face adjacent sub-modules at the site in closely engineered, planned and orchestrated construction sequences. This scheme failed badly when used by Westinghouse at its US Vogtle AP1000 project, and despite Rolls' claims to having overcome challenges encountered with this approach, little or no information is available to substantiate such a claim.

On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation in design features that would lend the plant safer or more economical than a conventional large PWR. Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from others by claiming 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred in manufacturing factories, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with power plant 'assembly' at the site. While an ambitious goal, this appears to indicate a lack of understanding of the actual realities of nuclear power plant construction logistics and realities and further indicates an immature design for construction. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration PGA of 0.3g. That said, the UK SMR includes seismic isolators under the reactor building, a novel design, construction, and licensing challenge. The information available makes no mention of consideration of or capability to cool the plant with ACCs, seemingly limiting its deployment to sites with available cooling water.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is a 300 MWe (net) advanced small modular reactor that can be deployed as a stand-alone single unit or in a cluster of units depending on the power need of the site.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Assured Operational and Environmental Safety
The Holtec SMR-300 reactor has a core damage frequency of <1E-7 and poses no credible risk to the environment and population proximate to the plant. It distinguishes itself (along with NuScale VOYGR) amongst the designs evaluated herein in achieving this level of safety without the use of pumps, offsite power, active safety systems or operator actions. Accordingly, it’s safer than the BWRX-300 and UK SMR which rely on active safety systems and limited coping periods.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Capacity Factor Improvement by Eliminating Load Following
The term "load-following" refers to the power plant adjusting its power output to meet the contemporaneous demand for electricity. Because the demand fluctuates throughout the 24-hour day cycle, the power plant’s output must be adjusted accordingly to stay aligned with the demand. Nuclear plants are typically designed to serve as base load generators with the power output adjustment function of a grid rendered by smaller fossil power plants. The SMR-300 can render this variable output function by several means such as bypassing turbine steam directly to the condenser and/or adjusting the position of the control rods. However, load-following by burning the fuel less efficiently is an inherently inefficient strategy; it is far more efficient to produce the motive steam at full capacity and bifurcate it with only the needed amount for the power generation directed to the turbogenerator. The balance of the steam can be directed to a Green Boiler which serves as a giant heat capacitor. As explained in the attachments to this report, the Green Boiler contains a large quantity of a specially engineered material called FeotermTM which has a large specific heat and a reasonably high conductivity. The Green Boiler conserves the thermal energy stored in its FeotermTM mass losing less than .5% of its enthalpy per day. The Green Boiler has a built-in steam generator which can be activated on demand to produce motive steam to power the site’s turbines. Thus, using the Green Boiler, the power output from a single unit Holtec SMR-300 plant can be varied within a wide range. In this manner, an SMR-300 plant can be producing its rated thermal energy, but its electric power output can be modulated to accord with the power demand. The overall power cycle capacity factor is near 100% and the reactors spared the wear and tear of cycling and associated expenditure of fatigue life.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Power Output Flexibility
Each Holtec SMR-300 plant is autonomous with its own turbogenerator and waste heat rejection system. A client can have one or more SMR-300 NPPs arrayed at a site. SMR-300 can be deployed in clusters to make a large power station or in single units for distributed generation giving the owner the full range of flexibility.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Reactor Performance Stability
SMR-300 is designed to circulate the reactor coolant with the flow rate sufficiently vigorous to ensure full turbulence at full and partial power loads. The steam is produced in the SG which boils water in the capacious shell-side space around the tubes, as is the traditional design practice. This ensures large hydraulic inertia in the system and a stable performance.

entries.text: According to NuScale Power, the NuScale Power Module (NPM) is a small, light-water-cooled pressurized- water reactor (PWR). NuScale VOYGR SMR plants are scalable and can be built to accommodate a varying number of NPMs to meet customer’s energy demands. NuScale standard plants include the VOYGR-4 at 308 MW(e), the VOYGR-6 at 462 MW(e), and the VOYGR-12 at 924 MW(e). Each NPM is a self- contained module that operates independently of the other modules in a multi-module configuration. All modules are managed from a single control room. The NuScale design is a modular reactor for electricity production, with the capability for flexible operations to load follow, and for non-electrical process heat applications, including the cogeneration of heat and electricity. The NuScale VOYGR SMR plant design adopts design simplification, proven light-water reactor technology, modular nuclear steam supply system, factory-fabricated power modules, and passive safety systems that allow for unlimited reactor cooling time after a beyond design basis accident without ac or DC power, operator action, or makeup water. There are no design basis accidents that uncover the core or require operator action. The NPM is designed to operate efficiently at full-power conditions using natural circulation as the means of providing core coolant flow, eliminating the need for reactor coolant pumps. NuScale Power has developed a 12-reactor 600 MWe gross output nuclear power plant, for which it has received 10CFR52 design certification (Feb.2023) from the US NRC. That design has now been heavily modified and resubmitted (Jan.2023) to the US NRC for standard design approval in accord with 10CFR52 for a 6-reactor 462 MWe gross output nuclear power plant called VOYGR USA460. Its licensing status is uncertain owing to its substantially changed design specification relative to the original 600 MWe plant.

NSSS Nuclear Steam Supply System The nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) consists of a reactor core, two helical coil steam generators, and a pressurizer within a reactor pressure vessel (RPV). The NSSS is enclosed in an approximately cylindrical containment vessel (CNV) — the RPV and CNV are integrated to form a NuScale Power Module (NPM). Each of up to twelve ~800–900 metric ton NPMs are hung from module supports built into the reactor building walls and foundation. The containment is evacuated and maintained at near-vacuum during power operations to reduce convective heat transfer losses from the reactor to the CNV and surrounding pool of water and forms an integral part of the reactor’s Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS) system, providing pressure relief, and condensate return to the reactor vessel via natural circulation following a loss of cooling accident. The CNV is immersed in a large reactor pool, which provides an assured passive heat sink for containment heat removal under LOCA conditions. Each power module is connected to a dedicated turbine-generator unit and balance-of-plant systems. The 50 MWe 12-NPM plant is rated at 600 MWe gross output, while a recent 6-NPM VOYGR plant design is rated at 462 MWe gross electric output using 77 MWe power modules.

Reactor Core The core configuration for the NPM consists of 37 fuel assemblies and 16 control rod assemblies. The fuel assembly design is modelled from an atypical 17 x 17 PWR fuel assembly with 24 guide tube locations for control rod fingers and a central instrument tube. The assembly is nominally half the height of standard plant fuel and is supported by five spacer grids. The fuel is UO2 with Gd2O3 as a burnable absorber homogeneously mixed within the fuel for select rod locations. The U235 enrichment is below the current U.S. manufacturer limit of 4.95% enrichment.

Reactivity Control Reactivity control in each NPM is achieved mainly through soluble boron in the primary coolant and 16 control rod assemblies. The control rods are organized into two groups: a control group, and a shutdown group. The control group, consisting of four rods symmetrically located in the core, functions as a regulating group that is used during normal plant operation to control reactivity. The shutdown group comprising 12 rods is used during shutdown and scram events. Control rods absorber material is B4C.

Reactor Coolant System The RCS is a subsystem of the NPM that provides for the circulation of the primary coolant relying on natural circulation. Hence, the RCS does not require reactor coolant pumps or an external piping system. The RCS includes the RPV and integral pressurizer, integral helical coil steam generators, the reactor vessel internals, the reactor safety valves, RCS piping inside the containment vessel and others.

Reactor Pressure Vessel and Internals The RPV consists of a cylindrical steel vessel with an inside diameter of 2.7 m, an overall height of approximately 17.7 m, and is designed for an operating pressure of 13.8 MPa. The upper and lower heads are torispherical and the lower portion of the vessel has flanges just above the core region to provide access for refueling. To be clear, unlike conventional light water reactors (PWRs and BWRs) which for maintenance and refueling are disassembled in-place and from the top down, the NuScale NPM (RPV + CNV) is transported by large crane within the reactor building to be disassembled from the bottom up, unbolting and lifting the integrated upper reactor and internals and containment to expose the core for refueling. The RPV upper head supports the control rod drive mechanisms. Nozzles on the RPV upper head

entries.text: The SMR-300 is designed to provide unconditional safety with assured cooling of fuel in both the reactor and the spent fuel pool, for all conditions of the plant. In the event of a LOCA, the spent fuel pool is cooled by the PCCS, along with the fuel in the RPV.
Through power conversion and reliable active systems, like Residual Heat Removal System
Through Passive Core Cooling System, including Primary & Secondary Decay Heat Removal Systems
Indefinite, passive, and secure coolability through Passive Containment Heat Removal System

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: Heat is removed from the RCS by rejecting heat to the steam turbine and condenser during power operations, and through active system operating with pumps and heat exchangers during refueling. Several available active systems are cross tied to further improve reliability (such as the Residual Heat Removal and Spent Fuel Pool Cooling systems) but are not credited or depended upon for assured safety.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: For response to anticipated operational occurrences and postulated events, SMR-300 safety systems include the Passive Core Cooling System (PCCS) and the Passive Containment Heat Removal System (PCHR).

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The Passive Core Cooling System (PCCS) is comprised of four individual subsystems: the Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDRHR), the Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDRHR), the Automatic Depressurization System (ADS), and the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCMS).

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The PDRHR and SDRHR are designed to reject decay heat from the RCS during all initiating events with the reactor coolant pressure boundary intact, where the normal heat rejection path is assumed to be lost. The PDRHR system is individually capable of removing 100% of the plant's decay heat indefinitely. The PDRHR rejects its heat to the Passive Core Makeup Water Tank (PCMWT) inside containment, while the SDRHR rejects its heat to the AR outside containment.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The ADS and the PCMWS are designed to provide core cooling near-and long-term for the complete range of loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA) required to be considered by nuclear licensing regulations.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-6: SMR-300 Cooling Mechanisms for all Modes & States
entries.text: The safety level achieved by the above systems is superior to that of large reactors. All engineered safety systems have redundancy and meet the single-failure-proof criterion, relying solely on the automatic one-time actuation of valves that are powered by Class 1E (safety) DC power or check valves to perform their safety function.

The PCCS provides a robust pathway to reject the plant's decay heat using conventional passive heat exchangers that rely on water-to-water heat transfer (PDHR). The PCCS is comprised of four subsystems, each of which is described briefly and exhibited separately below. These systems are designed to ensure there are no adverse inter-system interactions.
Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDRHR)
Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDRHR)
Automatic Depressurization System (ADS)

entries.text: The RPV assembly consists of an RPV body, a tori-spherical closure head assembly and a bolting arrangement comprising studs, washers, and mechanical seals. The RPV diameter is constrained to be less than 15 feet to ensure that the UK road transport height of 16 feet is not exceeded.

Primary circuit pressure is controlled by electrical heaters located at the base of the pressurizer and spray from a nozzle located at the top. Steam and water are maintained in equilibrium to provide the necessary overpressure. The pressurizer is a vertical, cylindrical vessel constructed from low alloy steel, sized to provide passive fault response for bounding faults with accidents causing either rapid and significant cooldown or heat-up accommodated.

Nuclear fuel includes UO2 enriched up to 4.95%, clad with a zirconium alloy and arranged in a 17x17 assembly. The core contains 121 fuel assemblies and has an active fueled length of approximately 9 feet, delivering a thermal power of 1358 MWth. Each fuel assembly contains 264 fuel rods, with 40 rods incorporating 8 wt% Gd2O3. The design includes 89 control rod assemblies, nearly twice the reactor core control rod density as compared to conventional PWRs.

No concentration of soluble boron is maintained in the primary coolant for reactivity or power control. Reactivity control is instead provided entirely via movement of control rods. No description is available as to the number and type (grey, shutdown, other) of control rod groups other than 89 total CRAs.

A vertical u-tube SG configuration has been selected as a mature and readily deployable technology. Other designs have been considered but deemed insufficiently mature for commercial deployment in 2030 in the first of a kind plant. Each of the three steam generators removes approximately 452 MWth of heat from the primary circuit, generating dry steam which drives the turbine to generate electricity. The SG design includes an economizer which preferentially directs feedwater to the cold leg of the tube bundle, and the majority of the recirculated water to the hot leg, resulting in an increased thermal efficiency compared to a conventional equivalent design.

The pump and motor in the RCP are combined in a sealless design; this avoids potential issues with seals which have been a cause of leaks in previous RCP designs. Each RCP is fitted with a flywheel to achieve an extended pump coast-down time, ensuring sufficient cooling flow is pumped through the core in case of a loss of electrical power. The RCP design provides a flow rate of 3.95 m3/s and generates 56 m of head (4 bar). This is somewhat in contrast to Rolls Royce claims that the reactor operates via natural circulation for DBAs.

The UK SMR operates on an 18-24-month fuel cycle, with a three-core shuffle. The duration of refueling outage is currently estimated at 18 days. Refueling is managed through the provision of an in-containment refueling pool which temporarily stores both new and spent fuel during a refueling outage. Spent fuel is subsequently transferred to an external spent fuel pool for storage prior to transfer to long term dry cask storage.

entries.section_title: With a compact, high power density plant configuration, the SMR-300 NPPs requires far less material and land per net MWe output than the GEH BWRX-300 or Rolls Royce UK SMR.
entries.text: With a compact, high power density plant configuration, the SMR-300 NPPs requires far less material and land per net MWe output than the GEH BWRX-300 or Rolls Royce UK SMR.

Where economies of land and capital resources matter, the SMR-300 stands out when compared to other lwr SMRs. At nearly 50% more MW per acre than competing technologies, the SMR-300 minimizes land requirements to maximize power deployment where NPP new build opportunities are limited by the number and sizes of available sites. The small SMR-300 Power Block – the reactor and turbine island – and large net power output yields better economies of scale than the GEH and Rolls Royce power plants. The plant is further differentiated from competing technologies by being uniquely offered with a practical and commercially available air-cooled condenser (ACC) cooling option. The SMR-300 Standard Plant integrates Holtec’s state-of-the-art life-cycle fuel management solutions and integrated capital equipment with a UMAX Spent Fuel Storage Facility, for turnkey fuel management solutions thru the life of the plant.

entries.text: The Rolls Royce UKR SMR comprises a Reactor Island, Turbine Island, Cooling Water Island, and Balance of Plant.

The UK SMR Reactor Island includes the SSCs that house the reactor, the transfer, handling, and storage of new and used fuel, and associated nuclear auxiliary systems. It is approximately 137 m long and 84 m wide for a total NI area of 11,500 m², equivalent to 3 acres. The exhibits below indicate the Reactor Island within the overall power block and estimated 30acre site general arrangement.

entries.section_title: Figure 6-10 Rolls Royce UK SMR Reactor Island
entries.text: The Reactor Island includes major area or 'Process Blocks' including: Fuel Block - houses the Spent Fuel Storage and Cask Loading System, which comprises the Spent Fuel Pool, Underpin Pit and Cask Loading Pit. Electrical and I&C Block - surrounds the Containment and houses the main control room and safety-critical electrical and I&C systems with associated heating, ventilation and air conditioning system and back-up cooling system, within four separate trains. Fluids Blocks - The Fluids Blocks (2) house systems associated with the reactor plant and the cooling of the fuel temperature within the Reactor Island. Auxiliary Block - The Auxiliary Block houses the systems and functions required for the collection, storage, treatment, processing, and disposal of solid, liquid, and gaseous radioactive waste. Waste Processing Block - The Waste Processing Block houses functions for decontamination and processing and packing of low-level waste. Outage Block - The Outage Block houses the containment preparation and laydown area, which provides a space directly adjacent to the Containment Vessel and interspace to facilitate EMI and replacement activities. Access Block - The Access Block houses the primary personnel access point into the Reactor Island area, radiologically controlled areas and health physics. It also houses the site security control center, the outage control center, the emergency response center, and the technical support center.

entries.text: 8.1 SMR Power Plant Economy by Scale, Sizes and Area Comparison

Most striking are the comparative efficiencies of the plant designs when viewed from a resource per unit power perspective. The SMR-300 appears to be logically more efficient than the competing designs based on side-by-side comparisons of plant areas and volumes of constructed plant structures and equipment. A high-level plot plan and power block comparison between the Holtec International SMR-300, GEH BWRX-300, and Rolls Royce UK SMR designs demonstrates the relative differences between the power plants, for example, and helps emphasize the benefits realizable via the SMR-300 dual-reactor standard nuclear plant configuration with shared non-safety and power block commodities, equipment, resources, and land, as compared to competing lwr SMR designs assessed herein.

Single-reactor SMR plant sizes simply do not scale efficiently to power. From the figure below, we can see that the BWRX-300 Integrated Reactor Building displaces 80% to the volume of the ESBWR Reactor Building, from which this 'small' plant has been derived (implies BWRX requires 80% of 1600MW nuclear island commodities, equipment, direct + indirect costs, whilst producing less than 20% of the ESBWR net electric output). The comparison below is effectively a starting demonstration of the discrepancies of scale realized when scaling down a large nuclear plant to essentially a small version of the same thing.

The SMR-300 Standard Plant design configuration has been reengineered on the advice of Industry and Corporate advisors, to optimize the capital cost-to-power ratio to overcome the diseconomies of SMR scale inherent in 'smalled-down' versions of large single reactor designs. To achieve this, the SMR-300 power block includes twin-reactors in two Containment Enclosure Structures (CES) enclosed by a single Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB), paired with twin turbine buildings, with shared RadWaste and Control and Electrical buildings and shared non-safety essential BOP and yard resources. The result is a plant optimized for efficient use of material, capital, labor and environmental resources.

entries.section_title: SMR-300, BWRX-300, and RR UK SMR building areas and arrangements are compared below, and the results indicate a stark difference in physical land and material requirements between these three lwr SMRs. Requiring far less material and land per MW than the BWRX-300 or RR UK SMR, the SMR-300 Standard Plant includes life-cycle fuel management solutions with integrated capital equipment and UMAX Spent Fuel Storage Facility, unlike any other SMR assessed herein. Designs lacking integrated spent fuel solutions can expect to face future $100m+ costs to engineer, license and construct integrated spent fuel storage facilities. Furthermore, the SMR-300 is the only design proposing to facilitate air cooling, while noting the air-cooled configuration is made practical with Holtec's off-the-shelf HI-KOOL ACCs, itself an extraordinary differentiator among SMRs on offer in the market today, assessed herein or not.

entries.text: cooling trains, each aligned to an RCS loop. The three cooling trains are independent and configured such that 2oo3 trains can provide 72 hours of decay heat removal. Decay heat is transferred from the fuel assemblies to RCS coolant. This coolant flows through the loops to the Steam Generation System where the secondary water boils to generate pressurized steam. Steam is transferred from the SG to the Main Steam System and onwards to a dedicated PDHR heat exchanger in the Passive Steam Condensing System (PSCS). The steam is then condensed through heat transfer into a body of water located in the LUHS; the condensed coolant falls by gravity through PSC drain lines to the Feedwater System, and water in the LUHS boils to atmosphere to provide ultimate heat removal from the power station.

This process is passive and does not rely on pumped flow from the RCPs. Inventory of the primary coolant needs to be maintained during operation of the PDHR due to contracting coolant as the temperature falls, and due to losses of coolant during a small LOCA fault. Inventory control can be provided by any one of the following three systems, initiated upon detection of low level in the pressurizer:
• Level and Volume Control System
• High Pressure Injection System (HPIS) should the LVCS be unavailable
• Low Pressure Injection System (LPIS) should the LVCS and HPIS be unavailable.
Passive Containment Cooling

Steam generated in the RCS throughout a LOCA transient is discharged via a low-pressure blowdown line to the Containment Structure. Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) heat exchangers, located within containment, condense the discharged steam allowing it to collect in the containment sump for recirculation. The PCC heat exchangers are fed by coolant from the LUHS tank. Heat is transferred from the PCC heat exchangers to coolant within the LUHS tank. As heat is transferred, water in the LUHS tank heats up, boils off and is discharged to the atmosphere.
Figure 6-3: Passive Containment Cooling System

The Local Ultimate Heatsink System comprises of three trains, each containing an LUHS tank and its associated ancillary equipment, including the provision of fill, drain and sampling functions. Each LUHS tank corresponds to a single PCC train. The LUHS tanks are arranged such that each tank (and most of the supporting equipment) is currently located outside containment in the interspace, adjacent to the Steam Generator (SG) with which it interfaces. Cross-connects are provided between each tank to enable the

unused water in one tank to be gravity drained into a tank that is available to cool the plant. The final location and geometry of the LUHS tanks are still to be finalized. The PCC heat exchangers are cooled by water from the LUHS tank, which circulates water in a closed loop between the LUHS tank and PCC heat exchanger via natural circulation. It is noted that the LUHS cooling capability is shared between both the ECCS and Passive Decay Heat Sink (PDHS) protective safety measures, as well as the mitigative safety measure In-Vessel Retention (IVR). The ECCS and IVR share the in-containment PCC heat exchangers that are cooled by the LUHS water inventory, whereas the heat exchangers located inside the LUHS vessels are dedicated to PDHS.

The UK SMR fuel handling system covers the fuel route from initial receipt of new fuel to final disposal. The primary function of the system is to move fuel between the outside containment storage and the RPV, providing cooling and shielding of the fuel throughout. The key aspects of the fuel handling system are the fuel handling machine, the in-containment refueling pool, the spent fuel pool, and the long-term storage facility. During refueling operations, the RPV head, stud tensioner and RPV internals are lifted and moved away from the RPV body to facilitate the movement of fuel. Fuel assemblies are lifted in and out of the RPV using a fuel handling machine mounted on rails to and from the refueling pool. The refueling pool temporarily stores both new and spent fuel during a refueling outage. In the refueling pool, spent fuel is re-orientated using an upender and subsequently transported out of containment horizontally through an underwater transfer channel, directly into the spent fuel pool. The spent fuel pool is designed to store fuel assemblies for up to 5 years prior to transferring the fuel to dry storage casks. Transporting new fuel into the RPV is achieved using the reverse of the spent fuel route, following initial receipt and inspection. Both the refueling pool and spent fuel pool are supported by a dedicated chemistry control and heat removal system. The UK SMR operates on an 18-24-month fuel cycle, with a three-core shuffle.

Heat from the reactor is transferred from the primary circuit to the secondary circuit in the three SGs. Feedwater present in the SGs is converted to steam which is then routed by the Steam System through the one high pressure and two low pressure turbines. The turbines are coupled to and rotate a generator, thereby generating the plant's electrical output. The steam leaving the low-pressure turbines is condensed by heat exchange with the cooling water in the Main Cooling Water System (MCWS). The resulting condensate is then deaerated, pre-heated, and fed back into the SGs.

entries.section_title: NuScale Passive Decay Heat Removal System
entries.text: has a passive condenser immersed in the reactor pool. During normal operations, the DHRS condensers are maintained with sufficient water inventory for stable and effective operation. The NuScale passive DHRS is capable of transferring core decay heat from either of the two steam generators to isolation condensers immersed in the reactor pool. Feedwater accumulators and long-term boiling and condensing heat transfer provide the driving head for DHRS flow. The DHRS, shown in Figure 4-2, is capable of decay heat removal for a minimum of 3 days without pumps or power.

The ECCS provides a passive means of decay heat removal in the event of a LOCA. The ECCS consists of two independent reactor vent valves and two independent reactor recirculation valves. All four valves are closed during normal operation. During ECCS operation, the reactor vent valves vent steam from the RPV into the CNV where the steam condenses and collects in the bottom of the containment. The reactor recirculation valves allow water to reenter the RPV and be naturally circulated through the core. When reactor coolant temperature is reduced to below the boiling point, core cooling continues via conduction through the CNV to the reactor pool.

The NPM design utilizes ECCS valves. The design includes reactor vent valves (RVVs) located on the reactor vessel pressurizer, with reactor recirculation valves (RRVs) located on the reactor vessel downcomer. The RVVs and RRVs are functionally similar in design; however, the RVVs are larger than the RRVs. Each of the ECCS valves is pilot operated by remote-mounted trip and reset solenoid valves located at the reactor containment boundary. The design includes a novel inadvertent actuation block (IAB) feature, located inside containment on each RRV main valve. Preliminary bench and prototype tests indicate these IABs are capable of functioning properly. A complex ECCS actuation system including these IAB devices is shown here.

entries.section_title: Lack of Safety System Assurance and Diversity
entries.text: BWRX-300 Emergency Core Cooling System relies entirely on the ICS to supply water and handle over pressure with fail safe (closed) double isolation valves integrated to reactor vessel for steam, feed, ICS exit and ICS return pipes. This is an extraordinary departure from the concept of diverse and redundant safety systems, and the double isolation valves appear not to be able to satisfy USNRC and international regulatory requirements regarding 10 CFR 50.46 (the ECCS Rule) and the single failure criterion. Accordingly, this design feature could prove a fatal flaw in the eyes of many regulators.

entries.section_title: Lack of Passive Makeup Water Injection
entries.text: There is no additional water makeup other than active injection via the FMCRds in case the single ICS safety system fails to perform, or a small undetectable RPV penetration break occurs – itself an unisolatable LOCA.
This novel, small, dry containment is not sized to handle LOCA enthalpy if the ICS fails, or in case an RPV isolation valve were to break.

entries.text: This report provides a succinct summary of four candidate light water SMR technologies, namely, Holtec International's SMR-300, GE-Hitachi's BWRX-300, NuScale's VOYGR and Rolls Royce's UK SMR. Emphasis is placed on the inherent strengths and weaknesses of each technology.

Holtec SMR-300 Sized to produce 340MW(net), the SMR-300 light water reactor has been designed with numerous design features that reflect the lessons from seven decades of nuclear energy generation and answer the imperatives of the 21st century such as the need for a terror-resistant nuclear reactor to support a resilient power grid. Among its key attributes are unconditional safety, absence of reliance on a local water source and a hassle-free long-term management solution of its used fuel. Serving equally well as the anchor of a mini-grid to power a country's rural population centers or as a baseload replacement for its aging fossil plants, the Holtec SMR-300 is a water-cooled small modular reactor that would produce 340 MW electric power (net) using conventional enriched uranium fuel available from current worldwide commercial suppliers. The SMR-300 is noted especially for its intrinsic safety because it does not rely on any safety-related pump or motor for its safe operation. Another important feature is that in the case of an accident from any source (including sabotage or terrorist action), the reactor does not rely upon human intervention to safely shut down. In other words, the Holtec SMR-300 is an unconditionally benign installation to its host community; its presence in any population center would pose no risk of a Chernobyl or Fukushima type catastrophe.

SMR-300 is a ready-for-market clean energy solution for any nation committed to decarbonizing its economy and creating a sustainable and competitive clean energy infrastructure. This report summarizes the Holtec SMR-300's technology differentiators and its compelling case for global adoption. Using the metrics of merit approach, the Holtec SMR-300 scores 93.3% of the maximum available score making it far and away the most eligible reactor for deployment in global markets considered.

GEH BWRX-300 Considered the 10th evolution of the GE boiling water reactor, the BWRX-300 is touted be both imminently licensable and a less expensive option for developers, as compared with other large reactor and SMR designs. GEH claims that the power plant is expected to incur up to 60% less capital cost per MW when compared with a typical water-cooled SMRs and be cost competitive with natural gas-fired power plants. However, these claims do not stand up to scrutiny. The design appears to have disproportionately large Reactor Island and Turbine Island structures in proportion to its 270MWe net electric power rating, certainly as compared to large BWRs like the ESBWR.

The GEH BWRX-300 appears to include designs features that introduce extraordinary licensing risk, but with no apparent or evidenced basis to substantiate claims of licensibility and particularly noting that GEH apparently must seek an exemption to the USNRC ECCS Rule, Title 10 Part 50.46 of Code of Federal Regulations. No previous LWR exemption request to 10 CFR 50.46 has been submitted to the USNRC, let alone been approved. Holtec has direct experience learning the expectations and limits of NRC acceptance criteria regarding that Rule when applied to the design and analysis and testing of pressure vessel components and weldments, engineered with solid mechanics in accord with ASME BPVC Class 1, Section III, Subsection NB nuclear pressure vessel requirements, to demonstrate a mechanistically failure-proof large, forged vessel component. The risk of this design seems extraordinary to us with this experience and perspective. The power plant seems substantially oversized for its small 270MWe net power output, and its radioactive Turbine Island seems an ordeal many markets in the world haven't and are unlikely to deploy, in part as a result. Using the metrics of merit approach, BWRX-300 scores 79.0% of the maximum available score.

entries.section_title: NuScale VOYGR (not updated in this revision (02))
entries.text: The NuScale VOYGR is essentially an SMR power plant comprised of modular factory-fabricated nuclear steam supply systems, assembled within a large, wet reactor building. At nearly 850 metric tons, each NPM is said to be shipped from a factory by rail, barge, or road to construction sites for rapid deployment. Having said this, NuScale provides no insight or proof that this is possible. It is inconceivable that the roads, bridges and transport infrastructure of most countries and Ukraine can handle such massive loads, undermining NuScale Power's claims regarding transportability, and further noting that few factories in the world have the capacity to turn these massive modules out. Astoundingly, each 77 MWe NuScale reactor module weighs nearly the same as a GEH ESBWR reactor vessel which is capable of 1600 MWe.

entries.section_title: NuScale VOYGR (not updated in this revision (02))
entries.text: Employing extraordinary unconventional operational and maintenance and refueling maneuvers and practices, the plant design eschews existing OPEX, and lessons learned from decades of operating light water reactors – a potential recipe for disaster. The plant incorporates a 1000mt single-failure proof NOG-1 crane, the largest of its kind in the world; any crane issue can threaten the ability to operate plant owing to its essentially continuous model refueling architecture and strategy. Individual 850t integrated power modules (RPV + CNV) require massive fabrication, transport and construction facilities, cranes, logistics. Disconnecting reactor power modules from steam and feed piping and transporting those modules past operating reactors in a common pool is a precarious and risky operation, conducted almost constantly to facilitate staggered module refueling. And with unproven and uncertified helical coil steam generators which cannot be replaced without replacing an entire reactor power module, this concept fails the commonsense test.

entries.section_title: NuScale VOYGR (not updated in this revision (02))
entries.text: The NuScale VOYGR has significant unproven and uncommon operational characteristics, and its cost is now estimated by its developer to dramatically exceed prior estimates. Using the metrics of merit approach, NuScale scores 75.4% of the maximum available score.

The Rolls Royce UK SMR is an unconventional forced circulation 3-loop PWR including both active and passive safety systems. The design relies on conventional PWR control rod assemblies (CRAs) for power control and scram, while lacking boron for shim and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the short (~9 feet) core comprising 121-fuel assemblies includes 89 control rods, nearly twice the control/fuel assembly ration as compared to typical PWRs (with FA/CRA ratios ~0.4), introducing a fuel cycle distinctly different, FOAK, to PWR OPEX and associated cycle and exposure dependent fuel mechanical limits of operation, a reactivity, power distribution, and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded power operation and attendant sequence exchanges, potentially with associated fuel conditioning safety or warranty requirements. The design includes an active low pressure boron injection for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of a transient or design basis earthquake.

On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation or design features that would lend the plant safer of more economical than a conventional large PWR. Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from others by claiming 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred in manufacturing factories, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with power plant 'assembly' at the site. While an ambitious goal, this appears practically unachievable when examining Ch09 of the Rolls Royce UK SMR Civil Construction Safety Case7, with its large conventional major underground and concrete structures, and an FOAK raft foundation and aseismic bearing, with no prior endorsed regulatory acceptance criteria or OPEX precedent, proof or practice.
