entries.text: reactor coolant pump in the cold leg, and one vertical u-tube Steam Generator (SG). One of the loops contains the pressurizer connected to the hot leg, to maintain pressure within the primary reactor circuit and avoid boiling of the coolant. The operational pressure of the primary circuit is 15.5 MPa.

The RPV is a cylindrical steel vessel designed to withstand the high temperatures, pressures, and radiation of the reactor. The RPV houses the reactor core, in-core instrumentation, and the reactor internals. The reactor core is made up of 121 fuel rod assemblies and 89 control rod assemblies. Each fuel assembly is arranged in a 17x17 array of fuel rods consisting of a metallic zirconium alloy cladding housing the nuclear fuel, which is now in the form of small ceramic pellets, which contain up to 4.95% enriched uranium dioxide fuel. The hemispherical upper head of the RPV is removable to allow refueling of the reactor every 18 months.

Water is used as the primary coolant, to extract the heat from the reactor, and as a moderator to maintain the nuclear reaction in the core. Hot water from the core outlet passes into the SGs, where it flows through thousands of heat exchange tubes which transfer the heat to the secondary coolant on the outside of the tubes which is allowed to boil and produce steam. It is this steam produced in the secondary side of the SGs that drives a turbine that ultimately, via a generator, produces electricity. The primary coolant leaving the SGs, which is now at lower temperature, is then pumped back into the reactor via the cold legs. The flowrate of the primary coolant is such that the flow through each loop takes only a few seconds.

Unlike other commercial PWRs, the generic Rolls-Royce SMR design is designed to operate without soluble boron during normal operations. Rolls-Royce SMR Limited claim that, in addition to simplification of the design, this provides safety benefits including full shutdown margin delivered by the control rods and elimination of boron dilution faults.

A range of safety measures are present in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide cooling, control criticality and contain radioactivity under faulted conditions. Active components and supporting electrical supply are claimed not to be significantly risk important. As such, hazards which render active systems unavailable such as complete loss of electrical supplies (station blackout) are claimed to present very low risk. Similarly,
failures of operator actions in delivery of safety functions are identified as not significantly important. As a result, a period of 72 hours is predicted before offsite support is required.

The Rolls-Royce SMR employs both active and passive decay heat removal systems. Condenser decay heat removal utilizes the SGs and the normal duty steam condenser to cool the RCS. Passive Decay Heat Removal (PDHR) is a dedicated safety system that utilizes the SGs and the Local Ultimate Heatsink System (LUHS) to cool the RCS. In the PDHR decay heat is transferred to the LUHS water tanks via dedicated submerged heat exchangers. Boiling of the LUHS water to atmosphere provides the ultimate heat sink via passive means which rely on natural circulation.
Figure 6-8: Passive Decay Heat Removal System (PDHR)

When steam generators are unavailable for decay heat removal, for example in LOCA, the ECCS provides a passive, redundant, diverse, and segregated protective safety measure. This system provides core cooling in a sequence which involves blowdown of the RCS to the containment through dedicated relief valves, water injection from three accumulator tanks, gravity injection from the refueling pool and auxiliary LOCA pool and passive circulation from water accumulated within the containment sumps.
Additional protection is available from the High-Pressure Injection System (HPIS) for smaller leaks, which uses pumped flow to introduce water into the RCS.

Shutdown of the reactor in faults can be achieved using both the scram function and Emergency Boron Injection (EBI) system. The scram function isolates power to the Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDM), causing the control rods to be rapidly inserted. The alternative shutdown function is provided by the EBI system which delivers boron solution to the RCS. The EBI system operates at low pressure and is therefore dependent on the HPIS pumps and AC power. These non-safety systems are triggered from independent and diverse control and instrumentation systems.

The containment incorporates features to minimize and mitigate postulated severe accident phenomena. These include passive hydrogen re-combiners to prevent hydrogen explosions and containment vessel overpressure protection via filtered containment venting. The design also includes a Reactor Vessel Cavity Injection System (RVCIS) which has been designed to achieve In-Vessel Retention (IVR) of molten core

entries.text: qualification testing to provide confidence in the ability of the valves to maintain their required performance after extended periods in an operational environment. Failing to demonstrate such will require a redesign of this safety system.

The integrity and performance of the steam generators have not yet been sufficiently validated because of uncertainties associated with unstable density wave oscillations (DWO) on the steam generator secondary side. Accelerated wear of the alloy 690TT (thermally treated) steam generator tubing material is also a potential concern. Without an ability to repair or replace SG tubes in damaged SG, this could be a fatal flaw.

The coolant in the downcomer will decorate for a range of design basis accidents, including small-break LOCA. The estimated time for the boron concentration to drop below the critical boron concentration in the downcomer for these events is within a few hours. Operator recovery actions raise the possibility of an influx of deborated water into the core, which may result in re-criticality, return to power, and the potential for core damage.
According to Rolls Royce, the UK SMR design is based on an optimized and enhanced use of proven technology, with a single unit, three-loop pWR rated at 1385MWe, 470MWt (gross) and 425 MWe (net).

The Reactor Island includes the systems that form the reactor, transfer, and storage of new and used fuel, and any associated nuclear auxiliary systems. The purpose of Reactor Island is to use the heat from a controlled nuclear fission reaction to generate steam, which is then passed to the Turbine Island. The Reactor Island includes the Reactor Plant, Handling of Nuclear Equipment and Nuclear Auxiliary Systems.
The Handling of Nuclear Equipment includes those systems that cover the fuel route from initial receipt of new fuel to final disposal.
The Auxiliary Systems comprise those systems supporting reactor plant operations.
The Electrical Power System is located within Reactor Island.

The UK SMR primary circuit comprises a reactor core, containing the reactor fuel, mounted in an RPV that is closely coupled through large bore pipework to three SGs. The baseline architecture for the RCS consists of three vertical u-tube Steam Generators (SGs) with associated pipework loops and a single Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) in each loop, mounted to the SG outlet. The configuration of the SG, pipework and pump layout in each loop provides thermal driving head for natural circulation flow during fault conditions. The system also contains a pump induced spray pressurizing system with associated pressure relief system.

entries.text: The PCHR passively maintains the containment atmospheric pressure and temperature within design limits in the event of a postulated accident by utilizing the metal containment structure and the water inventory in the annular reservoir. PCHR is a completely passive system that removes heat from the containment environment after an RCS energy release to containment. It does not require any actuations of components or an actuation signal to perform its functions.

During a postulated high energy loss of coolant accident, steam is released into the containment environment. The steam condenses on the inside surface of the containment structure as heat is transferred through the containment wall to the annular reservoir. The large heat transfer area and high conductance of the steel containment structure results in rapid heat rejection from the containment to the annular reservoir. As the water inventory in the reservoir is heated, it rejects heat to the environment through the discharge of clean vapor (no radioactivity) through a vent at the top of the Containment Enclosure Structure.

Water inventory is maintained in the annular reservoir at a certain level during normal operation to assure passive containment heat removal is available for at least 72 hours after a postulated accident without operator action. The water inventory can be replenished using an accessible connection outside of containment as part of the Holtec SMR-300 flexible coping strategy.

The Holtec SMR-300 reactor coolant loop is coupled with a thermally efficient simplified Rankine superheat steam cycle. In the event of a reactor trip with loss of power, the SMR-300 RCS can operate purely by natural circulation, as reactor coolant can circulate entirely because of the density difference between the primary water columns within the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) and steam generator (SG).

Passive, fail-safe, safety systems for emergency core cooling and containment heat removal eliminate the need for alternating current (ac) power under all accident conditions. All water required to mitigate loss of coolant accidents is located inside the containment in accumulators and tanks. The core damage frequency (CDF) is several orders of magnitude below U.S. regulatory thresholds without crediting any operator actions or non-safety systems.

entries.section_title: Offset Integrated Reactor and Steam Generator
entries.text: The SG is connected directly to the RPV by a set of two thick-walled pipes that deliver the cooled primary water to the down comer region of the Reactor Vessel. Each line features a booster pump, a non-safety equipment whose sole function is to increase the circulation in the RCS loop on demand. The two hot legs of the reactor coolant consist of heavy wall pipes that serve the heated primary water to the top header of the OTSG. There are no penetrations in the RPV below the RCS direct vessel injection nozzles, and the top of the core is well below this point, ensuring water stays within and above the active core. With a water volume to power ratio several times larger than traditional PWRs, the Holtec SMR-300 benefits from a large heat removal buffer for postulated transients and a large SG shell-side volume to prevent rapid SG dry-out during transients.

entries.section_title: Offset Integrated Reactor and Steam Generator
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 reactor is distinguished from other integral pressurized water reactors prevalent in the small modular reactor market which integrate the SG within the RPV. The Holtec SMR-300’s innovative offset design vastly simplifies refueling operations compared to iPWRs, while reducing or eliminating complex bolting and heavy load rigging and lifts. For refueling operations, the reactor head is readily removed to access the core in the same manner as current reactors, with the proximity of the spent fuel pool eliminating the need for complex fuel transfer equipment.

The PCSS is designed to provide emergency core cooling and makeup water following design basis accidents (DBAs), and unlike other SMRs designs, relies on no first of a kind components, valves, or actuation features not readily and reliably available. The system uses passive means such as natural circulation for core cooling, and compressed gas expansion and gravity injection for makeup, without the use of pumps. The design automatically manages and mitigates the effects of leaks and small break LOCA’s.

The passive safety systems rely on buoyancy driven flow and one-time opening of valves, eliminating the need for Class 1E AC power. A heat sink reservoir incorporated directly in the design surrounds the above grade CS and eliminates the need for safety-related cooling systems, while the passive core makeup water system (PCMWS) located inside the CS eliminates the need for external water supplies for safety injection. Small chemical and volume control system (CVCS) throughput equates to slow ion exchange resin consumption and little crud/lower resin radiological loading, resulting in low quantities of secondary waste streams. Because of the reduced plant size, reduced staffing, short refueling outages, and fewer plant systems, the Holtec SMR-300 yields less low-level waste than current facilities.

The Containment Enclosure (CS) is enveloped by the containment enclosure structure (CES), a steel and concrete structure assembled from CSSM modules that protects the CS from incident missiles and malevolent acts such as a crashing aircraft and contains a large reservoir of water in the annular region formed between the CES and Containment. This technology is proven and broadly deployed by Holtec, and its proprietary HI-STORM spent fuel storage system, licensed, and deployed in the US and numerous countries overseas.

The CES walls are constructed of extremely robust steel-concrete modules designed to withstand an impact from large commercial aircraft and other potential hazards. In addition to preventing the release of radioactive fission products to the environment, the containment system acts as a large passive heat exchanger. The containment system is partially embedded, with approximately half of the total height located below grade to maximize protection against external hazards and dampen seismic effects for critical components.

entries.section_title: Integrated Spent Nuclear Fuel Systems and Technologies
entries.text: The plant design incorporates a licensed spent fuel handling solution that accommodates discharge of spent fuel assemblies to underground dry storage in the HI-STORM UMAX Storage System, in conjunction with a tiny spent fuel pool passively cooled in the event of a design basis accident and protected inside the containment and CES. On-site interim dry storage within the HI-STORM UMAX system accommodates all the spent nuclear fuel for the design life of the Holtec SMR-300 reactor. When dry storage is performed during the refueling outage, the same HI-TRAC transfer cask that was used to bring in the new fuel will be used to move spent assemblies to dry storage. After the new fuel has been removed, and with the HI-TRAC still within the spent fuel pool (SFP), discharged spent fuel assemblies are loaded into the HI-TRAC using the fuel handling bridge and then the internal canister is prepared for on-site storage or off-site transport.

entries.section_title: Integrated Spent Nuclear Fuel Systems and Technologies
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 has been developed with construction and decommissioning in mind. Major plant buildings employ shallow and wide layouts to ease construction and make equipment installation uncomplicated. Plant buildings and other SSCs are arranged in a manner that readily befits decommissioning with minimal work, cost and material movements and transport. During decommissioning, the time, work, cost and material to unload spent fuel from the Holtec SMR-300 reactor and spent fuel pool after final shutdown is dramatically reduced as compared to a conventional reactor plant because at the end of design life most fuel will already have been removed from the SFP and placed in dry storage.

entries.section_title: 7.4 Notable Attributes of Rolls Royce Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text: At 1358 MWe, the UK SMR is a three-loop medium sized reactor. The plant design includes a novel seismic isolation system, and an unconventional approach to large power plant construction, more akin to submarine construction, albeit without the benefit of an adjacent marine factory and assembly environment.

The generic Rolls-Royce SMR design also includes aseismic bearings for a base isolation system within the reactor island. The main benefit of this system is that it is claimed to allow the superstructure to be standardized, along with the equipment in the power station, regardless of site-specific seismicity. The base isolation system comprises the raft foundation, the concrete pedestals, and aseismic bearings and the basemat. The raft foundation, basemat, and major Reactor Island building structures (e.g., Containment Support Structure) are filed constructed via conventional reinforced concrete materials and methods.

A hazard shield, consisting of a reinforced concrete wall and roof, is included in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide protection against radioactivity release due to external hazards. The bounding case for the hazard shield is based on an aircraft impact hazard, aiming to ensure confinement of fuel, prevention of criticality, protection of reactor shutdown and cooling systems and protection of monitoring systems. The hazard shield covers portions of the Reactor Island - the containment building and the fuel and control buildings - to ensure Class 1 SSCs are protected. The Hazard Shield, measuring 200 feet by 300 feet, is essentially a very large cover over the top of the plant’s nuclear assets.

Unlike other commercial PWRs, the generic Rolls-Royce SMR design is designed to operate without soluble boron during normal operations. Rolls-Royce claim that, in addition to simplification of the design, this provides safety benefits including full shutdown margin delivered by the control rods and elimination of boron dilution faults. This feature will however greatly complicate power operations and maneuvers, and may ultimately prove unworkable, lacking a second independent passive means to shut down the reactor.

The plant’s coping period after a design basis accident is limited to 72hrs. before operator actions are required – a significant shortfall in safety achievement compared to the other SMR plants evaluated herein.

The design also includes a Reactor Vessel Cavity Injection System (RVCIS) which has been designed to achieve In-Vessel Retention (IVR) of molten core material in a severe accident. This is achieved by externally cooling the RPV lower head by gravity flooding the reactor cavity pit with water, and allowing this to boil, condense and return to the pit. In the event of a LOCA, steam released into the containment throughout the transient is cooled by the LUHS Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) system heat exchangers.

Section 7 includes Rolls Royce disclosed plant information including major plant buildings, dimensions and areas. Those areas are compared to the same for other technologies evaluated herein (Reactor Island, Turbine Island, Plot Plan) to compare one against the other.

entries.text: The onsite distribution system is fed from the offsite power system during plant startup, normal or emergency shutdown, or during plant outages. During normal plant operations, it is fed from the main generator. If there is a loss of offsite power without a turbine trip, the plant will operate in island mode where the reactor will run back to a reduced power and the main generator will power all house loads. The Holtec SMR-300 is designed to provide flexible power output and perform load following based on grid demand. The Holtec SMR-300 is capable of quickly reducing from 100% to 0% power without a plant trip and is designed for continuous operation at low power or a return to higher power levels within hours.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: SMR-300 has been designed with special focus on a long service life marked by the absence of stress corrosion cracking failures and unscheduled shutdowns. While an accurate service life projection is not possible, the SMR-300 includes specific design features to overcome known reactor plant operational challenges, to best ensure it exceeds 80yr design life:

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Ensuring absence of laminar conditions: Holtec understands that laminar or transitional flow conditions which typically afflict thermosiphon-based designs and is caused by a small driving head is a threat to the system reliability of any reactor system. To ensure that the Holtec SMR-300 will be free of such a problem, the turbulence level in the RCS and elsewhere in the plant is required to be at least four times the upper end of the transition zone at the lowest power output condition.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Protecting the RCS pressure boundary: SCC and cyclic fatigue from thermal transients have been identified as the twin threats to the integrity of the pressure boundary in reactor vessels and steam generators. These threats have been ameliorated in the Holtec SMR-300 by ensuring that the RCS temperature changes are not abrupt, made possible by the large thermal inertia of the entire RCS, and by employing a thermal liner throughout the pressure boundary which blunts the thermal shock to the pressure boundary material (a patented Holtec invention).

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Protecting Steam Generator tubes from Wastage: The wisdom received from the spate of steam generator failures in the 1990s in the United States has been incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 SG design. The tubes are made of thermally treated Inconel 690, All-Volatile Treatment (AVT) water chemistry treatment is employed, and the blow-down rate to continuously purge the SG sludge is two times that used in the latest LWR designs. In addition, a tube installation sequence has been developed to pre-stress the most severely loaded tubes to mitigate tube axial stresses during operations. Non-segmental tube supports (based on an expired Patent patent and extensively used by the Company over the past 30 years) have been incorporated in the design to minimize vibration producing cross flows. It can be said that the Holtec SMR-300’s SG design incorporates all the chastening lessons learned from seven decades of PWR operations.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Vibration: Vibration of slender parts such as tubes in feedwater heaters, control condensers, steam generators, moisture separator reheaters, auxiliary feed exchangers, surface rod extensions, and piping runs has been a persistent operating problem in nuclear plants. In the Holtec SMR-300, this ubiquitous problem is systematically solved by requiring that the fundamental natural frequency of the part be at least two times the highest frequency of the excitation source. In heat exchangers, principal excitation sources are fluid elastic coupling and turbulent buffeting. Piping runs are vulnerable to the harmonics associated with earthquakes.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Pressure retaining weld seams: Pressure retaining welds in the RCS are known to be vulnerable to failure and are thus subject to periodic in-service inspection that increases outage duration. In the Holtec SMR-300, Holtec proprietary design strategies have been employed to significantly reduce the number of weld seams.

entries.text: The wisdom received from the spate of steam generator failures in the 1990s in the United States has been incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 SG design. entries.text: Importantly, the RIV design features may may prove un-licensable in certain domains and markets, as these nuclear safety components fail to comport with the 10 CFR 50.46 Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS) prescription, which effectively mandates Loss of Coolant Accident (LOCA) breaks at both inbound and outboard terminal ends of such devices. According to the USNRC, from pre-application meetings and submittals associated with the BWRX-300, GEH has essentially described an "alternate licensing framework" as their (or more correctly, a future applicant's) intended approach to address US regulations and acceptance criteria, that will require significant exemptions to NRC regulations, alternatives to the NRC 10 CFR Part 50, Appendix A, General Design Criteria (GDCs), and deviations to NRC regulatory guidance including NUREG-0800. Furthermore, the NRC recently performed a readiness review of the TVA-Clinch River draft PSAR, which implements the BWRX-300 design (letter: ML24302A104). Therein, the NRC observed that "staff identified major gaps in the content of information in the areas of key risk insights and quantitative results for the design, dominant accident sequences, design features that are major risk contributors, and quantified risk metrics. If not addressed... these gaps have the potential to challenge an effective and efficient review of the CP application...".

While unto itself this does not indicate the design cannot be licensed in the US, it does speak to the extraordinary commercial and regulatory risk GEH and its clients can expect when ultimately applying to build a BWRX-300 in the US, or UK/EU markets with arguably more demanding acceptance criteria than the USNRC. The BWRX-300 is essentially a scaled, or 'smalled-down', ESBWR reactor that appears to retain much of the Nuclear and Turbine Island structural area and volumes of the larger plant, resulting in a design that appears inefficient in terms of material and land use per MWe produced. The design information available provides no indication of, or allowance for adoption of air cooling via ACCs, and BWR turbine performance is far more sensitive to changes in back pressure than the PWR turbine. As such the plant appears to be limited to wet site deployments. The standard plant is limited by a bounding peak ground acceleration earthquake of 0.3g.

GE Hitachi's BWRX-300 completed the first two phases of the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission (CNSC)'s vendor design review. In April 2024, the CNSC confirmed that the existing environmental assessment for the Darlington New Nuclear Project (DNN) remains valid and applicable to the BWRX-300 technology. OPG applied in October 2022 for a construction license for a single BWRX-300 reactor, and in April 2025, the Commission authorized OPG to construct the first BWRX-300 unit at DNN.

Since December 2019, the NRC has engaged in pre-application review of GEH's BWRX-300, including topical reports and design white papers. In April 2025, TVA officially submitted the first part of the CPA—the environmental report—to the NRC, with the preliminary safety analysis report submitted in May 2025. The NRC has docketed the application for review and anticipates completing its review in 17 months—targeting December 2026.

The NuScale VOYR, discussed in Section 5 of this report, is a so-called "integral reactor" design, whereby the reactor internals, steam generator, and pressurizer are housed inside a single pressure vessel. An extraordinary feature of this integral design configuration is that secondary water is boiled and converted into steam inside the tubes which are helical in shape to fit into the limited available space.

This and other highly novel and untried features render the NuScale VOYR plant into a package of first-of-a-kind embodiments that challenge the plant's viability for broad commercial investments and operations. Several unique and novel means of construction and operation compared to normative, known, safe and reliable nuclear power plant operations are its obvious drawbacks. Despite having achieved USNRC conditional design certification for a 12 X 50 MWe (600 MWe total) NuScale Power Module
(NPM) plant in early 2023, several key open items were carved out of that certification, including the helical coil steam generators.

To enhance performance and economics, NuScale pursued an uprated design with 77MWe modules. They submitted their Standard Design Approval (SDA) application for the VOYR-6 (a six-module configuration) in January 2023. As of May 2025, the NRC completed the review and issued a Standard Design Approval for the US460 which corresponds to the VOYR-6 configuration of 77 MWe modules (462 MWe gross, estimated 420 MWe net).

Licensing issues and concerns aside, the entire VOYR power plant departs from proven nuclear power plant design functions for operability and presents unique features and operational challenges never previously incorporated or proven, presenting non-quantifiable risks and uncertainties to potential clients. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration PGA of 0.5g.

The Rolls Royce UK SMR, described in Section 6 of this report, is an unconventional forced circulation 3-loop PWR, including both active and passive safety systems. This lack of conventionality owes to the design relying on PWR control rod assemblies (CRAs) for power control and scram, as the plant does not employ boron for reactivity control and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the 121-fuel assembly core includes 89 control rods for a Fuel Assembly (FA) to Control Rod Assembly (CRA) ratio of 0.75, as compared to typical PWRs with a FA/CRA ratio ~0.4 - introducing a reactivity and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded operation. While it is important not to objectively overstate technical, commercial, or regulatory risks associated with this fuel cycle, it is equally important to point out the novelty of this PWR core and fuel cycle, with its attendant uncertainties regarding exposure dependent and transient fuel and clad performance. GE and BWR operators learned much about exposure dependent impacts to fuel mechanical performance from rodded-exposure and the thermal-physics of that fuel, as compared to the homogenous PWR core control. Time will tell, as lessons are learned and adopted to improve fuel performance for this novel fuel cycle.

The design includes active low pressure boron injection requiring AC power for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of certain transients including a design basis earthquake. On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation or design features that would render the plant economically competitive with conventional large PWR, while appearing to be significantly over-engineered in terms of redundant trains and divisions common to earlier generation PWRs and UK relevant good practice (RGP).

That said, Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from existing PWRs by 1) constructing the plant's Reactor Island in its entirety on a seismically isolated basement as a raft foundation and retaining wall, all of which is composed entirely of rebar-reinforced concrete (RC). entries.section_title: With a compact, high power density plant configuration, the SMR-300 NPPs requires far less material and land per net MWe output than the GEH BWRX-300 or Rolls Royce UK SMR.
entries.text: With a compact, high power density plant configuration, the SMR-300 NPPs requires far less material and land per net MWe output than the GEH BWRX-300 or Rolls Royce UK SMR.

Where economies of land and capital resources matter, the SMR-300 stands out when compared to other lwr SMRs. At nearly 50% more MW per acre than competing technologies, the SMR-300 minimizes land requirements to maximize power deployment where NPP new build opportunities are limited by the number and sizes of available sites. The small SMR-300 Power Block – the reactor and turbine island – and large net power output yields better economies of scale than the GEH and Rolls Royce power plants. The plant is further differentiated from competing technologies by being uniquely offered with a practical and commercially available air-cooled condenser (ACC) cooling option. The SMR-300 Standard Plant integrates Holtec’s state-of-the-art life-cycle fuel management solutions and integrated capital equipment with a UMAX Spent Fuel Storage Facility, for turnkey fuel management solutions thru the life of the plant.

This report provides a succinct summary of four candidate light water SMR technologies, namely, Holtec International's SMR-300, GE-Hitachi's BWRX-300, NuScale's VOYGR and Rolls Royce's UK SMR. Emphasis is placed on the inherent strengths and weaknesses of each technology.

Holtec SMR-300 Sized to produce 340MW(net), the SMR-300 light water reactor has been designed with numerous design features that reflect the lessons from seven decades of nuclear energy generation and answer the imperatives of the 21st century such as the need for a terror-resistant nuclear reactor to support a resilient power grid. Among its key attributes are unconditional safety, absence of reliance on a local water source and a hassle-free long-term management solution of its used fuel. Serving equally well as the anchor of a mini-grid to power a country's rural population centers or as a baseload replacement for its aging fossil plants, the Holtec SMR-300 is a water-cooled small modular reactor that would produce 340 MW electric power (net) using conventional enriched uranium fuel available from current worldwide commercial suppliers. The SMR-300 is noted especially for its intrinsic safety because it does not rely on any safety-related pump or motor for its safe operation. Another important feature is that in the case of an accident from any source (including sabotage or terrorist action), the reactor does not rely upon human intervention to safely shut down. In other words, the Holtec SMR-300 is an unconditionally benign installation to its host community; its presence in any population center would pose no risk of a Chernobyl or Fukushima type catastrophe.

SMR-300 is a ready-for-market clean energy solution for any nation committed to decarbonizing its economy and creating a sustainable and competitive clean energy infrastructure. This report summarizes the Holtec SMR-300's technology differentiators and its compelling case for global adoption. Using the metrics of merit approach, the Holtec SMR-300 scores 93.3% of the maximum available score making it far and away the most eligible reactor for deployment in global markets considered.

GEH BWRX-300 Considered the 10th evolution of the GE boiling water reactor, the BWRX-300 is touted be both imminently licensable and a less expensive option for developers, as compared with other large reactor and SMR designs. GEH claims that the power plant is expected to incur up to 60% less capital cost per MW when compared with a typical water-cooled SMRs and be cost competitive with natural gas-fired power plants. However, these claims do not stand up to scrutiny. The design appears to have disproportionately large Reactor Island and Turbine Island structures in proportion to its 270MWe net electric power rating, certainly as compared to large BWRs like the ESBWR.

The GEH BWRX-300 appears to include designs features that introduce extraordinary licensing risk, but with no apparent or evidenced basis to substantiate claims of licensibility and particularly noting that GEH apparently must seek an exemption to the USNRC ECCS Rule, Title 10 Part 50.46 of Code of Federal Regulations. No previous LWR exemption request to 10 CFR 50.46 has been submitted to the USNRC, let alone been approved. Holtec has direct experience learning the expectations and limits of NRC acceptance criteria regarding that Rule when applied to the design and analysis and testing of pressure vessel components and weldments, engineered with solid mechanics in accord with ASME BPVC Class 1, Section III, Subsection NB nuclear pressure vessel requirements, to demonstrate a mechanistically failure-proof large, forged vessel component. The risk of this design seems extraordinary to us with this experience and perspective. The power plant seems substantially oversized for its small 270MWe net power output, and its radioactive Turbine Island seems an ordeal many markets in the world haven't and are unlikely to deploy, in part as a result. Using the metrics of merit approach, BWRX-300 scores 79.0% of the maximum available score.

entries.text: NSSS Nuclear Boiler Components in the BWRX-300 NSSS include the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), with integrated RIVs and fine motion control rod drives (FMCRDs). The NSSS delivers steam from the RPV to the turbine via the main steam system, while the condensate and feedwater system delivers feedwater to the core as subcooled and provides overpressure protection of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB).

Reactor Core The reactor core of the BWRX-300 is arranged as an upright cylinder containing 240 fuel assemblies located within a core shroud. During operation, the coolant/moderator enters the bottom of the core as subcooled water and exits the core as saturated steam. The BWRX-300 utilizes GNF2 fuel, typical of much of the BWR fleet today. The GNF2 fuel assembly comprises a 10x10 array of 78 full-length fuel rods, 14 part-length rods and two large central water rods.

Reactivity Control Reactivity control is provided by control rods loaded with either B4C or Hf neutron absorbers and burnable neutron absorbers loaded in the fuel rods. Cruciform control rods are moved using FMCRDs successfully deployed in the ABWRs in Japan. FMCRDs have two independent means of moving the control rods—motor driven fine control for reactivity control during normal operation and hydraulic rapid insertion during a scram.

Reactor Coolant System The reactor coolant system (RCS) is natural circulation driven and provides cooling of the reactor core in all operational states and all postulated off normal conditions. The BWRX-300 leverages natural circulation modelling and operational information from the ESBWR and the Downwind Nuclear Power Plant that operated in the Netherlands. That said, this natural circulation BWR's coolant is effectively propelled by high-pressure feedwater condensate pumped directly in the reactor vessel downcomer during power operations,

Reactor Pressure Vessel and Internals The BWRX-300's RPV assembly consists of a pressure vessel with removable head, internal components, and appurtenances. The reactor internals include the core, control rods and nuclear instrumentation, core support and alignment structures (shroud, shroud support, top guide, core plate, control rod guide tube and orifice fuel support), chimney (chimney head and steam separator assembly and steam dryer assembly).

Engineered Safety Systems The BWRX-300 is designed using IAEA guidelines countries. The basic BWRX-300 safety design philosophy is built on utilization of inherent margins (e.g., large structure volumes and water inventory) to eliminate system challenges to accommodate transients. Natural circulation safety-related systems mitigate design basis. The BWRX-300 defense in depth concept uses Fundamental Safety Functions (FSF) to define the interface between the defense lines and the physical barriers.

Decay Heat Removal System The normal, non-Safety Class 1, shutdown cooling (SDC) system for decay heat removal comprises two independent pumps and heat exchanger trains. These trains provide redundant decay heat cooling capacity. The major components of each train are a pump and an HX, along with valves, piping, instrumentation and controls, and power inputs.

entries.section_title: Emergency Core Cooling Isolation Condenser System (ICS)
entries.text: The ECCS for the BWRX-300 is the Isolation Condenser System (ICS). The ICS removes decay heat after any reactor isolation and shutdown from power operations under normal or abnormal conditions. The ICS consists of three independent loops each containing a heat exchanger (HX) and isolation condenser (IC) with capacity of approximately 33 MWth. The ICS tubes condense steam from the RPV on the inside surface and transfer heat on the outside surface to the IC pool which is at atmospheric pressure. This steam condensation and gravity allow BWRX-300 to cool itself for a minimum of seven days without power or operator action.
Safety relief valves have been eliminated from the reactor coolant system. The ICS provides over pressure protection and decay heat removal with water makeup to the RCS after a LOCA.

The BWRX-300 design attempts to eliminate non-isolable LOCAs by utilizing novel, redundant RIVs integral to the RPV. All fluid pipes systems inside containment >50mm in diameter are equipped with double isolation valves integrated within the RPV ASME Section-III code boundary.

entries.text: Critical features are noted in Table 2-2, to evaluate and compare candidate technologies as possible. Each technology is presented and discussed in a distinct section of the report, in sections 3 through 6. A summary assessment relative to these critical features (to the extent practical via the available public information for each) can be found in four tables in section 7. Those tables include weighted scores of metrics envisaged to be roughly in descending order of significance to an NPP owner, with a maximum score that can be earned for each metric (critical feature or parameter).

The above-mentioned drawbacks of large reactors have prompted industry to seek the obverse of largeness, namely small reactors, defined empirically as a reactor that has less than 300 MWe design basis output. It was reasoned that because the “small” reactor has a small inventory of thermal energy at any one time, the dissipation of that heat during a postulated loss of coolant accident should be manageable. Also, a small reactor ought to be built and commissioned in a relatively short time, and the cost of capital per unit output ought to be smaller than large reactors. Proponents of small reactors also hoped that they would be largely factory built, maximizing the benefits inherent in serial manufacturing while minimizing site construction costs. The notion of manufacturing most parts and sub-components in a factory and limiting site construction to a minimum was conceived as the antidote to the awful labor efficiency at construction sites. Thus, the term “modular” became attached to small reactors, resulting in the now commonly used term “small modular reactor,” and its acronym “SMR.”

In this report, Holtec’s attention is focused on the light water SMRs which, because of the maturity of light water technology, hold the promise of immediate deployment. This report accordingly focuses on the merits and demerits of four SMR technologies which have progressed their designs and gained varying levels of acceptance. Because none has been yet deployed, Holtec’s appraisal is founded on the design features that define the prognosis for their future performance based on solid science, not conjectures and speculations. entries.text: inspection access to the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) using traditional methods. This configuration maximizes the use of operating experience from the current fleet and distinguishes the Holtec SMR-300 from iPWRs prevalent in the small modular reactor market, designs which integrate the steam generator and reactor in one embodiment, vastly complicating refueling, inspection, maintenance, and related activities.

The Holtec SMR-300 spent fuel solution is part of an integrated fuel management system, circumventing any need for costly plant modifications typical for current LWRs. The Holtec SMR-300 utilizes on-site interim spent fuel storage within the Holtec HI-STORM UMAX system, containing Multi-Purpose Canisters (MPCs). HI-STORM UMAX is an underground Vertical Ventilated Module (VVM) dry, spent fuel storage system. Each HI-STORM UMAX VVM provides storage of one MPC inside a cylindrical cavity located entirely below the top-of-grade. The Holtec SMR-300 is designed for on-site interim storage of all discharged fuel assemblies within an array of HI-STORM UMAX modules for the full design life of the Holtec SMR-300 with all necessary – developed and proven – structures, systems, and ancillary components to move the fuel in and out of the reactor and plant for safe and compact storage on-site.

Unlike some of the other SMR designs evaluated herein, the Holtec SMR-300 power plant is capable of a) being started from cold conditions without energy from the transmission grid, and b) and closing the output circuit breaker to a dead transmission bus to recover the electrical transmission system. Additionally, the plant derives power for house loads from the main generator, allowing the facility to operate without grid power. Together, these features allow the Holtec SMR-300 to be both black-start capable and island-mode capable, providing extreme robustness to any local or regional electricity distribution system.

The Holtec SMR-300 operates with large margins to criticality and thermal mechanical limits and employs a layered approach to mitigate the consequences of a postulated event, consistent with USNRC and IAEA guidelines. The passive safety systems incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 power plant comply with US and international guidelines in both letter and spirit.

The Holtec SMR-300 power plant is self-coping and designed to place itself in a safe condition in the event of a postulated accident. Independent and redundant layers of defense are engineered to anticipate, overcome and compensate for potential human errors and mechanical failures. Importantly, the containment of the Holtec SMR-300 is designed to remain intact and sealed during all power operating modes and postulated events, and to reject its internal energy to the large body of water surrounding the CS in the event of a design basis accident. Large releases of radioactivity postulated to occur for current large nuclear reactors in the case of an accident cannot occur with the Holtec SMR-300.

The Holtec SMR-300 design also incorporates flexible features such as emergency equipment, piping connections to important fluid systems, and spare batteries to address the potential occurrence of an event not yet conceived. The Holtec SMR-300 is a robust and safe power plant with large design and operating margins, and these flexible features make the plant well-equipped to handle events that far exceed the design basis loadings like in the case of Fukushima.

An 80-year design life is engineered into the Holtec SMR-300 by ensuring that every operational parameter has been optimized to increase NSSS longevity. Life-limiting factors such as neutron embrittlement and thermal shock to the reactor pressure boundary have been ameliorated.

Passive safety features and a simplified plant design enhance the safety, security, construction, operation, and maintenance of the plant. Where possible, inspections, tests, and maintenance requirements are simplified or eliminated for the life of the plant to reduce operating costs. Laydown space, for maintenance

The Holtec SMR-300 incorporates the Mitsubishi Electric Total Advanced Controller (MELTAC) architecture developed by MELCO.

MELTAC is a simplified and highly integrated 2-safety division, 4-channel distributed control system. The design includes significant automation (e.g., no operator action required for postulated accidents) and completely computer-based procedures. MELTAC has undergone extensive human system interface integration testing and is licensed and deployed around the world. MELCO and their MELTAC platform

entries.text: SMR-300 uses conventional length PWR fuel, available initially from Framatome, and expected to be sourced from numerous international suppliers.

The critically important components in the Holtec SMR-300, such as the RPV, the SG, and the pressurizer as well as the connecting piping are readily inspectable. The large hatches in the containment dome and the containment enclosure building allow all capital equipment, including the SG, to be replaced.

SMR-300 features a small fuel pool which is lined with a stainless liner as is conventional in modern nuclear plants. Unfortunately, liners are known to leak in service. For this reason, the fuel racks in the pool are designed to be freestanding; they can be removed, and a liner leak readily fixed if one were to develop. The free-standing racks can then be re-emplaced for use.
The SMR-300 CS operates at ambient pressure with a peak 80 psig in the event of a bounding loss of cooling accident.
SMR-300 is envisaged to have one outage every 18-24 months.

entries.text: The SMR-300 utilizes commercially available fuel assemblies as those employed in existing PWRs today. The fuel assemblies are comprised of a 17 x 17 square lattice of 12-foot fuel rods. The fuel rods are of a standard size and utilize a zirconium-based alloy for cladding. Each fuel rod consists of high density ceramic UO2 fuel pellets stacked within zircaloy cladding that is evacuated, backfilled with helium, and sealed with zircaloy end plugs. Instrumentation/guide tubes are included as part of the fuel assembly. Spacer grids are distributed throughout the assembly to provide structural support for the fuel rods. Dissolved boron is used for reactivity shim and control. The distribution of the uranium enrichment and gadolinia concentration within each fuel assembly is optimized to minimize intra-assembly power peaking to increase margin to thermal-mechanical limits.
The reactor core is designed for an 18-month refueling cycle with a maximum enrichment of 4.95 wt% U235, with the option for shorter or longer cycles depending upon utility requirements.

The core is loaded with sixty-nine (69) fuel assemblies arranged in an octane symmetric pattern. The core includes twenty-five (25) Rod Control Cluster Assemblies (RCCAs) for reactivity and temperature control, which are connected via drive shafts to Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDMs) welded to integrated nozzles on the reactor head.

The SMR-300 is designed to provide unconditional safety with assured cooling of fuel in both the reactor and the spent fuel pool, for all conditions of the plant. In the event of a LOCA, the spent fuel pool is cooled by the PCCS, along with the fuel in the RPV.

entries.text: Key new features of manufacturing, construction or operational challenges:

Individual reactors are to be installed and commissioned in series, creating challenging or impractical construction operations while adjacent to operating reactors in a common reactor pool. Steel lined reactor building pool – such steel lined pools always leak and accordingly have leak detection systems to detect, with controls to limit and remediate such. In the case of the NuScale VOYGR plant, the design does include leak channels and detectors underneath the pool between the liner and the concrete floor of the reactor building foundation. The pool is filled with boric acid with expected leakage to cause concrete erosion and structural material (rebars) to corrode, thereby weakening the structure. Furthermore, there appears to no way repair such eroded/corroded concrete sub-structures, or even any practical way to detect or monitor such …. A big risk for a 60yr investment

Failures of these unique hydraulically operated ECCS valves are one of the most important risk contributors identified in the NuScale PRA. The PRA results and confidence in the safety of the design depend on ensuring that these valves operate reliably. NuScale will perform extensive

qualification testing to provide confidence in the ability of the valves to maintain their required performance after extended periods in an operational environment. Failing to demonstrate such will require a redesign of this safety system.

The integrity and performance of the steam generators have not yet been sufficiently validated because of uncertainties associated with unstable density wave oscillations (DWO) on the steam generator secondary side. Accelerated wear of the alloy 690TT (thermally treated) steam generator tubing material is also a potential concern. Without an ability to repair or replace SG tubes in damaged SG, this could be a fatal flaw.

The coolant in the downcomer will decorate for a range of design basis accidents, including small-break LOCA. The estimated time for the boron concentration to drop below the critical boron concentration in the downcomer for these events is within a few hours. Operator recovery actions raise the possibility of an influx of deborated water into the core, which may result in re-criticality, return to power, and the potential for core damage.

entries.text: The Nuclear Steam Supply System (NSSS) is referred to as the NuScale Power Module (NPM) and consists of a reactor core, two helical-coil Steam Generators (SG), and a pressurizer integrated within the RPV. The RPV is enclosed within a Containment Vessel (CNV) that is partially immersed in the reactor pool. The reactor core is located below the helical-coil SGs inside the RPV. An extremely unique NSSS, the RPV and CNV are constructed and integrated as co-joined vessels in a factory prior to transport to a construction site. The 77 MWe assembled power module is massive and estimated to weigh 850mt. The reactor building crane capacity has been increased to 950mt for the 77 MWe power module.
Two decay heat removal system (DHRS) heat exchangers are major elements of the ECCS and mounted outside the CNV.

The power modules are designed to be disconnected from each respective units' main steam and condensate feed pipes and electric and control connects to allow the modules to be transported within the reactor building to a refueling area.
The reactor vessel internals are not readily removeable, and a steam generator failure would cause a complete loss or replacement of that affected reactor power module.

Each NuScale Power Module (NPM) incorporates two once-through, helical-coil SGs inside the RPV for steam production. The SGs are in the annular space between the reactor hot leg riser and the RPV inside diameter wall. The SG consists of tubes connected to feed and steam plenums with tube sheets. Preheated feedwater enters the lower feed plenum through nozzles on the RPV. As feedwater flows through the interior of the SG tubes, heat is transferred across the SG tube wall from the reactor coolant to the feedwater. The feedwater changes phase and exits the SG as superheated steam.

The NuScale steam generators are unique in that they boil water to produce steam INSIDE (tube-side) the SG tubes, vs more conventional and robust nuclear power plant and boiler designs that convert water to steam OUTSIDE (shell-side).
The SGs and respective steam and feed connections are integrally to the reactor vessel. The SGs cannot be replaced without replacing the reactor vessel.

The NPM design utilizes ECCS valves. The reactor vent valves (RVVs) are located on the reactor vessel pressurizer, and the reactor recirculation valves (RRVs) are located on the reactor vessel downcomer. The RVVs and RRVs are functionally similar in design; however, the RVVs are larger than the RRVs. Each of the ECCS valves is pilot operated by remote-mounted trip and reset solenoid valves located at the reactor containment boundary. The design includes a novel inadvertent actuation block (IAB) feature, located inside containment on each RVV main valve.

entries.text: 5.1 Overview According to NuScale Power, the NuScale Power Module (NPM) is a small, light-water-cooled pressurized- water reactor (PWR). NuScale VOYGR SMR plants are scalable and can be built to accommodate a varying number of NPMs to meet customer’s energy demands. NuScale standard plants include the VOYGR-4 at 308 MW(e), the VOYGR-6 at 462 MW(e), and the VOYGR-12 at 924 MW(e). Each NPM is a self- contained module that operates independently of the other modules in a multi-module configuration. All modules are managed from a single control room. The NuScale design is a modular reactor for electricity production, with the capability for flexible operations to load follow, and for non-electrical process heat applications, including the cogeneration of heat and electricity. The NuScale VOYGR SMR plant design adopts design simplification, proven light-water reactor technology, modular nuclear steam supply system, factory-fabricated power modules, and passive safety systems that allow for unlimited reactor cooling time after a beyond design basis accident without ac or DC power, operator action, or makeup water. There are no design basis accidents that uncover the core or require operator action. The NPM is designed to operate efficiently at full-power conditions using natural circulation as the means of providing core coolant flow, eliminating the need for reactor coolant pumps.

NuScale Power has developed a 12-reactor 600 MWe gross output nuclear power plant, for which it has received 10CFR52 design certification (Feb.2023) from the US NRC. That design has now been heavily modified and resubmitted (Jan.2023) to the US NRC for standard design approval in accord with 10CFR52 for a 6-reactor 462 MWe gross output nuclear power plant called VOYGR USA460. Its licensing status is uncertain owing to its substantially changed design specification relative to the original 600 MWe plant.

entries.text: The Seismic Isolation System is supported by the raft foundation and comprises a series of RC pedestals and aseismic bearings, which in turn support an RC Basemat. The seismic isolation is provided between the Basemat and pedestals by the aseismic bearings, which decouple the horizontal accelerations.

Rolls Royce is pursuing a different strategy with respect to factory manufacturing and modularity, focusing on the use steel-framed Process Clusters within the Reactor Island, and its respective blocks, or areas, while relying heavily on traditional RC materials and methods for major civil structures and construction techniques.

Reactor Island Process Blocks are those buildings and structures around the Containment Support Structure that are assembled in part from 'Process Clusters'. Process clusters are defined as the conglomeration of 'system modules' into discrete structural framing systems, and house mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. System modules are formed from module units and can vary in length depending on the systems within the major Reactor Island Process Blocks: Fuel Block Electrical and I&C Block Fluids Blocks Auxiliary Block Waste Processing Block

A series of ‘process clusters’ are housed within Process Blocks locks within the Reactor Island. Process clusters are defined as the conglomeration of ‘system modules’ into discrete structural framing systems, and house mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. System modules are formed from module units and can vary in length depending on the systems within them.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: A three-loop, close-coupled PWR, the UK SMR provides an estimated power output of 425 MWe from 1358 MWth using industry standard UO2 fuel. Coolant is circulated via three centrifugal Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCP) to three corresponding vertical U-tube Steam Generators (SGs). The design includes multiple active and passive safety systems.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: Strengths are Difficult to Identify: While Rolls Royce claims that 90% of the capital power plant cost will be incurred in a manufacturing factory, this claim appears to be less than credible upon close examination. The available information indicates that Rolls Royce intends to construct a massive cover under which to perform site construction and assembly operations. If true, this claim would be a strength, implying sophisticated and advanced proven module manufacturing practices. There is, however, no proof in Rolls Royce’s literature to substantiate these claims.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: Weaknesses are Apparent: The design relies on conventional PWR CRAs for power control and scram, while lacking bor on for shim and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the 121-fuel assembly core includes 89 control rods, a fuel assembly to control rad assembly (FA/CRA) ratio of 0.75, as compared to typical PWRs with a FA/CRA ratio ~0.4 – introducing a reactivity and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded operation.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: The design includes an active non-safety, low pressure boron injection for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of a transient or design basis earthquake. This secondary shutdown function is provided by the EBI system which delivers boron solution to the RCS. The EBI system operates at low pressure and is therefore dependent on the HPIS

entries.text: NuScale Power submitted the final revision of the NuScale DCA, Revision 5, in July 2020 (ADAMS Accession No. ML20225A071). In August 2020, the NRC issued a final safety evaluation report after the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) performed its final independent review and issued its July 29, 2020, letter to the Commission on its findings and recommendations. The final safety evaluation report is a collection of reports written by the NRC documenting the safety findings from its review of the standard design application, and it reflects all changes resulting from interactions with the ACRS as well as changes in the final version of the DCA. The final safety evaluation report, as elaborated on by the Response to DPO Tasking, reflects that NuScale Power has resolved all technical and safety issues except for the three issues discussed below.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: The NRC identified three issues as not resolved within the meaning of § 52.63(a)(5). There was insufficient information available for the NRC to resolve issues regarding:

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text:
• the shielding wall design in certain areas of the plant,
• the potential for contaminant leakage from the combustible gas monitoring system, and
• the ability of the steam generator tubes to maintain structural and leakage integrity during density wave oscillations in the secondary fluid system, including the method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations from reverse flow.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: Of most relevant significance and concern are issues associated with the steam generator design and associated unresolved density wave oscillation impacts.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: This steam generator design issue stems from the effects of density wave oscillations in the secondary fluid system on steam generator tubes to maintain structural and leakage integrity, including the method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations including reverse flow. Appendix G to 10 CFR part 52, Section VI, "Issue Resolution," clarifies that this issue is not resolved, and states that the COL applicant is responsible for providing the design information to address this issue.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: As a result, NuScale Power has not demonstrated that the flow oscillations that are predicted to occur on the secondary side of the steam generators will not cause failure of the inlet flow restrictors. Structural and leakage integrity of the inlet flow restrictors in the steam generators is necessary to avoid damage to multiple steam generator tubes, caused directly by broken parts or indirectly by unexpected density wave oscillation loads. Damage to multiple steam generator tubes could disrupt normal circulation in the reactor coolant pathway and interfere with the decay heat removal system and the emergency core cooling system, which is relied upon to cool the reactor core in a NuScale power module. The failure of multiple steam generator tubes resulting from failure of an inlet flow restrictor has not been included within the scope of the NuScale accident analyses in DCA Part 2, Tier 1, Chapter 15. Therefore, the NRC concludes that NuScale Power has not demonstrated compliance with 10 CFR 52.47(a)(2)(iv) and Appendix A to 10 CFR part 50, GDC 4 and GDC 31, relative to potential impacts on steam generator tube integrity from inlet flow restrictor failure.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: According to the NRC, the NuScale Power design requires a method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations including reverse flow. NuScale power did not provide verification and validation for its proposed method of analysis to demonstrate it is appropriate for this purpose, and accordingly the Design Certification includes a carve out for this critical item.

entries.section_title: Steam Generator Density Wave Oscillation (DWO) - USNRC codified remarks:
entries.text: The design and performance of the NuScale Power Module SGs are not sufficiently validated because of uncertainties associated with unstable DWO on the SG secondary side (inside the SG tubes), the NRC stability map differs greatly from the NuScale stability map, Accelerated wear of alloy 690TT SG tubing material is a potential concern, Concerns that the TF-2 test apparatus is not a prototypical test for the NuScale SG design.

entries.section_title: Steam Generator Density Wave Oscillation (DWO) - USNRC codified remarks:
entries.text: The NRC Safety Evaluation Report (SER) did not finalize review of the NuScale analysis methodology of secondary side instabilities in the helical coil SGs.

entries.section_title: Steam Generator Density Wave Oscillation (DWO) - USNRC codified remarks:
entries.text: Furthermore, the NRC created a COL Item 3.9-14 addressing this DWO matter: "A COL applicant that references the NuScale Power Plant design certification will develop an evaluation methodology for the analysis of secondary-side instabilities in the steam generator design. This methodology will address the identification of potential density wave oscillations in the steam generator tubes, and qualification of the applicable portions of the reactor coolant system integral reactor pressure vessel and steam generator given the occurrence of density wave oscillations, including the effects of reverse fluid flows within the tubes."

Regarding the recently submitted Standard Design Approval Application (SDAA) for the uprated 77 MWe power module (reference FSAR for 50 MWe module), the NRC conveyed the below observations in a letter to NuScale Power on Nov.15.2022, Subject: Preapplication Readiness Assessment Report of The NuScale Power, LLC Standard Design Approval Draft Application:

"In conducting the Readiness Assessment, the staff used a phased approach with groupings of relevant chapters and sections. The collection of observations in the report is organized by chapter and any chapters that did not have observations are absent from the report. Overall, the staff has identified several challenging and/or significant issues that could be focus areas for the SDAA acceptance and/or safety review. While there has been some early engagement on these topics, the staff would encourage continued engagement on these topics until the SDAA's submittal. entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: NuScale is a large reactor installation consisting of individual reactors each rated at 77 MWe making its total rated capacity between 308 MWe and 924 MWe. All reactors are housed in a single reactor building the size of a football field. In as much as each reactor is immersed in a large volume of borated water, it can be safely stated that the NuScale design does not suffer from the risk of a criticality accident such as those that befell Chernobyl or Fukushima.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Power Output Flexibility NuScale requires a fixed cluster of reactors to be built as a single plant, each reactor with its own turbogenerator and waste heat rejection system. Recently the reactor designer has announced the decision to abandon the 50 MWe module and increase the capacity of each of the six reactors comprising the standard plant design to 77 MWe which will make it a 462 MWe installation. Abandoning the 50 MWe design results in a substantial re-work of the design and noting much of the licensing work over the past decade will have to be re-performed.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Reactor Performance Stability The most critical performance metric, thermal hydraulic stability of the RCS, has been questioned by the US Regulator because the reactor is configured to boil water inside the helical tubes of the SG driven by natural circulation, and has been shown analytically to experience density wave oscillations. The risk of unequal flow among the helical tubes of different radii of curvature in the bundle, the small quantity of water in the tubes at any time instant and the lack of control on the expanding volume of steam created inside each tube raise concerns about tube dry-out and flow instability. Classical heat transfer equipment design theory supports boiling outside the tube under natural convection conditions. NuScale has run tests that have thus far failed to solve this potentially crippling drawback. Currently, the issue is unresolved.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Fuel Design NuScale uses half-length PWR fuel which is new in the industry. A small benefit of a short fuel design would be reduced risk of fretting damage of the tubes.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Refueling of the Reactor The refueling of the reactor in NuScale is an elaborate operation. The combined reactor module including its Containment Vessel (CV) and Reactor Vessel (RV) is lifted from its two protruding trunnions to transport the module for maintenance and refueling. To prepare a NuScale reactor module for refueling, all feedwater, steam piping, electrical and instrument lines must be disconnected to allow the combined vessels to be lifted free of many attachments. The freed CV including its RV, weighing approximately 850 metric tons, is next moved through a central aisle in the reactor building and brought to a reactor refueling stand where the lower containment and reactor vessels are disassembled. The act of unfastening the massive flange bolts must occur some 25 meters under water in the presence of an intense radiation field, making it necessary to employ a robot. In multiple moves and heavy lifts, the bottoms of CV and RV heads are remotely disconnected from their vessels so that the upper part of the combined CV and RV can be lifted and set aside, providing access to the fuel for change-out. After refueling the reactor core, the process must be re-traced: the RV reassembled and CV lower head replaced and carried back to its operating station where all piping, electrical, mechanical and instrumentation connections are re-made, and the CV is evacuated of water (set under vacuum). This operation involves many firsts in the industry which raises the un-fastening of the CV and the RV flanges featuring large bolts is only one stripped thread from a total stop of operations; leakage of any of the many gaskets that must be installed to join the pipes, and other connections can prevent reactor’s re-start, etc. No one has attempted the feat required to complete such a complex re-fueling; only time will tell if this “move the loaded CV” strategy is viable. The drop accident

The entire reactor coolant system sits under a 25-meter pool of borated water in a VOYGR plant. The RV is entirely inaccessible as is the steam generator. If they fail, there is no obvious means to fix or replace them. The power plant design includes numerous first of a kind components, instruments, valves, and electrical penetrations that are not environmentally qualified for use in the nuclear industry today.

In the NuScale power plant, the reactor building pool liner covers the entire extent of the football field-sized reactor building cavity which means numerous liner seams. The cavity liner is not accessible for repair only if a leak develops. Likewise, the NuScale helical coil steam generators are accessible for repair only by repair of underwater robotics, and the SGs are not replaceable – they are integral to the RV shell.

A NuScale power module containment operates under full vacuum, which makes its internal temperature rise to over 300 C. It is not apparent how the instrumentation and wiring in the containment will fare in a heavy radiation and hot temperature field. Furthermore, the NuScale power module containment must be designed to an accident condition pressure of over 10000 psi. Hydro-testing the CV for 10000 psi pressure at each outage is likely to be extremely arduous.

NuScale reactor refueling involves complex operations. A 12 module VOYGR reactor building must perform 6 refueling operations each year, meaning the plant will have virtually continuous outages. Performing refueling on a module while the adjacent ones are operating, may be viewed as inherently hazardous by experienced plant operators, and transporting a fueled reactor via heavy lift past operating reactors is likely to be disallowed in some regulatory regimes.
The NuScale plant must be located next to a river, lake, or sea. It cannot be deployed away from a natural source of water.
The approach to manage used fuel produced by VOYGR plants has not been articulated by NuScale Power at this time.

NuScale Power is a new company; it has no customers or sales revenue and hence, no performance record. Its sole income is from the funds contributed by its equity holders and the US DOE, and may experience ownership changes as it continues its search for new investors to sustain its operations.
