entries.text: The above-mentioned drawbacks of large reactors have prompted industry to seek the obverse of largeness, namely small reactors, defined empirically as a reactor that has less than 300 MWe design basis output. It was reasoned that because the “small” reactor has a small inventory of thermal energy at any one time, the dissipation of that heat during a postulated loss of coolant accident should be manageable. Also, a small reactor ought to be built and commissioned in a relatively short time, and the cost of capital per unit output ought to be smaller than large reactors. Proponents of small reactors also hoped that they would be largely factory built, maximizing the benefits inherent in serial manufacturing while minimizing site construction costs. The notion of manufacturing most parts and sub-components in a factory and limiting site construction to a minimum was conceived as the antidote to the awful labor efficiency at construction sites. Thus, the term “modular” became attached to small reactors, resulting in the now commonly used term “small modular reactor,” and its acronym “SMR.”

In this report, Holtec’s attention is focused on the light water SMRs which, because of the maturity of light water technology, hold the promise of immediate deployment. This report accordingly focuses on the merits and demerits of four SMR technologies which have progressed their designs and gained varying levels of acceptance. Because none has been yet deployed, Holtec’s appraisal is founded on the design features that define the prognosis for their future performance based on solid science, not conjectures and speculations. The candidate reactor designs considered are listed in Table 2-1 below, with reported or estimated* net electric outputs.
Table 2-1: SMR Technologies Considered in this Report Copyright Holtec International © 2025, all rights reserved

Critical features are noted in Table 2-2, to evaluate and compare candidate technologies as possible. Each technology is presented and discussed in a distinct section of the report, in sections 3 through 6. A summary assessment relative to these critical features (to the extent practical via the available public information for each) can be found in four tables in section 7. Those tables include weighted scores of metrics envisaged to be roughly in descending order of significance to an NPP owner, with a maximum score that can be earned for each metric (critical feature or parameter).
Holtec International formed SMR LLC in 2011 with the mission to develop an inherently safe and economically viable small modular reactor to de-carbonize electric power generation around the world.

The result of the long development effort is the Holtec SMR-300 pressurized light-water small modular reactor which generates approximately 1050 MWt, with a minimum of 340 MWe net electric output. The Standard Plant design is a twin-reactor configuration with shared non-safety systems and structures, to optimize cost and power plant flexibility for a cost-effective SMR power plant producing 680 MWe net (minimum 640) electric output. All safety-related components in the reactor coolant system are passive. Specifically, the pumps used to boost thermal performance are not safety related. The power plant relies upon simple and passive systems to achieve its absolute safety goals and competitive economic performance. Among its key attributes summarized herein are unconditional safety, absence of reliance on a local water source, and a convenient long-term management solution of its spent used fuel. Progressive nuclear companies such as Mitsubishi Electric Corporation (Japan and US), Hyundai Engineers & Constructors (South Korea), and Framatome (France and US) play important roles in the Holtec SMR-300’s development, complementing the company’s R&D team as needed for expedited completion of the detailed design and licensing documents needed for plant construction and operation.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is an innovative pressurized water reactor (PWR) that has natural circulation as an integral feature of its performance which is central to its ability to cope with all conceivable accident conditions. The Holtec SMR-300 reactor is also characterized by supplemental recirculation pumps situated between the steam generator and the reactor vessel in each of its two cold legs. These pumps serve to boost the velocity and turbulence level in the core and the steam generator tubes leading to high coolant flow rates and heat transfer coefficients for a high-power density light water reactor coolant system. These pumps are a part of the reactor coolant system’s pressure boundary but are not safety-related system because their failure does not threaten the radiological, structural or criticality safety of the reactor.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The evolutionary features of the Holtec SMR-300 ensure a long service life by ameliorating life limiting causative factors such as stress corrosion cracking, erosion, wear, neutron embrittlement and flow induced vibration. The likelihood of core damage has been rendered negligible with improved operational reliability as compared to conventional reactors and is informed by lessons learned from over seven decades of light water reactor (LWR) operations.

entries.section_title: 3.2 Essential Features of the Holtec SMR-300
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 owes its unconditional assured safety to the thermosiphon-actuated circulation of its reactor coolant and engineered safety systems that remove heat from the reactor core and spent fuel pool by passive means in the event of postulated accidents. No operator action is required to mitigate events deemed to be credible for consideration in the safety analysis by regulatory agencies. The Holtec SMR-300 leverages gravity-driven convective and conductive heat transfer to provide for an unlimited post-accident coping period. The plant design provides redundant and diverse pathways to reject heat from the core and does so by incorporating only existing and proven materials and environmentally qualified components, penetrations, and instruments in the plant design.

entries.text: The Containment Inerting System precludes the combustion of hydrogen and prevents damage to essential equipment and structures. It establishes and maintains an inert atmosphere (4% dry-basis-percent (DB%) oxygen) within containment during plant operating modes except during shutdown for refueling/maintenance and for limited periods of time during low power operation for inspection. The system also maintains a slightly positive pressure in containment to prevent air (oxygen) in-leakage into the inerted spaces from the Reactor Building.

Composite (DP-SC) modules are being utilized for the basement, walls, floors, and roof of the Reactor Building. Before concrete casting, the diaphragm plates and steel faceplates provide stiffness and strength to the empty steel modules. DP-SC modules are stiff and stable in the empty module configuration due to the continuous support provided by the diaphragm plates to the steel faceplates. After concrete casting, the diaphragm plates provide structural integrity to the composite section by preventing delamination of the concrete core. Furthermore, diaphragm plates provide composite action between the steel faceplates and the concrete infill, and out-of-plane shear reinforcement for the composite section. Additional ties or shear stud anchors may be used to anchor the steel faceplates to the concrete infill and control faceplate local buckling.

DP-SC panels are fabricated in factories in sizes that can be shipped to the construction site via truck, rail or barge depending on the location of the site. The panels are then assembled into modules at site before being lifted into final position. A multi-layered water proofing application is utilized to ensure leak tightness. A waterproof membrane is installed between the shaft wall and the DP-SC outer plate for a first protective layer. A grouting or concrete medium is then placed between the membrane and the steel liner. The DP-SC outer plate provides an additional layer of sealing.

A NuScale power module containment operates under full vacuum, which makes its internal temperature rise to over 300 C. It is not apparent how the instrumentation and wiring in the containment will fare in a heavy radiation and hot temperature field.

Furthermore, the NuScale power module containment must be designed to an accident condition pressure of over 10000 psi. Hydro-testing the CV for 10000 psi pressure at each outage is likely to be extremely arduous.

NuScale reactor refueling involves complex operations. A 12 module VOYGR reactor building must perform 6 refueling operations each year, meaning the plant will have virtually continuous outages. Performing refueling on a module while the adjacent ones are operating, may be viewed as inherently hazardous by experienced plant operators, and transporting a fueled reactor via heavy lift past operating reactors is likely to be disallowed in some regulatory regimes.
The NuScale plant must be located next to a river, lake, or sea. It cannot be deployed away from a natural source of water.
The approach to manage used fuel produced by VOYGR plants has not been articulated by NuScale Power at this time.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: GEH describes the BWRX-300 as requiring no core injection for LOCA mitigation, while noting the design includes high pressure injection via the fine motion control drive system. The BWRX-300 Emergency Core Cooling System relies entirely on the ICS to supply water and handle over pressure with fail safe (closed) double isolation valves integrated to reactor vessel for steam, feed, ICS exit and ICS return pipes.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: There is no additional water makeup other than active injection via the FMCRds. The containment is not sized to handle LOCA enthalpy if the ICS fails, or in case an RPV isolation valve were to break.

entries.section_title: KEY RISKS, Challenges, Potential Fatal Flaws
entries.text: The plant safety basis depends on the reliable integrity of the RPV double isolation valves. In accord with 10 CFR 50.46, an applicant can be expected to demonstrate the reactor fuel will survive a double-ended break of the most limiting valve. The design appears unable to withstand this postulated break, which would result in an unattenuated loss of cooling accident and potential core meltdown and associated radiological release.

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: The BWRX-300 control blades are used for power control, fuel reactivity management and power shaping, and for shutdown, startup, and scram. As such, the basic design does not include a second independent means to shut down the reactor, as expected and required by many competent regulators. While the design includes a Boron Injection System (BIS), this system will be credited to add negative reactivity but has no dedicated independent instrumentation or actuation logic and is not automated. Accordingly, it is not a credited shut down system according to today's interpreted regulations in the US, Canada, the UK, and other internationally regulated nuclear domains. Furthermore, it is not obvious how the plant can achieve assured safe shutdown for seven days without operator actions as the developer claims, as the BIS included in the plant design for an Anticipated Transient Without Scram (ATWS) is not automated and requires operator actions to actuate if or when needed. The FOIAK application in Canada will need to overcome the matter that Canadian regulations plainly require two independent shutdown systems.

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: There is a logical basis for Canadian regulations requiring independent shutdown systems, owing to the nature of CANDU reactors, and accordingly an expectation that GEH will be able to overcome this rule:

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: CANDU power plants have a positive void coefficient of reactivity. As a result, power can increase rapidly following postulated LOCA. This design characteristic is the primary driver for having two shutdown systems in current CANDUs. In addition, CANDU accident analysis for LOCA events defines performance requirements for key reactivity control measures (e.g., shutdown system speed and reactivity depth). Like most LWRs, the BWRX-300 has a negative void coefficient of reactivity, whereby void formations decrease reactivity and tend to shut LWRs down. For these LWRs, many of the traditional safety analysis issues in CANDU LOCA do not exhibit power excursions. However, for BWRs, the dominant reactivity phenomena that leads to a potential power increase is void reduction rather than void formation. Since anticipated operational

occurrence events such as a turbine trip or an RPV isolation can quickly collapse voids in an operating BWR, these events feature prominently in BWR safety analysis and may emphasize regulatory insistence for a second independent shutdown system in the BWRX-300.

Furthermore, Canadian and International regulations requiring independence between process systems and shutdown systems. The BWRX-300 control blades are used for power level control, fuel reactivity management and power shaping, and for shutdown, startup, and scram. As such, the basic design does not satisfy the fundamental Canadian and European requirement for independence of process and shutdown systems.

GEH is attempting to mechanically eliminate all substantial actual and postulated loss of coolant accidents - contrary to regulatory requirements to evaluate credible or postulated LOCA for pipe and valve connections at terminal ends - by designing a fail process system of components and operations that eliminate the possibility of saving or recovering the reactor in case such a postulated loss of coolant accident was to occur. To do so, they include a novel concept of double isolation valves integrated to the reactor pressure vessel for all piping penetrations larger than 2".

To do so, the BWRX-300 incorporates a novel feature: isolating the reactor vessel to protect against LOCA by placing two integral RPV isolation valves on each major RPV connection, e.g., between the reactor vessel and each of the steam, feed, isolation condenser feed and return pipes inside containment. As the designer of these valves, GEH (with no apparent consideration or component construction or qualification experience to Holtec's knowledge), will need to describe and prove, verify, and validate (V&V) the control system, power supply and failure modes for these new components, since any common cause failure will essentially invalidate many claims and conclusions in the designer's safety case. Any leak, crack or break in valve casing in the inner most isolation valve for any of these numerous reactor-vessel-integrated valves would cause a break or leak that cannot be isolated by the BWRX-300 engineered safety systems. While details of the RPV vessel are not available for public scrutiny, it is not clear how GEH intends to develop, test, validate and license these FOAK safety components, demonstrating to the competent licensing authorities that, as a minimum, that the integrity of the valve bodies, welds, packings, stems, and seals will be of the same mechanical and operational reliability as the RPV vessel itself. No such valve can be dedicated from a commercial quality class than to one designed explicitly to ASME Section-III requirements for nuclear power reactors; these nuclear valves do not exist in the market for this type of application, and as such, the deployment and licensing claims made by the designer are very optimistic. For context, Holtec expects that a future applicant wishing to build the GEH BWRX-300 via 10CFR50 in the US (for example) will have a heavy lift satisfying the intent and acceptance criteria of the 10CFR 50.46 ECCS rule, even in the case GEH is able to construct these numerous and different sized valves in accord with the ASME code. GEH claims in public facing documents and presentations that this breakthrough innovation - these integral nuclear reactor vessel isolation valves - are patented and approved via a USNRC Licensing Topical Report. In fact, no such approval has been granted by the NRC for use of these isolation valves, lacking any proof, verification or prior nuclear OPEX.

The BWRX-300 includes three identical trains of an Isolation Condenser safety system to remove decay heat, protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from over pressurization, and to provide makeup water in case of AOOs and loss of coolant accidents. By lacking a second diverse engineered safety feature to ensure these safety functions for all anticipated or postulated accidents, the plant design may not be able to adequately address the intent and application of national regulations and normative standards.
10CFR50 Appendix A General Design Criterion 35, for example, requires 'suitable redundancy in components and features, and suitable interconnections, leak detection, isolation, and containment

entries.text: Rolls-Royce claims its UK SMR has been developed to deliver a market driven, affordable, low carbon, energy generation capability. Rolls Royce claims that rapid, certain, and repeatable build is enhanced through site layout optimization and maximizing modular build, standardization, and commoditization. The UK SMR is primarily intended to supply baseload electricity for both coastal and inland siting. The design can be configured to support other heat-requiring or cogeneration applications, as well as provide a primary, carbon free, power source to produce e-fuels.

The main nuclear structures are associated with the reactor island. These include the containment building, fuel and control building, radioactive waste building, access building and auxiliary building.

A hazard shield is included in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide protection against radioactivity release due to external hazards. The bounding case for the hazard shield is based on an aircraft impact hazard, aiming to ensure confinement of fuel, prevention of criticality, protection of reactor shutdown and cooling systems and protection of monitoring systems. The hazard shield is engineered to ensure all class 1 SSCs functions are protected from that bounding aircraft hazard ( e.g., post A1 fire and mechanical shock and LOLA).

The Hazard Shield is a large, reinforced concrete (RC) structure that protects critical SSCs from external hazards, including accidental and malicious aircraft impacts. It is approximately 91 m long, 61 m wide and extends 45 m above ground level. The Hazard Shield houses the Containment Internal Structures, Interspace, Fueling Block, Electrical, Control and Instrumentation (EC&I) Systems and Fluid Systems blocks.

The containment building holds a containment vessel that encloses the reactor, providing confinement of radiation sources and preventing release to the environment in accident conditions. The containment vessel is a large steel pressure vessel, designed to American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) III specifications, which contains the components of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS). The vessel is cylindrical and includes a top and bottom dome. The bottom dome is embedded into concrete and supported upon the aseismic bearing. The vessel is approximately 32m in diameter, 37m in height with an internal free air volume of around 18,000m³.

entries.text: NSSS Nuclear Steam Supply System The nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) consists of a reactor core, two helical coil steam generators, and a pressurizer within a reactor pressure vessel (RPV). The NSSS is enclosed in an approximately cylindrical containment vessel (CNV) — the RPV and CNV are integrated to form a NuScale Power Module (NPM). Each of up to twelve ~800–900 metric ton NPMs are hung from module supports built into the reactor building walls and foundation. The containment is evacuated and maintained at near-vacuum during power operations to reduce convective heat transfer losses from the reactor to the CNV and surrounding pool of water and forms an integral part of the reactor’s Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS) system, providing pressure relief, and condensate return to the reactor vessel via natural circulation following a loss of cooling accident. The CNV is immersed in a large reactor pool, which provides an assured passive heat sink for containment heat removal under LOCA conditions. Each power module is connected to a dedicated turbine-generator unit and balance-of-plant systems. The 50 MWe 12-NPM plant is rated at 600 MWe gross output, while a recent 6-NPM VOYGR plant design is rated at 462 MWe gross electric output using 77 MWe power modules.

Reactor Core The core configuration for the NPM consists of 37 fuel assemblies and 16 control rod assemblies. The fuel assembly design is modelled from an atypical 17 x 17 PWR fuel assembly with 24 guide tube locations for control rod fingers and a central instrument tube. The assembly is nominally half the height of standard plant fuel and is supported by five spacer grids. The fuel is UO2 with Gd2O3 as a burnable absorber homogeneously mixed within the fuel for select rod locations. The U235 enrichment is below the current U.S. manufacturer limit of 4.95% enrichment.

Reactivity Control Reactivity control in each NPM is achieved mainly through soluble boron in the primary coolant and 16 control rod assemblies. The control rods are organized into two groups: a control group, and a shutdown group. The control group, consisting of four rods symmetrically located in the core, functions as a regulating group that is used during normal plant operation to control reactivity. The shutdown group comprising 12 rods is used during shutdown and scram events. Control rods absorber material is B4C.

Reactor Coolant System The RCS is a subsystem of the NPM that provides for the circulation of the primary coolant relying on natural circulation. Hence, the RCS does not require reactor coolant pumps or an external piping system. The RCS includes the RPV and integral pressurizer, integral helical coil steam generators, the reactor vessel internals, the reactor safety valves, RCS piping inside the containment vessel and others.

Reactor Pressure Vessel and Internals The RPV consists of a cylindrical steel vessel with an inside diameter of 2.7 m, an overall height of approximately 17.7 m, and is designed for an operating pressure of 13.8 MPa. The upper and lower heads are torispherical and the lower portion of the vessel has flanges just above the core region to provide access for refueling. To be clear, unlike conventional light water reactors (PWRs and BWRs) which for maintenance and refueling are disassembled in-place and from the top down, the NuScale NPM (RPV + CNV) is transported by large crane within the reactor building to be disassembled from the bottom up, unbolting and lifting the integrated upper reactor and internals and containment to expose the core for refueling. entries.text: Fukushima Daiichi OPEX will lead to reasonable concerns and attract certain scrutiny of accidents and safety system and isolation valve(s) reliability leading to severe core damage. The BWRX design presumably includes design improvements to prevent the ICS isolation that occurred at the Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 reactor, leading to core melting and a large radiation release to the public. Without a complete and reliable PSA model and analyses, designed, engineered, constructed, and tested isolation valves to inform associated reliability estimates, it is unknown whether this ICS design will be sufficient for regulatory approval of the overall plant design. If the BWRX-300 PSA can confirm that ICS reliability is high enough to practically eliminate severe core damage leading to a large release, then fundamental redesign of the reactor and engineered safety features and reactor protection system will not be required. On the other hand, if regulators conclude that ICS failure probability is not sufficiently low to preclude a large release, then licensing scrutiny will focus on containment robustness and function under severe accident conditions, and the plant and containment and ECCS may likely need to be redesigned.

entries.section_title: FOAK Application Envelope for Safety Analysis Codes – Methods and Models
entries.text: The BWRX-300, while representing the tenth generation of GE’s family of reactors, is undoubtedly a first-of-a-kind reactor, that relies on natural circulation for its assured operation and safety, with a single passive decay heat removal and over pressure protection system, and a fundamental different approach to system design, safety system components, and plant safety logic than prior licensed and operated BWRs. GEH design, safety system components, and plant safety logic than prior licensed and operated BWRs.

currently employs USNRC approved safety analysis and design codes (e.g., TRACG, PANACII, PRIME, etc.) to calculate fundamental thermal hydraulic and material parameters for operating and licensed BWRs and uses those same best estimate tools to calculate the same with estimated margins to limits for the BWRX-300 as well, for normal operations, AOOS and DBAs. The approved application envelopes associated with those codes may not, and in some cases certainly do not encompass all the BWRX-300 operating conditions, as they have not been proven to calculate actual or benchmarked BWRX-300 critical parameters with uncertainties. Absent relevant OPEX for this unique BWR plant - its reactor and engineered safety system configuration and design - a separate and integral effects test program will most certainly be required by competent regulators in North America and Europe, yet no such test plan has been described or committed by GEH publicly to Holtec's knowledge. GEH's approach appears to be one to convince regulators to accept the design based on prior art, BWR OPEX, and importantly the ESBWR .... albeit noting that design has never been built or operated. Assuming regulators will accept the best estimate code calculations without accounting for operational variations and modeling uncertainties is a risky proposition.

Some examples regarding uncertainty: coolant flow rate distribution in the core through each fuel channel will be based on hydraulic resistance and its distribution along the assembly channel and including the orifice at the bottom of the assembly, and with the respective void fraction/two-phase multiplier for each channel, as there is close coupling between bundle power, hydraulic loss coefficients and void fraction. Reactor physics will be affected due to the strong coupling between thermal hydraulics and reactor physics as a function of the reactor's negative void coefficient, and due to design basis accidents, which collapse voids in the core.

Also note: a natural circulation BWR is susceptible to coupled nuclear thermal hydraulic instability, and Holtec believes GEH will have a substantial amount of test/qualification work to gain regulator acceptance of their methods here, particularly during operation of the ICS/ECCS system.

Another unusual aspect of the design that will challenge safety certainty is the fact that ICS condensate return is to the chimney above the core instead of the traditional way of returning ICS flow to the downcomer to enhance natural circulation in BWRs. The current approach for the BWRX-300 could impede natural circulation flow after a LOCA/scram, or as a minimum require a scale testing program to validate new phenomenon associated with this unique RCS geometry and injection/flow path.

Adding cold ICS return condensate water into the chimney region impairs and can completely stop natural circulation, potentially severely impairing fuel cooling. The ICS in existing BWRs returns condensate water to the downcomer - whether the BWRX-300 configuration will be effective cannot be determined from OPEX for existing reactors which do not envelope the BWRX-300 design. Impairing or stopping natural circulation would result in counter-current flow from the chimney into the fuel region. Scaled experimental evidence is necessary to ensure adequate fuel cooling during DBA's and to ensure core stability, requiring accurate modelling/experiments and quantitative validation of counter-current flow in complex geometries. The current design of decay heat ECCS seems akin to shutting off or slowing down the recirculation pumps during accidents in traditional BWRs that require pressure relief or emergency core cooling.

The plant design results in a hot (radioactive) BOP, whereby most of the plant is isolated and can't be maintained or serviced while the reactor is operating. And radioactive steam is seen as a serious limitation for process heat applications (as compared to clean PWR steam).

The ICS heat exchangers and spent fuel pool are located outside the primary containment, on top of the reactor building, making that safety system and radioactive fuel susceptible to being targetable by drone or shape charge - with no way to cool the reactor or provide makeup if ICS fails or breaches.

entries.text: Mitsubishi Electric Company (MELCO) is working closely with Holtec to optimize the Holtec SMR-300 Instrumentation and Control (I&C) systems and components pertaining to the Plant Control System (PCS) and Plant Safety System (PSS), which together form the operating system for the plant. The Holtec SMR-300 incorporates the Mitsubishi Electric Total Advanced Controller (MELTAC) architecture developed by MELCO.

MELTAC is a simplified and highly integrated 2-safety division, 4-channel distributed control system. The design includes significant automation (e.g., no operator action required for postulated accidents) and completely computer-based procedures. MELTAC has undergone extensive human system interface integration testing and is licensed and deployed around the world. MELCO and their MELTAC platform

The Holtec SMR-300 is a light water PWR reactor that utilizes borated water in its primary side operating in a closed loop. The reactor, steam generator and pressurizer assemblage is configured to produce a gravity-driven circulation of the reactor coolant where the heat energy generated in the core is extracted from the reactor coolant in the steam generator. In normal plant operating mode, the rate of steam production is developed by the booster pumps connecting the Steam Generator to the reactor vessel. The booster pumps are sized to quadruple the through-flow of the reactor coolant (as compared to the natural circulation flow rate), enabling the core to be operated with an efficient uranium burn-up and a corresponding heat generation rate.

The primary coolant circulating through the Once-Through Steam Generator (OTSG) produces superheated steam, and a large pressurizer volume ensures operational reliability while eliminating the need for Power Operated Relief Valves (PORVs). The once through design also significantly reduces the accumulation of contaminants (i.e., crud) typical to recirculating-type steam generators, increasing service life.

The hot leg of the reactor coolant system consists of two parallel pipes emanating from the shrouded region of the core and running parallel to the body of the OTSG, ending at the inlet nozzles located in the top header of the OTSG. There are no RPV penetrations below the RCS safety injection nozzles.

The Holtec SMR-300 has a considerably larger water volume to power ratio compared to traditional PWRs. This results in a large heat removal buffer for transients due to the large SG shell-side volume (with secondary flow outside the SG tubes).

entries.section_title: Emergency Core Cooling Isolation Condenser System (ICS)
entries.text: The ECCS for the BWRX-300 is the Isolation Condenser System (ICS). The ICS removes decay heat after any reactor isolation and shutdown from power operations under normal or abnormal conditions. The ICS consists of three independent loops each containing a heat exchanger (HX) and isolation condenser (IC) with capacity of approximately 33 MWth. The ICS tubes condense steam from the RPV on the inside surface and transfer heat on the outside surface to the IC pool which is at atmospheric pressure. This steam condensation and gravity allow BWRX-300 to cool itself for a minimum of seven days without power or operator action.
Safety relief valves have been eliminated from the reactor coolant system. The ICS provides over pressure protection and decay heat removal with water makeup to the RCS after a LOCA.

The BWRX-300 design attempts to eliminate non-isolable LOCAs by utilizing novel, redundant RIVs integral to the RPV. All fluid pipes systems inside containment >50mm in diameter are equipped with double isolation valves integrated within the RPV ASME Section-III code boundary.

The BWRX-300 Primary Containment Vessel (PCV) encloses the RPV, provides radiation shielding and acts as a boundary for radioactive released from the RPV. It is integral to and surrounded by the Reactor Building (RB). The PCV is dry and is located mostly below grade.

There is no suppression pool or makeup water inside containment. The BWRX-300 containment is a vertical cylinder approximately 18 meters in diameter and 38 meters high. It comprises a Steel-Plate Composite Containment Vessel (SCCV), consisting of steel-plate composite cylindrical wall, basemat, and top slab, and a steel containment closure head. The containment structure is completely enclosed within a deeply embedded reactor building and includes personnel/equipment hatches and containment penetrations. The SCCV is integrated with the reactor building and the integrated structure is supported by a common steel-plate composite basemat. The design includes a nitrogen-inerted containment atmosphere during most operating modes. The containment has provisions for personnel access during plant outages to perform maintenance, inspections, and tests for critical parts, including the novel RIV, and has a design life of 60 years.

entries.text: The reactor building houses the NuScale Power Modules (NPMs) in a large subterranean reactor pool. The building is a seismic Category-1 structure, constructed with rebar reinforced concrete. The building is approximately 100m long and 50m wide and includes a large steel-lined pool of borated water, within which the NPMs (RPV + CNV) are suspended from the interior walls of the building. This pool of water provides the plant's ultimate heat sink and further provides reactivity control for the reactor during accidents or refueling, and the spent fuel pool.
Regardless of the number of modules, the same major capital civil and mechanical structures, crane and refueling and disassembly area and equipment are required for each VOYGR plant.

The Nuclear Steam Supply System (NSSS) is referred to as the NuScale Power Module (NPM) and consists of a reactor core, two helical-coil Steam Generators (SG), and a pressurizer integrated within the RPV. The RPV is enclosed within a Containment Vessel (CNV) that is partially immersed in the reactor pool. The reactor core is located below the helical-coil SGs inside the RPV. An extremely unique NSSS, the RPV and CNV are constructed and integrated as co-joined vessels in a factory prior to transport to a construction site. The 77 MWe assembled power module is massive and estimated to weigh 850mt. The reactor building crane capacity has been increased to 950mt for the 77 MWe power module.
Two decay heat removal system (DHRS) heat exchangers are major elements of the ECCS and mounted outside the CNV.

The power modules are designed to be disconnected from each respective units' main steam and condensate feed pipes and electric and control connects to allow the modules to be transported within the reactor building to a refueling area.
The reactor vessel internals are not readily removeable, and a steam generator failure would cause a complete loss or replacement of that affected reactor power module.

entries.text: This report (updated Aug 2025) documents a comparison of several competing light water SMR technologies and associated power plants using public domain information, including US NRC and UK ONR websites (Holtec, GEH, Rolls Royce, NuScale Power), to evaluate the relative merits, strengths, and weaknesses of each SMR technology. This comparative assessment focusing on three US and one UK SMR vendor technologies, with a discourse on the essential features and distinguishing aspects of Holtec's SMR-300. These technologies are (i) Holtec International's SMR-300, in a standard design twin-reactor configuration (ii) GE-Hitachi's single-reactor BWR-X-300, (iii) NuScale Power's multi-reactor VOYGR, and (iv) Rolls Royce's single-reactor UK SMR. While the AP300 SMR is on offer from Westinghouse, very little information is available, via published public or government documents or websites, to sufficiently inform this comparison. As such, the AP300 is not assessed herein. Furthermore, this update includes no new information or changes to the NuScale VOYGR design assessment that was provided in the Nov.2023 version of this document. At the time of that writing, the estimated delivered cost of the NuScale VOYGR plant had exceeded $20,000 per kilowatt electricity, leading to the cancellation of that first US project. The next update to this report will incorporate a contemporary evaluation of the latest NuScale design approved via USNRC Standard Design Approval.

Section 1 of this report provides a brief Overview of each technology. Section 2 defines Critical Features that are important to assess any SMR, and to evaluate and compare candidate technologies as objectively as possible. Each technology is presented and discussed in a distinct section of the report. A summary comparison of the technologies evaluated herein will be presented relative to these critical features to the extent practical via the available public information for each technology. Sections 3 through 6 present Differentiating Features and/or novel systems, components or licensing approaches of each technology assessed, and to characterize their respective overall practical viability and technological readiness for commercial construction and operations. Section 7 articulates Notable Attributes of each technology from an Owner's Perspective, and Section 8 provides the report's Conclusions with a discussion on SMR Power Plant Scale, including comparisons of power block and power plant areas and land use per MWe for the technologies assessed in this update.

Design and licensing information via US NRC and UK ONR web sites provides much of the information assessed in this report. Exhibits and narrative excerpts to this report are sourced from GEH, Rolls Royce, NuScale Power and Holtec International reference documents1. NuScale is not pursuing a Generic Design Assessment in the UK, and Westinghouse has not released public information, or is not sufficiently advanced in either US or UK pre-application reviews to facilitate available useful design information for this assessment.

The Holtec SMR-300, GEH BWRX-300, Rolls Royce UK SMR, and (possibly) Westinghouse AP300 technologies and power plants are being developed actively for commercial projects in North America and global markets. Little is known about Westinghouse and Rolls Royce aspirations or project developments in the US. Rolls Royce was singularly selected by the UK Govt to proceed SMR FOAK deployments under the Great British Nuclear domestic funding umbrella and initiative. Holtec and GEH continue forward, to complete their respective 2-Step Generic Design Assessments by the UK ONR. Holtec has keen insights, interests and serious engagements with global parties and partners to pursue commercial SMR-300 new build projects in the UK, Ukraine and India. While NuScale Power works with their US project developer ENTR1 to generate business thru projects, there don't seem to be any positive or certain project deployment works underway in either the US or UK, while noting they remain active developing a first project in Romania.

entries.text: Each NuScale Power Module (NPM) incorporates two once-through, helical-coil SGs inside the RPV for steam production. The SGs are in the annular space between the reactor hot leg riser and the RPV inside diameter wall. The SG consists of tubes connected to feed and steam plenums with tube sheets. Preheated feedwater enters the lower feed plenum through nozzles on the RPV. As feedwater flows through the interior of the SG tubes, heat is transferred across the SG tube wall from the reactor coolant to the feedwater. The feedwater changes phase and exits the SG as superheated steam.

The NuScale steam generators are unique in that they boil water to produce steam INSIDE (tube-side) the SG tubes, vs more conventional and robust nuclear power plant and boiler designs that convert water to steam OUTSIDE (shell-side).
The SGs and respective steam and feed connections are integrally to the reactor vessel. The SGs cannot be replaced without replacing the reactor vessel.

The NPM design utilizes ECCS valves. The reactor vent valves (RVVs) are located on the reactor vessel pressurizer, and the reactor recirculation valves (RRVs) are located on the reactor vessel downcomer. The RVVs and RRVs are functionally similar in design; however, the RVVs are larger than the RRVs. Each of the ECCS valves is pilot operated by remote-mounted trip and reset solenoid valves located at the reactor containment boundary. The design includes a novel inadvertent actuation block (IAB) feature, located inside containment on each RVV main valve.

The entire Nuclear Island reactor building is unconventional compared to the operating fleet. The reactor modules sit in a borated pool that is common to all modules and serves as a heat sink during the first 72 hours of an accident when off-site power may be unavailable. This pool is an integral part of both the decay heat removal system and the containment heat removal system. Refueling of the modules occurs in a separate pool attached to the containment cooling pool by a central canal. This allows refueling operations to occur separately and distant from the operating modules. During refueling, the two pools are isolated from each other using a gate or installed weir.

To initiate the refueling process, an individual reactor is shut down and the primary system temperature is lowered using the normal feed system and the steam generators. Once the reactor has been cooled below 100°C via the steam generators, the containment vacuum is broken, and the containment is partially flooded via the vacuum system to provide decay heat removal. Flooding the containment vessel provides a passive decay heat removal path that relies only on conduction and convection and, ultimately, the heat sink represented by the containment cooling/refueling pools. While the pools are serviced by active cooling systems, they have a passive capacity to provide at least three days of cooling.

After initial cool-down, the RPV+CNV module is disconnected from its supporting fluid systems and I&C leads. The 850-ton power module is then moved via an overhead crane to the module assembly/disassembly facility where it is remotely disassembled into the lower containment vessel, the lower reactor vessel (includes the reactor core), and the upper module section. While the core is being refueled, the upper module section is moved to a partial dry-dock facility for inspection and maintenance. Refueling of the core is accomplished by transporting upright fuel assemblies between the lower reactor vessel section and the adjacent spent fuel pool via a weir located in the wall that separates the spent fuel pool from the reactor pool. Spent fuel assemblies are stored in the used fuel pool for initial cool-down and later moved to an on-site dry-cask storage facility or interim fuel storage facility if available. After refueling, the module is reassembled, moved to its operating location, and reconnected to all support fluid (steam, feed, CVCS, RHR), electrical and instrumentation and control cables.

entries.text: Each Holtec SMR-300 reactor and NSSS produces 1050MWt, with a conventional PWR connected to a once-through steam generator with integrated pressurizer, and using non-safety booster pumps. The booster pumps feature two speed motors which together, at maximum design basis flow increase the total primary natural circulation flow by approximately a factor of four, eliminating the risks of flow stagnation attendant to the purely thermosiphon flow regime The hot legs of the reactor coolant system are external to the steam generator facilitating convenient in-service inspection.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 plant has no penetrations in the lower 2/3rd of the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV). An Annular Reservoir (AR) containing over one million gallons of water surrounds the containment vessel which is enclosed by the Containment Enclosure Structure (CES). This reservoir can provide cooling to the containment for greater than 90 days in the event of a loss of cooling accident, followed by a transition to indefinite air cooling; no operator action is necessary to achieve this - the plant is walk-away safe. The above-grade steel Containment Structure (CS) serves as both a containment and a large passive heat exchanger to reject decay heat through the containment wall into the annular reservoir. The deeply embedded CS is protected from aircraft and missile impact by the thick CES, with the plant's nuclear commodities - reactor, core and spent fuel pool - located below grade. The CES, characterized by a deep below-ground foundation with a cylindrical cross section assembled from CSSM modules is configured expressly to withstand impulsive and impactive loads.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 design specification includes evaluation of the highest earthquake and most severe environmental phenomena loads, yielding an adaptable bounding standard plant design which will envelope most US and global sites. This approach fixes the plant's anatomy during the design phase, with enough additional margin embedded in each critical area to preclude the need for gross site-specific design changes. Site conditions and utility functional requirements may inform the electric power output, but not the standard plant design. The energy allocated to electric power and process-heat may be adjusted to suit local needs, lending SMR-300 plants to broad load-following capabilities. Coupled with an energy storage system, the Holtec SMR-300 can further enhance grid stability and energy efficiencies.

entries.section_title: Figure 3-1: The Holtec SMR-300 in perspective view
entries.text: The CES and surrounding seismic category 1 structures (the most resilient type, required to assure nuclear safety in a worst case earthquake) are designed to prevent damage to any components of the nuclear steam supply system (NSSS) or any radiological release to the atmosphere in the event of a design basis earthquake, aircraft impact or any other external hazards. SMR-300 core components and reactor internals are readily removable for refueling, inspection, maintenance or change-out without disassembly of the reactor coolant system (RCS), or disconnection from its principal safety systems. The steam generator allows easy access for eddy current inspections as performed in the current US PWR fleet, and convenient in-service inspection.

inspection access to the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) using traditional methods. This configuration maximizes the use of operating experience from the current fleet and distinguishes the Holtec SMR-300 from iPWRs prevalent in the small modular reactor market, designs which integrate the steam generator and reactor in one embodiment, vastly complicating refueling, inspection, maintenance, and related activities.

The Holtec SMR-300 spent fuel solution is part of an integrated fuel management system, circumventing any need for costly plant modifications typical for current LWRs. The Holtec SMR-300 utilizes on-site interim spent fuel storage within the Holtec HI-STORM UMAX system, containing Multi-Purpose Canisters (MPCs). HI-STORM UMAX is an underground Vertical Ventilated Module (VVM) dry, spent fuel storage system. Each HI-STORM UMAX VVM provides storage of one MPC inside a cylindrical cavity located entirely below the top-of-grade. The Holtec SMR-300 is designed for on-site interim storage of all discharged fuel assemblies within an array of HI-STORM UMAX modules for the full design life of the Holtec SMR-300 with all necessary – developed and proven – structures, systems, and ancillary components to move the fuel in and out of the reactor and plant for safe and compact storage on-site.

Unlike some of the other SMR designs evaluated herein, the Holtec SMR-300 power plant is capable of a) being started from cold conditions without energy from the transmission grid, and b) and closing the output circuit breaker to a dead transmission bus to recover the electrical transmission system. Additionally, the plant derives power for house loads from the main generator, allowing the facility to operate without grid power. Together, these features allow the Holtec SMR-300 to be both black-start capable and island-mode capable, providing extreme robustness to any local or regional electricity distribution system.

The Holtec SMR-300 operates with large margins to criticality and thermal mechanical limits and employs a layered approach to mitigate the consequences of a postulated event, consistent with USNRC and IAEA guidelines. The passive safety systems incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 power plant comply with US and international guidelines in both letter and spirit.

The Holtec SMR-300 power plant is self-coping and designed to place itself in a safe condition in the event of a postulated accident. Independent and redundant layers of defense are engineered to anticipate, overcome and compensate for potential human errors and mechanical failures. Importantly, the containment of the Holtec SMR-300 is designed to remain intact and sealed during all power operating modes and postulated events, and to reject its internal energy to the large body of water surrounding the CS in the event of a design basis accident. Large releases of radioactivity postulated to occur for current large nuclear reactors in the case of an accident cannot occur with the Holtec SMR-300.

The Holtec SMR-300 design also incorporates flexible features such as emergency equipment, piping connections to important fluid systems, and spare batteries to address the potential occurrence of an event not yet conceived. The Holtec SMR-300 is a robust and safe power plant with large design and operating margins, and these flexible features make the plant well-equipped to handle events that far exceed the design basis loadings like in the case of Fukushima.

An 80-year design life is engineered into the Holtec SMR-300 by ensuring that every operational parameter has been optimized to increase NSSS longevity. Life-limiting factors such as neutron embrittlement and thermal shock to the reactor pressure boundary have been ameliorated.

Passive safety features and a simplified plant design enhance the safety, security, construction, operation, and maintenance of the plant. entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is a 300 MWe (net) advanced small modular reactor that can be deployed as a stand-alone single unit or in a cluster of units depending on the power need of the site.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Assured Operational and Environmental Safety
The Holtec SMR-300 reactor has a core damage frequency of <1E-7 and poses no credible risk to the environment and population proximate to the plant. It distinguishes itself (along with NuScale VOYGR) amongst the designs evaluated herein in achieving this level of safety without the use of pumps, offsite power, active safety systems or operator actions. Accordingly, it’s safer than the BWRX-300 and UK SMR which rely on active safety systems and limited coping periods.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Capacity Factor Improvement by Eliminating Load Following
The term "load-following" refers to the power plant adjusting its power output to meet the contemporaneous demand for electricity. Because the demand fluctuates throughout the 24-hour day cycle, the power plant’s output must be adjusted accordingly to stay aligned with the demand. Nuclear plants are typically designed to serve as base load generators with the power output adjustment function of a grid rendered by smaller fossil power plants. The SMR-300 can render this variable output function by several means such as bypassing turbine steam directly to the condenser and/or adjusting the position of the control rods. However, load-following by burning the fuel less efficiently is an inherently inefficient strategy; it is far more efficient to produce the motive steam at full capacity and bifurcate it with only the needed amount for the power generation directed to the turbogenerator. The balance of the steam can be directed to a Green Boiler which serves as a giant heat capacitor. As explained in the attachments to this report, the Green Boiler contains a large quantity of a specially engineered material called FeotermTM which has a large specific heat and a reasonably high conductivity. The Green Boiler conserves the thermal energy stored in its FeotermTM mass losing less than .5% of its enthalpy per day. The Green Boiler has a built-in steam generator which can be activated on demand to produce motive steam to power the site’s turbines. Thus, using the Green Boiler, the power output from a single unit Holtec SMR-300 plant can be varied within a wide range. In this manner, an SMR-300 plant can be producing its rated thermal energy, but its electric power output can be modulated to accord with the power demand. The overall power cycle capacity factor is near 100% and the reactors spared the wear and tear of cycling and associated expenditure of fatigue life.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Power Output Flexibility
Each Holtec SMR-300 plant is autonomous with its own turbogenerator and waste heat rejection system. A client can have one or more SMR-300 NPPs arrayed at a site. SMR-300 can be deployed in clusters to make a large power station or in single units for distributed generation giving the owner the full range of flexibility.

entries.section_title: Notable Attributes of the Holtec SMR-300 Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text:
Reactor Performance Stability
SMR-300 is designed to circulate the reactor coolant with the flow rate sufficiently vigorous to ensure full turbulence at full and partial power loads. The steam is produced in the SG which boils water in the capacious shell-side space around the tubes, as is the traditional design practice. This ensures large hydraulic inertia in the system and a stable performance.
SMR-300 uses conventional length PWR fuel, available initially from Framatome, and expected to be sourced from numerous international suppliers.

The critically important components in the Holtec SMR-300, such as the RPV, the SG, and the pressurizer as well as the connecting piping are readily inspectable. The large hatches in the containment dome and the containment enclosure building allow all capital equipment, including the SG, to be replaced.

SMR-300 features a small fuel pool which is lined with a stainless liner as is conventional in modern nuclear plants. Unfortunately, liners are known to leak in service. For this reason, the fuel racks in the pool are designed to be freestanding; they can be removed, and a liner leak readily fixed if one were to develop. The free-standing racks can then be re-emplaced for use.
The SMR-300 CS operates at ambient pressure with a peak 80 psig in the event of a bounding loss of cooling accident.
SMR-300 is envisaged to have one outage every 18-24 months.

The SMR-300 can be deployed at any location in a country that has maximum 100-year return ground acceleration in the range of 0.4 g's to 0.6 g's (depending on the stiffness profile of the site's subgrade and undergrade) without any site-specific analysis. The plant can be on arid land or adjacent to a body of water.
The used fuel at the Holtec SMR-300 plant will reside in subterranean storage cavities known as HI-STORM UMAX for an indefinite period.

The SMR's developer is Holtec, which is a proven turnkey supplier of complex engineered systems to over 140 nuclear units around the world. Holtec has been delivering turnkey nuclear projects with full responsibility for design, licensing, manufacturing, site construction and commissioning on five continents since the early 1990s. Holtec's quality and worker safety program, continuously exercised on scores of ongoing projects, is well regarded in the industry.

Fukushima Daiichi OPEX will lead to reasonable concerns and attract certain scrutiny of accidents and safety system and isolation valve(s) reliability leading to severe core damage. The BWRX design presumably includes design improvements to prevent the ICS isolation that occurred at the Fukushima Daiichi Unit 1 reactor, leading to core melting and a large radiation release to the public. Without a complete and reliable PSA model and analyses, designed, engineered, constructed, and tested isolation valves to inform associated reliability estimates, it is unknown whether this ICS design will be sufficient for regulatory approval of the overall plant design. The Rolls-Royce SMR employs both active and passive decay heat removal systems. Condenser decay heat removal utilizes the SGs and the normal duty steam condenser to cool the RCS. Passive Decay Heat Removal (PDHR) is a dedicated safety system that utilizes the SGs and the Local Ultimate Heatsink System (LUHS) to cool the RCS. In the PDHR decay heat is transferred to the LUHS water tanks via dedicated submerged heat exchangers. Boiling of the LUHS water to atmosphere provides the ultimate heat sink via passive means which rely on natural circulation.
Figure 6-8: Passive Decay Heat Removal System (PDHR)

When steam generators are unavailable for decay heat removal, for example in LOCA, the ECCS provides a passive, redundant, diverse, and segregated protective safety measure. This system provides core cooling in a sequence which involves blowdown of the RCS to the containment through dedicated relief valves, water injection from three accumulator tanks, gravity injection from the refueling pool and auxiliary LOCA pool and passive circulation from water accumulated within the containment sumps.
Additional protection is available from the High-Pressure Injection System (HPIS) for smaller leaks, which uses pumped flow to introduce water into the RCS.

Shutdown of the reactor in faults can be achieved using both the scram function and Emergency Boron Injection (EBI) system. The scram function isolates power to the Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDM), causing the control rods to be rapidly inserted. The alternative shutdown function is provided by the EBI system which delivers boron solution to the RCS. The EBI system operates at low pressure and is therefore dependent on the HPIS pumps and AC power. These non-safety systems are triggered from independent and diverse control and instrumentation systems.

The containment incorporates features to minimize and mitigate postulated severe accident phenomena. These include passive hydrogen re-combiners to prevent hydrogen explosions and containment vessel overpressure protection via filtered containment venting. The design also includes a Reactor Vessel Cavity Injection System (RVCIS) which has been designed to achieve In-Vessel Retention (IVR) of molten core
The Rolls Royce UKR SMR comprises a Reactor Island, Turbine Island, Cooling Water Island, and Balance of Plant.

The UK SMR Reactor Island includes the SSCs that house the reactor, the transfer, handling, and storage of new and used fuel, and associated nuclear auxiliary systems. It is approximately 137 m long and 84 m wide for a total NI area of 11,500 m², equivalent to 3 acres. entries.text: The design includes a Containment Cooling System (CCS) to maintain bulk average temperature inside containment during normal operations. The CCS is a closed loop recirculating cooling comprising redundant trains of air handling units. The containment is designed to maintain an inerted nitrogen atmosphere during operation. The CCS does not perform any safety functions but does assist with containment cooldown following a Loss-of-Offsite Power (LOOP) during the period from hot shutdown to cold shutdown and limits containment temperature during LOOP.

The PCCS is a passive system that removes decay heat and maintains the containment within its pressure limits for design basis accidents such as LOCA. It consists of several independent low pressure heat exchangers suspended inside the primary containment vessel.

The containment, or PCS, is enclosed within an Integrated Reactor Building. At approximately 200 feet tall and 35 meters in diameter, the PCS share a common modular basemat with the reactor building, which when constructed is embedded to a depth of 120 feet below grade.

The Control Building, Turbine Building, and RadWaste Building structures are built on a near-surface basement foundation adjacent to the deeply embedded RB structure. The Control Building includes the plant's control room, electrical, control, and instrumentation equipment. The RadWaste Building houses rooms and equipment for handling, processing, and packaging liquid and solid radioactive wastes. The Turbine Building encloses the turbine generator, main condenser, condensate and feed systems, condensate purification system, off gas, and turbine generator support systems, and bridge crane. The power block is comprised of the Reactor Building, the Control and Services Buildings, the Turbine Building, RadWaste Building, and Turbine Maintenance Building. The footprint of the power block is approximately 148 m x 78 m.

entries.text: Highest power density of any light water reactor SMR in development for cost economy of scale.
Passive engineered safety systems rely on natural circulation with no need for off-site power.
Utilizes existing (no FOAK materials components) environmentally qualified components and equipment for safety functions.
80yr design life by eliminating causative failures in equipment, leveraging manufacturing expertise (design for manufacture).
Entirely modular Nuclear Island, assembly via patented CSSMs civil modules for rapid and efficient field erection of Standard Plant.

An ASME Certified Material Organization (CMO), Holtec maintains an in-house lab to support material dedication and upgrading, in addition to an independent network of qualified material test labs on its Approved Vendor List, with objectives to maintain multiple vendors for the same scope of supply; competitively bid packages based on quality, schedule, and price; and to establish and maintain alliance/partnerships for key components with limited supply flexibility.
Manages vendors through Purchase Order portal, and controls inventory to support availability and drive bulk pricing for routine production.

Enables vendor flexibility through “smart” licensing, defining Equivalent Materials and Components in the plant licensing basis, with design envelopes that bound multiple supplier’s materials and components.
Conventional, off-the-shelf fuel and CRDS/CRAs with flexibility of supply.
Robust Containment Enclosure System – part of the ICS – with Annular Reservoir for unlimited coping period with no operator actions needed.
Integrated, licensed proprietary spent fuel management solutions and equipment, including underground ISFSI for life of the plant.

Technology, factories and experience fabricating and supplying ASME Section-III capital nuclear equipment, vessels, and heat exchangers; largest capital nuclear equipment exporter in US, with a multi-unit configurable plant design for optimal capital and operating costs, best optimizing the resource/power ratios of designs assessed herein.

4.1 Overview The BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe (gross), 270 MWe (net) SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of GEH's U.S. NRC-certified ESBWR. The key simplifications of the BWRX- 300 are the use of a dry containment with integral reactor pressure vessel isolation valves (RIVs) that mitigate the impacts of LOCAs, and large capacity Isolation Condensers (ICs) that provide over pressure protection without the need for safety relief valves. The ICs also act as the reactor plant's Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS), a vital and mandatory engineered safety feature mandated by US nuclear regulatory requirements per 10 CFR 50.46. This is important to note, given the critical regulatory treatment the NRC typically imposes on ECCS systems, with attendant loss of coolant accident assumptions for safety analyses.

Target applications include base load electricity generation, with a slow power ramp rate (0.5%/min) and load following electrical generation within a range of 50 to 100% power, district heating, synthetic fuel production, hydrogen production and other process heat applications. The BWRX-300 leverages the U.S. NRC-approved ESBWR design, proven in-use materials, off-the-shelf components, and operational parameters within the range of the existing BWR experience base, with a well-defined, robust, procedure driven process to direct cost-effective design decisions.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: The NuScale reactor plant is based on a small light water reactor developed at Oregon State University in the early 2000s. It consists of one or more NuScale power modules (hereafter referred to as power module(s)). A power module is a natural circulation light water reactor composed of a reactor core, a pressurizer, and two helical coil steam generators located in a common reactor pressure vessel that is integrated within a compact cylindrical steel containment. The NuScale reactor building is designed to hold up to 12 power modules. Each power module of the NRC-certified design has a rated thermal output of 160 MWth and gross electrical output of 50 MWe, yielding a total capacity of 600 MWe for 12 power modules. The NuScale power modules are partially submerged in a large common safety-related pool of borated water, which is also the ultimate heat sink for up to 12 power modules. The pool portion of the reactor building is located below grade. The design utilizes several first-of-a-kind approaches for accomplishing key safety functions.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: The twelve-reactor (50 MWe per power module) NuScale small modular reactor design certification final rule was published in the US federal register effective Feb.21.2023. Review of the design and final safety analysis report indicates a design with inherent safety characteristics owing to the reactor maintaining substantial margin to fuel and reactor coolant system thermal-mechanical safety limits.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: In Jan.2023, NuScale submitted a Standard Design Application (SDA) for an updated small modular reactor design, which is on a six-module VOYGR plant configuration powered by an uprated 77 MWe reactor power module. In a press release announcing submission of the SDA to the US NRC, NuScale indicated that the design uprate was done with select changes to support customer's capacity needs and to improve power plant economics. This design uprate includes a substantial 54% increase in thermal energy output per reactor module, with associated necessary fundamental physical and analytical changes required to satisfy regulatory and operability requirements.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: Extraordinarily unconventional operational and maintenance and refueling maneuvers and practices with no prior or existing OPEX FOAK tooling and 1000mt single-failure proof NOG-1 crane, biggest in the world; any crane issue can threaten ability to operate plant owing to its essentially continuous model refueling architecture and strategy 850t integrated power module (RPV + CNV) requiring massive fabrication, transport and construction facilities, cranes, logistics, Disconnecting reactor power modules from steam and feed piping and transporting past operating reactors in a common pool No ability to replace helical coil steam generators without replacing entire power module; and noting outstanding lack of proof for operability owing to SG DWOs Novel FOAK

NuScale Power submitted the final revision of the NuScale DCA, Revision 5, in July 2020 (ADAMS Accession No. ML20225A071). In August 2020, the NRC issued a final safety evaluation report after the Advisory Committee on Reactor Safeguards (ACRS) performed its final independent review and issued its July 29, 2020, letter to the Commission on its findings and recommendations. The final safety evaluation report is a collection of reports written by the NRC documenting the safety findings from its review of the standard design application, and it reflects all changes resulting from interactions with the ACRS as well as changes in the final version of the DCA. The final safety evaluation report, as elaborated on by the Response to DPO Tasking, reflects that NuScale Power has resolved all technical and safety issues except for the three issues discussed below.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: The NRC identified three issues as not resolved within the meaning of § 52.63(a)(5). There was insufficient information available for the NRC to resolve issues regarding:

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text:
• the shielding wall design in certain areas of the plant,
• the potential for contaminant leakage from the combustible gas monitoring system, and
• the ability of the steam generator tubes to maintain structural and leakage integrity during density wave oscillations in the secondary fluid system, including the method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations from reverse flow.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: Of most relevant significance and concern are issues associated with the steam generator design and associated unresolved density wave oscillation impacts.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: This steam generator design issue stems from the effects of density wave oscillations in the secondary fluid system on steam generator tubes to maintain structural and leakage integrity, including the method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations including reverse flow. Appendix G to 10 CFR part 52, Section VI, "Issue Resolution," clarifies that this issue is not resolved, and states that the COL applicant is responsible for providing the design information to address this issue.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: As a result, NuScale Power has not demonstrated that the flow oscillations that are predicted to occur on the secondary side of the steam generators will not cause failure of the inlet flow restrictors. Structural and leakage integrity of the inlet flow restrictors in the steam generators is necessary to avoid damage to multiple steam generator tubes, caused directly by broken parts or indirectly by unexpected density wave oscillation loads. Damage to multiple steam generator tubes could disrupt normal circulation in the reactor coolant pathway and interfere with the decay heat removal system and the emergency core cooling system, which is relied upon to cool the reactor core in a NuScale power module. The failure of multiple steam generator tubes resulting from failure of an inlet flow restrictor has not been included within the scope of the NuScale accident analyses in DCA Part 2, Tier 1, Chapter 15. Therefore, the NRC concludes that NuScale Power has not demonstrated compliance with 10 CFR 52.47(a)(2)(iv) and Appendix A to 10 CFR part 50, GDC 4 and GDC 31, relative to potential impacts on steam generator tube integrity from inlet flow restrictor failure.

entries.section_title: Issues Not Resolved by the Design Certification
entries.text: According to the NRC, the NuScale Power design requires a method of analysis to predict the thermal-hydraulic conditions of the steam generator secondary fluid system and resulting loads, stresses, and deformations from density wave oscillations including reverse flow. NuScale power did not provide verification and validation for its proposed method of analysis to demonstrate it is appropriate for this purpose, and accordingly the Design Certification includes a carve out for this critical item.

entries.section_title: Lack of Safety System Assurance and Diversity
entries.text: BWRX-300 Emergency Core Cooling System relies entirely on the ICS to supply water and handle over pressure with fail safe (closed) double isolation valves integrated to reactor vessel for steam, feed, ICS exit and ICS return pipes. This is an extraordinary departure from the concept of diverse and redundant safety systems, and the double isolation valves appear not to be able to satisfy USNRC and international regulatory requirements regarding 10 CFR 50.46 (the ECCS Rule) and the single failure criterion. Accordingly, this design feature could prove a fatal flaw in the eyes of many regulators.

entries.section_title: Lack of Passive Makeup Water Injection
entries.text: There is no additional water makeup other than active injection via the FMCRds in case the single ICS safety system fails to perform, or a small undetectable RPV penetration break occurs – itself an unisolatable LOCA.
This novel, small, dry containment is not sized to handle LOCA enthalpy if the ICS fails, or in case an RPV isolation valve were to break.

entries.section_title: Lack of Independence for Shut Down System (SDS)
entries.text: The BWRX-300 control blades are used for power level control, fuel reactivity management and power shaping, and for shutdown, startup, and scram. As such, the basic design does not include a second independent means to shut down the reactor, as expected and required by many competent regulators.
The design includes no manually actuated relief valves or automatic depressurization of the RPV.

entries.text: cooling trains, each aligned to an RCS loop. The three cooling trains are independent and configured such that 2oo3 trains can provide 72 hours of decay heat removal. Decay heat is transferred from the fuel assemblies to RCS coolant. This coolant flows through the loops to the Steam Generation System where the secondary water boils to generate pressurized steam. Steam is transferred from the SG to the Main Steam System and onwards to a dedicated PDHR heat exchanger in the Passive Steam Condensing System (PSCS). The steam is then condensed through heat transfer into a body of water located in the LUHS; the condensed coolant falls by gravity through PSC drain lines to the Feedwater System, and water in the LUHS boils to atmosphere to provide ultimate heat removal from the power station.

This process is passive and does not rely on pumped flow from the RCPs. Inventory of the primary coolant needs to be maintained during operation of the PDHR due to contracting coolant as the temperature falls, and due to losses of coolant during a small LOCA fault. Inventory control can be provided by any one of the following three systems, initiated upon detection of low level in the pressurizer:
• Level and Volume Control System
• High Pressure Injection System (HPIS) should the LVCS be unavailable
• Low Pressure Injection System (LPIS) should the LVCS and HPIS be unavailable.
Passive Containment Cooling

Steam generated in the RCS throughout a LOCA transient is discharged via a low-pressure blowdown line to the Containment Structure. Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) heat exchangers, located within containment, condense the discharged steam allowing it to collect in the containment sump for recirculation. The PCC heat exchangers are fed by coolant from the LUHS tank. Heat is transferred from the PCC heat exchangers to coolant within the LUHS tank. As heat is transferred, water in the LUHS tank heats up, boils off and is discharged to the atmosphere.

The Local Ultimate Heatsink System comprises of three trains, each containing an LUHS tank and its associated ancillary equipment, including the provision of fill, drain and sampling functions. Each LUHS tank corresponds to a single PCC train.
