entries.text: RIVs are located on RPV nozzles for the Main Steam System, Reactor Water Cleanup System, the supply and return lines of the ICS system, the Head Vent, and the Feed Water System. The RIV concept consists of two RIVs in series, with each RIV to be able to independently isolate its respective line. On loss of power, the RPV isolation valves fail in the closed position. However, the RIVs for the ICS steam supply and condensate return lines are exceptions. The ICS RIVs fail as-is because they perform safety functions during transient and LOCA events. The fail-as-is RIVs for the ICS steam supply and condensate return piping automatically close on indication of a break in the ICS train in which the RIV is located.

The RIVs are mounted in a double valve body made from an integral assembly attached to the RPV using flanged connections, within an ASME B&PV Code Section III, Class 1 construction. These double isolation valves are integrated to the reactor vessel for all pipes (steam, feed, DHRs (ICS feed and return)) inside containment with diameters greater than 2", to isolate the RCS+ICS (isolation condenser system) and to preserve RPV inventory in the event of a LOCA.

One of the design objectives of the BWRX-300 Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary (RCPB) is to minimize the risks associated with LOCAs by reducing the number of nozzles attached to the RPV, reducing associated pipe lengths and nominal pipe diameters, and by incorporating double RPV isolation valves integrated to the RPV to isolate the RCS for long-term safe shutdown cooling without the need or facility for makeup water or RCS safety relief valves. To be clear, this innovation appears to rely on a mechanistic argument that these components are designed to code to preclude a non-isolable break upstream of each outer most isolation valve boundary. Undoubtedly - and GEH claims - this innovation should enable simpler passive safety systems, a more compact containment that is dry, and a simpler Reactor Building compared to prior LWR designs. A simpler, safer, smaller plant should be cheaper to own and operate. However, the design includes significant regulatory risk in many global jurisdictions in our opinion, having seen firsthand the NRC resistance to any design or exemption to the intent of 10 CFR 50.46, and a closer look (Section 7) at BWRX-300 nuclear and conventional island areas and volumes seemingly disprove that claim.

The ICS removes decay heat after any reactor isolation and shutdown event during power operations. The ICS decay heat removal limits the increase in steam pressure and maintains the RPV pressure and water inventory at an acceptable level. The ICS consists of three independent loops that each contain a Heat Exchanger (HX) with a capacity of approximately 33 MWth, or approximately 3.7% of rated thermal power, or 3X50% decay heat removal HXs. Thermal energy removal condenses steam on the tube side and transfers heat by heating/evaporating water in the Isolation Condenser (IC) pools which are vented to atmosphere.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: NuScale is a large reactor installation consisting of individual reactors each rated at 77 MWe making its total rated capacity between 308 MWe and 924 MWe. All reactors are housed in a single reactor building the size of a football field. In as much as each reactor is immersed in a large volume of borated water, it can be safely stated that the NuScale design does not suffer from the risk of a criticality accident such as those that befell Chernobyl or Fukushima.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Power Output Flexibility NuScale requires a fixed cluster of reactors to be built as a single plant, each reactor with its own turbogenerator and waste heat rejection system. Recently the reactor designer has announced the decision to abandon the 50 MWe module and increase the capacity of each of the six reactors comprising the standard plant design to 77 MWe which will make it a 462 MWe installation. Abandoning the 50 MWe design results in a substantial re-work of the design and noting much of the licensing work over the past decade will have to be re-performed.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Reactor Performance Stability The most critical performance metric, thermal hydraulic stability of the RCS, has been questioned by the US Regulator because the reactor is configured to boil water inside the helical tubes of the SG driven by natural circulation, and has been shown analytically to experience density wave oscillations. The risk of unequal flow among the helical tubes of different radii of curvature in the bundle, the small quantity of water in the tubes at any time instant and the lack of control on the expanding volume of steam created inside each tube raise concerns about tube dry-out and flow instability. Classical heat transfer equipment design theory supports boiling outside the tube under natural convection conditions. NuScale has run tests that have thus far failed to solve this potentially crippling drawback. Currently, the issue is unresolved.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Fuel Design NuScale uses half-length PWR fuel which is new in the industry. A small benefit of a short fuel design would be reduced risk of fretting damage of the tubes.

entries.section_title: 7.3 Notable Attributes of the NuScale Plant from Owner’s Perspective:
entries.text: Refueling of the Reactor The refueling of the reactor in NuScale is an elaborate operation. The combined reactor module including its Containment Vessel (CV) and Reactor Vessel (RV) is lifted from its two protruding trunnions to transport the module for maintenance and refueling. To prepare a NuScale reactor module for refueling, all feedwater, steam piping, electrical and instrument lines must be disconnected to allow the combined vessels to be lifted free of many attachments. The freed CV including its RV, weighing approximately 850 metric tons, is next moved through a central aisle in the reactor building and brought to a reactor refueling stand where the lower containment and reactor vessels are disassembled. The act of unfastening the massive flange bolts must occur some 25 meters under water in the presence of an intense radiation field, making it necessary to employ a robot. In multiple moves and heavy lifts, the bottoms of CV and RV heads are remotely disconnected from their vessels so that the upper part of the combined CV and RV can be lifted and set aside, providing access to the fuel for change-out. After refueling the reactor core, the process must be re-traced: the RV reassembled and CV lower head replaced and carried back to its operating station where all piping, electrical, mechanical and instrumentation connections are re-made, and the CV is evacuated of water (set under vacuum). This operation involves many firsts in the industry which raises the un-fastening of the CV and the RV flanges featuring large bolts is only one stripped thread from a total stop of operations; leakage of any of the many gaskets that must be installed to join the pipes, and other connections can prevent reactor’s re-start, etc. No one has attempted the feat required to complete such a complex re-fueling; only time will tell if this “move the loaded CV” strategy is viable. entries.text: With all of its nuclear assets deeply embedded underground, the SMR-300 addresses common industry challenges associated with protection of a plant's spent nuclear fuel by locating the reactor's spent fuel pool inside containment with a small number of racked fuel assemblies. The design has eliminated the traditional LWR fuel transfer tunnel for vastly simplified fuel transfers into and out of the reactor building, and there is no need for future plant modifications to facilitate long term onsite interim spent fuel storage.

As a result of the in-containment spent fuel pool and integrated fuel management approach, the Holtec SMR-300 nuclear fuel assets are inherently self-protected, with no personnel access inside containment during operation.

Modularizing SMR-300 Nuclear Island civil structures (Figure 3.4-a) - beyond the ICS(CS + CES), including the Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) and Intermediate Buildings (steam tunnels) (IB) - is fundamental to developing a cost-efficient Standard SMR-300 power plant. Automated rebar reinforced concrete materials, methods, and manpower with factory fabricated-for-transport field welded and efficiently assembled CSSMs is expected to drastically improve craft (field and factory) productivity while dramatically reducing manpower labor hours constructing SMR-300 NI civil buildings, and CS internals. With a major portion of typical US NPP construction cost expended on inefficient craft and supervisory costs and expenses, Holtec expects to realize substantial cost reductions from the FOAK to NOAK NPPs.
modules to erect SMR-300 Standard plants by optimizing manufacture and assembly of CSSMs

These SMR-300 CSSMs (Figure 3.4-c) are inspired by Holtec's patented HI-STORM spent fuel storage cask - itself a concrete strengthend steel module, which is shipped to an NPP site to be installed - lifted, grouted, inspected for commissioning and use- before being loaded with spent nuclear fuel.

With decades of experience designing, licensing, fabricating, transporting, handling, installing, and loading HI-STORM CSSMs, and via regular improvements and repeat manufacture and installation, Holtec has benchmark actuals to validate the value of learning form to FOAK to NOAK. From early HI-STORMs, with attendant supply chain and manufacturing lead times, factory handling and labor hours, documentation production and management and QA practices, and field erection times to modern automated fabrication at AMD in Camden, NJ, with attendant savings, and improvements better than 10X in time and labor for site logistics, placement, grouting and loading - the benefits of practice are real. Leveraging that experience and learning, Holtec expects to speed the time and number of NNPs to realize FOAK to NOAK cost benefits through the significant and repeated use of SMR-300 CSSMs.

The SMR-300 utilizes commercially available fuel assemblies as those employed in existing PWRs today. The fuel assemblies are comprised of a 17 x 17 square lattice of 12-foot fuel rods. The fuel rods are of a standard size and utilize a zirconium-based alloy for cladding. Each fuel rod consists of high density ceramic UO2 fuel pellets stacked within zircaloy cladding that is evacuated, backfilled with helium, and sealed with zircaloy end plugs. Instrumentation/guide tubes are included as part of the fuel assembly. Spacer grids are distributed throughout the assembly to provide structural support for the fuel rods. Dissolved boron is used for reactivity shim and control. The distribution of the uranium enrichment and gadolinia concentration within each fuel assembly is optimized to minimize intra-assembly power peaking to increase margin to thermal-mechanical limits.
The reactor core is designed for an 18-month refueling cycle with a maximum enrichment of 4.95 wt% U235, with the option for shorter or longer cycles depending upon utility requirements.

The core is loaded with sixty-nine (69) fuel assemblies arranged in an octane symmetric pattern. The core includes twenty-five (25) Rod Control Cluster Assemblies (RCCAs) for reactivity and temperature control, which are connected via drive shafts to Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDMs) welded to integrated nozzles on the reactor head.

entries.text: The PDHR and SDHR are designed to remove decay heat from the RCS when normal cooling is not available. The ADS and the PCMWS are designed to provide core cooling for the complete range of loss-of-coolant accidents (LOCA) required to be considered by nuclear regulations. The ADS is a staged energy relieving system for the primary circuit, separate from the ASME Boiler & Pressure Vessel Code safety relief valves. All makeup water required for LOCA events is inside containment, such that the containment can be fully isolated to prevent release of radioactivity.

The PDHR provides diverse passive core cooling for non-LOCA accidents by removing core decay heat directly via closed-loop decay heat transfer directly from reactor coolant to PCMWT inside containment. The PDHR operates passively with liquid water via natural circulation. All system components are safely located and protected within the CES.

The SDHR provides diverse passive core cooling for non-LOCA accidents by removing core decay heat indirectly from the RCS via the steam generator shell side coolant and rejecting it to the annular reservoir via the SDHR heat exchanger located in the reservoir. The SDHR operates by condensing shell side steam and returning the condensate to the feedwater line of the steam generator much like the auxiliary steam systems of some current reactors but operating entirely passively. All system components are safely and securely located within the CES.

For a postulated loss of coolant accident (LOCA), the Automatic Depressurization System works in conjunction with the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCMWS) to depressurize the RCS to allow for passive safety injection from pressurized accumulators and atmospheric tanks. Decay heat is dissipated to the containment environment in the form of steam. The water that condenses on the inner metallic wall of the containment from a LOCA then returns to spent fuel pool where it can reenter the reactor primary loop via adjoining sump-strainers located in the PCMWS to support long-term cooling. The accumulators and PCMWS contain borated water for injection to the RPV as RCS pressure reduces, ensuring the reactor core is both cooled and rendered subcritical. All components are safely located and protected within the CES.

The PCHR passively maintains the containment atmospheric pressure and temperature within design limits in the event of a postulated accident by utilizing the metal containment structure and the water inventory in the annular reservoir. PCHR is a completely passive system that removes heat from the containment environment after an RCS energy release to containment. It does not require any actuations of components or an actuation signal to perform its functions.

During a postulated high energy loss of coolant accident, steam is released into the containment environment. The steam condenses on the inside surface of the containment structure as heat is transferred through the containment wall to the annular reservoir. The large heat transfer area and high conductance of the steel containment structure results in rapid heat rejection from the containment to the annular reservoir. As the water inventory in the reservoir is heated, it rejects heat to the environment through the discharge of clean vapor (no radioactivity) through a vent at the top of the Containment Enclosure Structure.

Water inventory is maintained in the annular reservoir at a certain level during normal operation to assure passive containment heat removal is available for at least 72 hours after a postulated accident without operator action. The water inventory can be replenished using an accessible connection outside of containment as part of the Holtec SMR-300 flexible coping strategy.

The Holtec SMR-300 reactor coolant loop is coupled with a thermally efficient simplified Rankine superheat steam cycle. In the event of a reactor trip with loss of power, the SMR-300 RCS can operate purely by natural circulation, as reactor coolant can circulate entirely because of the density difference between the primary water columns within the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) and steam generator (SG).

Passive, fail-safe, safety systems for emergency core cooling and containment heat removal eliminate the need for alternating current (ac) power under all accident conditions. All water required to mitigate loss of coolant accidents is located inside the containment in accumulators and tanks. The core damage frequency (CDF) is several orders of magnitude below U.S. regulatory thresholds without crediting any operator actions or non-safety systems.

entries.section_title: Offset Integrated Reactor and Steam Generator
entries.text: The SG is connected directly to the RPV by a set of two thick-walled pipes that deliver the cooled primary water to the down comer region of the Reactor Vessel. Each line features a booster pump, a non-safety equipment whose sole function is to increase the circulation in the RCS loop on demand. The two hot legs of the reactor coolant consist of heavy wall pipes that serve the heated primary water to the top header of the OTSG. There are no penetrations in the RPV below the RCS direct vessel injection nozzles, and the top of the core is well below this point, ensuring water stays within and above the active core. With a water volume to power ratio several times larger than traditional PWRs, the Holtec SMR-300 benefits from a large heat removal buffer for postulated transients and a large SG shell-side volume to prevent rapid SG dry-out during transients.

entries.section_title: Offset Integrated Reactor and Steam Generator
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 reactor is distinguished from other integral pressurized water reactors prevalent in the small modular reactor market which integrate the SG within the RPV. The Holtec SMR-300’s innovative offset design vastly simplifies refueling operations compared to iPWRs, while reducing or eliminating complex bolting and heavy load rigging and lifts. For refueling operations, the reactor head is readily removed to access the core in the same manner as current reactors, with the proximity of the spent fuel pool eliminating the need for complex fuel transfer equipment.

entries.text: 7.4 Notable Attributes of Rolls Royce Plant from Owner's Perspective
8 Conclusions and Recommendations
8.1 SMR Power Plant Economy by Scale, Sizes and Area Comparison
8.2 Concluding Remarks

This report (updated Aug 2025) documents a comparison of several competing light water SMR technologies and associated power plants using public domain information, including US NRC and UK ONR websites (Holtec, GEH, Rolls Royce, NuScale Power), to evaluate the relative merits, strengths, and weaknesses of each SMR technology. This comparative assessment focusing on three US and one UK SMR vendor technologies, with a discourse on the essential features and distinguishing aspects of Holtec's SMR-300. These technologies are (i) Holtec International's SMR-300, in a standard design twin-reactor configuration (ii) GE-Hitachi's single-reactor BWR-X-300, (iii) NuScale Power's multi-reactor VOYGR, and (iv) Rolls Royce's single-reactor UK SMR. While the AP300 SMR is on offer from Westinghouse, very little information is available, via published public or government documents or websites, to sufficiently inform this comparison. As such, the AP300 is not assessed herein. Furthermore, this update includes no new information or changes to the NuScale VOYGR design assessment that was provided in the Nov.2023 version of this document. At the time of that writing, the estimated delivered cost of the NuScale VOYGR plant had exceeded $20,000 per kilowatt electricity, leading to the cancellation of that first US project. The next update to this report will incorporate a contemporary evaluation of the latest NuScale design approved via USNRC Standard Design Approval.

Section 1 of this report provides a brief Overview of each technology. Section 2 defines Critical Features that are important to assess any SMR, and to evaluate and compare candidate technologies as objectively as possible. Each technology is presented and discussed in a distinct section of the report. A summary comparison of the technologies evaluated herein will be presented relative to these critical features to the extent practical via the available public information for each technology. Sections 3 through 6 present Differentiating Features and/or novel systems, components or licensing approaches of each technology assessed, and to characterize their respective overall practical viability and technological readiness for commercial construction and operations. Section 7 articulates Notable Attributes of each technology from an Owner's Perspective, and Section 8 provides the report's Conclusions with a discussion on SMR Power Plant Scale, including comparisons of power block and power plant areas and land use per MWe for the technologies assessed in this update.

Design and licensing information via US NRC and UK ONR web sites provides much of the information assessed in this report. Exhibits and narrative excerpts to this report are sourced from GEH, Rolls Royce, NuScale Power and Holtec International reference documents1. NuScale is not pursuing a Generic Design Assessment in the UK, and Westinghouse has not released public information, or is not sufficiently advanced in either US or UK pre-application reviews to facilitate available useful design information for this assessment.

entries.text: currently employs USNRC approved safety analysis and design codes (e.g., TRACG, PANACII, PRIME, etc.) to calculate fundamental thermal hydraulic and material parameters for operating and licensed BWRs and uses those same best estimate tools to calculate the same with estimated margins to limits for the BWRX-300 as well, for normal operations, AOOS and DBAs. The approved application envelopes associated with those codes may not, and in some cases certainly do not encompass all the BWRX-300 operating conditions, as they have not been proven to calculate actual or benchmarked BWRX-300 critical parameters with uncertainties. Absent relevant OPEX for this unique BWR plant - its reactor and engineered safety system configuration and design - a separate and integral effects test program will most certainly be required by competent regulators in North America and Europe, yet no such test plan has been described or committed by GEH publicly to Holtec's knowledge. GEH's approach appears to be one to convince regulators to accept the design based on prior art, BWR OPEX, and importantly the ESBWR .... albeit noting that design has never been built or operated. Assuming regulators will accept the best estimate code calculations without accounting for operational variations and modeling uncertainties is a risky proposition.

Some examples regarding uncertainty: coolant flow rate distribution in the core through each fuel channel will be based on hydraulic resistance and its distribution along the assembly channel and including the orifice at the bottom of the assembly, and with the respective void fraction/two-phase multiplier for each channel, as there is close coupling between bundle power, hydraulic loss coefficients and void fraction. Reactor physics will be affected due to the strong coupling between thermal hydraulics and reactor physics as a function of the reactor's negative void coefficient, and due to design basis accidents, which collapse voids in the core.

Also note: a natural circulation BWR is susceptible to coupled nuclear thermal hydraulic instability, and Holtec believes GEH will have a substantial amount of test/qualification work to gain regulator acceptance of their methods here, particularly during operation of the ICS/ECCS system.

Another unusual aspect of the design that will challenge safety certainty is the fact that ICS condensate return is to the chimney above the core instead of the traditional way of returning ICS flow to the downcomer to enhance natural circulation in BWRs. The current approach for the BWRX-300 could impede natural circulation flow after a LOCA/scram, or as a minimum require a scale testing program to validate new phenomenon associated with this unique RCS geometry and injection/flow path.

Adding cold ICS return condensate water into the chimney region impairs and can completely stop natural circulation, potentially severely impairing fuel cooling. The ICS in existing BWRs returns condensate water to the downcomer - whether the BWRX-300 configuration will be effective cannot be determined from OPEX for existing reactors which do not envelope the BWRX-300 design. Impairing or stopping natural circulation would result in counter-current flow from the chimney into the fuel region. Scaled experimental evidence is necessary to ensure adequate fuel cooling during DBA's and to ensure core stability, requiring accurate modelling/experiments and quantitative validation of counter-current flow in complex geometries. The current design of decay heat ECCS seems akin to shutting off or slowing down the recirculation pumps during accidents in traditional BWRs that require pressure relief or emergency core cooling.

The plant design results in a hot (radioactive) BOP, whereby most of the plant is isolated and can't be maintained or serviced while the reactor is operating. And radioactive steam is seen as a serious limitation for process heat applications (as compared to clean PWR steam).

The ICS heat exchangers and spent fuel pool are located outside the primary containment, on top of the reactor building, making that safety system and radioactive fuel susceptible to being targetable by drone or shape charge - with no way to cool the reactor or provide makeup if ICS fails or breaches.

5.1 Overview According to NuScale Power, the NuScale Power Module (NPM) is a small, light-water-cooled pressurized- water reactor (PWR). NuScale VOYGR SMR plants are scalable and can be built to accommodate a varying number of NPMs to meet customer’s energy demands. NuScale standard plants include the VOYGR-4 at 308 MW(e), the VOYGR-6 at 462 MW(e), and the VOYGR-12 at 924 MW(e). Each NPM is a self- contained module that operates independently of the other modules in a multi-module configuration. All modules are managed from a single control room. The NuScale design is a modular reactor for electricity production, with the capability for flexible operations to load follow, and for non-electrical process heat applications, including the cogeneration of heat and electricity. The NuScale VOYGR SMR plant design adopts design simplification, proven light-water reactor technology, modular nuclear steam supply system, factory-fabricated power modules, and passive safety systems that allow for unlimited reactor cooling time after a beyond design basis accident without ac or DC power, operator action, or makeup water. There are no design basis accidents that uncover the core or require operator action. The NPM is designed to operate efficiently at full-power conditions using natural circulation as the means of providing core coolant flow, eliminating the need for reactor coolant pumps.

NuScale Power has developed a 12-reactor 600 MWe gross output nuclear power plant, for which it has received 10CFR52 design certification (Feb.2023) from the US NRC. That design has now been heavily modified and resubmitted (Jan.2023) to the US NRC for standard design approval in accord with 10CFR52 for a 6-reactor 462 MWe gross output nuclear power plant called VOYGR USA460. Its licensing status is uncertain owing to its substantially changed design specification relative to the original 600 MWe plant.

entries.section_title: NuScale Passive Decay Heat Removal System
entries.text: has a passive condenser immersed in the reactor pool. During normal operations, the DHRS condensers are maintained with sufficient water inventory for stable and effective operation. The NuScale passive DHRS is capable of transferring core decay heat from either of the two steam generators to isolation condensers immersed in the reactor pool. Feedwater accumulators and long-term boiling and condensing heat transfer provide the driving head for DHRS flow. The DHRS, shown in Figure 4-2, is capable of decay heat removal for a minimum of 3 days without pumps or power.

The ECCS provides a passive means of decay heat removal in the event of a LOCA. The ECCS consists of two independent reactor vent valves and two independent reactor recirculation valves. All four valves are closed during normal operation. During ECCS operation, the reactor vent valves vent steam from the RPV into the CNV where the steam condenses and collects in the bottom of the containment. The reactor recirculation valves allow water to reenter the RPV and be naturally circulated through the core. When reactor coolant temperature is reduced to below the boiling point, core cooling continues via conduction through the CNV to the reactor pool.

entries.text: A NuScale power module containment operates under full vacuum, which makes its internal temperature rise to over 300 C. It is not apparent how the instrumentation and wiring in the containment will fare in a heavy radiation and hot temperature field. Furthermore, the NuScale power module containment must be designed to an accident condition pressure of over 10000 psi. Hydro-testing the CV for 10000 psi pressure at each outage is likely to be extremely arduous.

NuScale reactor refueling involves complex operations. A 12 module VOYGR reactor building must perform 6 refueling operations each year, meaning the plant will have virtually continuous outages. Performing refueling on a module while the adjacent ones are operating, may be viewed as inherently hazardous by experienced plant operators, and transporting a fueled reactor via heavy lift past operating reactors is likely to be disallowed in some regulatory regimes.

The NuScale plant must be located next to a river, lake, or sea. It cannot be deployed away from a natural source of water. The approach to manage used fuel produced by VOYGR plants has not been articulated by NuScale Power at this time.

NuScale Power is a new company; it has no customers or sales revenue and hence, no performance record. Its sole income is from the funds contributed by its equity holders and the US DOE, and may experience ownership changes as it continues its search for new investors to sustain its operations.

entries.text: The NPM design utilizes ECCS valves. The design includes reactor vent valves (RVVs) located on the reactor vessel pressurizer, with reactor recirculation valves (RRVs) located on the reactor vessel downcomer. The RVVs and RRVs are functionally similar in design; however, the RVVs are larger than the RRVs. Each of the ECCS valves is pilot operated by remote-mounted trip and reset solenoid valves located at the reactor containment boundary. The design includes a novel inadvertent actuation block (IAB) feature, located inside containment on each RRV main valve. Preliminary bench and prototype tests indicate these IABs are capable of functioning properly. A complex ECCS actuation system including these IAB devices is shown here.

The Ultimate Heat Sink (UHS) is a pool of water located in the reactor building. The UHS consists of the reactor pool, the refueling pool, and the spent fuel pool. During normal plant operations, heat is removed from the pool with a pool cooling and cleanup system. In a design basis accident involving a sustained loss of AC power, decay heat is removed from the NPMs through passive heat transfer to the pool resulting in pool heat up and boiling. Water inventory in the reactor pool is adequate to cool the NPMs for at least 72 hours without adding water.

The functions of Containment Vessel (CNV) are to contain the release of radioactivity following postulated accidents, to protect the RPV from external hazards, and to provide heat rejection to the reactor pool following ECCS actuation. Each CNV consists of a steel cylinder with an outside diameter of 4.5 m and an overall height of 23.1 m. The CNV houses the RPV, control rod drive mechanisms, and associated piping and components of the NSSS. The CNV is immersed in the reactor pool of borated water, which is the plant's passive heat sink for containment heat removal under LOCA conditions. During normal power operation, the containment atmosphere is evacuated (less than 1psia) to provide an insulating vacuum to reduce heat loss from the reactor vessel.

The CNV is an evacuated pressure vessel fabricated with a combination of martensitic and austenitic stainless steel that houses, supports, and protects the reactor pressure vessel (RPV) from external hazards and provides a barrier to the release of fission products. The CNV is partially immersed in a below grade, borated water filled, stainless steel lined, reinforced concrete pool to facilitate heat removal. The CNV is an American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code (BPVC) Class MC (steel) containment whose design, analysis, fabrication, inspection, testing, and stamping conform to ASME BPVC Class 1 pressure vessel requirements in accordance with Section III, Subsection NB.

entries.text: Holtec understands that laminar or transitional flow conditions which typically afflict thermosiphon-based designs and is caused by a small driving head is a threat to the system reliability of any reactor system. To ensure that the Holtec SMR-300 will be free of such a problem, the turbulence level in the RCS and elsewhere in the plant is required to be at least four times the upper end of the transition zone at the lowest power output condition.

SCC and cyclic fatigue from thermal transients have been identified as the twin threats to the integrity of the pressure boundary in reactor vessels and steam generators. These threats have been ameliorated in the Holtec SMR-300 by ensuring that the RCS temperature changes are not abrupt, made possible by the large thermal inertia of the entire RCS, and by employing a thermal liner throughout the pressure boundary which blunts the thermal shock to the pressure boundary material (a patented Holtec invention).

entries.section_title: Protecting Steam Generator tubes from Wastage
entries.text: The wisdom received from the spate of steam generator failures in the 1990s in the United States has been incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 SG design. The tubes are made of thermally treated Inconel 690, All-Volatile Treatment (AVT) water chemistry treatment is employed, and the blow-down rate to continuously purge the SG sludge is two times that used in the latest LWR designs. In addition, a tube installation sequence has been developed to pre-stress the most severely loaded tubes to mitigate tube axial stresses during operations. Non-segmental tube supports (based on an expired Patent patent and extensively used by the Company over the past 30 years) have been incorporated in the design to minimize vibration producing cross flows. It can be said that the Holtec SMR-300’s SG design incorporates all the chastening lessons learned from seven decades of PWR operations.

Vibration of slender parts such as tubes in feedwater heaters, control condensers, steam generators, moisture separator reheaters, auxiliary feed exchangers, surface rod extensions, and piping runs has been a persistent operating problem in nuclear plants. In the Holtec SMR-300, this ubiquitous problem is systematically solved by requiring that the fundamental natural frequency of the part be at least two times the highest frequency of the excitation source. In heat exchangers, principal excitation sources are fluid elastic coupling and turbulent buffeting. Piping runs are vulnerable to the harmonics associated with earthquakes.

Pressure retaining welds in the RCS are known to be vulnerable to failure and are thus subject to periodic in-service inspection that increases outage duration. In the Holtec SMR-300, Holtec proprietary design strategies have been employed to significantly reduce the number of weld seams.
Highest power density of any light water reactor SMR in development for cost economy of scale.
Passive engineered safety systems rely on natural circulation with no need for off-site power.
Utilizes existing (no FOAK materials components) environmentally qualified components and equipment for safety functions.
80yr design life by eliminating causative failures in equipment, leveraging manufacturing expertise (design for manufacture).
Entirely modular Nuclear Island, assembly via patented CSSMs civil modules for rapid and efficient field erection of Standard Plant.

An ASME Certified Material Organization (CMO), Holtec maintains an in-house lab to support material dedication and upgrading, in addition to an independent network of qualified material test labs on its Approved Vendor List, with objectives to maintain multiple vendors for the same scope of supply; competitively bid packages based on quality, schedule, and price; and to establish and maintain alliance/partnerships for key components with limited supply flexibility.
Manages vendors through Purchase Order portal, and controls inventory to support availability and drive bulk pricing for routine production.

Enables vendor flexibility through “smart” licensing, defining Equivalent Materials and Components in the plant licensing basis, with design envelopes that bound multiple supplier’s materials and components.
Conventional, off-the-shelf fuel and CRDS/CRAs with flexibility of supply.
Robust Containment Enclosure System – part of the ICS – with Annular Reservoir for unlimited coping period with no operator actions needed.
Integrated, licensed proprietary spent fuel management solutions and equipment, including underground ISFSI for life of the plant.

Technology, factories and experience fabricating and supplying ASME Section-III capital nuclear equipment, vessels, and heat exchangers; largest capital nuclear equipment exporter in US, with a multi-unit configurable plant design for optimal capital and operating costs, best optimizing the resource/power ratios of designs assessed herein.

entries.text: 4.1 Overview The BWRX-300 is a 300 MWe (gross), 270 MWe (net) SMR with passive safety systems that leverages the design and licensing basis of GEH's U.S. NRC-certified ESBWR. The key simplifications of the BWRX- 300 are the use of a dry containment with integral reactor pressure vessel isolation valves (RIVs) that mitigate the impacts of LOCAs, and large capacity Isolation Condensers (ICs) that provide over pressure protection without the need for safety relief valves. The ICs also act as the reactor plant's Emergency Core Cooling System (ECCS), a vital and mandatory engineered safety feature mandated by US nuclear regulatory requirements per 10 CFR 50.46. This is important to note, given the critical regulatory treatment the NRC typically imposes on ECCS systems, with attendant loss of coolant accident assumptions for safety analyses.

Target applications include base load electricity generation, with a slow power ramp rate (0.5%/min) and load following electrical generation within a range of 50 to 100% power, district heating, synthetic fuel production, hydrogen production and other process heat applications. The BWRX-300 leverages the U.S. NRC-approved ESBWR design, proven in-use materials, off-the-shelf components, and operational parameters within the range of the existing BWR experience base, with a well-defined, robust, procedure driven process to direct cost-effective design decisions.

entries.text: Reactor Island structures are supported on a rectangular 2acre raft foundation 400ft long and 230ft wide, the top of which is 37ft below grade. The Containment Support Structure (45m (150ft) square on each side) supports the Containment Vessel and provides access into and out of Containment Vessel for construction and examination, maintenance, inspection, and testing activities. The Containment Vessel is 32m in diameter (105ft) and 37m high (121ft).

The Reactor Island is covered by a Hazard Shield (not shown), a large, reinforced concrete (RC) structure that protects safety critical SSCs from external hazards, including accidental and malicious aircraft impacts. This concrete roof over the top of the Reactor Island is 300ft long 200ft wide and extends 150ft above grade. The Hazard Shield covers and is credited in the plant's design and licensing basis with protecting the Reactor Island structures from external hazards, natural and man-made. Unlike typical reactor and SMR designs which incorporate a robust shield building or containment enclosure structure,

An RC Raft Foundation provides support to the Reactor Island structures which are themselves supported on a Basemat, separated by an Aseismic Bearing. A retaining wall is integral to the raft foundation at its base and retains the external ground and groundwater surrounding the Reactor Island. The retaining wall is physically separated from the Hazard Shield and Basemat.

The Seismic Isolation System is supported by the raft foundation and comprises a series of RC pedestals and aseismic bearings, which in turn support an RC Basemat. The seismic isolation is provided between the Basemat and pedestals by the aseismic bearings, which decouple the horizontal accelerations.

Rolls Royce is pursuing a different strategy with respect to factory manufacturing and modularity, focusing on the use steel-framed Process Clusters within the Reactor Island, and its respective blocks, or areas, while relying heavily on traditional RC materials and methods for major civil structures and construction techniques.

Reactor Island Process Blocks are those buildings and structures around the Containment Support Structure that are assembled in part from 'Process Clusters'. Process clusters are defined as the conglomeration of 'system modules' into discrete structural framing systems, and house mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. System modules are formed from module units and can vary in length depending on the systems within the major Reactor Island Process Blocks: Fuel Block Electrical and I&C Block Fluids Blocks Auxiliary Block Waste Processing Block

entries.text: Small modular reactors (SMRs) have increasingly become a centerpiece of the nuclear industry’s aspiration to play a critical role in decarbonizing the world’s national economies which many view as an existential struggle for ensuring continued habitability of our planet. Developers of nuclear power plants around the world have responded to the challenge by proposing novel small modular reactor designs based on the classical light water technology which originated in the US in the 1950s and rapidly became the most popular reactor architecture leading to over 400 plants built over the past eight decades and operated around the world. Guided by the ostensibly sound reasoning that bigger reactors would bring down per kilowatt cost, each generation of reactors grew steadily in size and power output. Unfortunately, the conventional wisdom did not hold in the case of the commercial nuclear industry and the unit per kilowatt cost of power continued to rise in tandem with the reactor’s size. Other drawbacks inherent to large reactors also came to the fore, such as long period of construction, increased complexity, need for significant investment in power delivery infrastructure and the need for copious quantities of water to reject the plant’s waste heat (which is over 65% of the total power produced by the reactor). The industry’s standing with the public suffered serious setbacks when a boiling water reactor suffered a core melt-down in Fukushima, Japan in March 2011. That accident rekindled memories of the horrific accident at the Russian-built RBMK reactor at Chernobyl in 1986, which was preceded by an accident at TMI unit 2 in 1979. The increasing high costs and safety performance of large reactors have kept them at the being embraced more universally, even as humankind desperately seeks to stem the rise of carbon in the atmosphere.

The above-mentioned drawbacks of large reactors have prompted industry to seek the obverse of largeness, namely small reactors, defined empirically as a reactor that has less than 300 MWe design basis output. It was reasoned that because the “small” reactor has a small inventory of thermal energy at any one time, the dissipation of that heat during a postulated loss of coolant accident should be manageable. Also, a small reactor ought to be built and commissioned in a relatively short time, and the cost of capital per unit output ought to be smaller than large reactors. Proponents of small reactors also hoped that they would be largely factory built, maximizing the benefits inherent in serial manufacturing while minimizing site construction costs. The notion of manufacturing most parts and sub-components in a factory and limiting site construction to a minimum was conceived as the antidote to the awful labor efficiency at construction sites. Thus, the term “modular” became attached to small reactors, resulting in the now commonly used term “small modular reactor,” and its acronym “SMR.”

In this report, Holtec’s attention is focused on the light water SMRs which, because of the maturity of light water technology, hold the promise of immediate deployment. This report accordingly focuses on the merits and demerits of four SMR technologies which have progressed their designs and gained varying levels of acceptance. Because none has been yet deployed, Holtec’s appraisal is founded on the design features that define the prognosis for their future performance based on solid science, not conjectures and speculations. The candidate reactor designs considered are listed in Table 2-1 below, with reported or estimated* net electric outputs.

entries.text: The Containment Inerting System precludes the combustion of hydrogen and prevents damage to essential equipment and structures. It establishes and maintains an inert atmosphere (4% dry-basis-percent (DB%) oxygen) within containment during plant operating modes except during shutdown for refueling/maintenance and for limited periods of time during low power operation for inspection. The system also maintains a slightly positive pressure in containment to prevent air (oxygen) in-leakage into the inerted spaces from the Reactor Building.

Composite (DP-SC) modules are being utilized for the basement, walls, floors, and roof of the Reactor Building. Before concrete casting, the diaphragm plates and steel faceplates provide stiffness and strength to the empty steel modules. DP-SC modules are stiff and stable in the empty module configuration due to the continuous support provided by the diaphragm plates to the steel faceplates. After concrete casting, the diaphragm plates provide structural integrity to the composite section by preventing delamination of the concrete core. Furthermore, diaphragm plates provide composite action between the steel faceplates and the concrete infill, and out-of-plane shear reinforcement for the composite section. Additional ties or shear stud anchors may be used to anchor the steel faceplates to the concrete infill and control faceplate local buckling.

DP-SC panels are fabricated in factories in sizes that can be shipped to the construction site via truck, rail or barge depending on the location of the site. The panels are then assembled into modules at site before being lifted into final position. A multi-layered water proofing application is utilized to ensure leak tightness. A waterproof membrane is installed between the shaft wall and the DP-SC outer plate for a first protective layer. A grouting or concrete medium is then placed between the membrane and the steel liner. The DP-SC outer plate provides an additional layer of sealing.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH claims to achieve "dramatic design simplification, using a licensed and proven fuel design, and the incorporation of proven components and supply chain expertise, to allow the BWRX-300 to become the lowest-risk, most cost-competitive and quickest to market SMR in the market." In essence, GEH claims much, even all the technology and systems/components embodied in the BWRX-300 are already licensed, and as such, a BWRX-300 can effectively be deployed from a toolbox of licensing packages and IP, quickly and readily. These claims will be seriously challenged, and the tools and methods developed and used for licensed and operating BWR reactors and technologies will be shown to require significant extended qualification through testing and engineering analyses to be qualified as applicable to the BWRX-300. The reactor coolant pressure boundary and dry containment design are major departures from prior wet containment BWRs with diverse safety systems. GEH has gambled on a very stripped-down safety system nuclear power plant concept - incorporating RIVs with a dry containment into the DNA of the design - valves that are neither developed, qualified, or available in the marketplace. Their design may prove difficult to license without some fundamental design changes to incorporate added safety capacity, as it will challenge regulatory normative standards, regulations, and subjective acceptance criteria with respect to NRC and international regulatory intents and risk postures.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH and its partners are developing a design and a SAR to satisfy universal, and initially Canadian nuclear regulations, as needed to construct and license an FOAK reactor. The design includes certain basic features that will challenge regulations both in Canada, and in competent nuclear design regions around the world, given different cultures, experiences, insights and OPEX in those regions. Certain fundamental elements of the design introduce first-of-a-kind components, operations and technologies not previously developed, tested, or proven for use in nuclear reactor applications, and these elements introduce significant risks and challenges to the concept as currently envisioned. The design relies on a single Isolation Condenser System to perform numerous crucial safety functions, with no capability to ensure a safely cooled and shutdown reactor in case that ICS fails for any reason, foreseeable or not. The Fukushima accident is still fresh in the minds and memories of the world, where the unit-1 reactor core melted after the ICS did not perform as expected. GEH has promised that they have learned from this accident and improved the ICS - but have eliminated all other BWR safety systems in pursuit of cost reduction.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: Construction and Operations

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: While this BWRX-300 reactor and engineered safety system design is certainly revolutionary, GEH appears to have done little to address the complexity and severe operating environment and costs associated with commercial island of plant operations and costs, considering BWRs essentially contaminate most of the commercial island with radioactive steam. This not only adds to capital cost for shielding and separation of hot systems but dramatically limits the operations and maintenance work that can be performed while the reactor plant is in operating mode. Furthermore, the radioactive steam is not available for process heat applications and will require entirely separate systems and capital costs to facilitate such, as compared to PWRs and SMR-300. Ultimately the TI and associated systems yield a power block very difficult to scale, resulting in a plant very physically similar in size to the ESBWR, albeit with less than 20% of that plant's power output.

entries.section_title: 4.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the BWRX-300
entries.text: GEH claims to dramatically reduce the plant cost substantially through elimination of concrete as compared to prior BWRs, by replacing conventional concrete with DP-SC modules, but without eliminating the need for the associated BOP systems and structures. There is little or no evidence or FOAK to NOAK basis - GEH has no prior experience designing, fabricating or constructing such - to suggest that this will reduce plant capital cost, and in fact it may prove to dramatically increase constructed (vs estimated) cost when FOAK and early learnings are realized.

entries.section_title: 7.4 Notable Attributes of Rolls Royce Plant from Owner’s Perspective
entries.text: At 1358 MWe, the UK SMR is a three-loop medium sized reactor. The plant design includes a novel seismic isolation system, and an unconventional approach to large power plant construction, more akin to submarine construction, albeit without the benefit of an adjacent marine factory and assembly environment.

The generic Rolls-Royce SMR design also includes aseismic bearings for a base isolation system within the reactor island. The main benefit of this system is that it is claimed to allow the superstructure to be standardized, along with the equipment in the power station, regardless of site-specific seismicity. The base isolation system comprises the raft foundation, the concrete pedestals, and aseismic bearings and the basemat. The raft foundation, basemat, and major Reactor Island building structures (e.g., Containment Support Structure) are filed constructed via conventional reinforced concrete materials and methods.

A hazard shield, consisting of a reinforced concrete wall and roof, is included in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide protection against radioactivity release due to external hazards. The bounding case for the hazard shield is based on an aircraft impact hazard, aiming to ensure confinement of fuel, prevention of criticality, protection of reactor shutdown and cooling systems and protection of monitoring systems. The hazard shield covers portions of the Reactor Island - the containment building and the fuel and control buildings - to ensure Class 1 SSCs are protected. The Hazard Shield, measuring 200 feet by 300 feet, is essentially a very large cover over the top of the plant’s nuclear assets.

Unlike other commercial PWRs, the generic Rolls-Royce SMR design is designed to operate without soluble boron during normal operations. Rolls-Royce claim that, in addition to simplification of the design, this provides safety benefits including full shutdown margin delivered by the control rods and elimination of boron dilution faults. This feature will however greatly complicate power operations and maneuvers, and may ultimately prove unworkable, lacking a second independent passive means to shut down the reactor.

The plant’s coping period after a design basis accident is limited to 72hrs. before operator actions are required – a significant shortfall in safety achievement compared to the other SMR plants evaluated herein.

The design also includes a Reactor Vessel Cavity Injection System (RVCIS) which has been designed to achieve In-Vessel Retention (IVR) of molten core material in a severe accident. This is achieved by externally cooling the RPV lower head by gravity flooding the reactor cavity pit with water, and allowing this to boil, condense and return to the pit. In the event of a LOCA, steam released into the containment throughout the transient is cooled by the LUHS Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) system heat exchangers.

Section 7 includes Rolls Royce disclosed plant information including major plant buildings, dimensions and areas. Those areas are compared to the same for other technologies evaluated herein (Reactor Island, Turbine Island, Plot Plan) to compare one against the other.

entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300, GEH BWRX-300, Rolls Royce UK SMR, and (possibly) Westinghouse AP300 technologies and power plants are being developed actively for commercial projects in North America and global markets. Little is known about Westinghouse and Rolls Royce aspirations or project developments in the US. Rolls Royce was singularly selected by the UK Govt to proceed SMR FOAK deployments under the Great British Nuclear domestic funding umbrella and initiative. Holtec and GEH continue forward, to complete their respective 2-Step Generic Design Assessments by the UK ONR. Holtec has keen insights, interests and serious engagements with global parties and partners to pursue commercial SMR-300 new build projects in the UK, Ukraine and India. While NuScale Power works with their US project developer ENTR1 to generate business thru projects, there don't seem to be any positive or certain project deployment works underway in either the US or UK, while noting they remain active developing a first project in Romania.

The Holtec SMR-300 is deemed both safe and practical, with design features and functions that prioritize SAFETY and ease of OPERATIONS. The power plant is designed in a Standard Plant configuration and incorporates innovative Concrete Strengthened Steel Modules (CSSMs) for major nuclear island civil structures and supports, to optimize construction safety, quality, cost and schedule. The Holtec SMR-300 pressurized water reactor (PWR) coolant system has a large water mass per megawatt compared to typical PWRs and includes gravity-driven engineered safety features that eliminate active components and AC power needed in typical PWRs and BWRs. The design reflects decades of PWR operating experience and lessons learned. Holtec has emphasized elimination of fundamental causative failures in reactor operations and maintenance, e.g., stress corrosion cracking of reactor vessel and steam generator materials and components, for a long and assured plant lifetime of 80 yrs1. The design incorporates an innovative robust integrated containment and enclosure structure and reactor auxiliary building with intermediate buildings (combined these building form the Standard Plant Nuclear Island) constructed substantially from CSSMs, facilitating expedient assembly of the standard plant, while providing assured plant safety and security against accidents, natural disasters and terrorist threats. The CSSM design and deployment plan is predicated on decades of Holtec's proven, licensed HI-STORM fuel storage casks and associated modular construction technologies. The plant design includes an integrated and licensed spent fuel management system and provides for life-of-the-plant on-site storage of used fuel in an NRC-licensed subterranean configuration. Equipped with passive engineered safety features, the plant provides assured walk-away safety with no operator actions for an unlimited duration. The Holtec SMR-300 design is differentiated by including an alternative waste heat rejection system that utilizes a Holtec-proprietary air-cooled heat exchanger technology to facilitate siting the plant in water challenged regions.

The reactor coolant system features gravity-driven circulation which assures removal of decay heat from the core if the plant trips or the mechanical devices to boost primary flow fail. A not-important-to-safety pump in each of the two cold legs helps generate a highly turbulized flow regime in the reactor core and the steam generator, eliminating concerns of localized flow stagnation. The power plant produces clean super-heated steam ideal for both electricity generation and process heat applications. The plant is offered in both a single unit and a standard dual-unit configuration, the latter to optimize construction and operating costs, and to eliminate single-shaft failure risk to the production of thermal and electric power. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration (PGA) earthquake in the range of 0.4g to 0.6g depending on the shear wave velocity of the site subgrade. The design incorporates two divisions of multi-channel state-of-the-art electrical and digital control architectures with passive safety systems to simplify systems, equipment, cabinets and cables compared to other complex 3 and 4 safety division SMRs with active safety systems, to reduce capital and operating costs and complexities.

Structural safety analysis of the Holtec SMR-300 plant has been performed using design basis loadings that bound the highest environmental loadings that are likely to occur at any of the sites where the plant is likely to be sited. The design thus developed and qualified is referred to as the Bounding Design. The object of this approach is to make sure that all plants, no matter where deployed, shall be virtually identical and standardized, helping minimize construction time and cost and facilitating the use of standard plant procedures.

entries.text: The BWRX-300 Primary Containment Vessel (PCV) encloses the RPV, provides radiation shielding and acts as a boundary for radioactive released from the RPV. It is integral to and surrounded by the Reactor Building (RB). The PCV is dry and is located mostly below grade.

There is no suppression pool or makeup water inside containment. The BWRX-300 containment is a vertical cylinder approximately 18 meters in diameter and 38 meters high. It comprises a Steel-Plate Composite Containment Vessel (SCCV), consisting of steel-plate composite cylindrical wall, basemat, and top slab, and a steel containment closure head. The containment structure is completely enclosed within a deeply embedded reactor building and includes personnel/equipment hatches and containment penetrations. The SCCV is integrated with the reactor building and the integrated structure is supported by a common steel-plate composite basemat. The design includes a nitrogen-inerted containment atmosphere during most operating modes. The containment has provisions for personnel access during plant outages to perform maintenance, inspections, and tests for critical parts, including the novel RIV, and has a design life of 60 years.

The design includes a Containment Cooling System (CCS) to maintain bulk average temperature inside containment during normal operations. The CCS is a closed loop recirculating cooling comprising redundant trains of air handling units. The containment is designed to maintain an inerted nitrogen atmosphere during operation. The CCS does not perform any safety functions but does assist with containment cooldown following a Loss-of-Offsite Power (LOOP) during the period from hot shutdown to cold shutdown and limits containment temperature during LOOP.

The PCCS is a passive system that removes decay heat and maintains the containment within its pressure limits for design basis accidents such as LOCA. It consists of several independent low pressure heat exchangers suspended inside the primary containment vessel.

The containment, or PCS, is enclosed within an Integrated Reactor Building. At approximately 200 feet tall and 35 meters in diameter, the PCS share a common modular basemat with the reactor building, which when constructed is embedded to a depth of 120 feet below grade.

8.1 SMR Power Plant Economy by Scale, Sizes and Area Comparison

Most striking are the comparative efficiencies of the plant designs when viewed from a resource per unit power perspective. The SMR-300 appears to be logically more efficient than the competing designs based on side-by-side comparisons of plant areas and volumes of constructed plant structures and equipment. A high-level plot plan and power block comparison between the Holtec International SMR-300, GEH BWRX-300, and Rolls Royce UK SMR designs demonstrates the relative differences between the power plants, for example, and helps emphasize the benefits realizable via the SMR-300 dual-reactor standard nuclear plant configuration with shared non-safety and power block commodities, equipment, resources, and land, as compared to competing lwr SMR designs assessed herein.

Single-reactor SMR plant sizes simply do not scale efficiently to power. From the figure below, we can see that the BWRX-300 Integrated Reactor Building displaces 80% to the volume of the ESBWR Reactor Building, from which this 'small' plant has been derived (implies BWRX requires 80% of 1600MW nuclear island commodities, equipment, direct + indirect costs, whilst producing less than 20% of the ESBWR net electric output). The comparison below is effectively a starting demonstration of the discrepancies of scale realized when scaling down a large nuclear plant to essentially a small version of the same thing.

The SMR-300 Standard Plant design configuration has been reengineered on the advice of Industry and Corporate advisors, to optimize the capital cost-to-power ratio to overcome the diseconomies of SMR scale inherent in 'smalled-down' versions of large single reactor designs. To achieve this, the SMR-300 power block includes twin-reactors in two Containment Enclosure Structures (CES) enclosed by a single Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB), paired with twin turbine buildings, with shared RadWaste and Control and Electrical buildings and shared non-safety essential BOP and yard resources. The result is a plant optimized for efficient use of material, capital, labor and environmental resources.

entries.text: A series of ‘process clusters’ are housed within Process Blocks locks within the Reactor Island. Process clusters are defined as the conglomeration of ‘system modules’ into discrete structural framing systems, and house mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. System modules are formed from module units and can vary in length depending on the systems within them.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: A three-loop, close-coupled PWR, the UK SMR provides an estimated power output of 425 MWe from 1358 MWth using industry standard UO2 fuel. Coolant is circulated via three centrifugal Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCP) to three corresponding vertical U-tube Steam Generators (SGs). The design includes multiple active and passive safety systems.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: Strengths are Difficult to Identify: While Rolls Royce claims that 90% of the capital power plant cost will be incurred in a manufacturing factory, this claim appears to be less than credible upon close examination. The available information indicates that Rolls Royce intends to construct a massive cover under which to perform site construction and assembly operations. If true, this claim would be a strength, implying sophisticated and advanced proven module manufacturing practices. There is, however, no proof in Rolls Royce’s literature to substantiate these claims.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: Weaknesses are Apparent: The design relies on conventional PWR CRAs for power control and scram, while lacking bor on for shim and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the 121-fuel assembly core includes 89 control rods, a fuel assembly to control rad assembly (FA/CRA) ratio of 0.75, as compared to typical PWRs with a FA/CRA ratio ~0.4 – introducing a reactivity and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded operation.

entries.section_title: 6.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the UK SMR
entries.text: The design includes an active non-safety, low pressure boron injection for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of a transient or design basis earthquake. This secondary shutdown function is provided by the EBI system which delivers boron solution to the RCS. The EBI system operates at low pressure and is therefore dependent on the HPIS

pumps and AC power. A significant departure from the most advanced light water reactors, likely made possible by the large number of RCCAs included in the design. Control rod drive mechanisms are expensive components, and the sheer number of RCCAs and RCCA adds substantially to the plant capital cost. While likely able to shut the reactor down, the absence of a second independent and passive shutdown system is very likely a fatal flaw in many international regulatory regimes.

Furthermore, Holtec suspects that the fundamental reactor physics and safety basis will be difficult to demonstrate for a boron-free PWR core lacking boron shim, heavy fuel Gd2O3 poison loadings, or RCCAs enriched in boron-10. Controlling power and criticality with RCCAs alone (no shim) is a complicated operation requiring constant control rod sequence exchanges to prevent a phenomenon known as control rod history effect, whereby controlled fuel rods in an unborated chemistry breed plutonium in fuel rods, which must be burned to prevent the rods from becoming too 'hot.' Typical of BWRs, it is a complex control scheme, and this feature is an extraordinary departure from PWR OPEX.

Rolls Royce can expect significant challenges satisfying regulatory expectations with respect to the design and construction of the plant's Reactor Island seismic isolation system over raft foundation. While novel in application to an NPP, Rolls Royce provides no information or insights to the maintenance, inspection, testing and serviceability of these complex nuclear structures, introducing substantial regulatory and commercial asset risk to the design and potential future projects.

Regarding modularity, Rolls Royce intends to use construction modules — or Process Clusters — 'conglomerations of 'system modules' manufactured into discrete structural framing systems, housing mechanical, electrical and plumbing (MEP) equipment that can be assembled in an offsite factory. Essentially, these clusters are site bolted and welded mechanical and process equipment frames containing spools and system sub-assemblies with signal and power cable, with associated mechanical/electrical/control interfaces connections prepped for site assembly — to be shipped and connected to face adjacent sub-modules at the site in closely engineered, planned and orchestrated construction sequences. This scheme failed badly when used by Westinghouse at its US Vogtle AP1000 project, and despite Rolls' claims to having overcome challenges encountered with this approach, little or no information is available to substantiate such a claim.

On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation in design features that would lend the plant safer or more economical than a conventional large PWR. Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from others by claiming 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred in manufacturing factories, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with power plant 'assembly' at the site. While an ambitious goal, this appears to indicate a lack of understanding of the actual realities of nuclear power plant construction logistics and realities and further indicates an immature design for construction. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration PGA of 0.3g. That said, the UK SMR includes seismic isolators under the reactor building, a novel design, construction, and licensing challenge. The information available makes no mention of consideration of or capability to cool the plant with ACCs, seemingly limiting its deployment to sites with available cooling water.

entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is deemed both safe and practical, with design features and functions that prioritize SAFETY and ease of OPERATIONS. The power plant is designed in a Standard Plant configuration and incorporates innovative Concrete Strengthened Steel Modules (CSSMs) for major nuclear island civil structures and supports, to optimize construction safety, quality, cost and schedule. The Holtec SMR-300 pressurized water reactor (PWR) coolant system has a large water mass per megawatt compared to typical PWRs and includes gravity-driven engineered safety features that eliminate active components and AC power needed in typical PWRs and BWRs. The design reflects decades of PWR operating experience and lessons learned. Holtec has emphasized elimination of fundamental causative failures in reactor operations and maintenance, e.g., stress corrosion cracking of reactor vessel and steam generator materials and components, for a long and assured plant lifetime of 80 yrs1. The design incorporates an innovative robust integrated containment and enclosure structure and reactor auxiliary building with intermediate buildings (combined these building form the Standard Plant Nuclear Island) constructed substantially from CSSMs, facilitating expedient assembly of the standard plant, while providing assured plant safety and security against accidents, natural disasters and terrorist threats. The CSSM design and deployment plan is predicated on decades of Holtec's proven, licensed HI-STORM fuel storage casks and associated modular construction technologies. The plant design includes an integrated and licensed spent fuel management system and provides for life-of-the-plant on-site storage of used fuel in an NRC-licensed subterranean configuration. Equipped with passive engineered safety features, the plant provides assured walk-away safety with no operator actions for an unlimited duration. The Holtec SMR-300 design is differentiated by including an alternative waste heat rejection system that utilizes a Holtec-proprietary air-cooled heat exchanger technology to facilitate siting the plant in water challenged regions.

The reactor coolant system features gravity-driven circulation which assures removal of decay heat from the core if the plant trips or the mechanical devices to boost primary flow fail. A not-important-to-safety pump in each of the two cold legs helps generate a highly turbulized flow regime in the reactor core and the steam generator, eliminating concerns of localized flow stagnation. The power plant produces clean super-heated steam ideal for both electricity generation and process heat applications. The plant is offered in both a single unit and a standard dual-unit configuration, the latter to optimize construction and operating costs, and to eliminate single-shaft failure risk to the production of thermal and electric power. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration (PGA) earthquake in the range of 0.4g to 0.6g depending on the shear wave velocity of the site subgrade. The design incorporates two divisions of multi-channel state-of-the-art electrical and digital control architectures with passive safety systems to simplify systems, equipment, cabinets and cables compared to other complex 3 and 4 safety division SMRs with active safety systems, to reduce capital and operating costs and complexities.

Structural safety analysis of the Holtec SMR-300 plant has been performed using design basis loadings that bound the highest environmental loadings that are likely to occur at any of the sites where the plant is likely to be sited. The design thus developed and qualified is referred to as the Bounding Design. The object of this approach is to make sure that all plants, no matter where deployed, shall be virtually identical and standardized, helping minimize construction time and cost and facilitating the use of standard plant procedures.

With these simplifications, the SMR-300 twin-reactor configuration with shared non-safety and BOP systems and structures is expected to provide a distinctly improve plant economics and resource utilization needed to make it cost competitive.

For the supply of SMRs, Holtec is in an exclusive global teaming relationship with Hyundai E&C (HDEC) which designates them as Holtec's EPC construction partner. With its EPC construction partner Hyundai E&C (HDEC), Holtec's first SMR-300 is planned to be constructed and operated by 2031 at Palisades, MI in the US, with a Limited Work Authorization request submitted to the USNRC in Q1.2026 to begin site excavation and underground works, followed by a 10 CFR 50 Construction Permit Application submitted not later than Q3.2027, for construction and operation with an initial 40-yr operating license. Holtec has affirmed its ability and commitment to fund the project with internal and partner equity and debt financing. The Palisades LLWR PPA off-taker has a right-of-first refusal and plan for the SMR-300 electricity output. The FOAK SMR-300 power plant will be located adjacent to the exiting Palisades Large Light Water reactor in Covert MI, owned, due to be restarted by the 2025 year end, and operated by Holtec. The Twin SMRs at the Palisades site will benefit from common services and resources across the Palisades Nuclear Energy Center.

Described in Section 4 of this report, the GEH BWRX-300 is a practical boiling water reactor (BWR) power plant from a control and operations perspective. It uses substantially developed and proven technologies and components, leveraging decades of BWR operating experience - and excepting its revolutionary use of Reactor Isolation Valves (RIV) with a Dry Containment - its design is otherwise very similar to conventional generation large BWRs. A 'natural circulation reactor' with 100% high-pressure pumped condensate reactor feedwater during power operations, the plant is relatively easy to refuel during an outage, but its radioactive condenser steam both limits the plants application flexibility and greatly complicates turbine island and balance of plant outage maintenance issues and costs as compared to PWR SMRs. Unique aspects of the reactor plant include the use of unproven first-of-a-kind integrated nuclear RIVs. In conjunction with a single isolation condenser safety system performing multiple crucial safety functions and a small dry containment, GEH's BWRX-300 will challenge US, Canadian and international regulators to change certain key regulatory acceptance criteria to be able to license the plant.

GEH has attempted to simplify the reactor's engineered safety systems by eliminating diverse means and systems to cool or shutdown the reactor in case of accidents. The reactor relies on fine motion control rod drives (FMCRDs) for startup, control and scram, and those rods can be passively scrammed by pressurized accumulators. The FMCRDS include a secondary means of insertion for that same shutdown function, albeit one relying on non-safety AC powered screw drives. Another independent means to shut down the reactor relies on a manually actuated enriched boron liquid injection system reliant on non-safety AC power in case of an Anticipated Transient Without Scram (ATWS). It's clear how the design is able to assure shutdown in the event of an ATWS concurrent with a Loss of Offsite Power (LOOP) without reliance on non-safety AC power. The experience of the Fukushima Daiichi accident is certain to elicit heightened scrutiny of this single safety system design, which includes no ability to provide makeup water to the reactor in case of an unanticipated accident. The design incorporates hybrid composite steel plates originally developed and tested by Modular Wall Systems (Scotland, UK), now modified with a derivative Diaphragm Plate Steel Composite (DP-SC) module that GEH is developing in-house. The BWRX-300 integrated reactor building is substantially below grade, and to be constructed entirely with these DP-SC modules (in lieu of conventional rebar-concrete construction) within a deep excavated shaft. Like Holtec's CSSM civil modules and construction approach for major nuclear island structures, DP-SC panels are expected to be fabricated in factories in sizes that can be shipped to construction sites to be further assembled before being lifted into final position for grouting.
