entries.text: The containment building holds a containment vessel that encloses the reactor, providing confinement of radiation sources and preventing release to the environment in accident conditions. The containment vessel is a large steel pressure vessel, designed to American Society of Mechanical Engineers (ASME) III specifications, which contains the components of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS). The vessel is cylindrical and includes a top and bottom dome. The bottom dome is embedded into concrete and supported upon the aseismic bearing. The vessel is approximately 32m in diameter, 37m in height with an internal free air volume of around 18,000m³.

The RCS is a three-loop PWR configured to facilitate natural circulation when pumped flow is unavailable. Each loop consists of primary pipes going into and out of the reactor pressure vessel, with a single seal-less

reactor coolant pump in the cold leg, and one vertical u-tube Steam Generator (SG). One of the loops contains the pressurizer connected to the hot leg, to maintain pressure within the primary reactor circuit and avoid boiling of the coolant. The operational pressure of the primary circuit is 15.5 MPa.

The RPV is a cylindrical steel vessel designed to withstand the high temperatures, pressures, and radiation of the reactor. The RPV houses the reactor core, in-core instrumentation, and the reactor internals. The reactor core is made up of 121 fuel rod assemblies and 89 control rod assemblies. Each fuel assembly is arranged in a 17x17 array of fuel rods consisting of a metallic zirconium alloy cladding housing the nuclear fuel, which is now in the form of small ceramic pellets, which contain up to 4.95% enriched uranium dioxide fuel. The hemispherical upper head of the RPV is removable to allow refueling of the reactor every 18 months.

Water is used as the primary coolant, to extract the heat from the reactor, and as a moderator to maintain the nuclear reaction in the core. Hot water from the core outlet passes into the SGs, where it flows through thousands of heat exchange tubes which transfer the heat to the secondary coolant on the outside of the tubes which is allowed to boil and produce steam. It is this steam produced in the secondary side of the SGs that drives a turbine that ultimately, via a generator, produces electricity. The primary coolant leaving the SGs, which is now at lower temperature, is then pumped back into the reactor via the cold legs. The flowrate of the primary coolant is such that the flow through each loop takes only a few seconds.

Unlike other commercial PWRs, the generic Rolls-Royce SMR design is designed to operate without soluble boron during normal operations. Rolls-Royce SMR Limited claim that, in addition to simplification of the design, this provides safety benefits including full shutdown margin delivered by the control rods and elimination of boron dilution faults.

A range of safety measures are present in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide cooling, control criticality and contain radioactivity under faulted conditions. Active components and supporting electrical supply are claimed not to be significantly risk important. entries.text: A NuScale power plant in any power module configuration (6x, 12x, other) has two separate turbine buildings, each housing up to six turbines and air-cooled generators. The turbine buildings are above-grade structures that house the turbine-generators with their auxiliaries, the condensers, condensate systems, and the feedwater systems. Each turbine-generator is associated with a single NPM and has dedicated condensate and feedwater pumps. As such, a 6-module 462 MWe power plant includes nearly six times as much equipment to be procured, constructed, and maintained as a single reactor power plant producing the same output. This SMR design attempts to benefit by eliminating the single-shaft risk associated with large LWRs, with a novel small reactor (77 MWe) concept deployed in multiples, albeit one where individual small reactors weigh nearly 850 metric tons each.

The NuScale Power includes an extremely novel and untested sequence of refueling operations, with complex heavy lifts and first-of-a-kind tooling. Reactor/containment modules are refueled on a staggered 24-month cycle, by moving them via a 1000 metric ton overhead crane to a common refueling area adjacent to the spent fuel pool following module separation from all piping connections, and disassembly of the containment and reactor vessels.

Each module resides under a biological shield in a three-sided bay that is open to the common pool. Also included in the pool is the module assembly/disassembly facility, which is used for installation of new modules into the plant in conjunction with the building crane. The reactor building layout and equipment is designed for refueling to be completed for a single module while the other modules continue to generate power. This staggered refueling of individual modules is performed by a permanent team of plant personnel.

The reactor building houses the NuScale Power Modules (NPMs) in a large subterranean reactor pool. The building is a seismic Category-1 structure, constructed with rebar reinforced concrete. The building is approximately 100m long and 50m wide and includes a large steel-lined pool of borated water, within which the NPMs (RPV + CNV) are suspended from the interior walls of the building. This pool of water provides the plant's ultimate heat sink and further provides reactivity control for the reactor during accidents or refueling, and the spent fuel pool.
Regardless of the number of modules, the same major capital civil and mechanical structures, crane and refueling and disassembly area and equipment are required for each VOYGR plant.

entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 is a light water PWR reactor that utilizes borated water in its primary side operating in a closed loop. The reactor, steam generator and pressurizer assemblage is configured to produce a gravity-driven circulation of the reactor coolant where the heat energy generated in the core is extracted from the reactor coolant in the steam generator. In normal plant operating mode, the rate of steam production is developed by the booster pumps connecting the Steam Generator to the reactor vessel. The booster pumps are sized to quadruple the through-flow of the reactor coolant (as compared to the natural circulation flow rate), enabling the core to be operated with an efficient uranium burn-up and a corresponding heat generation rate.

The primary coolant circulating through the Once-Through Steam Generator (OTSG) produces superheated steam, and a large pressurizer volume ensures operational reliability while eliminating the need for Power Operated Relief Valves (PORVs). The once through design also significantly reduces the accumulation of contaminants (i.e., crud) typical to recirculating-type steam generators, increasing service life.

The hot leg of the reactor coolant system consists of two parallel pipes emanating from the shrouded region of the core and running parallel to the body of the OTSG, ending at the inlet nozzles located in the top header of the OTSG. There are no RPV penetrations below the RCS safety injection nozzles.

The Holtec SMR-300 has a considerably larger water volume to power ratio compared to traditional PWRs. This results in a large heat removal buffer for transients due to the large SG shell-side volume (with secondary flow outside the SG tubes).

REACTOR DESIGN NAME SMR-300 Thermal Power (MWth) 1050 Electrical Power (MWe, net) 340 Primary circulation Forced FA number in core 69 Fuel assembly length (ft) 12 Effective core diameter (ft) 7.0 Core height-to-diameter ratio 1.7 Power density (w/cc) 80 Average linear heat rate (kW/ft) 4.8 Fuel cycle (month) 18 Core-average enrichment (wt%) 4.8-4.9 Number of fresh FA per cycle 25 Average discharge burnup (GWD/MTU) 54

The Holtec SMR-300 plant incorporates numerous barriers for plant safety, including a thick enclosure constructed from steel plate and concrete, a large reservoir of water, and a composite steel and CSSM containment vessel. This layered approach provides substantial protection to the reactor and its safety systems, and allows the Holtec SMR-300 to guarantee a negligible predicted release of radioactivity with no relevant risk to health and safety of the public.

The NuScale VOYGR design introduces numerous novel features and functions that may be proving to be unacceptable to experienced nuclear owner/operators, not least owing to the plant's unique reactor refueling environment, structures, processes and requirements, with associated FOAK operational risks and impacts.

Licensing issues and concerns aside, the entire VOYR power plant departs from proven nuclear power plant design functions for operability and presents unique features and operational challenges never previously incorporated or proven, presenting non-quantifiable risks and uncertainties to potential clients. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration PGA of 0.5g.

The Rolls Royce UK SMR, described in Section 6 of this report, is an unconventional forced circulation 3-loop PWR, including both active and passive safety systems. This lack of conventionality owes to the design relying on PWR control rod assemblies (CRAs) for power control and scram, as the plant does not employ boron for reactivity control and assured shutdown.

Highly atypical for a PWR, the 121-fuel assembly core includes 89 control rods for a Fuel Assembly (FA) to Control Rod Assembly (CRA) ratio of 0.75, as compared to typical PWRs with a FA/CRA ratio ~0.4 - introducing a reactivity and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded operation.

While it is important not to objectively overstate technical, commercial, or regulatory risks associated with this fuel cycle, it is equally important to point out the novelty of this PWR core and fuel cycle, with its attendant uncertainties regarding exposure dependent and transient fuel and clad performance.

GE and BWR operators learned much about exposure dependent impacts to fuel mechanical performance from rodded-exposure and the thermal-physics of that fuel, as compared to the homogenous PWR core control. Time will tell, as lessons are learned and adopted to improve fuel performance for this novel fuel cycle.

The design includes active low pressure boron injection requiring AC power for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of certain transients including a design basis earthquake.

On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation or design features that would render the plant economically competitive with conventional large PWR, while appearing to be significantly over-engineered in terms of redundant trains and divisions common to earlier generation PWRs and UK relevant good practice (RGP).

That said, Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from existing PWRs by 1) constructing the plant's Reactor Island in its entirety on a seismically isolated basement as a raft foundation and retaining wall, all of which is composed entirely of rebar-reinforced concrete (RC). The Reactor Building is further covered by a large Hazard Shield, essentially a large RC roof over the top of the Reactor Island, 300ft long 200ft wide and extending 150ft above grade, and further claiming that 2) 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred fabricating and assembling factory fabricated modules, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with traditional power plant 'assembly' at the site.

Small modular reactors (SMRs) have increasingly become a centerpiece of the nuclear industry’s aspiration to play a critical role in decarbonizing the world’s national economies which many view as an existential struggle for ensuring continued habitability of our planet. Developers of nuclear power plants around the world have responded to the challenge by proposing novel small modular reactor designs based on the classical light water technology which originated in the US in the 1950s and rapidly became the most popular reactor architecture leading to over 400 plants built over the past eight decades and operated around the world. Guided by the ostensibly sound reasoning that bigger reactors would bring down per kilowatt cost, each generation of reactors grew steadily in size and power output. Unfortunately, the conventional wisdom did not hold in the case of the commercial nuclear industry and the unit per kilowatt cost of power continued to rise in tandem with the reactor’s size. Other drawbacks inherent to large reactors also came to the fore, such as long period of construction, increased complexity, need for significant investment in power delivery infrastructure and the need for copious quantities of water to reject the plant’s waste heat (which is over 65% of the total power produced by the reactor). The industry’s standing with the public suffered serious setbacks when a boiling water reactor suffered a core melt-down in Fukushima, Japan in March 2011. That accident rekindled memories of the horrific accident at the Russian-built RBMK reactor at Chernobyl in 1986, which was preceded by an accident at TMI unit 2 in 1979. The increasing high costs and safety performance of large reactors have kept them at the being embraced more universally, even as humankind desperately seeks to stem the rise of carbon in the atmosphere.

The above-mentioned drawbacks of large reactors have prompted industry to seek the obverse of largeness, namely small reactors, defined empirically as a reactor that has less than 300 MWe design basis output. It was reasoned that because the “small” reactor has a small inventory of thermal energy at any one time, the dissipation of that heat during a postulated loss of coolant accident should be manageable. Also, a small reactor ought to be built and commissioned in a relatively short time, and the cost of capital per unit output ought to be smaller than large reactors. Proponents of small reactors also hoped that they would be largely factory built, maximizing the benefits inherent in serial manufacturing while minimizing site construction costs. The notion of manufacturing most parts and sub-components in a factory and limiting site construction to a minimum was conceived as the antidote to the awful labor efficiency at construction sites. Thus, the term “modular” became attached to small reactors, resulting in the now commonly used term “small modular reactor,” and its acronym “SMR.”

In this report, Holtec’s attention is focused on the light water SMRs which, because of the maturity of light water technology, hold the promise of immediate deployment. This report accordingly focuses on the merits and demerits of four SMR technologies which have progressed their designs and gained varying levels of acceptance. entries.text: According to Rolls Royce, the UK SMR design is based on an optimized and enhanced use of proven technology, with a single unit, three-loop pWR rated at 1385MWe, 470MWt (gross) and 425 MWe (net).

The Reactor Island includes the systems that form the reactor, transfer, and storage of new and used fuel, and any associated nuclear auxiliary systems. The purpose of Reactor Island is to use the heat from a controlled nuclear fission reaction to generate steam, which is then passed to the Turbine Island. The Reactor Island includes the Reactor Plant, Handling of Nuclear Equipment and Nuclear Auxiliary Systems.
The Handling of Nuclear Equipment includes those systems that cover the fuel route from initial receipt of new fuel to final disposal.
The Auxiliary Systems comprise those systems supporting reactor plant operations.
The Electrical Power System is located within Reactor Island.

The UK SMR primary circuit comprises a reactor core, containing the reactor fuel, mounted in an RPV that is closely coupled through large bore pipework to three SGs. The baseline architecture for the RCS consists of three vertical u-tube Steam Generators (SGs) with associated pipework loops and a single Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) in each loop, mounted to the SG outlet. The configuration of the SG, pipework and pump layout in each loop provides thermal driving head for natural circulation flow during fault conditions. The system also contains a pump induced spray pressurizing system with associated pressure relief system.

The RPV assembly consists of an RPV body, a tori-spherical closure head assembly and a bolting arrangement comprising studs, washers, and mechanical seals. The RPV diameter is constrained to be less than 15 feet to ensure that the UK road transport height of 16 feet is not exceeded.

Primary circuit pressure is controlled by electrical heaters located at the base of the pressurizer and spray from a nozzle located at the top. Steam and water are maintained in equilibrium to provide the necessary overpressure. The pressurizer is a vertical, cylindrical vessel constructed from low alloy steel, sized to provide passive fault response for bounding faults with accidents causing either rapid and significant cooldown or heat-up accommodated.

Nuclear fuel includes UO2 enriched up to 4.95%, clad with a zirconium alloy and arranged in a 17x17 assembly. The core contains 121 fuel assemblies and has an active fueled length of approximately 9 feet, delivering a thermal power of 1358 MWth. Each fuel assembly contains 264 fuel rods, with 40 rods incorporating 8 wt% Gd2O3. The design includes 89 control rod assemblies, nearly twice the reactor core control rod density as compared to conventional PWRs.

No concentration of soluble boron is maintained in the primary coolant for reactivity or power control. Reactivity control is instead provided entirely via movement of control rods. No description is available as to the number and type (grey, shutdown, other) of control rod groups other than 89 total CRAs.

A vertical u-tube SG configuration has been selected as a mature and readily deployable technology. Other designs have been considered but deemed insufficiently mature for commercial deployment in 2030 in the first of a kind plant. Each of the three steam generators removes approximately 452 MWth of heat from the primary circuit, generating dry steam which drives the turbine to generate electricity. The SG design includes an economizer which preferentially directs feedwater to the cold leg of the tube bundle, and the majority of the recirculated water to the hot leg, resulting in an increased thermal efficiency compared to a conventional equivalent design.

The pump and motor in the RCP are combined in a sealless design; this avoids potential issues with seals which have been a cause of leaks in previous RCP designs. Each RCP is fitted with a flywheel to achieve an extended pump coast-down time, ensuring sufficient cooling flow is pumped through the core in case of a loss of electrical power. The RCP design provides a flow rate of 3.95 m3/s and generates 56 m of head (4 bar). This is somewhat in contrast to Rolls Royce claims that the reactor operates via natural circulation for DBAs.

The UK SMR operates on an 18-24-month fuel cycle, with a three-core shuffle. The duration of refueling outage is currently estimated at 18 days. Refueling is managed through the provision of an in-containment refueling pool which temporarily stores both new and spent fuel during a refueling outage. Spent fuel is subsequently transferred to an external spent fuel pool for storage prior to transfer to long term dry cask storage.

entries.text: This 3X100% ICS HX design includes redundancy for defense-in-depth, but the design lacks any diversity regarding any other passive or active safety systems. The ICS is initiated automatically on high RPV pressure indicating an overpressure event or on signals indicating a LOCA. To start an IC train, the IC condensate return valve is opened whereupon the standing condensate drains into the reactor and the steam water interface in the IC tube bundle moves downward below the lower headers.

During normal reactor operation, the steam supply valve to the ICS is open so that the steam condenses and fills the ICS pipes and the common collectors with condensate water. This condensate is also cooled down to parameters well below the saturation line to facilitate condensed primary coolant back into the reactor when the condensate valves are opened, and to keep the reactor core covered to prevent core melt during design basis accidents. Condensation in the heat exchanger apparatus is carried out by transferring heat to an external water reservoir via the walls of the ICS vertical tubes. ICS heat exchangers are submerged in water tanks above the reactor and containment closure head and dissipate decay heat by evaporation to the atmosphere. The coolant moves by natural circulation due to the density difference in the steam supply and condensate discharge pipework. The volume of the reservoirs is designed for continuous cooling of the reactor core for seven days without makeup or operator actions.

Unlike conventional BWRs that incorporate IC Systems, whereby the condensate is returned to the downcomer for circulation back through the core, the BWRX-300 IC condensate is returned at or near the top of the RPV chimney, functioning like a core spray system. The ICS is the plant's safety feature (ECCS) engineered to protect against reactor overpressure, heat decay and makeup water. This singular plant safety system, part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, is OUTSIDE containment, and located at top of Integrated Reactor Building and potentially susceptible to external hazards, natural and terroristic.

The Passive Containment Cooling System (PCCS) is a passive containment heat removal system that maintains the containment within its pressure limits for design basis accidents such as a LOCA. It consists of several low-pressure natural circulation heat exchangers that transfer heat from the containment to the reactor cavity pool which is located above the containment upper head and is filled with water during normal operation. The reactor cavity pool is vented to the atmosphere. There are no containment isolation valves between the PCCS HXs and the containment.

entries.text: A hazard shield, consisting of a reinforced concrete wall and roof, is included in the Rolls-Royce SMR design to provide protection against radioactivity release due to external hazards. The bounding case for the hazard shield is based on an aircraft impact hazard, aiming to ensure confinement of fuel, prevention of criticality, protection of reactor shutdown and cooling systems and protection of monitoring systems. The hazard shield covers portions of the Reactor Island - the containment building and the fuel and control buildings - to ensure Class 1 SSCs are protected. The Hazard Shield, measuring 200 feet by 300 feet, is essentially a very large cover over the top of the plant’s nuclear assets.

Unlike other commercial PWRs, the generic Rolls-Royce SMR design is designed to operate without soluble boron during normal operations. Rolls-Royce claim that, in addition to simplification of the design, this provides safety benefits including full shutdown margin delivered by the control rods and elimination of boron dilution faults. This feature will however greatly complicate power operations and maneuvers, and may ultimately prove unworkable, lacking a second independent passive means to shut down the reactor.

entries.section_title: Coping Period after Design Basis Accident
entries.text: The plant’s coping period after a design basis accident is limited to 72hrs. before operator actions are required – a significant shortfall in safety achievement compared to the other SMR plants evaluated herein.

The design also includes a Reactor Vessel Cavity Injection System (RVCIS) which has been designed to achieve In-Vessel Retention (IVR) of molten core material in a severe accident. This is achieved by externally cooling the RPV lower head by gravity flooding the reactor cavity pit with water, and allowing this to boil, condense and return to the pit.

entries.section_title: LOCA and Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) System
entries.text: In the event of a LOCA, steam released into the containment throughout the transient is cooled by the LUHS Passive Containment Cooling (PCC) system heat exchangers.

entries.text: The entire Nuclear Island reactor building is unconventional compared to the operating fleet. The reactor modules sit in a borated pool that is common to all modules and serves as a heat sink during the first 72 hours of an accident when off-site power may be unavailable. This pool is an integral part of both the decay heat removal system and the containment heat removal system. Refueling of the modules occurs in a separate pool attached to the containment cooling pool by a central canal. This allows refueling operations to occur separately and distant from the operating modules. During refueling, the two pools are isolated from each other using a gate or installed weir.

To initiate the refueling process, an individual reactor is shut down and the primary system temperature is lowered using the normal feed system and the steam generators. Once the reactor has been cooled below 100°C via the steam generators, the containment vacuum is broken, and the containment is partially flooded via the vacuum system to provide decay heat removal. Flooding the containment vessel provides a passive decay heat removal path that relies only on conduction and convection and, ultimately, the heat sink represented by the containment cooling/refueling pools. While the pools are serviced by active cooling systems, they have a passive capacity to provide at least three days of cooling.

After initial cool-down, the RPV+CNV module is disconnected from its supporting fluid systems and I&C leads. The 850-ton power module is then moved via an overhead crane to the module assembly/disassembly facility where it is remotely disassembled into the lower containment vessel, the lower reactor vessel (includes the reactor core), and the upper module section. While the core is being refueled, the upper module section is moved to a partial dry-dock facility for inspection and maintenance. Refueling of the core is accomplished by transporting upright fuel assemblies between the lower reactor vessel section and the adjacent spent fuel pool via a weir located in the wall that separates the spent fuel pool from the reactor pool. Spent fuel assemblies are stored in the used fuel pool for initial cool-down and later moved to an on-site dry-cask storage facility or interim fuel storage facility if available. After refueling, the module is reassembled, moved to its operating location, and reconnected to all support fluid (steam, feed, CVCS, RHR), electrical and instrumentation and control cables.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: The NuScale reactor plant is based on a small light water reactor developed at Oregon State University in the early 2000s. It consists of one or more NuScale power modules (hereafter referred to as power module(s)). A power module is a natural circulation light water reactor composed of a reactor core, a pressurizer, and two helical coil steam generators located in a common reactor pressure vessel that is integrated within a compact cylindrical steel containment. The NuScale reactor building is designed to hold up to 12 power modules. Each power module of the NRC-certified design has a rated thermal output of 160 MWth and gross electrical output of 50 MWe, yielding a total capacity of 600 MWe for 12 power modules. The NuScale power modules are partially submerged in a large common safety-related pool of borated water, which is also the ultimate heat sink for up to 12 power modules. The pool portion of the reactor building is located below grade. The design utilizes several first-of-a-kind approaches for accomplishing key safety functions.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: The twelve-reactor (50 MWe per power module) NuScale small modular reactor design certification final rule was published in the US federal register effective Feb.21.2023. Review of the design and final safety analysis report indicates a design with inherent safety characteristics owing to the reactor maintaining substantial margin to fuel and reactor coolant system thermal-mechanical safety limits.

entries.section_title: 5.4 Strengths and Weaknesses of the NuScale VOYGR
entries.text: In Jan.2023, NuScale submitted a Standard Design Application (SDA) for an updated small modular reactor design, which is on a six-module VOYGR plant configuration powered by an uprated 77 MWe reactor power module. In a press release announcing submission of the SDA to the US NRC, NuScale indicated that the design uprate was done with select changes to support customer's capacity needs and to improve power plant economics. This design uprate includes a substantial 54% increase in thermal energy output per reactor module, with associated necessary fundamental physical and analytical changes required to satisfy regulatory and operability requirements.

entries.text: RIVs are located on RPV nozzles for the Main Steam System, Reactor Water Cleanup System, the supply and return lines of the ICS system, the Head Vent, and the Feed Water System. The RIV concept consists of two RIVs in series, with each RIV to be able to independently isolate its respective line. On loss of power, the RPV isolation valves fail in the closed position. However, the RIVs for the ICS steam supply and condensate return lines are exceptions. The ICS RIVs fail as-is because they perform safety functions during transient and LOCA events. The fail-as-is RIVs for the ICS steam supply and condensate return piping automatically close on indication of a break in the ICS train in which the RIV is located.

The RIVs are mounted in a double valve body made from an integral assembly attached to the RPV using flanged connections, within an ASME B&PV Code Section III, Class 1 construction. These double isolation valves are integrated to the reactor vessel for all pipes (steam, feed, DHRs (ICS feed and return)) inside containment with diameters greater than 2", to isolate the RCS+ICS (isolation condenser system) and to preserve RPV inventory in the event of a LOCA.

One of the design objectives of the BWRX-300 Reactor Coolant Pressure Boundary (RCPB) is to minimize the risks associated with LOCAs by reducing the number of nozzles attached to the RPV, reducing associated pipe lengths and nominal pipe diameters, and by incorporating double RPV isolation valves integrated to the RPV to isolate the RCS for long-term safe shutdown cooling without the need or facility for makeup water or RCS safety relief valves. To be clear, this innovation appears to rely on a mechanistic argument that these components are designed to code to preclude a non-isolable break upstream of each outer most isolation valve boundary. Undoubtedly - and GEH claims - this innovation should enable simpler passive safety systems, a more compact containment that is dry, and a simpler Reactor Building compared to prior LWR designs. A simpler, safer, smaller plant should be cheaper to own and operate. However, the design includes significant regulatory risk in many global jurisdictions in our opinion, having seen firsthand the NRC resistance to any design or exemption to the intent of 10 CFR 50.46, and a closer look (Section 7) at BWRX-300 nuclear and conventional island areas and volumes seemingly disprove that claim.

The ICS removes decay heat after any reactor isolation and shutdown event during power operations. The ICS decay heat removal limits the increase in steam pressure and maintains the RPV pressure and water inventory at an acceptable level. The ICS consists of three independent loops that each contain a Heat Exchanger (HX) with a capacity of approximately 33 MWth, or approximately 3.7% of rated thermal power, or 3X50% decay heat removal HXs. Thermal energy removal condenses steam on the tube side and transfers heat by heating/evaporating water in the Isolation Condenser (IC) pools which are vented to atmosphere.

This 3X100% ICS HX design includes redundancy for defense-in-depth, but the design lacks any diversity regarding any other passive or active safety systems. The ICS is initiated automatically on high RPV pressure indicating an overpressure event or on signals indicating a LOCA. To start an IC train, the IC condensate return valve is opened whereupon the standing condensate drains into the reactor and the steam water interface in the IC tube bundle moves downward below the lower headers.

During normal reactor operation, the steam supply valve to the ICS is open so that the steam condenses and fills the ICS pipes and the common collectors with condensate water. This condensate is also cooled down to parameters well below the saturation line to facilitate condensed primary coolant back into the reactor when the condensate valves are opened, and to keep the reactor core covered to prevent core melt during design basis accidents. Condensation in the heat exchanger apparatus is carried out by transferring heat to an external water reservoir via the walls of the ICS vertical tubes. ICS heat exchangers are submerged in water tanks above the reactor and containment closure head and dissipate decay heat by evaporation to the atmosphere. The coolant moves by natural circulation due to the density difference in the steam supply and condensate discharge pipework. The volume of the reservoirs is designed for continuous cooling of the reactor core for seven days without makeup or operator actions.

Unlike conventional BWRs that incorporate IC Systems, whereby the condensate is returned to the downcomer for circulation back through the core, the BWRX-300 IC condensate is returned at or near the top of the RPV chimney, functioning like a core spray system. The ICS is the plant's safety feature (ECCS) engineered to protect against reactor overpressure, heat decay and makeup water. This singular plant safety system, part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary, is OUTSIDE containment, and located at top of Integrated Reactor Building and potentially susceptible to external hazards, natural and terroristic.

The Passive Containment Cooling System (PCCS) is a passive containment heat removal system that maintains the containment within its pressure limits for design basis accidents such as a LOCA. It consists of several low-pressure natural circulation heat exchangers that transfer heat from the containment to the reactor cavity pool which is located above the containment upper head and is filled with water during normal operation. The reactor cavity pool is vented to the atmosphere. There are no containment isolation valves between the PCCS HXs and the containment.

entries.text: The PCSS is designed to provide emergency core cooling and makeup water following design basis accidents (DBAs), and unlike other SMRs designs, relies on no first of a kind components, valves, or actuation features not readily and reliably available. The system uses passive means such as natural circulation for core cooling, and compressed gas expansion and gravity injection for makeup, without the use of pumps. The design automatically manages and mitigates the effects of leaks and small break LOCA’s.

The passive safety systems rely on buoyancy driven flow and one-time opening of valves, eliminating the need for Class 1E AC power. A heat sink reservoir incorporated directly in the design surrounds the above grade CS and eliminates the need for safety-related cooling systems, while the passive core makeup water system (PCMWS) located inside the CS eliminates the need for external water supplies for safety injection. Small chemical and volume control system (CVCS) throughput equates to slow ion exchange resin consumption and little crud/lower resin radiological loading, resulting in low quantities of secondary waste streams. Because of the reduced plant size, reduced staffing, short refueling outages, and fewer plant systems, the Holtec SMR-300 yields less low-level waste than current facilities.

The Containment Enclosure (CS) is enveloped by the containment enclosure structure (CES), a steel and concrete structure assembled from CSSM modules that protects the CS from incident missiles and malevolent acts such as a crashing aircraft and contains a large reservoir of water in the annular region formed between the CES and Containment. This technology is proven and broadly deployed by Holtec, and its proprietary HI-STORM spent fuel storage system, licensed, and deployed in the US and numerous countries overseas.

The CES walls are constructed of extremely robust steel-concrete modules designed to withstand an impact from large commercial aircraft and other potential hazards. In addition to preventing the release of radioactive fission products to the environment, the containment system acts as a large passive heat exchanger. The containment system is partially embedded, with approximately half of the total height located below grade to maximize protection against external hazards and dampen seismic effects for critical components.

entries.section_title: Integrated Spent Nuclear Fuel Systems and Technologies
entries.text: The plant design incorporates a licensed spent fuel handling solution that accommodates discharge of spent fuel assemblies to underground dry storage in the HI-STORM UMAX Storage System, in conjunction with a tiny spent fuel pool passively cooled in the event of a design basis accident and protected inside the containment and CES. On-site interim dry storage within the HI-STORM UMAX system accommodates all the spent nuclear fuel for the design life of the Holtec SMR-300 reactor. When dry storage is performed during the refueling outage, the same HI-TRAC transfer cask that was used to bring in the new fuel will be used to move spent assemblies to dry storage. After the new fuel has been removed, and with the HI-TRAC still within the spent fuel pool (SFP), discharged spent fuel assemblies are loaded into the HI-TRAC using the fuel handling bridge and then the internal canister is prepared for on-site storage or off-site transport.

entries.section_title: Integrated Spent Nuclear Fuel Systems and Technologies
entries.text: The Holtec SMR-300 has been developed with construction and decommissioning in mind. Major plant buildings employ shallow and wide layouts to ease construction and make equipment installation uncomplicated. Plant buildings and other SSCs are arranged in a manner that readily befits decommissioning with minimal work, cost and material movements and transport. During decommissioning, the time, work, cost and material to unload spent fuel from the Holtec SMR-300 reactor and spent fuel pool after final shutdown is dramatically reduced as compared to a conventional reactor plant because at the end of design life most fuel will already have been removed from the SFP and placed in dry storage.

The onsite distribution system is fed from the offsite power system during plant startup, normal or emergency shutdown, or during plant outages. During normal plant operations, it is fed from the main generator. If there is a loss of offsite power without a turbine trip, the plant will operate in island mode where the reactor will run back to a reduced power and the main generator will power all house loads. The Holtec SMR-300 is designed to provide flexible power output and perform load following based on grid demand. The Holtec SMR-300 is capable of quickly reducing from 100% to 0% power without a plant trip and is designed for continuous operation at low power or a return to higher power levels within hours.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: SMR-300 has been designed with special focus on a long service life marked by the absence of stress corrosion cracking failures and unscheduled shutdowns. While an accurate service life projection is not possible, the SMR-300 includes specific design features to overcome known reactor plant operational challenges, to best ensure it exceeds 80yr design life:

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Ensuring absence of laminar conditions: Holtec understands that laminar or transitional flow conditions which typically afflict thermosiphon-based designs and is caused by a small driving head is a threat to the system reliability of any reactor system. To ensure that the Holtec SMR-300 will be free of such a problem, the turbulence level in the RCS and elsewhere in the plant is required to be at least four times the upper end of the transition zone at the lowest power output condition.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Protecting the RCS pressure boundary: SCC and cyclic fatigue from thermal transients have been identified as the twin threats to the integrity of the pressure boundary in reactor vessels and steam generators. These threats have been ameliorated in the Holtec SMR-300 by ensuring that the RCS temperature changes are not abrupt, made possible by the large thermal inertia of the entire RCS, and by employing a thermal liner throughout the pressure boundary which blunts the thermal shock to the pressure boundary material (a patented Holtec invention).

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Protecting Steam Generator tubes from Wastage: The wisdom received from the spate of steam generator failures in the 1990s in the United States has been incorporated in the Holtec SMR-300 SG design. The tubes are made of thermally treated Inconel 690, All-Volatile Treatment (AVT) water chemistry treatment is employed, and the blow-down rate to continuously purge the SG sludge is two times that used in the latest LWR designs. In addition, a tube installation sequence has been developed to pre-stress the most severely loaded tubes to mitigate tube axial stresses during operations. Non-segmental tube supports (based on an expired Patent patent and extensively used by the Company over the past 30 years) have been incorporated in the design to minimize vibration producing cross flows. It can be said that the Holtec SMR-300’s SG design incorporates all the chastening lessons learned from seven decades of PWR operations.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Vibration: Vibration of slender parts such as tubes in feedwater heaters, control condensers, steam generators, moisture separator reheaters, auxiliary feed exchangers, surface rod extensions, and piping runs has been a persistent operating problem in nuclear plants. In the Holtec SMR-300, this ubiquitous problem is systematically solved by requiring that the fundamental natural frequency of the part be at least two times the highest frequency of the excitation source. In heat exchangers, principal excitation sources are fluid elastic coupling and turbulent buffeting. Piping runs are vulnerable to the harmonics associated with earthquakes.

entries.section_title: 3.10 SMR-300 Design Attributes that ensure 80-year minimum service life
entries.text: Pressure retaining weld seams: Pressure retaining welds in the RCS are known to be vulnerable to failure and are thus subject to periodic in-service inspection that increases outage duration. In the Holtec SMR-300, Holtec proprietary design strategies have been employed to significantly reduce the number of weld seams.

entries.text: The Control Building, Turbine Building, and RadWaste Building structures are built on a near-surface basement foundation adjacent to the deeply embedded RB structure. The Control Building includes the plant's control room, electrical, control, and instrumentation equipment. The RadWaste Building houses rooms and equipment for handling, processing, and packaging liquid and solid radioactive wastes. entries.text: (NPM) plant in early 2023, several key open items were carved out of that certification, including the helical coil steam generators.

To enhance performance and economics, NuScale pursued an uprated design with 77MWe modules. They submitted their Standard Design Approval (SDA) application for the VOYR-6 (a six-module configuration) in January 2023. As of May 2025, the NRC completed the review and issued a Standard Design Approval for the US460 which corresponds to the VOYR-6 configuration of 77 MWe modules (462 MWe gross, estimated 420 MWe net).

Licensing issues and concerns aside, the entire VOYR power plant departs from proven nuclear power plant design functions for operability and presents unique features and operational challenges never previously incorporated or proven, presenting non-quantifiable risks and uncertainties to potential clients. The standard plant is bounded by a peak ground acceleration PGA of 0.5g.

The Rolls Royce UK SMR, described in Section 6 of this report, is an unconventional forced circulation 3-loop PWR, including both active and passive safety systems. This lack of conventionality owes to the design relying on PWR control rod assemblies (CRAs) for power control and scram, as the plant does not employ boron for reactivity control and assured shutdown. Highly atypical for a PWR, the 121-fuel assembly core includes 89 control rods for a Fuel Assembly (FA) to Control Rod Assembly (CRA) ratio of 0.75, as compared to typical PWRs with a FA/CRA ratio ~0.4 - introducing a reactivity and control scheme more akin to a BWR than a PWR, and with the complexities of fully-rodded operation. While it is important not to objectively overstate technical, commercial, or regulatory risks associated with this fuel cycle, it is equally important to point out the novelty of this PWR core and fuel cycle, with its attendant uncertainties regarding exposure dependent and transient fuel and clad performance. GE and BWR operators learned much about exposure dependent impacts to fuel mechanical performance from rodded-exposure and the thermal-physics of that fuel, as compared to the homogenous PWR core control. Time will tell, as lessons are learned and adopted to improve fuel performance for this novel fuel cycle.

The design includes active low pressure boron injection requiring AC power for a secondary shutdown system and further includes active safety systems to keep the reactor and fuel cooled in case of certain transients including a design basis earthquake. On balance, the UK SMR design includes little innovation or design features that would render the plant economically competitive with conventional large PWR, while appearing to be significantly over-engineered in terms of redundant trains and divisions common to earlier generation PWRs and UK relevant good practice (RGP).

That said, Rolls Royce appears to differentiate the plant from existing PWRs by 1) constructing the plant's Reactor Island in its entirety on a seismically isolated basement as a raft foundation and retaining wall, all of which is composed entirely of rebar-reinforced concrete (RC). The Reactor Building is further covered by a large Hazard Shield, essentially a large RC roof over the top of the Reactor Island, 300ft long 200ft wide and extending 150ft above grade, and further claiming that 2) 90% of the UK SMR capital cost will be incurred fabricating and assembling factory fabricated modules, while the remaining 10% will be the cost associated with traditional power plant 'assembly' at the site. With respect to 1) maintenance of these complex foundation and seismic bearing structures, Rolls Royce claims that the serviceability design of these RC structures shall be carried out in accordance with ACI 349M-13 and ACI 318M-08, without any publicly available information to substantiate such. Rolls Royce intends to use low-damping laminated rubber bearings for the plant Seismic Isolation System and claims these will be designed to the general performance requirements and preferred methods of analysis and testing per ASCE 4-16 and section 9 of ASCE 43-19. The novelty of this civil seismic isolation design, integrated with the Reactor Island basement and raft foundation may pose a serious challenge for regulatory acceptance, and the potential need or

In this report, the design attributes of each reactor technology are presented using information available in the public domain. From the body of information compiled herein, it's practical to assess or evaluate each in accord with a list of Critical SMR Features. Holtec's global nuclear manufacturing business experience, combined with its quality assurance and supply chain expertise, and with capital construction and commissioning experience in US and global markets, substantially informs our thinking when considering which of these vendor/technologies are most broadly licensable and deployable. From this we conclude that the Holtec SMR-300 is the most eligible technology for immediate deployment in US and global markets. A comparison between technologies considering safety, plant robustness and design life, siting and operational flexibility, life cycle fuel management and resource/area bases implies distinct and compelling operational and economic advantages to the SMR-300 power plant design when compared to the other lwr SMR technologies assessed herein. The SMR-300 standard plant's twin-reactor configuration maximizes the value for money through optimally shared non-safety plant structures and systems, to overcome the disadvantages of smaller power plants.

Designs lacking integrated spent fuel solutions can expect to face future $100m+ costs to engineer, license and construct integrated spent fuel storage facilities. entries.text: To demonstrate that the SMR-300 RPV shells, heads, and nozzles sizing are sufficient with respect to regulatory and design requirements, a design-by-analysis approach of Reference [4] is completed. When the actual piping loads and moments are available, the angle and direction may not be oriented at one of these, 0, 45, 90-degree type orientations. It is assumed that varying the orientations by 45 degrees will be sufficient at this time, to provide the most severe orientation. Figure: A-1 shows the model geometry and a sample setup. As stated in Section 3.0, a stress analysis is performed to determine the RPV stresses during Design and Test conditions. For the limited scope of this report for initial superimposed piping loads, Design Pressure and Temperature loadings, deadweight, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions, a finite element analysis (FEA) of the RPV is completed to determine the stresses. The following sections describe the FEA preprocessing, solution, and results.

The geometry described in Section 6.1 was imported in ANSYS. Edits were performed to aid in mesh generation and boundary condition application, such as adding extensions to the nozzles, end caps to both the nozzles and CRDM penetrations. Additionally, many bodies were suppressed as they were not needed, and no geometry for the RVI or reactor coolant fluid was included. The RPV cladding geometry contained in the CAD model, as defined in Reference [1], was not included with the exception of the portion of cladding at the closure head to vessel interface. This portion was retained to better enable the connection between the head and vessel. According to Reference [4], no structural strength due to cladding is permitted for primary stress evaluation. Since the scope of this report is limited to the previously mentioned geometry and load conditions, only primary stresses will result. Therefore, the cladding is not included, except as previously mentioned. For further details of the FEA geometry see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf. Figure 9-1 shows the geometry used in the FEA.

The materials used in the FEA are given in Section 6.3. Modifications to certain material properties are made as described in Section 9.5.1. For further details of the FEA materials see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf
To simulate threaded and welded attachments between certain components, bonded contact connections were created at the following interfaces:

Also, for simplification purposes and since the torque values are unknown at this time, it was assumed (see Section 5.0) that the Closure Studs will prevent any separation between the Closure Head and Vessel during service conditions. In other words, the Closure Stud preload will be sufficient to maintain a tight joint during all service conditions. Therefore, bonded contact was created between the Closure Head Cladding and Vessel Cladding. For further details of the FEA connections see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf.
The RPV components were represented using solid elements, with the majority being hexahedral shaped. The nozzle and CRDM penetration end caps were represented with shell elements.

entries.text: This report documents one of several mechanical analyses performed for the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), as defined in Reference [1], for the SMR-300. The included analyses are performed to demonstrate that the sizing of the design is structurally adequate to meet the design requirements and acceptance criteria set forth by 10 CFR 50 with endorsements to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code. This, and other analyses, will ensure all aspects of the RPV design assembly, will satisfy all structural and functional requirements. This report focuses on the RPV heads, shells and nozzles sizing when subjected to Design Pressure, Design Temperature, Test Pressure, and estimated piping loads only. A minimum thickness calculation is also performed. Accordingly, only primary stress for these conditions was evaluated. Safety factors were computed, and recommendations are provided to remedy potential unsatisfactory conditions. The analysis focuses on the RPV geometry defined in Reference [1], and does not consider the geometry of any interfacing components. In addition to regulatory requirements, the SMR-300 RPV must satisfy the criteria specified in the Owners (i.e. Holtec International, as defined by ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NCA) (Reference [3]), certified RPV ASME Design Specification. The RPV ASME Design Specification classifies the RPV as a Division 1, Class 1 item (per NCA-2100), which requires the design and analysis to be completed in accordance with the rules contained in ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB (Reference [4]). The RPV ASME Design Specification is not currently available for this report. The scope of this report is therefore limited to initial superimposed loads, Design Pressure and Design Temperature loadings, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions. After the ASME Design Specification is completed, future analyses will be performed to show that the RPV satisfies all the criteria contained within the ASME Design Specification including all load combinations for ASME Service Levels A, B, C, and D. Stresses from superimposed mechanical loads on the RPV due to interactions with interfacing components such as the Control Rod Drive Mechanisms and Reactor Vessel Internals are not included in this report. Additionally, triaxial stress and comparison to the ASME limits were not included in this report.

The purpose of this report is to provide a detailed mechanical analysis of the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) for the SMR-300, ensuring that the design meets all structural and functional requirements as per the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code and the SMR-300 RPV ASME Design Specification.

The methodology employed in this report involves the analysis of the RPV under various loading conditions, including Design Pressure, Design Temperature, Test Pressure, and estimated piping loads. The analysis is performed using finite element analysis (FEA) to evaluate the structural integrity of the RPV components.

The acceptance criteria for this analysis are based on the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code and the SMR-300 RPV ASME Design Specification. The primary stress evaluated under the specified loading conditions must meet the criteria set forth in these documents.

The allowable stress limits are derived from the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code and are used to ensure that the RPV components do not exceed the permissible stress levels under the specified loading conditions.

Deformation limits are established to ensure that the RPV components do not undergo excessive deformation under the specified loading conditions, which could compromise the structural integrity of the vessel.
External pressure conditions are considered in the analysis to ensure that the RPV components can withstand the external forces applied during operation and testing.
A minimum thickness calculation is performed to ensure that the RPV components have sufficient thickness to withstand the specified loading conditions without failure.

Several assumptions are made in the analysis, including the geometry of the RPV components, the material properties, and the loading conditions. These assumptions are necessary to simplify the analysis and ensure that the results are accurate and reliable.

The input data for the analysis includes the geometry of the RPV components, the material properties, and the loading conditions. This data is used to perform the finite element analysis and evaluate the structural integrity of the RPV.

The geometry of the RPV components is defined in Reference [1] and is used as the basis for the finite element analysis. The geometry includes the RPV heads, shells, and nozzles, which are subjected to the specified loading conditions.

The input loads for the analysis include Design Pressure, Design Temperature, Test Pressure, and estimated piping loads. These loads are applied to the RPV components to evaluate their structural integrity under various operating conditions.

The material properties of the RPV components are used in the finite element analysis to evaluate their structural integrity under the specified loading conditions. These properties include the material's strength, stiffness, and other relevant characteristics.

The finite element analysis is performed using specialized computer codes that simulate the behavior of the RPV components under the specified loading conditions. These codes are essential for accurately evaluating the structural integrity of the RPV.

The computer files used in the analysis include the geometry files, material property files, and loading condition files. These files are essential for performing the finite element analysis and evaluating the structural integrity of the RPV.

The analysis involves performing the finite element analysis using the specified computer codes and input data. The results of the analysis are used to evaluate the structural integrity of the RPV components under the specified loading conditions.
The finite element analysis geometry is defined based on the RPV components' geometry and is used to simulate their behavior under the specified loading conditions.
The finite element analysis materials are defined based on the material properties of the RPV components and are used to simulate their behavior under the specified loading conditions.
The finite element analysis connections are defined based on the connections between the RPV components and are used to simulate their behavior under the specified loading conditions.
The finite element analysis mesh is defined based on the geometry of the RPV components and is used to simulate their behavior under the specified loading conditions.

The finite element analysis solutions are obtained by solving the equations of motion for the RPV components under the specified loading conditions. These solutions are used to evaluate the structural integrity of the RPV.

The results of the finite element analysis are used to evaluate the structural integrity of the RPV components under the specified loading conditions. These results include stress and deformation values, which are compared to the allowable limits to ensure compliance with the acceptance criteria.

The conclusions of the analysis are based on the results obtained from the finite element analysis. These conclusions provide recommendations for any necessary design modifications to ensure that the RPV components meet the structural and functional requirements.

The references section includes the documents and sources used in the analysis, such as the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code, the SMR-300 RPV ASME Design Specification, and other relevant references.

The list of appendices includes additional information and data used in the analysis, such as the RCS and DVI Piping Nozzle Study, Initial Piping Loads, RPV and Supported Weights, Allowable External Pressure, Minimum Vessel Thickness, and Mesh Study.

For the scope of this report for initial superimposed piping loads, Design Pressure and Design Temperature loadings, deadweight, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions, three steady state (static) solutions are performed to determine the resulting stresses from each individual load. The stress resulting from the weight of the RPV and components supported by the RPV, including the reactor coolant, due to standard earth gravity, was determined. The amount of weight was calculated in Appendix C. The RPV is supported by the four Trunnions vertically and tangentially about a cylindrical coordinate system where the Z axis is aligned with RPV shell axis. The RPV is unrestrained in the radial direction. Therefore, displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining those degrees of freedom.

The results will be scaled during post processing to achieve the desired pressures. Displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining the degrees of freedom as described in Section 9.5.1. As stated in Section 3.0, a stress analysis is performed to determine the RPV stresses during Design and Test conditions. For the limited scope of this report for initial superimposed piping loads, Design Pressure and Temperature loadings, deadweight, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions, a finite element analysis (FEA) of the RPV is completed to determine the stresses. The following sections describe the FEA preprocessing, solution, and results.

The geometry described in Section 6.1 was imported in ANSYS. Edits were performed to aid in mesh generation and boundary condition application, such as adding extensions to the nozzles, end caps to both the nozzles and CRDM penetrations. Additionally, many bodies were suppressed as they were not needed, and no geometry for the RVI or reactor coolant fluid was included. The RPV cladding geometry contained in the CAD model, as defined in Reference [1], was not included with the exception of the portion of cladding at the closure head to vessel interface. This portion was retained to better enable the connection between the head and vessel. According to Reference [4], no structural strength due to cladding is permitted for primary stress evaluation. Since the scope of this report is limited to the previously mentioned geometry and load conditions, only primary stresses will result. Therefore, the cladding is not included, except as previously mentioned. For further details of the FEA geometry see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf. Figure 9-1 shows the geometry used in the FEA.

For simplification purposes, a unit pressure load of 1000 psi was applied to all interior surfaces that are within the pressure boundary of the model. The results will be scaled during post processing to achieve the desired pressures. Displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining the degrees of freedom as described in Section 9.5.1. Since the evaluation is required to be performed at Design Temperature, the entire model was assigned the temperature given in Table 6-1. The piping loads are given in Table 6-1 for the hot and cold leg piping nozzles, and the DVI piping nozzle. The orientation of the loads was determined in Appendix A. The force and moments were applied to the nozzle faces. Displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining the degrees of freedom as described in Section 9.5.1. entries.text: This report documents the Mechanical Analysis performed for the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) for SMR-300 as shown in Figure 1-1. The RPV geometry and associated materials used in this analysis are defined in Reference [1].

The RPV is one of the major components (Reference [2]) of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS). The RPV is a cylindrical pressure vessel with an integrally welded lower hemispherical head and a removable flanged, upper hemispherical head (also called a closure head). It permits connections to the RCS leg piping (hot and cold legs), and direct vessel injection (DVI) piping. The RPV also provides external attachment points for Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDMs), and internal attachment locations for the Reactor Vessel Internal (RVI) components that support and maintain the position of the nuclear fuel. The RPV is supported externally by trunnions that interface with the surrounding containment concrete walls, as well as a horizontal restraint located at the bottom of the RPV containment cavity. During plant operation, the RPV forms part of the pressure boundary of the RCS, and is exposed to, and consequently providing shielding against, radiation from the reactor core.

The purpose of this report is to demonstrate the SMR-300 RPV sizing of the heads, shells, and nozzles will satisfy the appropriate regulatory and design requirements with respect to structural integrity, to ensure safe, reliable plant operations. Regulatory requirements include:
Also considered are the methods and guidance contained in Regulatory Guides 1.29, 1.122, 1.207, and 1.230, as well as NUREG/CR-6909 and NUREG-0800.

According to Regulatory Guide 1.29, the RPV is designated as a seismic category I structures, systems, and components (SSCs) since it forms part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary as defined in 10CFR Part 50.2.
In addition to regulatory requirements, the SMR-300 RPV must satisfy additional criteria, stated earlier in this report in the Statement of Limitations section of the Executive Summary.

To demonstrate that the SMR-300 RPV shells, heads, and nozzles sizing are sufficient with respect to regulatory and design requirements, a design-by-analysis approach of Reference [4] is completed. This includes the following analyses and evaluations:
Determination of the RPV stresses is accomplished by performing Engineering Simulations (modeling) and finite element analyses, as well as classical hand calculations.

Also, for simplification purposes and since the torque values are unknown at this time, it was assumed (see Section 5.0) that the Closure Studs will prevent any separation between the Closure Head and Vessel during service conditions. In other words, the Closure Stud preload will be sufficient to maintain a tight joint during all service conditions. Therefore, bonded contact was created between the Closure Head Cladding and Vessel Cladding. For further details of the FEA connections see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf.
The RPV components were represented using solid elements, with the majority being hexahedral shaped. The nozzle and CRDM penetration end caps were represented with shell elements.

entries.section_title: Appendix A RCS and DVI Piping Nozzle Study
entries.text: The direction of the loads and moments, or sense of action as termed in Reference [7], is unknown at this time. Therefore, a study was performed to determine the approximate nozzle to vessel interface load and moment orientations that result in the maximum stress in the RPV shell, and the four, RPV Trunnion support locations. It is not the goal of the study to determine the actual stress magnitudes, but rather to determine what orientation of load would result in the most severe stress.

entries.section_title: Appendix A RCS and DVI Piping Nozzle Study
entries.text: A FEA model of a 180-degree segment of the Upper RPV Shell, Nozzles, and Trunnion supports was used to apply nozzle loads with varying directions, and compute the resulting stress and reactions. Local coordinate systems were created at each nozzle location, where the X axis is parallel with the nozzle cylindrical axis. Symmetry conditions were applied to the shell to account for symmetric geometry, and displacement boundary conditions were applied at the top and bottom surfaces to represent closure head restraint and continuous shell length. Unit loads (forces) and moments were applied to the end of each nozzle where the force and moment varied by 45 degrees about each nozzle cylindrical axis, as well as a unit pressure load to all interior surfaces. When the actual piping loads and moments are available, the angle and direction may not be oriented at one of these, 0, 45, 90-degree type orientations. It is assumed that varying the orientations by 45 degrees will be sufficient at this time, to provide the most severe orientation. Figure: A-1 shows the model geometry and a sample setup. For further details of the FEA, see the attached file Nozzle Study Details.pdf.

This report documents the Mechanical Analysis performed for the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) for SMR-300 as shown in Figure 1-1. The RPV geometry and associated materials used in this analysis are defined in Reference [1].

The RPV is one of the major components (Reference [2]) of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS). The RPV is a cylindrical pressure vessel with an integrally welded lower hemispherical head and a removable flanged, upper hemispherical head (also called a closure head). It permits connections to the RCS leg piping (hot and cold legs), and direct vessel injection (DVI) piping. The RPV also provides external attachment points for Control Rod Drive Mechanisms (CRDMs), and internal attachment locations for the Reactor Vessel Internal (RVI) components that support and maintain the position of the nuclear fuel. The RPV is supported externally by trunnions that interface with the surrounding containment concrete walls, as well as a horizontal restraint located at the bottom of the RPV containment cavity. During plant operation, the RPV forms part of the pressure boundary of the RCS, and is exposed to, and consequently providing shielding against, radiation from the reactor core.

entries.text: This report documents one of several mechanical analyses performed for the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), as defined in Reference [1], for the SMR-300. The included analyses are performed to demonstrate that the sizing of the design is structurally adequate to meet the design requirements and acceptance criteria set forth by 10 CFR 50 with endorsements to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel code. This, and other analyses, will ensure all aspects of the RPV design assembly, will satisfy all structural and functional requirements. This report focuses on the RPV heads, shells and nozzles sizing when subjected to Design Pressure, Design Temperature, Test Pressure, and estimated piping loads only. A minimum thickness calculation is also performed. Accordingly, only primary stress for these conditions was evaluated. Safety factors were computed, and recommendations are provided to remedy potential unsatisfactory conditions. The analysis focuses on the RPV geometry defined in Reference [1], and does not consider the geometry of any interfacing components.

In addition to regulatory requirements, the SMR-300 RPV must satisfy the criteria specified in the Owners (i.e. Holtec International, as defined by ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NCA) (Reference [3]), certified RPV ASME Design Specification. The RPV ASME Design Specification classifies the RPV as a Division 1, Class 1 item (per NCA-2100), which requires the design and analysis to be completed in accordance with the rules contained in ASME Section III, Division 1, Subsection NB (Reference [4]).

The RPV ASME Design Specification is not currently available for this report. The scope of this report is therefore limited to initial superimposed loads, Design Pressure and Design Temperature loadings, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions. After the ASME Design Specification is completed, future analyses will be performed to show that the RPV satisfies all the criteria contained within the ASME Design Specification including all load combinations for ASME Service Levels A, B, C, and D.

Stresses from superimposed mechanical loads on the RPV due to interactions with interfacing components such as the Control Rod Drive Mechanisms and Reactor Vessel Internals are not included in this report. Additionally, triaxial stress and comparison to the ASME limits were not included in this report.

entries.text: For the scope of this report for initial superimposed piping loads, Design Pressure and Design Temperature loadings, deadweight, and Hydrostatic testing load conditions, three steady state (static) solutions are performed to determine the resulting stresses from each individual load. The Hydrostatic test conditions are evaluated with the RVI installed during the test. The stress resulting from the weight of the RPV and components supported by the RPV, including the reactor coolant, due to standard earth gravity, was determined. The amount of weight was calculated in Appendix C. The RPV is supported by the four Trunnions vertically and tangentially about a cylindrical coordinate system where the Z axis is aligned with RPV shell axis. The RPV is unrestrained in the radial direction. Therefore, displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining those degrees of freedom. The Design Internal Pressure and Hydrotest Pressures are shown in Table 6-1. Although in Reference [4], pressures are taken as a pressure above atmospheric pressure, atmospheric pressure is conservatively neglected in this analysis. For simplification purposes, a unit pressure load of 1000 psi was applied to all interior surfaces that are within the pressure boundary of the model. The results will be scaled during post processing to achieve the desired pressures. Displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining the degrees of freedom as described in Section 9.5.1. Since the evaluation is required to be performed at Design Temperature, the entire model was assigned the temperature given in Table 6-1. For further details of the FEA solution, see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf. The piping loads are given in Table 6-1 for the hot and cold leg piping nozzles, and the DVI piping nozzle. The orientation of the loads was determined in Appendix A. The force and moments were applied to the nozzle faces. Displacement boundary conditions are applied to the four Trunnions restraining the degrees of freedom as described in Section 9.5.1. Since the evaluation is required to be performed at Design Temperature, the entire model was assigned the temperature given in Table 6-1. For further details of the FEA solution, see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf. The analyses in Section 9.0 were then combined to maximize the stress results. This includes the scaling of the unit pressure analysis to achieve the Design and Test pressure conditions in Table 6-1. To determine membrane and bending stresses, stress classification lines (SCLs) are created through the thickness of each RPV component. The locations of SCLs were selected at areas of highest stress. Figure 10-1 and Figure 10-2 show locations of SCLs. For further details of the SCLs, see the attached file FEA Model Details.pdf.

The results show safety factors > 1.0 for the RPV components. The RPV ASME Design Specification will define the loads and load combinations, including actual piping nozzle loads. Based on existing PWR's, when it is available it will not available at this time. However, based on existing PWR's, when it is available it will define the loads and load combinations, including actual piping nozzle loads. These loads and any other criteria will need to be re-evaluated to ensure the requirements are satisfied. This includes test conditions to ensure the correct test temperature is being used.

entries.text: To determine the water weight, the total volume of the RPV cavity was determined using the CAD model. The total cavity volume, shown in Figure: C-3, is
It should be noted, that this RPV cavity volume neglects the RPV cladding thickness, resulting in a slightly larger cavity.
Subtracting the volume of the RVI, from the total cavity volume, results with the total water volume, and weight of
Wwater = ρwaterVwater = 147,235.8 lbf
ρwater = 0.036 lbm/in³ @ 70 °F
It should be noted that using the density of water at a higher temperature would reduce the water weight. Therefore, it is considered conservative to use density at 70 °F.
Therefore, the total calculated weight being supported by the RPV Trunnions is
Wtotal = WRPVFEA + WRVI + Wwater = 848,840 lbf

Since the RVI and fuel are not explicitly modeled, they are represented using a distributed mass attached to the RPV flange. This is the location where typical PW R RVI are supported. To represent the water weight, a hydrostatic pressure is applied to the inside of the RPV. Standard earth gravity, 1g acceleration, was applied to the entire model. Since the evaluation is required to be performed at Design Temperature, the entire model was assigned the temperature given in Table 6-1.
The resulting total model weight was computed as Wresult = 885,630 lbf

This is 36,790 lbf over the total weight supported by the RPV Trunnions. This is due to the hydrostatic pressure application, which assumes the RPV cavity is filled entirely with water (i.e. there are no solids in the cavity) which is not correct since the RVI and fuel exist in the cavity. Therefore, the water density of 0.036 lbf/in³ is scaled down to 0.02879 lbf/in³ to reduce the water weight.
The adjusted total model weight was then computed, shown in Figure: C-4, as WRPVTotal = 849,060 lbf
Which differs from the RPV total calculated weight, WTotal, by 220 lbf and is considered insignificant.
