entries.section_title: Supply forced flow during normal operations
entries.text: The reactor coolant pumps drive flow through the RCS to cool the core and ensure effective heat transfer to the SGE during power operations. During startup and shutdown the flow removes decay heat from the core and ensures uniform heat up or cooldown of RCS components.
The RCS provides a means to vent the reactor pressure vessel head and RCPs. The pressurizer steam space is vented via connections to other systems.

The reactor vessel head, RCP vent, and pressurizer head vent are used to fill the RCS during plant startup. The ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident (see PCC SDD [1]).

Reactor vessel head vent valves and the automatic depressurization system valves have the ability to be operated from the main control room. SMR-300 does not require the use of the reactor vessel head vent to provide safety-related core cooling following a postulated accident.
The RCS provides a means to perform a non-critical heat up of the plant during startup operations using heat from the RCPs.
Reactor Coolant System

The RCS equipment is arranged and designed to transfer heat from the reactor core to the SGE during normal operations using forced circulation. In the event of an AOO or DBA, decay heat can be transferred to the SGE or other interfacing systems such as PDH or RHR.

The reactor pressure vessel is designed to have two hot and two cold leg piping connections to a single steam generator. The steam generator, located adjacent to the RPV, is a once-through steam generator (OTSG) designed to produce superheated steam at full power conditions.

The pressurizer is attached to the steam generator above the upper tube sheet. The pressurizer is integral to the steam generator, this eliminates the need for a separate pressure vessel and associated surge piping to keep the RCS footprint in containment compact. An internal divider plate separates the pressurizer volume from the flowing RCS coolant volume. The pressurizer heaters are located above the divider plate. The pressurizer safety valves are located at the top of the pressurizer.

The low temperature overpressure protection for the RCS is provided by the relief valve in the Residual Heat Removal System [2]. Overpressure protection of the SGE secondary side is provided by the main steam safety valves in the Main Steam System [3].

The control rod drive mechanisms are mounted on the reactor pressure vessel upper hemispherical head. The reactor pressure vessel head vent discharges to the passive core make up water tank, which is part of the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCM).
Copyright Holtec International ©2024, all rights reserved [Export Controlled]
The major components of the RCS are described in this section.

Reactor coolant pressure boundary materials, including reactor pressure vessel materials in contact with reactor coolant, are selected to minimize corrosion. A water chemistry program will be established to control corrosion and maintain compatibility with RCS materials in accordance with SMR-300 water chemistry requirements.

Reflective metal insulation will be used to the extent practical for all RCS equipment, components, and SSC inside containment. Any fibrous insulation used will be encapsulated to prevent fibrous debris from clogging the strainers located in the Passive Core Make-up Water Tanks (PCMWTs) [5].

entries.text: 5.1 System Boundaries

For lines flowing into the RCS, the mechanical system boundary is at the outlet of the last isolation valve leaving the interfacing system, except for the interfaces listed below where the boundary is at the equipment nozzle (or otherwise noted).
Discharge line from the RHR. The boundary is at Cold Leg B.
Return line from CVC from the charging pump. The boundary is at the Cold leg upstream of each RCP.
Pressurizer spray supply line from CVC. The boundary is at the common spray supply line.
Direct vessel injection lines at the reactor pressure vessel from Passive Core Make Up Water System (PCM). The boundary is at the reactor pressure vessel.
Seal injection from CVC. The boundary is at the RCP seals.
Cooling water supply from CCW to the RCP. The boundary is the RCP.
Discharge line from the PDH. The boundary is at the SGE lower head.

For lines flowing out of the RCS, the mechanical system boundary is at the outlet of the last isolation valve leading to the interfacing system, except for the interfaces listed below where the boundary is at the RCS equipment nozzle (or otherwise noted).
Supply line to the RHR. The boundary is at Hot Leg B.
Letdown line to the CVC. The boundary is at the Cold Leg downstream of each RCP.
Supply line to the PDH. The boundary is at Hot Leg B.
RPV head vent line to passive core make up water tank in the PCM. The boundary is at the passive core makeup water tank.
High point vent line at the pressurizer to Gaseous Radwaste System and Liquid Radwaste System. The boundary is at the inlet of the first isolation valve.
Supply lines to the PSL. The boundary is at the outlet of the first isolation valve from the RCS.
The boundary between the electrical system and the RCS is at the connection of the electrical power to the component (i.e., motor).

entries.text: To transition from Refueling Operations (MODE 6) to Cold Shutdown (MODE 5) the Reactor Pressure Vessel head is reinstalled and closure head bolts are fully tensioned. During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary Non-safety-related components and instrumentation are powered with non-Class 1E power. For example, the reactor coolant pumps are supplied with non-Class 1E power since the pumps do not have a safety function, other than maintaining the reactor coolant pressure boundary. The Stand-by Diesel Generator System can provide backup non-class 1E AC power for the equipment listed below.

Startup Operation To transition from Refueling Operations (MODE 6) to Cold Shutdown (MODE 5) the Reactor Pressure Vessel head is reinstalled and closure head bolts are fully tensioned. During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary

Once the RCS is depressurized and reaches Cold Shutdown (MODE 5), the RCS is depressurized to atmospheric pressure with a vent path established and the RCS water inventory is reduced to facilitate refueling and maintenance activities. High point vent connections provide the ability to remotely vent non-condensable gases from the RCS and facilitate draining the RCS water level to the reactor pressure vessel head flange before refueling operations. The RHR and CVC systems are used to drain RCS inventory. Refueling (MODE 6) is entered when the first reactor pressure vessel head closure fastener is de-tensioned. After the water level in the reactor pressure vessel is confirmed as below the flange level, the reactor pressure vessel head is removed.
At reduced water inventory, the RCS water level is maintained above the level required to support RHR net positive suction head requirements for operation while keeping the core covered.

After the reactor pressure vessel head is removed for refueling operations, refueling water from the PCMWT and RWST fills the reactor cavity and spent fuel pool, this can be done using the RHR pumps or by gravity drain.

Once the refueling operations are complete, the refueling water is returned to the RWST and PCMWT. After the water level drains from the reactor cavity and reaches the reactor pressure vessel head flange, the reactor pressure vessel head can be installed.
When the reactor pressure vessel head fasteners are fully tensioned, the RCS is filled with reactor coolant, using the RHR or CVC.
3.3.5.1 Anticipated Operational Occurrences and Accident Scenarios

Initiating events that affect RCS operation will be listed in an SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Assessment with descriptions of the expected event sequence and the response of the safety-related systems available to mitigate.

The reactor trip and engineering safety feature actuation logic automatically prevents the RCS from exceeding the design limits of the system and mitigates design basis accidents using RCS instrumentation and SSC important to safety.

During accident conditions the reactor coolant pumps are not required to remain functional. The only safety functions of the RCPs are to provide adequate pump coast down to ensure reactor coolant continues to flow for a short time after pump trip and to maintain the RCPB.
3.3.5.2 Operator Actions during Beyond Design Basis Accident Conditions

The reactor vessel head vents are opened from the main control room to allow venting from the RPV head and RCS if non-condensable gases accumulate following an accident. The RPV head vent is not credited for venting as a safety function or a safety-related core cooling function. Note that the ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident. The PDH has provisions (high point vent) to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident.

Information on the Pressurizer, its role in maintaining system pressure, and relevant data.

This document defines the functional requirements and design basis for the Reactor Coolant System (RCS).
This document defines the functional requirements and design basis for the Reactor Coolant System (RCS).

The RCS transfers heat produced by the reactor core to the balance-of-plant power conversion system or the appropriate decay heat removal system (Residual Heat Removal System (RHR) or Passive Core Cooling System (PCC)) and maintains the pressure boundary integrity to contain the reactor coolant. The RCS is a dual leg primary heat transfer circuit with a single Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) and Steam Generator (SGE). The RCS is designed to use forced circulation at power and natural circulation for emergency cooling.

The principal RCS components are the RPV, SGE, RCPs, and the pressurizer (PZR) which is integral to the SGE. All components of the RCS are located completely within the containment. The reactor coolant is heated by the reactor core (heat source) and flows up to the top of the steam generator via two hot legs. The steam generator (heat sink) cools the reactor coolant as it transfers the energy from the reactor coolant to the shell side fluid (i.e., converts feedwater to steam). The cooler reactor coolant flows downward from the steam generator and splits between two cold legs, each with a reactor coolant pump which provides the motive force for coolant flow during normal operations. The RCS components are designed to enhance natural circulation flow during design basis accidents (DBA) and anticipated operational occurrences (AOO) when RCPs are not available. The predominant part of feedwater heating is performed by multi-stage feedwater heaters of the main feed system (MFS) as in traditional power plants. Once in the SGE, feedwater will be further heated to near saturation temperature by aspirating steam prior to entering the tube bundle.

The reactor coolant (water), which serves both as the moderator and the coolant, is boratated since conventional chemical shim is required for core reactivity control. The pressure in the RCS is controlled by maintaining a saturated liquid-steam interface in the pressurizer with the use of conventional electric-resistance heaters and water spray.

The RCS may be quickly depressurized in the event of an accident (such as a loss of coolant accident) via its interface with the automatic depressurization system to allow for passive safety injection. Additional information on this depressurization function is available in the PCC system design description [1].

    Requirement statements often include words such as "shall", "must", "will", or "is required to", but the absence of these keywords does NOT automatically mean the sentence is not a requirement.
    Conversely, sentences that do contain these keywords may not be requirements if they are purely descriptive, explanatory, or context-based.

entries.text: The major components of the RCS are described in this section.

Reactor coolant pressure boundary materials, including reactor pressure vessel materials in contact with reactor coolant, are selected to minimize corrosion. A water chemistry program will be established to control corrosion and maintain compatibility with RCS materials in accordance with SMR-300 water chemistry requirements.

Reflective metal insulation will be used to the extent practical for all RCS equipment, components, and SSC inside containment. Any fibrous insulation used will be encapsulated to prevent fibrous debris from clogging the strainers located in the Passive Core Make-up Water Tanks (PCMWTs) [5].

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: CRDMs are external to the RPV and penetrate the upper hemispherical head. The Rod Cluster Control Assemblies (RCCAs) provide a rapid means for reactivity control during both normal operating and accident conditions. There is a single control rod drive mechanism for each RCCA. Control rod drive mechanisms are externally attached to the control rod pressure housings. The upper hemispherical head also contains penetrations for the in-core instrumentation tubes and a high-point vent line. RPV level is measured with shared instrumentation for RCS inventory level (upper FPV volume down to the DVI lines) and in-core level (DVI lines to the bottom of the fuel envelope).

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The RPV internals for the SMR-300 consist of two primary sections: the upper internals and the lower internals. The reactor internals provide protection, alignment, and support for the core, the control rods, and the in-core instruments. Additionally, the reactor internals direct coolant flow to and from the fuel assemblies, and help absorb control rod dynamic loads, fuel assembly loads, and other loads resulting from design basis events. These loads are transmitted to the RPV, which provides overall structural rigidity.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The lower internals consist of the core barrel flange, core barrel cylinder, irradiation specimen baskets, lower support plate, radial key inserts, flow distribution device, and heavy reflector. The upper internals consist of the upper support assembly (including the flange, shell, and upper support plate), the upper core plate, control rod guide tubes and cards, and shell columns.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The external support for the RPV will be trunnions to the surrounding concrete walls and a lateral restraint at the bottom of the RPV cavity to help withstand seismic events.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: During operation, reactor coolant from the cold legs enters the RPV through the inlet nozzles and flows into the downcomer, which is the annulus formed by the space between the core barrel and the RPV inner wall. The flow then enters the lower plenum, which is the area at the bottom of the RPV. The flow then enters the flow distribution device (FDD) and is directed to the lower support plate (LSP) which is attached to the FDD. After traversing the core, the heated reactor coolant passes through the upper core plate (UCP) and enters the upper plenum, which is enclosed by the UCP, core barrel and upper support plate (USP). The flow then passes through and around the columns attaching the UCP and USP to reach the RPV outlet nozzles.

The SGE is a vertical shell and tube Once-Through Steam Generator (OTSG) [7]. The SGE is designed to utilize reactor coolant on the tube side and feedwater on the shell side. For requirements and guidance for the mechanical design and the fabrication of the OTSG see the Design Specification for the SMR-300 Steam Generator.

The hot legs connect the OTSG upper channel to the RPV outlet nozzles. The hot reactor coolant from the RPV flows down through the OTSG tubes to the lower head and into the cold leg connections back to the RPV. The primary coolant transfers heat to the feedwater flowing up the shell side of the OTSG to produce superheated steam.

The tube side of the SGE is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code [8]. The straight OTSG tubes provide easy access for in-service inspection and tube plugging as needed. The OTSG is designed for rated performance with a percentage of the tubes plugged.

entries.text: The pressurizer features a thick cylindrical shell with a top hemispherical head and is laterally restrained by supports [9]. The pressurizer has been sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure during operational maneuvers and transients. This eliminates the need for fast-acting power operated relief valves (PORVs).The lack of PORVs eliminates the need for a pressurizer relief tank and obviates potential PORV malfunctions common to operating PWRs.

The internal divider plate is designed to limit thermal communication between the volumes on either side to minimize the size of the PZR heaters while allowing sufficient flow into and out of the PZR for pressure control. The PZR controls the pressure of the RCS by maintaining a saturated steam-liquid interface. Pressure changes caused by the expansion and contraction of the reactor coolant are absorbed by condensing the steam using the PZR spray or generating steam using the PZR heaters. RCP discharge pressure drives normal spray flow. Continuous flow through the pressurizer spray line maintains the spray line warm which prevents thermal stratification while also keeping the pressurizer volume at a similar boron concentration as the rest of the RCS volume.

The primary function of the reactor coolant pump is to provide forced circulation of reactor coolant for transfer of core heat during reactor startup, shutdown, and power operations. The SMR-300 design does not include provisions to operate with a single pump running during power operations (Mode 1).

Two 50% capacity pumps are provided, one on each cold leg [10]. There are two safety related characteristics of the RCP. First, in the event of a reactor trip or loss of power, the pumps maintain flow to the core during pump coast down using a flywheel. Second, the RCPs serve as part of the RCS pressure boundary. The pumps are not required to perform any active safety functions and will be de-energized during LOCA or operation of the primary or secondary decay heat removal systems.
The reactor coolant pump is a vertical, centrifugal type pump. The pump is designed to use traditional seals designed to allow continued operation of the pump for a period of at least one

Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT.
The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients.

Reactor coolant piping is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. The reactor coolant piping maintains the reactor coolant pressure boundary and is designed to withstand the maximum RCS pressure and temperature under all expected modes of plant operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Seamless piping is used to avoid in-service inspection of longitudinal piping welds. The piping material for the hot legs and cold legs shall be carbon steel with stainless steel cladding. All other piping shall be stainless steel.

The application of Leak-Before-Break (LBB) analysis and criteria to portions of the RCS piping design of high energy piping systems is being developed. Using the Leak-Before-Break methodology approved by the NRC and other design considerations can justify a design basis that eliminates jet impingement shields and pipe whip restraints. This methodology requires the ability to detect leaks from cracks smaller than a critical flaw size.
RCS instrumentation is used for:
Measuring conditions of the RCS and providing measurement data to the Plant Safety System (PSS), which actuates reactor protection and engineered safety features.

Measuring conditions of the RCS and providing data to the Plant Control System (PCS) for the basis information regarding specification, regulatory, and operational requirements of primary instrumentation, see the Primary Instrumentation Strategy, and for instrumentation quantities, automatic functions, and setpoints, see Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System [11]. For steam generator secondary side instrumentation, refer to the Main Feed System (MFS) [12] and Main Steam System (MSS) [13] Control System Descriptions.

entries.text: Instrumentation is provided for operators to monitor the reactor coolant flow by four elbow tap differential pressure flow meter instruments in each cold leg, tapping into the 90° elbow located upstream of each RCP. There are pressure indicators located immediately upstream and downstream of each RCP to monitor differential pressure indicating the status of the pump.

The pressurizer safety valves are provided with full open and full closed position switches. The pressurizer safety valve discharge piping includes a temperature element to detect leakage or relief through the valve. The use of acoustic monitoring for leak detection will be determined later. Safety valve leakage detection is provided for operating personnel to be aware of the plant status of SSC important to safety and to perform timely corrective actions.

Leg temperatures are monitored by thermocouples and provide input signals for steam control and rod control. RCS temperature sensors utilize thermwells welded into the piping to provide isolation between the temperature sensor and the process fluid as opposed to direct immersion temperature sensors. The temperature probe and thermwell design allows easy removal and insertion for maintenance. Use of thermowells facilitates replacement of temperature sensors without requiring the RCS to be drained.
Excore instruments provide input signals to control feedwater demand, rod control, letdown, and charging.
The safety-related valves and instrumentation are supplied with safety-related Class 1E power to meet requirements for redundancy and reliability (see section 4.2.3 on single failure criterion).

Non-safety-related components and instrumentation are powered with non-Class 1E power. For example, the reactor coolant pumps are supplied with non-Class 1E power since the pumps do not have a safety function, other than maintaining the reactor coolant pressure boundary.
The Stand-by Diesel Generator System can provide backup non-class 1E AC power for the equipment listed below.

To transition from Refueling Operations (MODE 6) to Cold Shutdown (MODE 5) the Reactor Pressure Vessel head is reinstalled and closure head bolts are fully tensioned. During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary

entries.text: The safety components of the RCS are designed to withstand expected environmental conditions and a single failure with redundancy and independence (see section 4.2.2 Environmental Qualification and 4.2.3 Single Failure Criterion) for system reliability. System reliability is demonstrated through protection against:

To prevent a common failure and assure protection for pipe breaks, missiles, and fires, safety-related valves and components will meet the grouping and separation requirements described in section 4.2.4.

The pressurizer is sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure, which results in fewer reactor trips that would occur due to high Pressurizer water level or high Pressurizer pressure.

Redundant valves in series assure isolation of the RCS to maintain the reactor coolant pressure boundary and ensure an inadvertent actuation of a valve will not result in a LOCA. The RPV head vent forms the high point for the RPV and are designed with redundant valves in series to assure isolation in case an open vent valve cannot be closed. The failure mode and effects analysis in Appendix A provide a summary of the system response to a single failure of components with a safety function.
The following are system design features for reliability:
Programs will be developed for in-service inspection and testing activities during detailed design in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15].

The RCS will be designed with provisions for access and clearances around equipment, piping, and components that are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary to meet ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15]. The equipment arrangement inside containment will be designed to permit periodic inspection and testing. Sufficient space will be provided for
The reactor coolant pressure boundary SSC are examined to assess the structural leak-tight integrity to meet the examination requirements of ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8].

Steam generator manways are located near both tube sheets for access and inspection of tubes and tube sheets. The steam generator tubes can be inspected over the entire length for the detection of tube defects.
Provisions for disassembly and inspection of RCP components, including motors and seals, are accounted for in containment layout and will be developed in detail after pump selection.

The Leak Detection System will be developed for detecting and monitoring RCS leakage. Leak-Before-Break methodology and associated in-service inspection criterion leakage detection will be applied to portions of the RCS piping to minimize the probability of a pipe rupture.

System pressure tests (leakage and hydrostatic) will be performed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15]. The charging pump in the Chemical and Volume Control System can be used for the system leakage test at the RCS pressure corresponding to 100% rated reactor power, in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15] Article IWB-5000 for system pressure tests.

The pressurizer safety valves will be tested and qualified (10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(i)(x) for TMI Action Plan Item II.D.1 [16]) by the EPRI Test Program [17]. The LTOP relief valve that is part of the RHR has a set pressure less than the full RCS design pressure, therefore, this relief valve is excluded from the EPRI Test Program and will be covered by the test program that will be developed later.
Regulatory requirements that are applicable to the RCS, and their bases, are provided in the Reactor Coolant System Regulatory Compliance Report.
See the Reactor Coolant System Requirements, Open Items, and Interface Requirements Report for a more detailed overview of requirements applicable to the RCS.

entries.text: Non-safety-related components and instrumentation are powered with non-Class 1E power. For example, the reactor coolant pumps are supplied with non-Class 1E power since the pumps do not have a safety function, other than maintaining the reactor coolant pressure boundary. The Stand-by Diesel Generator System can provide backup non-class 1E AC power for the equipment listed below.

Startup Operation To transition from Refueling Operations (MODE 6) to Cold Shutdown (MODE 5) the Reactor Pressure Vessel head is reinstalled and closure head bolts are fully tensioned. During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary

entries.text: The reactor coolant pressure boundary SSC are examined to assess the structural leak-tight integrity to meet the examination requirements of ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8].

Steam generator manways are located near both tube sheets for access and inspection of tubes and tube sheets. The steam generator tubes can be inspected over the entire length for the detection of tube defects.
Provisions for disassembly and inspection of RCP components, including motors and seals, are accounted for in containment layout and will be developed in detail after pump selection.

The Leak Detection System will be developed for detecting and monitoring RCS leakage. Leak-Before-Break methodology and associated in-service inspection criterion leakage detection will be applied to portions of the RCS piping to minimize the probability of a pipe rupture.

System pressure tests (leakage and hydrostatic) will be performed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15]. The charging pump in the Chemical and Volume Control System can be used for the system leakage test at the RCS pressure corresponding to 100% rated reactor power, in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15] Article IWB-5000 for system pressure tests.

The pressurizer safety valves will be tested and qualified (10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(i)(x) for TMI Action Plan Item II.D.1 [16]) by the EPRI Test Program [17]. The LTOP relief valve that is part of the RHR has a set pressure less than the full RCS design pressure, therefore, this relief valve is excluded from the EPRI Test Program and will be covered by the test program that will be developed later.
Regulatory requirements that are applicable to the RCS, and their bases, are provided in the Reactor Coolant System Regulatory Compliance Report.
See the Reactor Coolant System Requirements, Open Items, and Interface Requirements Report for a more detailed overview of requirements applicable to the RCS.

entries.text: Once the RCS is depressurized and reaches Cold Shutdown (MODE 5), the RCS is depressurized to atmospheric pressure with a vent path established and the RCS water inventory is reduced to facilitate refueling and maintenance activities. High point vent connections provide the ability to remotely vent non-condensable gases from the RCS and facilitate draining the RCS water level to the reactor pressure vessel head flange before refueling operations. The RHR and CVC systems are used to drain RCS inventory. Refueling (MODE 6) is entered when the first reactor pressure vessel head closure fastener is de-tensioned. After the water level in the reactor pressure vessel is confirmed as below the flange level, the reactor pressure vessel head is removed.
At reduced water inventory, the RCS water level is maintained above the level required to support RHR net positive suction head requirements for operation while keeping the core covered.

After the reactor pressure vessel head is removed for refueling operations, refueling water from the PCMWT and RWST fills the reactor cavity and spent fuel pool, this can be done using the RHR pumps or by gravity drain.

Once the refueling operations are complete, the refueling water is returned to the RWST and PCMWT. After the water level drains from the reactor cavity and reaches the reactor pressure vessel head flange, the reactor pressure vessel head can be installed.
When the reactor pressure vessel head fasteners are fully tensioned, the RCS is filled with reactor coolant, using the RHR or CVC.
3.3.5.1 Anticipated Operational Occurrences and Accident Scenarios

Initiating events that affect RCS operation will be listed in an SMR-300 Probabilistic Safety Assessment with descriptions of the expected event sequence and the response of the safety-related systems available to mitigate.

The reactor trip and engineering safety feature actuation logic automatically prevents the RCS from exceeding the design limits of the system and mitigates design basis accidents using RCS instrumentation and SSC important to safety.

During accident conditions the reactor coolant pumps are not required to remain functional. The only safety functions of the RCPs are to provide adequate pump coast down to ensure reactor coolant continues to flow for a short time after pump trip and to maintain the RCPB.
3.3.5.2 Operator Actions during Beyond Design Basis Accident Conditions

The reactor vessel head vents are opened from the main control room to allow venting from the RPV head and RCS if non-condensable gases accumulate following an accident. The RPV head vent is not credited for venting as a safety function or a safety-related core cooling function. Note that the ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident. The PDH has provisions (high point vent) to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident.

The safety components of the RCS are designed to withstand expected environmental conditions and a single failure with redundancy and independence (see section 4.2.2 Environmental Qualification and 4.2.3 Single Failure Criterion) for system reliability. System reliability is demonstrated through protection against:

To prevent a common failure and assure protection for pipe breaks, missiles, and fires, safety-related valves and components will meet the grouping and separation requirements described in section 4.2.4.

The pressurizer is sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure, which results in fewer reactor trips that would occur due to high Pressurizer water level or high Pressurizer pressure.

Redundant valves in series assure isolation of the RCS to maintain the reactor coolant pressure boundary and ensure an inadvertent actuation of a valve will not result in a LOCA. The RPV head vent forms the high point for the RPV and are designed with redundant valves in series to assure isolation in case an open vent valve cannot be closed. The failure mode and effects analysis in Appendix A provide a summary of the system response to a single failure of components with a safety function.

Programs will be developed for in-service inspection and testing activities during detailed design in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15].

The RCS will be designed with provisions for access and clearances around equipment, piping, and components that are part of the reactor coolant pressure boundary to meet ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15]. entries.text: This document defines the functional requirements and design basis for the Reactor Coolant System (RCS).
This document defines the functional requirements and design basis for the Reactor Coolant System (RCS).

The RCS transfers heat produced by the reactor core to the balance-of-plant power conversion system or the appropriate decay heat removal system (Residual Heat Removal System (RHR) or Passive Core Cooling System (PCC)) and maintains the pressure boundary integrity to contain the reactor coolant. The RCS is a dual leg primary heat transfer circuit with a single Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV) and Steam Generator (SGE). The RCS is designed to use forced circulation at power and natural circulation for emergency cooling.

The principal RCS components are the RPV, SGE, RCPs, and the pressurizer (PZR) which is integral to the SGE. All components of the RCS are located completely within the containment. The reactor coolant is heated by the reactor core (heat source) and flows up to the top of the steam generator via two hot legs. The steam generator (heat sink) cools the reactor coolant as it transfers the energy from the reactor coolant to the shell side fluid (i.e., converts feedwater to steam). The cooler reactor coolant flows downward from the steam generator and splits between two cold legs, each with a reactor coolant pump which provides the motive force for coolant flow during normal operations. The RCS components are designed to enhance natural circulation flow during design basis accidents (DBA) and anticipated operational occurrences (AOO) when RCPs are not available. The predominant part of feedwater heating is performed by multi-stage feedwater heaters of the main feed system (MFS) as in traditional power plants. Once in the SGE, feedwater will be further heated to near saturation temperature by aspirating steam prior to entering the tube bundle.

The reactor coolant (water), which serves both as the moderator and the coolant, is boratated since conventional chemical shim is required for core reactivity control. The pressure in the RCS is controlled by maintaining a saturated liquid-steam interface in the pressurizer with the use of conventional electric-resistance heaters and water spray.

The RCS may be quickly depressurized in the event of an accident (such as a loss of coolant accident) via its interface with the automatic depressurization system to allow for passive safety injection. Additional information on this depressurization function is available in the PCC system design description [1].

The scope and level of detail of a System Design Description (SDD) will be updated during the design process based on a graded approach to the development of the SDD. As the design progresses, this SDD will be revised as necessary to incorporate design changes. Limitations of this SDD include the following:
This document is intended to compile system information in one location. When source documents are referenced, those should be consulted for the most current information.
Some project standards referred to in this SDD are not yet developed and will define project requirements applicable to the RCS design as described in Section 4.0.
System interfaces have been identified in Section 5.0, and systems not yet developed will be evaluated later to confirm details of the interface.
The design parameter values without a reference in Section 7.0 are based on preliminary scoping data.

entries.text: The RCS provides instrumentation to measure parameters which provide a signal to PSS for reactor protection and engineered safety feature actuation during DBAs and some AOOs. The RCS uses redundant instrumentation (using four independent channels) for protection functions (i.e. for the reactor trip and ESFA logic.

The RCS hot leg temperature (Thot) and cold leg temperature (Tcold) signals are processed by PSS and used for control room indication, inputs to various control systems, and inputs to the PSS logic. Thot and Tcold are each measured with 2 instrument sensors per leg, that are averaged out to provide the channel readings. The averaged signals for Thot and Tcold are used to generate RCS average temperature (Tavg) and delta temperature signals. The Tavg setpoint is used by PSS within the ESFA logic.
Pressurizer pressure instrumentation is provided for reactor trip and ESFA logic in the PSS and is part of the pressurizer pressure permissible used in the ESFA logic.
Pressurizer level instrumentation is provided for reactor trip and ADS actuation in the ESFA logic of the PSS.
RCS level instrumentation is provided to measure the RCS inventory, spanning from the top of the Pressurizer to the RPV DVI lines. RCS inventory is crucial to all stages of accident response.
The cold legs are provided with instrumentation for monitoring the reactor coolant pump flow. This instrumentation is provided for reactor trip logic in the PSS for loss of flow DNB protection.

The PSS shares measurement channels (with proper isolation for independence) with the PCS for non-safety control of the RCS. The PSS transmits signals via a unit safety bus to the PCS for control purposes and normal monitoring.
Excore instrumentation provides permissible setpoints and reactor trip signals in the PSS logic.
The RCS provides instrumentation to measure parameters which provide a signal to PCS for plant control and monitoring during normal operations and AOOs.

The pressurizer heaters are controlled by the PCS based on the pressurizer pressure instrumentation. The pressurizer level instrumentation provides input to the PCS to calculate and control the mass balance in the pressurizer. The purpose of the pressurizer level control system is to control charging and letdown flows, as well as heater operation, to maintain programmed level.

Pressure instrumentation is also provided in the pressurizer to measure RCS pressure for indication during normal operation. Pressurizer level is measured by narrow range level instruments. RCS inventory is measured by wide range level instruments spanning from the pressurizer to the DVI lines. Both of these level instruments have a common reference leg. These instruments allow operators to monitor the level in the PZR during normal operations and in the RPV while the RCS is at reduced inventory, such as during refueling operations.

Instrumentation is provided for operators to monitor the reactor coolant flow by four elbow tap differential pressure flow meter instruments in each cold leg, tapping into the 90° elbow located upstream of each RCP. There are pressure indicators located immediately upstream and downstream of each RCP to monitor differential pressure indicating the status of the pump.

The pressurizer safety valves are provided with full open and full closed position switches. The pressurizer safety valve discharge piping includes a temperature element to detect leakage or relief through the valve. The use of acoustic monitoring for leak detection will be determined later. Safety valve leakage detection is provided for operating personnel to be aware of the plant status of SSC important to safety and to perform timely corrective actions.

Leg temperatures are monitored by thermocouples and provide input signals for steam control and rod control. RCS temperature sensors utilize thermwells welded into the piping to provide isolation between the temperature sensor and the process fluid as opposed to direct immersion temperature sensors. The temperature probe and thermwell design allows easy removal and insertion for maintenance. Use of thermowells facilitates replacement of temperature sensors without requiring the RCS to be drained.
Excore instruments provide input signals to control feedwater demand, rod control, letdown, and charging.
The safety-related valves and instrumentation are supplied with safety-related Class 1E power to meet requirements for redundancy and reliability (see section 4.2.3 on single failure criterion).

Non-safety-related components and instrumentation are powered with non-Class 1E power. For example, the reactor coolant pumps are supplied with non-Class 1E power since the pumps do not have a safety function, other than maintaining the reactor coolant pressure boundary.
The Stand-by Diesel Generator System can provide backup non-class 1E AC power for the equipment listed below.

To transition from Refueling Operations (MODE 6) to Cold Shutdown (MODE 5) the Reactor Pressure Vessel head is reinstalled and closure head bolts are fully tensioned. During this transition the Residual Heat Removal System is in operation to control RCS temperature and provides low temperature overpressure protection (LTOP). Either RHHR or CVC is used to fill the RCS. Once the RCS is water solid, the operators energize the pressurizer heaters and discharge coolant via CVC letdown to draw a bubble in the Pressurizer to establish RCS pressure control. Operators establish pressure control below brittle fracture prevention limits (BFPL) and LTOP setpoints. Once system pressure is greater than NPSHR, the RCPs can begin circulating water in the RCS. The RCPs provide the heat input to raise RCS temperature. RCPs also provide heat for spray flow to allow mixing and pressure control in the pressurizer, CVC may be used to provide auxiliary spray flow as necessary prior to starting RCPs. Primary

entries.text: A master list of terms and acronyms can be found in the SMR-300 Acronyms and Glossary of Terms. The following are additional terms or acronyms used specifically in this SDD:
In the event of any discrepancy in the information presented for the system, the following documents shall take precedence, in the order that they are listed:
Third-party Supplied Information
The safety functions of the system are to:

The RCS provides a flow path for reactor coolant to remove heat from the reactor core, which supports maintaining the fuel condition within the operating bounds. Reactor coolant is transported through the RCS to transfer heat from the fuel to the balance of plant systems via the steam generator during Power Operation as well as in the Hot Standby and Safe Shutdown modes (when the reactor is subcritical). RCS transfers the core decay heat to the RHR system during the subsequent phases of Safe Shutdown, Cold Shutdown, and Refueling modes. During a design basis accident where the reactor coolant pressure boundary remains intact, the RCS transfers core decay heat from the fuel to the PCMWT via the Primary Decay Heat Removal System (PDH) and to the SGE via the Secondary Decay Heat Removal System (SDH). During design basis accidents where the reactor coolant pressure boundary fails, such as a loss of coolant accident (LOCA), connections at the reactor pressure vessel provide for direct safety injection of coolant to meet emergency core cooling requirements. During a loss of RCPs, the flywheel provides continued flow for a short period ensuring coast down requirements are met.

The RCS equipment, piping, and components contain radioactive material and assure the integrity of the reactor coolant pressure boundary (RCPB) as a fission product barrier. The primary coolant is isolated by the RCPB from the containment atmosphere during normal operation and design basis accidents other than a LOCA. The steam generator tubes and tube sheet boundary prevent the transfer of radioactive material from the reactor core to the secondary cooling systems.
The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection and prevent the RCS pressure exceeding design limits to protect the integrity of the RCPB and vacuum breakers on the outlet piping.
The non-safety functions of the system are to:

To ensure operational limits are not exceeded. The pressurizer maintains the system pressure during operation and limits pressure transients by establishing a saturated vapor-liquid interface (i.e., steam bubble). The pressurizer is sized to accommodate volume changes in the reactor coolant during a reduction or increase of plant load during power operations.

entries.section_title: Supply forced flow during normal operations
entries.text: The reactor coolant pumps drive flow through the RCS to cool the core and ensure effective heat transfer to the SGE during power operations. During startup and shutdown the flow removes decay heat from the core and ensures uniform heat up or cooldown of RCS components.
The RCS provides a means to vent the reactor pressure vessel head and RCPs. The pressurizer steam space is vented via connections to other systems.

The reactor vessel head, RCP vent, and pressurizer head vent are used to fill the RCS during plant startup. The ADS valves provide the capability to vent non-condensable gases from the RCS following an accident (see PCC SDD [1]).

Reactor vessel head vent valves and the automatic depressurization system valves have the ability to be operated from the main control room. SMR-300 does not require the use of the reactor vessel head vent to provide safety-related core cooling following a postulated accident.
The RCS provides a means to perform a non-critical heat up of the plant during startup operations using heat from the RCPs.
Reactor Coolant System

The RCS equipment is arranged and designed to transfer heat from the reactor core to the SGE during normal operations using forced circulation. In the event of an AOO or DBA, decay heat can be transferred to the SGE or other interfacing systems such as PDH or RHR.

The reactor pressure vessel is designed to have two hot and two cold leg piping connections to a single steam generator. The steam generator, located adjacent to the RPV, is a once-through steam generator (OTSG) designed to produce superheated steam at full power conditions.

The pressurizer is attached to the steam generator above the upper tube sheet. The pressurizer is integral to the steam generator, this eliminates the need for a separate pressure vessel and associated surge piping to keep the RCS footprint in containment compact. An internal divider plate separates the pressurizer volume from the flowing RCS coolant volume. The pressurizer heaters are located above the divider plate. The pressurizer safety valves are located at the top of the pressurizer.

The low temperature overpressure protection for the RCS is provided by the relief valve in the Residual Heat Removal System [2]. Overpressure protection of the SGE secondary side is provided by the main steam safety valves in the Main Steam System [3].

The control rod drive mechanisms are mounted on the reactor pressure vessel upper hemispherical head. The reactor pressure vessel head vent discharges to the passive core make up water tank, which is part of the Passive Core Makeup Water System (PCM).

entries.text: System pressure tests (leakage and hydrostatic) will be performed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15].

The charging pump in the Chemical and Volume Control System can be used for the system leakage test at the RCS pressure corresponding to 100% rated reactor power, in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section XI [15] Article IWB-5000 for system pressure tests.
The pressurizer safety valves will be tested and qualified (10 CFR 50.34(f)(2)(i)(x) for TMI Action Plan Item II.D.1 [16]) by the EPRI Test Program [17].

The LTOP relief valve that is part of the RHR has a set pressure less than the full RCS design pressure, therefore, this relief valve is excluded from the EPRI Test Program and will be covered by the test program that will be developed later.
Regulatory requirements that are applicable to the RCS, and their bases, are provided in the Reactor Coolant System Regulatory Compliance Report.
See the Reactor Coolant System Requirements, Open Items, and Interface Requirements Report for a more detailed overview of requirements applicable to the RCS.
5.1 System Boundaries

For lines flowing into the RCS, the mechanical system boundary is at the outlet of the last isolation valve leaving the interfacing system, except for the interfaces listed below where the boundary is at the equipment nozzle (or otherwise noted).
Discharge line from the RHR. The boundary is at Cold Leg B.
Return line from CVC from the charging pump. The boundary is at the Cold leg upstream of each RCP.
Pressurizer spray supply line from CVC. The boundary is at the common spray supply line.
Direct vessel injection lines at the reactor pressure vessel from Passive Core Make Up Water System (PCM). The boundary is at the reactor pressure vessel.
Seal injection from CVC. The boundary is at the RCP seals.
Cooling water supply from CCW to the RCP. The boundary is the RCP.
Discharge line from the PDH. The boundary is at the SGE lower head.

For lines flowing out of the RCS, the mechanical system boundary is at the outlet of the last isolation valve leading to the interfacing system, except for the interfaces listed below where the boundary is at the RCS equipment nozzle (or otherwise noted).
Supply line to the RHR. The boundary is at Hot Leg B.
Letdown line to the CVC. The boundary is at the Cold Leg downstream of each RCP.
Supply line to the PDH. The boundary is at Hot Leg B.
RPV head vent line to passive core make up water tank in the PCM. The boundary is at the passive core makeup water tank.
High point vent line at the pressurizer to Gaseous Radwaste System and Liquid Radwaste System. The boundary is at the inlet of the first isolation valve.
Supply lines to the PSL. The boundary is at the outlet of the first isolation valve from the RCS.
The boundary between the electrical system and the RCS is at the connection of the electrical power to the component (i.e., motor).
5.1.3 Instrumentation and Control

The instrumentation and control boundary are at the connection of the RCS instruments to the PCS or PSS. A summary of the quantities and basis for required instrumentation in the RCS can be found in the Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System [1]

entries.text: Two pressurizer safety valves protect the reactor coolant pressure boundary from excessive pressure during any transients. The pressurizer safety valves provide overpressure protection in accordance with ASME Boiler Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. Discharge lines are routed from the outlet of each pressurizer safety valve to the PCMWT.
The pressurizer safety valve sizing analysis will ensure the capability of the SMR-300 design to adequately cope with the most limiting overpressure transients.

Reactor coolant piping is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code Section III [8]. The reactor coolant piping maintains the reactor coolant pressure boundary and is designed to withstand the maximum RCS pressure and temperature under all expected modes of plant operation and anticipated operational occurrences. Seamless piping is used to avoid in-service inspection of longitudinal piping welds. The piping material for the hot legs and cold legs shall be carbon steel with stainless steel cladding. All other piping shall be stainless steel.

The application of Leak-Before-Break (LBB) analysis and criteria to portions of the RCS piping design of high energy piping systems is being developed. Using the Leak-Before-Break methodology approved by the NRC and other design considerations can justify a design basis that eliminates jet impingement shields and pipe whip restraints. This methodology requires the ability to detect leaks from cracks smaller than a critical flaw size.
RCS instrumentation is used for:
Measuring conditions of the RCS and providing measurement data to the Plant Safety System (PSS), which actuates reactor protection and engineered safety features.

Measuring conditions of the RCS and providing data to the Plant Control System (PCS) for the basis information regarding specification, regulatory, and operational requirements of primary instrumentation, see the Primary Instrumentation Strategy, and for instrumentation quantities, automatic functions, and setpoints, see Control System Description for Reactor Coolant System [11]. For steam generator secondary side instrumentation, refer to the Main Feed System (MFS) [12] and Main Steam System (MSS) [13] Control System Descriptions.

The RCS provides instrumentation to measure parameters which provide a signal to PSS for reactor protection and engineered safety feature actuation during DBAs and some AOOs. The RCS uses redundant instrumentation (using four independent channels) for protection functions (i.e. for the reactor trip and ESFA logic.

The RCS hot leg temperature (Thot) and cold leg temperature (Tcold) signals are processed by PSS and used for control room indication, inputs to various control systems, and inputs to the PSS logic. Thot and Tcold are each measured with 2 instrument sensors per leg, that are averaged out to provide the channel readings. The averaged signals for Thot and Tcold are used to generate RCS average temperature (Tavg) and delta temperature signals. The Tavg setpoint is used by PSS within the ESFA logic.
Pressurizer pressure instrumentation is provided for reactor trip and ESFA logic in the PSS and is part of the pressurizer pressure permissible used in the ESFA logic.
Pressurizer level instrumentation is provided for reactor trip and ADS actuation in the ESFA logic of the PSS.
RCS level instrumentation is provided to measure the RCS inventory, spanning from the top of the Pressurizer to the RPV DVI lines. RCS inventory is crucial to all stages of accident response.
The cold legs are provided with instrumentation for monitoring the reactor coolant pump flow. This instrumentation is provided for reactor trip logic in the PSS for loss of flow DNB protection.

The PSS shares measurement channels (with proper isolation for independence) with the PCS for non-safety control of the RCS. The PSS transmits signals via a unit safety bus to the PCS for control purposes and normal monitoring.
Excore instrumentation provides permissible setpoints and reactor trip signals in the PSS logic.
The RCS provides instrumentation to measure parameters which provide a signal to PCS for plant control and monitoring during normal operations and AOOs.

The pressurizer heaters are controlled by the PCS based on the pressurizer pressure instrumentation. The pressurizer level instrumentation provides input to the PCS to calculate and control the mass balance in the pressurizer. The purpose of the pressurizer level control system is to control charging and letdown flows, as well as heater operation, to maintain programmed level.

Pressure instrumentation is also provided in the pressurizer to measure RCS pressure for indication during normal operation. Pressurizer level is measured by narrow range level instruments. RCS inventory is measured by wide range level instruments spanning from the pressurizer to the DVI lines. Both of these level instruments have a common reference leg. These instruments allow operators to monitor the level in the PZR during normal operations and in the RPV while the RCS is at reduced inventory, such as during refueling operations.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: CRDMs are external to the RPV and penetrate the upper hemispherical head. The Rod Cluster Control Assemblies (RCCAs) provide a rapid means for reactivity control during both normal operating and accident conditions. There is a single control rod drive mechanism for each RCCA. Control rod drive mechanisms are externally attached to the control rod pressure housings. The upper hemispherical head also contains penetrations for the in-core instrumentation tubes and a high-point vent line. RPV level is measured with shared instrumentation for RCS inventory level (upper FPV volume down to the DVI lines) and in-core level (DVI lines to the bottom of the fuel envelope).

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The RPV internals for the SMR-300 consist of two primary sections: the upper internals and the lower internals. The reactor internals provide protection, alignment, and support for the core, the control rods, and the in-core instruments. Additionally, the reactor internals direct coolant flow to and from the fuel assemblies, and help absorb control rod dynamic loads, fuel assembly loads, and other loads resulting from design basis events. These loads are transmitted to the RPV, which provides overall structural rigidity.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The lower internals consist of the core barrel flange, core barrel cylinder, irradiation specimen baskets, lower support plate, radial key inserts, flow distribution device, and heavy reflector. The upper internals consist of the upper support assembly (including the flange, shell, and upper support plate), the upper core plate, control rod guide tubes and cards, and shell columns.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: The external support for the RPV will be trunnions to the surrounding concrete walls and a lateral restraint at the bottom of the RPV cavity to help withstand seismic events.

entries.section_title: System Design Description for the Reactor Coolant System
entries.text: During operation, reactor coolant from the cold legs enters the RPV through the inlet nozzles and flows into the downcomer, which is the annulus formed by the space between the core barrel and the RPV inner wall. The flow then enters the lower plenum, which is the area at the bottom of the RPV. The flow then enters the flow distribution device (FDD) and is directed to the lower support plate (LSP) which is attached to the FDD. After traversing the core, the heated reactor coolant passes through the upper core plate (UCP) and enters the upper plenum, which is enclosed by the UCP, core barrel and upper support plate (USP). The flow then passes through and around the columns attaching the UCP and USP to reach the RPV outlet nozzles.

The SGE is a vertical shell and tube Once-Through Steam Generator (OTSG) [7]. The SGE is designed to utilize reactor coolant on the tube side and feedwater on the shell side. For requirements and guidance for the mechanical design and the fabrication of the OTSG see the Design Specification for the SMR-300 Steam Generator.

The hot legs connect the OTSG upper channel to the RPV outlet nozzles. The hot reactor coolant from the RPV flows down through the OTSG tubes to the lower head and into the cold leg connections back to the RPV. The primary coolant transfers heat to the feedwater flowing up the shell side of the OTSG to produce superheated steam.

The tube side of the SGE is designed in accordance with ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code [8]. The straight OTSG tubes provide easy access for in-service inspection and tube plugging as needed. The OTSG is designed for rated performance with a percentage of the tubes plugged.

The pressurizer features a thick cylindrical shell with a top hemispherical head and is laterally restrained by supports [9]. The pressurizer has been sized to account for changes in pressurizer level and RCS pressure during operational maneuvers and transients. This eliminates the need for fast-acting power operated relief valves (PORVs).The lack of PORVs eliminates the need for a pressurizer relief tank and obviates potential PORV malfunctions common to operating PWRs.

The internal divider plate is designed to limit thermal communication between the volumes on either side to minimize the size of the PZR heaters while allowing sufficient flow into and out of the PZR for pressure control. The PZR controls the pressure of the RCS by maintaining a saturated steam-liquid interface. Pressure changes caused by the expansion and contraction of the reactor coolant are absorbed by condensing the steam using the PZR spray or generating steam using the PZR heaters. RCP discharge pressure drives normal spray flow. Continuous flow through the pressurizer spray line maintains the spray line warm which prevents thermal stratification while also keeping the pressurizer volume at a similar boron concentration as the rest of the RCS volume.

The primary function of the reactor coolant pump is to provide forced circulation of reactor coolant for transfer of core heat during reactor startup, shutdown, and power operations. The SMR-300 design does not include provisions to operate with a single pump running during power operations (Mode 1).

Two 50% capacity pumps are provided, one on each cold leg [10]. There are two safety related characteristics of the RCP. First, in the event of a reactor trip or loss of power, the pumps maintain flow to the core during pump coast down using a flywheel. Second, the RCPs serve as part of the RCS pressure boundary. The pumps are not required to perform any active safety functions and will be de-energized during LOCA or operation of the primary or secondary decay heat removal systems.

entries.text: The PSS employs a two-division design, where either division can initiate an RT or ESF function independent of the other. Each division receives two instrument inputs (U/X for Division A, and Y/Z for Division B) and performs the necessary bistable logic for those inputs. The bistable outputs are then shared to the other division through Data Links so that each division can perform two out of four (2oo4) voting independently. The results of this 2oo4 voting are used in logic for RT and ESF actuation.

The PSS employs 2oo4 voting logic, where any two of the four inputs being true, causes the output to be true. The logic includes the capability to bypass individual channels for maintenance or troubleshooting. Instrument channels are compared to setpoints, and a bistable output is provided that is true when the setpoint is exceeded and false when it is back to normal.

The actuation logic for RT and ESF functions uses a standard set of logic (Figure 4-1). Each actuation logic function is initiated automatically by some specific set of logic for that function and can also be manually initiated by the operator. Once initiated the function is latched at the division level, a manual reset is provided for the operators to reset the function once allowed.

Divisional manual initiation can be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and this initiation causes both divisions to actuate (Figure 4-1). Channelized manual initiation require two concurrent initiations (2oo2) from a division or from the PCS to help prevent a spurious actuation (Figure 4-2), and this initiation causes four channels to actuate.

Manual reset can also be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the reset causes both divisions to reset. The reset has a permissive that only allows it to be reset once the division senses that it can be reset. This prevents the other division or PCS from inadvertently resetting the actuation function. Each ESF function has it’s own reset permissive that is true when all the components in that division have reached their ESF state. For example, to reset containment isolation in Division A, all Division A containment isolation valves must be closed.

entries.text: The manual reactor trip can be initiated in two ways: Touch Screen Controls via the S-VDUs Physical Reactor trip switch The touch screen controls are at the division level. Controls for manual initiation and reset of a RT are provided on the S-VDU of each division, and via the PCS O-VDU. Initiation from any of these locations will call for both divisions to open the RTBs. The physical RT switch is located on the safety console. The two contacts of the physical switch are input to hardwired AND gate, which directly initiates the RT signal for the division. This division's RT signal also generates a logical RT signal through an OR gate, combined with the RT signal from other division via datalink. Therefore, each manual RT initiates both divisions.

The PSS monitors plant parameters to provide protective action, including Engineered Safety Features actuations, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates an ESF Actuation when required by actuating an ESF component (a valve or breaker) to its safe state. Separate ESF components are provided for each division of the PSS and are configured to meet single failure criteria. Appendix B contains a summary table of all ESF actuations, the components actuated, and the ESF reset permissive signal, explaining which status feedback of the device is used for the permissive signal and how the logic to monitor the necessary plant parameters and initiate an ESF actuation is implemented.

Manual initiation of an ESF action is initiated from touch screen controls via the S-VDUs. The touch screen controls can be at the division level or at the channel level, as shown in Figure 4-1 and Figure 4-2. Controls for manual initiation and reset of an ESF function are provided on the S-VDU of each division, and via the PCS O-VDU. Initiation from any of these locations will call for both divisions to initiate the ESF function.

The PSS monitors plant parameters and provides interlocks to ensure systems are aligned to support protective action, including Engineered Safety Features actuations, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates interlocks to ensure systems are aligned to allow ESF actuations to function in the modes required. The equipment receiving these interlocks is typically locked in its safe position in the modes it's required. The interlock provides an automatic position of these components to the required state if operators fail to position them prior to needing the function.

entries.text: The PSS employs a two-division design, where either division can initiate an RT or ESF function independent of the other. Each division receives two instrument inputs (U/X for Division A, and Y/Z for Division B) and performs the necessary bistable logic for those inputs. The bistable outputs are then shared to the other division through Data Links so that each division can perform two out of four (2oo4) voting independently. The results of this 2oo4 voting are used in logic for RT and ESF actuation. The PSS employs 2oo4 voting logic, where any two of the four inputs being true, causes the output to be true. The logic includes the capability to bypass individual channels for maintenance or troubleshooting. Instrument channels are compared to setpoints, and a bistable output is provided that is true when the setpoint is exceeded and false when it is back to normal.

entries.text: Certain protection logic may or may not be necessary depending on current plant conditions. In cases where a specific set of protection logic is not necessary for a given plant condition, the logic can be bypassed. This is called an Operating Bypass.
An Operating Bypass can be initiated and/or reset automatically by the protection system or manually by the operator.

A manual Operating Bypass can be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the bypass happens in both divisions. Resetting the bypass can also be accomplished by either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the reset removes the bypass in both divisions.

All Operating Bypasses have permissives that only allow the bypass to be initiated when allowed. This permissive utilizes 2oo4+1oo2 voting logic. This is similar to the 2oo4 logic, however it also requires one of the channels within its own division to call for the permissive. This protects a division from negative influence from outside its own division.

The standard logic shown in Figure 4-3 shows all available options for an Operating Bypass. When the Bypass can be initiated by the operator or the SR latch is used to latch the bypass until the reset conditions are true. The Operating Bypass can have permissives that allow the bypass to be initiated, and these can also automatically all reset the bypass or not. If they automatically reset the bypass, they are supplied through an OR to the reset of the latch, and if they do not automatically reset the bypass they are supplied through an AND to the set of the latch. If there is no manual initiation of the bypass, the automatic bypass is supplied through an AND gate with no latch.

The permissives are used to Operating Bypass, interlock, and actuation of reactor startup, shutdown, control rod withdrawal, and ESF. The parameters associated with permissives are presented in the Appendices of this document.

Permissives are identified as P-XX, where XX is a number which defines the unique permissive. For the detailed definition of permissive list, refer to Table 1 of the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2].

entries.text: Revision Description of Changes
1 - The Assumption formation of Section 3 has been modified according to HPP-8002-0024.
- Since MCH is not required as safety-related (HI-2240950), the following were deleted.
Main Control Room Isolation in Appendix B
Main Control Room Intake Radioactivity High 1 in Appendix D
- Since the release of RT&ESF Logic Basis (HI-2240747), Assumption 19 was deleted.
- Corrected Typo: Appendix C to Appendix D in the Section 3.0 Assumption
- In Section 1.2, changed 'individual system CSD' to 'individual system level CSD', and both I/O and Instrument Ranges are covered by individual system level CSDs.
- Changed Figure 4-1, 4-2, and 4-3.
- Added 'Section 4.5 Permissives'.
- Modified Note 1 as per figure 5-1.
- Added 'Reactor Coolant System Flow Rate Low 2' (Appendix A & D)
- Added 'ESF Reset Permissive' Column to clarify the component status required for ESF reset.

- Changed 'NONE' to 'manual bypass allowed below P3' in the Operating Bypass of Pressurizer Water Level High 2 for CV Charging Isolation

- Deleted Effluent makeup outside CIV (AOV-179-2) in CVC charging Isolation based on the CVCS P&ID (DWG-15211)

entries.text: The PSS monitors plant parameters to provide protective action, including reactor trip, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates a RT when required by opening reactor trip breakers. The output actuates both the undervoltage and shunt trip coils on the RTB. The RTBs are configured such that each division has two parallel breakers, where a reactor trip will occur if both breakers in either division open.
Appendix A contains a summary table of all reactor trips and explains how the logic, to monitor the necessary plant parameters and initiate a reactor trip, is implemented.
The manual reactor trip can be initiated in two ways:
Touch Screen Controls via the S-VDUs
Physical Reactor trip switch

The touch screen controls are at the division level. Controls for manual initiation and reset of a RT are provided on the S-VDU of each division, and via the PCS O-VDU. Initiation from any of these locations will call for both divisions to open the RTBs.

The physical RT switch is located on the safety console. The two contacts of the physical switch are input to hardwired AND gate, which directly initiates the RT signal for the division. This division's RT signal also generates a logical RT signal through an OR gate, combined with the RT signal from other division via datalink. Therefore, each manual RT initiates both divisions.

Main Control Room Isolation in Appendix B
Main Control Room Intake Radioactivity High 1 in Appendix D

- Modified Note 1 as per figure 5-1.

- Changed 'NONE' to 'manual bypass allowed below P3' in the Operating Bypass of Pressurizer Water Level High 2 for CV Charging Isolation
- Since the P&ID (DWG-15650) for the CBV has been released for the SMR-300, Assumption 3 and 14 has been deleted.
- RPV Vessel Water Level - Low 1 was changed to RCS Inventory Low 2. (Appendix B & D)
- Added Letdown inside/outside CIV (MOV-017-2/MOV-020-2) in Containment Isolation based on the CVCS P&ID (DWG-15211)
- Deleted Effluent makeup outside CIV (AOV-179-2) in CVC charging Isolation based on the CVCS P&ID (DWG-15211)
