The PSS employs a two-division design, where either division can initiate an RT or ESF function independent of the other. Each division receives two instrument inputs (U/X for Division A, and Y/Z for Division B) and performs the necessary bistable logic for those inputs. The bistable outputs are then shared to the other division through Data Links so that each division can perform two out of four (2oo4) voting independently. The results of this 2oo4 voting are used in logic for RT and ESF actuation.

The PSS employs 2oo4 voting logic, where any two of the four inputs being true, causes the output to be true. The logic includes the capability to bypass individual channels for maintenance or troubleshooting. Instrument channels are compared to setpoints, and a bistable output is provided that is true when the setpoint is exceeded and false when it is back to normal.

The actuation logic for RT and ESF functions uses a standard set of logic (Figure 4-1). Each actuation logic function is initiated automatically by some specific set of logic for that function and can also be manually initiated by the operator. Once initiated the function is latched at the division level, a manual reset is provided for the operators to reset the function once allowed.

Divisional manual initiation can be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and this initiation causes both divisions to actuate (Figure 4-1). Channelized manual initiation require two concurrent initiations (2oo2) from a division or from the PCS to help prevent a spurious actuation (Figure 4-2), and this initiation causes four channels to actuate.

Manual reset can also be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the reset causes both divisions to reset. The reset has a permissive that only allows it to be reset once the division senses that it can be reset. This prevents the other division or PCS from inadvertently resetting the actuation function. Each ESF function has it’s own reset permissive that is true when all the components in that division have reached their ESF state. For example, to reset containment isolation in Division A, all Division A containment isolation valves must be closed.

entries.section_title: Reactor Trip and Engineered Safety Features Control Description
entries.text: A manual Operating Bypass can be accomplished from either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the bypass happens in both divisions. Resetting the bypass can also be accomplished by either division of the PSS or from the PCS, and the reset removes the bypass in both divisions. All Operating Bypasses have permissives that only allow the bypass to be initiated when allowed. This permissive utilizes 2oo4+1oo2 voting logic. This is similar to the 2oo4 logic, however it also requires one of the channels within its own division to call for the permissive. This protects a division from negative influence from outside its own division.

entries.section_title: Reactor Trip and Engineered Safety Features Control Description
entries.text: The standard logic shown in Figure 4-3 shows all available options for an Operating Bypass. When the Bypass can be initiated by the operator or the SR latch is used to latch the bypass until the reset conditions are true. The Operating Bypass can have permissives that allow the bypass to be initiated, and these can also automatically all reset the bypass or not. If they automatically reset the bypass, they are supplied through an OR to the reset of the latch, and if they do not automatically reset the bypass they are supplied through an AND to the set of the latch. If there is no manual initiation of the bypass, the automatic bypass is supplied through an AND gate with no latch.

entries.section_title: Reactor Trip and Engineered Safety Features Control Description
entries.text: The permissives are used to Operating Bypass, interlock, and actuation of reactor startup, shutdown, control rod withdrawal, and ESF. The parameters associated with permissives are presented in the Appendices of this document. Permissives are identified as P-XX, where XX is a number which defines the unique permissive. For the detailed definition of permissive list, refer to Table 1 of the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2].

The PSS monitors plant parameters to provide protective action, including reactor trip, to prevent safety limits from being exceeded. The basis for the parameters and setpoints monitored are included in the SMR-300 Plant Safety System Logic Basis [2]. The PSS initiates a RT when required by opening reactor trip breakers. The output actuates both the undervoltage and shunt trip coils on the RTB. The RTBs are configured such that each division has two parallel breakers, where a reactor trip will occur if both breakers in either division open.
Appendix A contains a summary table of all reactor trips and explains how the logic, to monitor the necessary plant parameters and initiate a reactor trip, is implemented.
The manual reactor trip can be initiated in two ways:
Touch Screen Controls via the S-VDUs
Physical Reactor trip switch

The touch screen controls are at the division level. Controls for manual initiation and reset of a RT are provided on the S-VDU of each division, and via the PCS O-VDU. Initiation from any of these locations will call for both divisions to open the RTBs.

The physical RT switch is located on the safety console. The two contacts of the physical switch are input to hardwired AND gate, which directly initiates the RT signal for the division. This division's RT signal also generates a logical RT signal through an OR gate, combined with the RT signal from other division via datalink. Therefore, each manual RT initiates both divisions.

entries.text: This section contains the calculations necessary to create the input files for the multi-assembly reflector calculation. A 1D radial reflector input file is generated solely to provide the geometry of the assembly for the multi-assembly calculation [21]. Reference [11] indicates that reflectors should be at least 25 cm; however, 30 cm was selected for the radial reflectors to ensure that the flux is approximately zero at the outer boundary of the reflectors. The radial reflector is broken up azimuthally to more accurately capture the heterogeneity of the ex-core structures. The design of the reflector assemblies in this model are uniform axially. Figure A2-1 shows a depiction of the MxN reflector geometry as generated by CASMO5. The red box shows the location of the 1D segmented radial reflector and encompasses the components that the 1D radial reflector segment is modeling. The radial reflector is modeled as 30 cm homogenized slabs (water gap, baffle, water gap, barrel, and downcomer). The MxN radial reflector generates reflector data appropriate for each radial reflector location in the core from a single input file and incorporates 2D transport physics. The heavy reflector is modeled as accurately as possible given the limitations of CASMO5 for Holtec SMR specific geometry (Assumption A-6).

This section contains the calculations necessary to create the input files for the multi-assembly reflector calculation. A 1D radial reflector input file is generated solely to provide the geometry of the assembly for the multi-assembly calculation [21]. Reference [11] indicates that reflectors should be at least 25 cm; however, 30 cm was selected for the radial reflectors to ensure that the flux is approximately zero at the outer boundary of the reflectors. The radial reflector is broken up azimuthally to more accurately capture the heterogeneity of the ex-core structures. The design of the reflector assemblies in this model are uniform axially. Figure A2-1 shows a depiction of the MxN reflector geometry as generated by CASMO5. The red box shows the location of the 1D segmented radial reflector and encompasses the components that the 1D radial reflector segment is modeling. The radial reflector is modeled as 30 cm homogenized slabs (water gap, baffle, water gap, barrel, and downcomer). The MxN radial reflector generates reflector data appropriate for each radial reflector location in the core from a single input file and incorporates 2D transport physics. The heavy reflector is modeled as accurately as possible given the limitations of CASMO5 for Holtec SMR specific geometry (Assumption A-6).

entries.section_title: Base Input Deck Description for Reactor Core Neutronics
entries.text: This report documents all input data and derived input parameters required to model Holtec SMR fuel in the TRITON and ORIGAMI modules of SCALE 6.2.1. The TRITON and ORIGAMI input decks are described in detail for a single burnup / enrichment combination. Statement of Limitations: The core design, i.e. fuel types and loading pattern, presented here is consistent with the latest working Holtec SMR core model. The mechanical design parameters are consistent with Section 4.0 of the Main body and Section C1-4.0 of this appendix. There is no specific methodology for this report. There are no acceptance criteria for this report. All assumptions made for the development of TRITON and ORIGAMI input decks are described in Table C1-4-1.

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: Number Assumption Descriptor Justification

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: C-10 single irradiation cycle is assumed for all burnups. Simplification Increasing the amount of UO2 in the fuel pins increases the source terms.

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: Gadolinia in the fuel pins is replaced with UO2 for both TRITON and ORIGAMI models. Simplification

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: C-11 Lower enriched fuel blanket regions are not included in the model. The entire active fuel region is assumed to have the same enrichment. Simplification The top and bottom fuel blankets only account for about 4% of the active fuel assembly length each and have negligible fission power contribution due to the low neutron flux. Therefore, its impact on the assembly source term is insignificant.

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: C-12 Control Rod Assemblies are not modeled in the TRITON or ORIGAMI fuel lattices. Reasonable This is an acceptable assumption since the calculations are for full power, in which CRAs are fully removed.

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: C-13 Gamma and neutron energy groups are set to the SCALE default 19 and 27 energy group bins respectively. [28] Simplification These libraries were chosen when considering the downstream use of these source terms because they are common multi-group libraries used for shielding analysis of light water reactors.

entries.section_title: Table C1-4-1: Assumptions for the TRITON and ORIGAMI model of Holtec SMR
entries.text: C-14 Average boron concentration is assumed. Reasonable A typical average value when considering equilibrium cycle boron evolution is chosen.

entries.text: The cards provided here may be modified as desired by the user, they will not affect the results of the calculation. These cards control what data is printed to the output file. Exclusion of some of these may cause limited functionality of automated post-processing tools. Only the options that are explicitly used in the example basedeck of this report are presented. See Reference [13] for all options.

'PRI.CSV' 'onoff' / 'onoff' 'on' Generate a comma separated value file Local file name to which restart file is written If turned OFF, readCSV and calcCSV modules of the readSIM5 and calcSIM5 libraries will not function properly [26].
'PRI.INP' 'prinp(n)' / 'prinp(n)' (n=1) 'FMAP' Input edits List of input edits to print. Turns on printing of FUE.LAB, FUE.SER, FUE.ROT, FUE.TYP.

'PRI.STA' 'prista(i)' / There are many options and configuration of labels, i.e. number and characters, please refer to manual [13] for more explicit description. Note that only a few are shown for example, in a final safety analysis calculation there may be many more edits requested.
'prinp(n)' List of input edits to print.
Pin power reconstruction edit control. The 'ON' entry specifies that pin power reconstruction edits will be printed and common peaking factor edits will be printed in the 'Output Summary' section.
('pripin(i)') List of pin-by-pin reconstruction edits (see Ref [13] for more details of all available edits).
(n=1) 'SUMM' Produces an axial distribution summary of maximum peaking factors and a batch summary of maximum exposures and powers
(n=2) 'APXP' Axial averaged pin-by-pin distribution of relative pin-by-pin power density within an assembly (i.e. integrated pin power peaking factors)
(n=3) '3PXP' Pin-by-pin distribution of relative pin-by-pin linear power density within an assembly (i.e. 3D pin power peaking factors). Normalized so the core average value is 1.0.

The cards presented in this section define the fuel mechanical properties and hydraulic design of the core. For some input cards flow loss coefficients are input, all of these values are currently unverified assumptions and should be validated by a fuel vendor.
Value Description 'PWR.POR' 'tmpopt' 'flwdisopf & PWR core inlet condition and flow determination method
'tmpopt' 'TMPINL' Core inlet condition calculation method. 'TMPINL' specifies that core inlet conditions are determined using COR.TIN.

'flwdisopf 'FLWPBAL' Core flow distribution calculation method. 'FLWPBAL' specifies that radial core inlet flow distribution is determined by equating assembly pressure drops at actual operating conditions. This enables different assemblies to pull different flow rates, therefore will result in a distribution of assembly inlet flow rates. For this option to function properly with non-channeled fuel assemblies, crossflow must be enabled (see PWR.XFL).

entries.text: The provided report serves as the comprehensive basedeck, encompassing all data, dimensions, values, and intricate details pertinent to our reactor design. Its primary role is to serve as a reference point for all forthcoming calculation packages and reports. Within this report, a meticulous presentation of the essential data for the reactor core design is provided, with a detailed description of building the input files.

Statement of Limitations: This technical report is categorized under Quality Class Nuclear, with identified exceptions. These exceptions stem from specific reasons that, in certain instances, result in the document not fully adhering to all relevant procedural guidance:

The utilization of CMSS, including CASMO5 v3.09.00L, CMSLINK5 v1.23.00L, and SIMULATE5 v2.07.00L, lacks complete verification and validation for this specific use. Verification and validation will occur later in accordance with Studsvik Scand Power (SSP) procedures outlined in Topical Report SSP-14-P01/028-TR, deemed acceptable by the NRC for referencing in licensing applications for Pressurized Water Reactors (PWR). All other control and usage requirements for this computer code are fulfilled.

The report is based on a few assumptions outlined in Section 4.0 that have not been verified. These unverified assumptions must be addressed before utilizing the report for final design, licensing, or manufacturing purposes.
The input calculations are not included in this report but are documented in the Python script Data_pool_rev2.py.
All reactor operational parameters are based on assumptions provided by the Deterministic Safety Analysis Group. These aspects will be addressed in future revision.

This document compiles the necessary input data for modeling Holtec SMR reactor core using two core neutronics software, namely Studsvik CMS5 (CASMO/SIMULATE5) and SCALE (TRITON/ORIGAMI). The primary content of this report presents the input data, referencing all available relevant reports and drawings. The specific base decks for each core modeling software are detailed in a dedicated appendix.

Creating a core neutronics model and generating results using any of the discussed codes in this report (CASMO/SIMULATE or SCALE) involves the following general stages: Establish the scope and boundaries of the model Collect and organize information for model input calculations Develop the model The subsequent sub-sections detail the methodology for each of the aforementioned stages.
The model scope depends on the software being used:

CASMO 2D fuel assembly model that covers one fuel assembly pitch in both the x and y directions. Reflector lattices extend slightly beyond in the x and y directions to account for the non-fuel hardware geometry surrounding the core in radial and axial directions. For instance, the top and bottom reflectors reach into the upper and lower core plates (1D), respectively, and the radial reflectors (2D) extend into the heavy reflector and into the downcomer to the core vessel.

SIMULATE 3D full core model that spans from the lower core plate to the top of the fuel bundle in the axial direction. Radially, it extends into the heavy reflector and downcomer, with the specific radial reflector thickness being an input model option.
SCALE/TRITON 2D fuel assembly. The extent of the fuel segment models is one (1) fuel assembly pitch in the x and y directions.
SCALE/ORIGAMI 3D fuel assembly. The extent of the fuel assembly models is one (1) fuel assembly pitch in the radial direction and from the bottom to the top of the active fuel region.

All softwares necessitate comparable fundamental information, including: Assembly geometry and material distribution Boundary conditions Modeling options The subsequent sections delve into each of these areas.

It is essential to create four (4) distinct types of fundamental reflectors: 1D top and bottom
reflectors, a 1D radial reflector, and a 2D MxN radial reflector. The CASMO5 input file for the 1D
reflector models closely resembles that of a non-Gad fuel assembly input file, assuming a fuel
enrichment of 4.95 wt% 235U. The key difference lies in the exclusion of the smeared spacer card
from the reflector model. However, the 1D radial reflector is specifically employed to furnish
assembly-specific information to the 2D MxN radial reflector model [21]. The CASMO5 input file
for the 2D MxN radial reflector models 1/8th of the core out to the reactor pressure vessel.

A2-2.1 Bottom and Top Reflectors
To build the input for the bottom and top reflectors, it is imperative to ascertain the thickness and
material composition—essentially, the homogenization of materials—in each reflector region or
zone. Each material is characterized by volume fractions representing specific compositions, such
as coolant, zircaloy, stainless steel, and helium. Initially, segment thickness and material
compositions are calculated, followed by the specification of input cards.

entries.text: This appendix documents all input data and derived input parameters required to model Holtec's SMR fuel and reflector lattices in CASMO5. The CASMO5 input decks are described in detail for all necessary lattice configurations. Additionally, CMSLINK5 is discussed in this appendix.
Statement of Limitations: See limitations in the main body of this report.
There is no specific methodology for this report.
There are no acceptance criteria for this report.
All assumptions made for the development of CASMO5 input decks are described in Table A1-4-1.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: Number Assumption Descriptor Justification A-4 The total thickness of the radial reflector model in CASMO5 is 30 cm. Simplification Reference [11] (pp. 2-146-149) indicates that reflectors should be at least 25 cm to produce accurate results in SIMULATES. The thickness was increased slightly to be equal to approximately two fuel assemblies. In addition, the thickness was increased to ensure zero flux at the boundary.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-5 The cooling holes in the heavy reflector are assumed to be constant diameter. Simplification The increase in heavy reflector material is minimal and will have an inconsequential effect on the neutron flux distribution and spectrum within the heavy reflector region. Therefore, this will not have a significant effect on the results.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-6 The heavy reflector geometry in the CASMO model is an approximation and doesn't need to match the engineering drawing in detail. Simplification According to Studsvik [21], the MxN model is sufficient to approximate the overall area and position of the water in the reflector, as reflector cross-section generation mainly requires the general geometry and materials, not exact details.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-7 The temperature used when calculating the thermal expansion coefficient of the Q12 material (guide tubes and instrument tube) is set equal to the moderator temperature. Reasonable It is a reasonable assumption to assume the guide tubes and instrument tube are a similar temperature to the moderator that surrounds them.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-8 When determining spacer grid thicknesses, peripheral fins on HMP and GAIA spacer grids are excluded while mixing fins on IGM spacers are included. Reasonable Peripheral fins account for a very small volume when compared to entire spacer volume. However mixing fins occur across the entire span of the IGM spacer, so it is more reasonable to include these when determining thickness value.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-9 When calculating the smeared spacer mass per length, the bottom HMP spacer is ignored. Reasonable This assumption is in accordance with Studsvik guidance. Inconel is a strong neutron absorber and the bottom HMP spacer is located very close to the bottom of the active fuel region. Therefore, including its presence in the smeared spacer would result in unrealistic conditions.

entries.text: This report documents all input data and derived input parameters required to model Holtec SMR fuel in the TRITON and ORIGAMI modules of SCALE 6.2.1. The TRITON and ORIGAMI input decks are described in detail for a single burnup / enrichment combination. Statement of Limitations: The core design, i.e. fuel types and loading pattern, presented here is consistent with the latest working Holtec SMR core model. The mechanical design parameters are consistent with Section 4.0 of the Main body and Section C1-4.0 of this appendix. There is no specific methodology for this report. There are no acceptance criteria for this report. All assumptions made for the development of TRITON and ORIGAMI input decks are described in Table C1-4-1.

entries.text: This section contains the calculations necessary to create the input files for the multi-assembly reflector calculation. A 1D radial reflector input file is generated solely to provide the geometry of the assembly for the multi-assembly calculation [21]. Reference [11] indicates that reflectors should be at least 25 cm; however, 30 cm was selected for the radial reflectors to ensure that the flux is approximately zero at the outer boundary of the reflectors. The radial reflector is broken up azimuthally to more accurately capture the heterogeneity of the ex-core structures. The design of the reflector assemblies in this model are uniform axially. Figure A2-1 shows a depiction of the MxN reflector geometry as generated by CASMO5. The red box shows the location of the 1D segmented radial reflector and encompasses the components that the 1D radial reflector segment is modeling. The radial reflector is modeled as 30 cm homogenized slabs (water gap, baffle, water gap, barrel, and downcomer). The MxN radial reflector generates reflector data appropriate for each radial reflector location in the core from a single input file and incorporates 2D transport physics. The heavy reflector is modeled as accurately as possible given the limitations of CASMO5 for Holtec SMR specific geometry (Assumption A-6).

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: Number Assumption Descriptor Justification A-4 The total thickness of the radial reflector model in CASMO5 is 30 cm. Simplification Reference [11] (pp. 2-146-149) indicates that reflectors should be at least 25 cm to produce accurate results in SIMULATES. The thickness was increased slightly to be equal to approximately two fuel assemblies. In addition, the thickness was increased to ensure zero flux at the boundary.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-5 The cooling holes in the heavy reflector are assumed to be constant diameter. Simplification The increase in heavy reflector material is minimal and will have an inconsequential effect on the neutron flux distribution and spectrum within the heavy reflector region. Therefore, this will not have a significant effect on the results.

entries.section_title: Table A1-4-1: Assumptions for the CASMO5 model of the Holtec SMR (continued)
entries.text: A-6 The heavy reflector geometry in the CASMO model is an approximation and doesn't need to match the engineering drawing in detail. It is essential to create four (4) distinct types of fundamental reflectors: 1D top and bottom
reflectors, a 1D radial reflector, and a 2D MxN radial reflector. The CASMO5 input file for the 1D
reflector models closely resembles that of a non-Gad fuel assembly input file, assuming a fuel
enrichment of 4.95 wt% 235U. The key difference lies in the exclusion of the smeared spacer card
from the reflector model. However, the 1D radial reflector is specifically employed to furnish
assembly-specific information to the 2D MxN radial reflector model [21]. The CASMO5 input file
for the 2D MxN radial reflector models 1/8th of the core out to the reactor pressure vessel.

A2-2.1 Bottom and Top Reflectors
To build the input for the bottom and top reflectors, it is imperative to ascertain the thickness and
material composition—essentially, the homogenization of materials—in each reflector region or
zone. Each material is characterized by volume fractions representing specific compositions, such
as coolant, zircaloy, stainless steel, and helium. Initially, segment thickness and material
compositions are calculated, followed by the specification of input cards.

entries.text: The data required for calculating inputs are extracted from drawings and other references and includes, but not limited to: Number of fuel assemblies Number of fuel pins and guide tubes Number of control rod assemblies Array size of fuel pins and guide tubes Dimensions of fuel pins, guide tubes, control rods Fuel rod length (lower inactive fuel, active fuel, and upper inactive fuel) Spacer grid locations and loss coefficients Heavy reflector specifications Reactor pressure vessel specifications Types of materials Material properties (i.e. density, temperature, etc.) Material thickness

Boundary conditions may be applied at the inlet and/or outlet of the core/fuel assembly to mimic the response of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) during steady state and transient conditions. The input data required for boundary conditions is obtained from system thermal hydraulic analysis and includes: Core inlet mass flow rate Core inlet temperature Core exit pressure Apart from the thermal-hydraulic boundary conditions, each neutronics model has its distinct approach to handling neutrons at problem boundaries.

CASMO Fuel lattices use reflective boundary conditions for +/- x and +/- y. Radial reflector lattices use reflective boundary conditions for -x and +y and vacuum boundary conditions for +x and -y. Axial reflector lattices use reflective boundary conditions on -x and +/- y, while the +x boundary is vacuum boundary condition
SIMULATE The exterior boundary conditions are albedo boundary conditions, as described in Reference [1].
SCALE/TRITON The default modeling option is for reflective boundary conditions for +/- x and +/- y. This option may be changed by the user, but it is not typical for our application.
SCALE/ORIGAMI The same as specified for TRITON.

Every computer code comes with diverse model options related to solution methods, output control, thermal hydraulic feedback effects, and more. Each code must undergo verification and validation using test data supplied by either the fuel vendor or the code package provider (SPP). Studsvik provided code V&V and benchmarking in the generic licensing topical report [2]. Studsvik also provided computer modeling guidelines in accordance with the generic licensing topical HI-2230970 Rev. 2 Copyright Holtec International © 2023, all rights reserved

The input files for all the codes discussed in this report are formatted as ASCII text files. The CASMO/SIMULATE inputs rely on input cards and are typically free-form, allowing the cards to be input in any order (with some exceptions, particularly regarding restart files). In contrast, SCALE inputs are organized into groups of input cards, each with specific required entries.

Each appendix outlines the essential keywords/cards needed to construct the respective models. Generally, the input cards are presented in the recommended order for inclusion in the input file (with exceptions noted where applicable). Each appendix concludes with an example input file, showcasing all the input cards in ASCII text file format. This example serves as a reference for constructing new input files.
There are no acceptance criteria for this report.
Some dimensions or input data may be listed as an unverified assumption. Code-specific modeling assumptions or simplifications are identified and discussed in the respective Appendix.

entries.text: This document compiles the necessary input data for modeling Holtec SMR reactor core using two core neutronics software, namely Studsvik CMS5 (CASMO/SIMULATE5) and SCALE (TRITON/ORIGAMI). The primary content of this report presents the input data, referencing all available relevant reports and drawings. The specific base decks for each core modeling software are detailed in a dedicated appendix.

Creating a core neutronics model and generating results using any of the discussed codes in this report (CASMO/SIMULATE or SCALE) involves the following general stages: Establish the scope and boundaries of the model Collect and organize information for model input calculations Develop the model The subsequent sub-sections detail the methodology for each of the aforementioned stages.
The model scope depends on the software being used:

CASMO 2D fuel assembly model that covers one fuel assembly pitch in both the x and y directions. Reflector lattices extend slightly beyond in the x and y directions to account for the non-fuel hardware geometry surrounding the core in radial and axial directions. For instance, the top and bottom reflectors reach into the upper and lower core plates (1D), respectively, and the radial reflectors (2D) extend into the heavy reflector and into the downcomer to the core vessel.

SIMULATE 3D full core model that spans from the lower core plate to the top of the fuel bundle in the axial direction. Radially, it extends into the heavy reflector and downcomer, with the specific radial reflector thickness being an input model option.
SCALE/TRITON 2D fuel assembly. The extent of the fuel segment models is one (1) fuel assembly pitch in the x and y directions.
SCALE/ORIGAMI 3D fuel assembly. The extent of the fuel assembly models is one (1) fuel assembly pitch in the radial direction and from the bottom to the top of the active fuel region.

All softwares necessitate comparable fundamental information, including: Assembly geometry and material distribution Boundary conditions Modeling options The subsequent sections delve into each of these areas.

The data required for calculating inputs are extracted from drawings and other references and includes, but not limited to: Number of fuel assemblies Number of fuel pins and guide tubes Number of control rod assemblies Array size of fuel pins and guide tubes Dimensions of fuel pins, guide tubes, control rods Fuel rod length (lower inactive fuel, active fuel, and upper inactive fuel) Spacer grid locations and loss coefficients Heavy reflector specifications Reactor pressure vessel specifications Types of materials Material properties (i.e. density, temperature, etc.) Material thickness

Boundary conditions may be applied at the inlet and/or outlet of the core/fuel assembly to mimic the response of the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) during steady state and transient conditions. The input data required for boundary conditions is obtained from system thermal hydraulic analysis and includes: Core inlet mass flow rate Core inlet temperature Core exit pressure Apart from the thermal-hydraulic boundary conditions, each neutronics model has its distinct approach to handling neutrons at problem boundaries.

CASMO Fuel lattices use reflective boundary conditions for +/- x and +/- y. Radial reflector lattices use reflective boundary conditions for -x and +y and vacuum boundary conditions for +x and -y. Axial reflector lattices use reflective boundary conditions on -x and +/- y, while the +x boundary is vacuum boundary condition
SIMULATE The exterior boundary conditions are albedo boundary conditions, as described in Reference [1].
SCALE/TRITON The default modeling option is for reflective boundary conditions for +/- x and +/- y. This option may be changed by the user, but it is not typical for our application.
SCALE/ORIGAMI The same as specified for TRITON.

Every computer code comes with diverse model options related to solution methods, output control, thermal hydraulic feedback effects, and more. Each code must undergo verification and validation using test data supplied by either the fuel vendor or the code package provider (SPP). Studsvik provided code V&V and benchmarking in the generic licensing topical report [2]. Studsvik also provided computer modeling guidelines in accordance with the generic licensing topical HI-2230970 Rev. 2 Copyright Holtec International © 2023, all rights reserved

All other control and usage requirements for this computer code are fulfilled.

The terms GAIA and GAIA-AFM have been used interchangeably throughout the report to refer to GAIA-AFM fuel design. Revisions marked with rev bars throughout.

The provided report serves as the comprehensive basedeck, encompassing all data, dimensions, values, and intricate details pertinent to our reactor design. Its primary role is to serve as a reference point for all forthcoming calculation packages and reports. Within this report, a meticulous presentation of the essential data for the reactor core design is provided, with a detailed description of building the input files.

Verification and validation will occur later in accordance with Studsvik Scand Power (SSP) procedures outlined in Topical Report SSP-14-P01/028-TR, deemed acceptable by the NRC for referencing in licensing applications for Pressurized Water Reactors (PWR). All other control and usage requirements for this computer code are fulfilled.

The report is based on a few assumptions outlined in Section 4.0 that have not been verified. These unverified assumptions must be addressed before utilizing the report for final design, licensing, or manufacturing purposes.

The input calculations are not included in this report but are documented in the Python script Data_pool_rev2.py. All reactor operational parameters are based on assumptions provided by the Deterministic Safety Analysis Group. These aspects will be addressed in future revision.

entries.text: The heavy reflector geometry in the CASMO model is an approximation and doesn't need to match the engineering drawing in detail. Simplification According to Studsvik [21], the MxN model is sufficient to approximate the overall area and position of the water in the reflector, as reflector cross-section generation mainly requires the general geometry and materials, not exact details.

The temperature used when calculating the thermal expansion coefficient of the Q12 material (guide tubes and instrument tube) is set equal to the moderator temperature. Reasonable It is a reasonable assumption to assume the guide tubes and instrument tube are a similar temperature to the moderator that surrounds them.

When determining spacer grid thicknesses, peripheral fins on HMP and GAIA spacer grids are excluded while mixing fins on IGM spacers are included. Reasonable Peripheral fins account for a very small volume when compared to entire spacer volume. However mixing fins occur across the entire span of the IGM spacer, so it is more reasonable to include these when determining thickness value.

When calculating the smeared spacer mass per length, the bottom HMP spacer is ignored. Reasonable This assumption is in accordance with Studsvik guidance. Inconel is a strong neutron absorber and the bottom HMP spacer is located very close to the bottom of the active fuel region. Therefore, including its presence in the smeared spacer would result in unrealistic conditions.

An enrichment reduction or 'cutback' of 5% for each 1 w/o of Gd2O3 is applied in Reasonable Framatome has commitments to the USNRC that a gadolinia-bearing fuel rod will not become the limiting fuel rod with respect to calculated rod power in the
See Appendix A2 for all CASMO input data.

entries.section_title: 4.1.4 Procedure for Obtaining Automatic Water Level Measurements
entries.text: Automatic water level and barometric transducers will be installed in selected wells to monitor changes in groundwater elevations to supplement the monthly manual water level measurements.

entries.section_title: 4.1.4 Procedure for Obtaining Automatic Water Level Measurements
entries.text: The wells monitored, the measurement interval, and time period of monitoring are at the discretion of the HTDL.

entries.section_title: 4.1.4 Procedure for Obtaining Automatic Water Level Measurements
entries.text: Barometric efficiency of the aquifer can be determined by continuous monitoring of the depth to groundwater at the pumping well, observation wells, or slug test wells and the atmospheric barometric pressure prior to initiation of the pumping test or following completion of the recovery test. These observations are used to correct for the anticipated changes in the groundwater elevation due to changing barometric conditions at the test site, if needed.

1) Complete the “Well Information” section of the “Transducer Data Sheet” (Attachment B) for each well that will be monitored with a water level transducer system. Separate data sheets shall be completed for each well a transducer system is installed in.
2) Open well cap/seal. Cover any sharp edges of the well casing to protect the transducer cables.

3) Manually measure the initial water level in the well where the transducer will be installed as instructed in Section 4.1.3. Record the water level measurement on the “Transducer Data Sheet” in Attachment B.
4) Connect the water level transducer system components (cables, transducers, etc.) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
5) Lower the transducer and cable down the well until the transducer indicates contact with water. Visually inspect the condition of the cables as they are being lowered.
6) Raise the transducer slightly above the detected water level. Perform a zero-level reset of the water level transducer.

Perform pre-measurement operational and accuracy checks for the manual water level indicator prior to use on site. This shall be completed for each manual water level indicator used during the testing.

Record any equipment conditional defects:
1. If previously performed and documented per PI ESEPCOHOLTEC-00077-PI-001 or ESEPCOHOLTEC-00077-PI-004, Step 3 of this Attachment is not required.
2. Check here if not applicable per Step 1: and proceed to Step 4. Technical Staff initials: Date:

3. Prior to mobilization to the site, verify that the water level indicator electric tape accuracy has been checked by comparing to a steel reference tape, as described below: a. Operational Check: Perform a visual inspection of the water level indicator electric tape to ensure that it has not been damaged, spliced, or inaccurately marked. Also, dip the electrode tip into water to ensure that the audible alarm functions properly. Operational check satisfactory: Technical Staff initials: Date: b. Accuracy Check: Prior to site mobilization, visually verify the accuracy of the electric tape using a reference tape. i. Lay the electric tape and reference tape out straight on a flat surface. ii. Position the zero marks of both tapes exactly opposite one another. On the electric tape this will be the point on the electrode's sensor that first indicates contact with the water. iii. Compare the graduated measurement marks on the two tapes at 1-foot mark intervals. Record the comparative values on the accuracy verification sheet. iv. If there is a difference between the electric tape and reference tape, a correction must be applied to all depth-to-water measurements recorded with the electric tape. v. If an electric tape needs a correction value it should be determined to the nearest 0.01- foot. Record the correction value on the accuracy verification sheet and on the body of the tape reel. Accuracy verification sheet completed and satisfactory: Technical verification initials: Date:

entries.text: Project Manager (PM) – The PM is responsible for technical, administrative, and financial management of the project. The PM is also responsible for assuring compliance with this PI and approving any revisions to the PI.

Hydrology Task Discipline Lead (HTDL) – The HTDL is assigned the responsibility for technical adequacy, oversight of hydrologic field activities and compliance with QA program requirements for work conducted under this PI. The HTDL transmits project information to the technical staff and PM and submits the Project Field Log and/or field documentation to the PM. The HTDL also provides technical direction based on experience and subject matter knowledge. Based on a continuing evaluation of Ground Water Data, the HTDL will identify which wells will be tested and the required duration of the test.

Technical Staff – Field technical staff work under the direction of the HTDL to perform field data collection in accordance with this PI. Measurements and raw data are recorded in the Project Field Log and/or field documentation in accordance with this PI.

This PI is applicable to all personnel responsible for measuring, recording, or collecting SR field hydrological data. This PI provides administration controls for data acquisition, data documentation requirements, standard procedures for data collection, and a description of the supplies and equipment needed.
ASTM – American Society for Testing and Materials
bgs – below ground surface
btc – below top of casing
CPA – Construction Permit Aplication
HTDL – Hydrology Task Discipline Lead
Kd – distribution coefficient
M&TE – Measuring & Test Equipment
NIST - National Institute of Standard and Technology
PI – Project Instruction

Groundwater Level The level of the water table surrounding a borehole or well. The groundwater level may be represented as an elevation relative to mean sea level or as a depth below the ground surface.

Water Level Transducer System Commercially available devices consisting of a water level sensor, a separate barometric sensor, cabling, and a computer system to download the data produced by the sensors.

Water Level Indicator A commercially available water level measuring device consisting of a double-wired electric tape that is graduated in feet, tenths and hundredths of feet. The electric tape is commonly mounted on a manually-operated reel that contains space for the batteries and some device (“indicator”) for signaling when the groundwater surface is encountered (commonly referred to as a water level meter).
Bailer A hollow cylindrical container or pipe with a simple ball check valve at the bottom used to retrieve groundwater samples from monitoring wells.

Reference Tape A steel tape, graduated in feet, tenths and hundredths of foot. A reference tape is one that is maintained in the office and used only for verifying the accuracy of other tapes, such as the electric tape of the water level indicator. The reference tape is never used in the field.

entries.text: Open well cap/seal. Cover any sharp edges of the well casing to protect the transducer cables.

Manually measure the initial water level in the well where the transducer will be installed as instructed in Section 4.1.3. Record the water level measurement on the “Transducer Data Sheet” in Attachment B.
Connect the water level transducer system components (cables, transducers, etc.) according to the manufacturer’s instructions.
Lower the transducer and cable down the well until the transducer indicates contact with water. Visually inspect the condition of the cables as they are being lowered.
Raise the transducer slightly above the detected water level. Perform a zero-level reset of the water level transducer.

i. If the transducer measurements are not within 0.3 foot of the manual water level measurements, and installation problems or transducer malfunctions are not discovered, instrument drift is indicated. Instrument drift is a change in the electronic output over a period of time that is not a function of a change in the measured water level.

ii. If installation problems or transducer malfunctions are suspected, inspect the installation and operation of the installed transducer to ensure the cable has not slipped and it is operating properly (refer to Steps 9 and 10 above). If installation or transducer problems are discovered, these shall be corrected as needed and the transducer installation and operation shall be verified (refer to Steps 6 through 10 above).

b. Drift in excess of the manufacturer’s accuracy range is acceptable and will be corrected after leaving the field to within 0.3 foot by applying a linear pulleration with time, consistent with common industry practices.
14) At any time that the down-well transducer must be removed or disturbed (such as the completion of the monitoring period, sampling, or changes in testing):
a. Record the manual water level measurement in the well.
b. Stop the transducer data collection.
c. Slowly pull/reel the transducer cable to the surface. Visually inspect the cable as it is retrieved.
d. If required, re-install the water level transducer system following steps 4 through 11 above.
e. Record all removal and re-installation activities on the “Transducer Data Sheet” in Attachment B.
1) Complete the “Barometric Transducer” section of the “Transducer Data Sheet” (see Attachment B) for each well that will be monitored with a barometric transducer.
2) Secure the transducer cable to a stable, stationary object to prevent slippage.

entries.text: Lower the barometric transducer and cable into the monitoring well to the length of the transducer cable, but above the maximum expected water level in the well. The HTDL will determine a target installation depth for each transducer.

A barometric transducer is not required to be installed in each well equipped with a water level transducer. One barometric transducer is sufficient for all water level transducers installed within a one-mile radius.
Determination of barometric efficiency and any required data correction will be performed after leaving the field and during data evaluation activities.

ENERCON personnel will collect a minimum of two (2) soil/bedrock samples with accompanying groundwater samples (if groundwater is present) for submittal to a qualified analytical laboratory for determination of isotopic distribution coefficients (Kd).
The following list of materials and equipment will be required for collection of soil and groundwater samples for the analysis of soil distribution coefficients.
Project Field Log – as described in Section 4.1.1 of this PI;

Bailer with String or Rope Commercially-available bailers will be used to obtain groundwater for use in the analysis of soil distribution coefficients for this project. Each bailer will be new and discarded following each use or dedicated to one monitoring well. Bailers will be composed of an inert, non-conductive material, such as polypropylene. Bailers will be lowered into the well using string or rope of sufficient strength to retrieve the filled bailer and resist potential breakage from any sharp edges on the well casing. The bailer string will be composed of a similar inert, non-conductive material, such as nylon or polypropylene. Any used string or rope will be discarded between wells. There are no additional requirements or specifications for bailers used for groundwater sampling for this project. Commercially-available bailers, as described above, are adequate for use under this PI.
Laboratory supplied or designated sample containers;
Watch or clock– as described in Section 4.1.1 of this PI; and
Latex or nitrile gloves

1) One soil or bedrock sample will be obtained from each of two of the geotechnical borings installed at the site. The geotechnical borings to be sampled and sample depth interval will be determined in the field by the HTDL.

2) Soil samples for Kd analysis need not be collected at the time of drilling and may be collected from cores stored in the secured storage facility. Soil samples do not require chemical or thermal preservation methods.

3) Using an indelible ink pen, all sample containers shall be labeled at the time of sampling. Labels shall include as a minimum: a. sample location (boring identification and depth interval); b. unique sample number; c. sample date; and d. sample time; and e. initials of the sample collector.
4) Other comments pertaining to the sample collection should be noted as necessary. All information will be written in indelible ink.

5) Soil samples obtained from the geotechnical cores will be transferred to ENERCON personnel using chain-of-custody controls and packaged in appropriately sized glass laboratory sample jars. Filled laboratory sample jars will be packaged for shipment in an appropriate shipping container. A chain of custody form, as provided in Attachment C, or equivalent, will be completed and accompany samples during collection and shipment. Follow sample custody instructions in Section 4.2.4 of this PI.
1) If recoverable groundwater is not encountered in any installed monitoring well, instructions described in this subsection are not applicable and need not be performed.

2) Following installation and development of the site monitoring wells, groundwater samples will be obtained from the monitoring wells associated with the geotechnical borings where the soil samples collected for Kd analysis were obtained.
3) Grab groundwater samples will be obtained from each monitoring well using dedicated disposable polyethylene bailers and placed in laboratory specified sample containers.

entries.text: The HTDL will transmit QA records generated by this project to the PMT. Technical staff shall maintain the following field records and submit them to the HTDL at the completion of the 12-month data collection period, or more frequently as requested:
• the Project Field log;
• completed Manual Water Level Data Sheet(s), Attachment A;
• electronic water level transducer system download files, Attachment B;
• soil distribution coefficient analytic reports;
• completed chain of custody forms; and
• Electric Tape Accuracy Verification Sheet, Attachment C

Records of data should be legible and completed using indelible ink. To correct an entry, strike out the error with a single line so that the original entry remains legible. Record your initials and the date of the correction near the revised entry.

entries.text: This section provides field instructions for the collection of manual and automatic groundwater level measurements and soil and groundwater Kd samples.

Manual groundwater level measurements (also commonly referred to as groundwater gauging or depth-to-water measurements) are a SR activity that will be conducted in accordance with this PI. Manual groundwater level measurements will be collected from installed wells over a minimum 12-month period to determine a maximum groundwater elevation and characterize seasonal groundwater level fluctuations. Automatic water level transducers will be installed in selected wells to monitor changes in groundwater elevations to supplement the monthly manual water level measurements.
The following list of materials and equipment will be required for collection of manual and automated water level measurements.

Project Field Log - Field data may be recorded in a bound field logbook or on an appropriate form/data sheet. All recorded data will be in indelible ink. All original field data sheets in a loose format will be bound and numbered at the project completion to ensure against loss. Each field log will be specific to the fieldwork conducted for the HOLTEC SMR project and labeled with a start and end date (when known). If multiple field logs are necessary, each logbook shall be assigned a unique sequential number or identifier. For hydrology related tasks, field logs will be identified as HOLTEC SMR-HYD "x", where "x" is a sequential number starting with "01". A digital copy of all Field Logbooks should be kept in a separate location from the logbook itself. At the completion of each day's entry, or as soon as is practicable, a digital copy should be made and added to the electronic files maintained for the project. Digital records should be transferred to the project file at least weekly.

Steel Reference Tape: A steel reference tape will be used to measure linear distances as required for verification of the accuracy of the water level indicator (see Attachment A of this PI). The reference tape will be high quality steel with engineering markings. The reference tape will be a minimum of 300 feet in length to ensure that measurements can be obtained from a single tape. Commercially-available steel tapes have general accuracies of +/- 0.100 inches per 100-foot length (varying by manufacturer, but of similar order of magnitude). 1. If previously performed and documented per PI ESEPCOHOLTEC-00077-PI-001 or ESEPCOHOLTEC-00077-PI-004, Step 3 of this Attachment is not required.

3. Prior to mobilization to the site, verify that the water level indicator electric tape accuracy has been checked by comparing to a steel reference tape, as described below: a. Operational Check: Perform a visual inspection of the water level indicator electric tape to ensure that it has not been damaged, spliced, or inaccurately marked. Also, dip the electrode tip into water to ensure that the audible alarm functions properly. Operational check satisfactory: Technical Staff initials: Date: b. Accuracy Check: Prior to site mobilization, visually verify the accuracy of the electric tape using a reference tape. i. Lay the electric tape and reference tape out straight on a flat surface. ii. Position the zero marks of both tapes exactly opposite one another. On the electric tape this will be the point on the electrode's sensor that first indicates contact with the water. iii. Compare the graduated measurement marks on the two tapes at 1-foot mark intervals. Record the comparative values on the accuracy verification sheet. iv. If there is a difference between the electric tape and reference tape, a correction must be applied to all depth-to-water measurements recorded with the electric tape. v. If an electric tape needs a correction value it should be determined to the nearest 0.01- foot. Record the correction value on the accuracy verification sheet and on the body of the tape reel. entries.text: Groundwater Level The level of the water table surrounding a borehole or well. The groundwater level may be represented as an elevation relative to mean sea level or as a depth below the ground surface.

entries.text: The primary objective of this Project Instruction (PI) is to direct the efforts for the nuclear safety related (SR) hydrogeologic data acquisition and analysis in accordance with standards set in the ENERCON Project Plan (PP). This data will become part of the Construction Permit Application (CPA) for two new Small Modular Reactor (SMR) units planned for construction by Holtec International (Holtec) at the Palisades Nuclear Plant (PNP) site.

This PI deals specifically with the collection of hydrogeologic data that may be used for SR tasks to support the Holtec SMR CPA, such as Section 2.4 of the Site Safety Analysis Report (SSAR). SR field activities described in this PI associated with the groundwater investigation include:

1. Manual groundwater level measurements - These measurements will be used to determine the maximum site groundwater elevation to be used in hydrostatic loading analyses and the site groundwater flow characteristics to be used in postulated accidental release analyses.

2. Automatic Groundwater Level Measurement - Transducers will be installed in selected groundwater monitoring wells and will automatically log the groundwater elevation within the well for long term-continuous groundwater elevation trends that may be missed with the monthly manual gauging events performed for this PI.

3. Collection of geologic materials (soil and/or bedrock and groundwater) for laboratory isotopic distribution coefficient (Kd) analyses. Isotopic distribution coefficient data will be used in the postulated accidental release analyses.

Work completed during field operations will be performed in compliance with ENERCON's site-specific Health and Safety Plan. The site of the groundwater investigation is depicted on Figure 1. The approximate locations of planned subsurface borings and groundwater monitoring wells are shown in Figure 2.

Changes allowed under this PI include moving, deleting, and/or adding well locations due to utility conflicts, access restrictions, buried subsurface impediments, or observed subsurface conditions encountered during the course of the investigation. For example, if groundwater is not observed during the drilling of the geotechnical borings, the number of monitoring wells installed and monitored may be decreased after review and in consultation with the ENERCON Hydrology team and acceptance of the Project Manager.

Project Manager (PM) – The PM is responsible for technical, administrative, and financial management of the project. The PM is also responsible for assuring compliance with this PI and approving any revisions to the PI.

Hydrology Task Discipline Lead (HTDL) – The HTDL is assigned the responsibility for technical adequacy, oversight of hydrologic field activities and compliance with QA program requirements for work conducted under this PI. The HTDL transmits project information to the technical staff and PM and submits the Project Field Log and/or field documentation to the PM. The HTDL also provides technical direction based on experience and subject matter knowledge. Based on a continuing evaluation of Ground Water Data, the HTDL will identify which wells will be tested and the required duration of the test.

Technical Staff – Field technical staff work under the direction of the HTDL to perform field data collection in accordance with this PI. Measurements and raw data are recorded in the Project Field Log and/or field documentation in accordance with this PI.

This PI is applicable to all personnel responsible for measuring, recording, or collecting SR field hydrological data. This PI provides administration controls for data acquisition, data documentation requirements, standard procedures for data collection, and a description of the supplies and equipment needed.

entries.text: Groundwater samples collected for Kd analysis do not require chemical or thermal preservation methods.

All sample containers shall be labeled at the time of sampling and labels shall include as a minimum: a. sample location; b. unique sample number (corresponding to soil Kd sample); c. sample date; d. sample time; and e. initials of the sample collector.

If a representative ground water sample is not available, it should be documented in the Field Log. Other comments pertaining to the sample collection should be noted in the Project Field Log, as necessary. All information will be written in indelible ink.

A chain of custody form, supplied by the laboratory or as provided in Attachment C, will be completed and accompany groundwater samples during collection and shipment. Follow sample custody instructions in Section 4.2.4 of this PI.

ENERCON staff will maintain sample custody from the time the sample is obtained (such as when the soil sample is collected or when the groundwater sample is collected from the monitoring well) until the sample is released for transportation. A chain of custody form, as depicted below, or equivalent, will be completed to document the sample collector, sample transporter(s), and sample recipient. The sample transporter may include other ENERCON employees or freight companies. The original chain of custody form will accompany the samples throughout transportation. Samples shall be consumed at the laboratory; no sample material will be returned to ENERCON. The recipient laboratory will be requested to return the original chain of custody form with the completed analytical results. Technical staff will keep a copy of the chain of custody that is included in the sample shipment for submittal to the HTDL.

The HTDL will transmit QA records generated by this project to the PMT. Technical staff shall maintain the following field records and submit them to the HTDL at the completion of the 12-month data collection period, or more frequently as requested:
• the Project Field log;
• completed Manual Water Level Data Sheet(s), Attachment A;
• electronic water level transducer system download files, Attachment B;
• soil distribution coefficient analytic reports;
• completed chain of custody forms; and
• Electric Tape Accuracy Verification Sheet, Attachment C

Records of data should be legible and completed using indelible ink. To correct an entry, strike out the error with a single line so that the original entry remains legible. Record your initials and the date of the correction near the revised entry.

entries.section_title: Water Level Indicator (to be identified on Attachment A)
entries.text: A water level indicator(s) will be used to measure the depth to water within installed monitoring wells during the hydrogeologic investigation for this project.

entries.section_title: Water Level Indicator (to be identified on Attachment A)
entries.text: As defined in Sections 3.2 of this PI, water level indicators used for this project will be high quality, commercially-available instruments whose electric tapes are graduated in units of feet, tenths of feet, and hundredths of feet. For collection of manual water level measurements, an accuracy of 0.01 foot is required.

entries.section_title: Water Level Indicator (to be identified on Attachment A)
entries.text: Prior to use in the field, each water level indicator will be inspected, as instructed in Section 4.1.2 of this PI, to verify that the accuracy is adequate for use. Models acceptable for use are listed below:

As referenced in this PI, a watch or clock will be required to record the time of day when manual water level measurements are taken. An accuracy of +/- 5 minutes is required for this activity. Commercially-available watches and clocks generally have accuracies of +/- 10 seconds variation within 24 hours. Commercially-available watches or clocks will be adequate for the stated purpose of recording the time of data measurements. If multiple timepieces are used, the time of each will be synchronized to be within the 5-minute tolerance.

entries.section_title: Water Level Indicator Operation and Accuracy Check
entries.text: Prior to mobilization to the site, perform the water level indicator operational and accuracy checks per Attachment C.

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: Manual water level measurements will be collected monthly for a period of 12 months (minimum) from installed monitoring wells. Measurements will be recorded as instructed below, based on the ASTM Standard D4750-87 (2001).

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 1) Complete the "Water Level Indicator Information" section of the "Manual Water Level Data Sheet" in Attachment A.

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 2) Open well cap/seal.

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 3) Lower the electrode of the water level indicator down the well until the indicator shows that contact with the water surface is made.

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 4) Grasping the electric tape at the measuring point, read the depth to water to the nearest 0.01-foot below top-of-casing (btc). For consistency, the measuring point is defined as a marked/notched reference point on the top of the well riser/casing. Confirm the reading is stable by slightly raising and lowering the electrode and checking that the indicator depth is the same (repeat the measurement).

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 5) Record the well identification, date, time, depth-to-water measurement (from top of well casing), and unit of measurement (ft btc) on the "Manual Water Level Data Sheet" in Attachment A.

entries.section_title: Procedure for Obtaining Manual Water Level Measurements
entries.text: 6) Once the water level indicator has been withdrawn, replace the well cap ensuring that the well is sealed. Replace any locks or bolted covers.

entries.section_title: 4.1.4 Procedure for Obtaining Automatic Water Level Measurements
entries.text: Barometric efficiency of the aquifer can be determined by continuous monitoring of the depth to groundwater at the pumping well, observation wells, or slug test wells and the atmospheric barometric pressure prior to initiation of the pumping test or following completion of the recovery test. 1) Complete the “Well Information” section of the “Transducer Data Sheet” (Attachment B) for each well that will be monitored with a water level transducer system. Separate data sheets shall be completed for each well a transducer system is installed in.

5) Lower the transducer and cable down the well until the transducer indicates contact with water. Visually inspect the condition of the cables as they are being lowered.
6) Raise the transducer slightly above the detected water level. Perform a zero-level reset of the water level transducer.

entries.text: 1) One soil or bedrock sample will be obtained from each of two of the geotechnical borings installed at the site. The geotechnical borings to be sampled and sample depth interval will be determined in the field by the HTDL.

2) Soil samples for Kd analysis need not be collected at the time of drilling and may be collected from cores stored in the secured storage facility. Soil samples do not require chemical or thermal preservation methods.

3) Using an indelible ink pen, all sample containers shall be labeled at the time of sampling. Labels shall include as a minimum: a. sample location (boring identification and depth interval); b. unique sample number; c. sample date; and d. sample time; and e. initials of the sample collector.
4) Other comments pertaining to the sample collection should be noted as necessary. All information will be written in indelible ink.

5) Soil samples obtained from the geotechnical cores will be transferred to ENERCON personnel using chain-of-custody controls and packaged in appropriately sized glass laboratory sample jars. Filled laboratory sample jars will be packaged for shipment in an appropriate shipping container. A chain of custody form, as provided in Attachment C, or equivalent, will be completed and accompany samples during collection and shipment. Follow sample custody instructions in Section 4.2.4 of this PI.
1) If recoverable groundwater is not encountered in any installed monitoring well, instructions described in this subsection are not applicable and need not be performed.

2) Following installation and development of the site monitoring wells, groundwater samples will be obtained from the monitoring wells associated with the geotechnical borings where the soil samples collected for Kd analysis were obtained.
3) Grab groundwater samples will be obtained from each monitoring well using dedicated disposable polyethylene bailers and placed in laboratory specified sample containers.
Groundwater samples collected for Kd analysis do not require chemical or thermal preservation methods.

All sample containers shall be labeled at the time of sampling and labels shall include as a minimum: a. sample location; b. unique sample number (corresponding to soil Kd sample); c. sample date; d. sample time; and e. initials of the sample collector.

If a representative ground water sample is not available, it should be documented in the Field Log. Other comments pertaining to the sample collection should be noted in the Project Field Log, as necessary. All information will be written in indelible ink.

A chain of custody form, supplied by the laboratory or as provided in Attachment C, will be completed and accompany groundwater samples during collection and shipment. Follow sample custody instructions in Section 4.2.4 of this PI.

ENERCON staff will maintain sample custody from the time the sample is obtained (such as when the soil sample is collected or when the groundwater sample is collected from the monitoring well) until the sample is released for transportation. A chain of custody form, as depicted below, or equivalent, will be completed to document the sample collector, sample transporter(s), and sample recipient. The sample transporter may include other ENERCON employees or freight companies. The original chain of custody form will accompany the samples throughout transportation. Samples shall be consumed at the laboratory; no sample material will be returned to ENERCON. The recipient laboratory will be requested to return the original chain of custody form with the completed analytical results. Technical staff will keep a copy of the chain of custody that is included in the sample shipment for submittal to the HTDL.

entries.text: i. If the transducer measurements are not within 0.3 foot of the manual water level measurements, and installation problems or transducer malfunctions are not discovered, instrument drift is indicated. Instrument drift is a change in the electronic output over a period of time that is not a function of a change in the measured water level.

ii. If installation problems or transducer malfunctions are suspected, inspect the installation and operation of the installed transducer to ensure the cable has not slipped and it is operating properly (refer to Steps 9 and 10 above). If installation or transducer problems are discovered, these shall be corrected as needed and the transducer installation and operation shall be verified (refer to Steps 6 through 10 above).

b. Drift in excess of the manufacturer’s accuracy range is acceptable and will be corrected after leaving the field to within 0.3 foot by applying a linear pulleration with time, consistent with common industry practices.
14) At any time that the down-well transducer must be removed or disturbed (such as the completion of the monitoring period, sampling, or changes in testing):
a. Record the manual water level measurement in the well.
b. Stop the transducer data collection.
c. Slowly pull/reel the transducer cable to the surface. Visually inspect the cable as it is retrieved.
d. If required, re-install the water level transducer system following steps 4 through 11 above.
e. Record all removal and re-installation activities on the “Transducer Data Sheet” in Attachment B.
1) Complete the “Barometric Transducer” section of the “Transducer Data Sheet” (see Attachment B) for each well that will be monitored with a barometric transducer.
2) Secure the transducer cable to a stable, stationary object to prevent slippage.

Lower the barometric transducer and cable into the monitoring well to the length of the transducer cable, but above the maximum expected water level in the well. The HTDL will determine a target installation depth for each transducer.

A barometric transducer is not required to be installed in each well equipped with a water level transducer. One barometric transducer is sufficient for all water level transducers installed within a one-mile radius.
Determination of barometric efficiency and any required data correction will be performed after leaving the field and during data evaluation activities.

ENERCON personnel will collect a minimum of two (2) soil/bedrock samples with accompanying groundwater samples (if groundwater is present) for submittal to a qualified analytical laboratory for determination of isotopic distribution coefficients (Kd).
The following list of materials and equipment will be required for collection of soil and groundwater samples for the analysis of soil distribution coefficients.
Project Field Log – as described in Section 4.1.1 of this PI;

Bailer with String or Rope Commercially-available bailers will be used to obtain groundwater for use in the analysis of soil distribution coefficients for this project. Each bailer will be new and discarded following each use or dedicated to one monitoring well. Bailers will be composed of an inert, non-conductive material, such as polypropylene. Bailers will be lowered into the well using string or rope of sufficient strength to retrieve the filled bailer and resist potential breakage from any sharp edges on the well casing. The bailer string will be composed of a similar inert, non-conductive material, such as nylon or polypropylene. Any used string or rope will be discarded between wells. There are no additional requirements or specifications for bailers used for groundwater sampling for this project. Commercially-available bailers, as described above, are adequate for use under this PI.
Laboratory supplied or designated sample containers;
Watch or clock– as described in Section 4.1.1 of this PI; and
Latex or nitrile gloves

entries.text: The BEF is the most likely flow rate to occur in the RCS loop when the plant is operating at normal full-power conditions. This operating state is the design basis point for the RCP. The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions. The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

Uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions are accounted for individually in the TDH calculations at TDF and MDF conditions. These uncertainties are applied to their respective parts of Equation (3) and a new TDH is calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the new TDH based on a specific uncertainty, results in an uncertainty with a dimension (unit) of TDH. These TDH uncertainties are then then combined using the root sum of squares method:

Where: Utotal = Total uncertainty (ft) Ufr = Uncertainty in flow resistance (including SGE tube plugging) (ft) Ufm = Uncertainty in flow measurement (ft) Uoc = Uncertainty in operating conditions (temperature and pressure) (ft)
The uncertainty is then added to the nominal TDH at TDF conditions and subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions:
Where: TDHtotal = TDH at TDF conditions plus uncertainty (ft) TDHnominal = TDH at TDF conditions without uncertainty (ft) UTDHFfr = nominal TDH uncertainty in flow resistance at TDF conditions (ft)

The RCP TDH is dependent on flow resistance. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainties associated with flow resistance. Uncertainties for flow resistance are taken from Reference [4]. These uncertainties are applied (added for TDF, subtracted for MDF) to each section within the RCS flow loop.
The flow resistance uncertainty can be assumed to have a normal distribution. With a normal distribution, one-sided tolerance limits can be calculated as:

x = Weighted average of the TDH uncertainty. This is calculated by determining the differences between the nominal TDH and TDH with uncertainty at each section with the RCS loop. The weighted average is calculated by summing the squares of the differences in TDH and dividing by the sum of the TDH differences.
k = Coverage factor used to determine the range within which a certain proportion of the flow resistance uncertainty lies within a specific level of confidence.
o = Standard deviation of the flow resistance uncertainty.
Ufr = Total flow resistance uncertainty

The coverage factor (k) is taken from Table 2.1 of Reference [5]. The k factor is selected such that there is a 99.5% probability that 99.0% of the possible TDH combinations due to flow resistance uncertainty are less than Ufr.
The new TDHs calculated for each section are summed up and the difference between the new total TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The TDF flow resistance uncertainty also accounts for SGE tube plugging, since the tube plugging will increase resistance. The MDF flow resistance uncertainty does not account for tube plugging because largest RCS flow will not occur with plugged tubes.

The flow resistance uncertainty does not account for geometry changes due to temperature changes, wear, or manufacturing tolerances. The TDHs of each section are added up for a new total TDH. This is statistically conservative because it assumes that all flow resistance uncertainties occur in the conservative direction at the same time, unlike the root sum of squares. Therefore, this conservative statistical approach bounds minor changes in geometry.
