entries.text: The RCP TDH is dependent on flow resistance. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainties associated with flow resistance. Uncertainties for flow resistance are taken from Reference [4]. These uncertainties are applied (added for TDF, subtracted for MDF) to each section within the RCS flow loop.
The flow resistance uncertainty can be assumed to have a normal distribution. With a normal distribution, one-sided tolerance limits can be calculated as:

x = Weighted average of the TDH uncertainty. This is calculated by determining the differences between the nominal TDH and TDH with uncertainty at each section with the RCS loop. The weighted average is calculated by summing the squares of the differences in TDH and dividing by the sum of the TDH differences.
k = Coverage factor used to determine the range within which a certain proportion of the flow resistance uncertainty lies within a specific level of confidence.
o = Standard deviation of the flow resistance uncertainty.
Ufr = Total flow resistance uncertainty

The coverage factor (k) is taken from Table 2.1 of Reference [5]. The k factor is selected such that there is a 99.5% probability that 99.0% of the possible TDH combinations due to flow resistance uncertainty are less than Ufr.
The new TDHs calculated for each section are summed up and the difference between the new total TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The TDF flow resistance uncertainty also accounts for SGE tube plugging, since the tube plugging will increase resistance. The MDF flow resistance uncertainty does not account for tube plugging because largest RCS flow will not occur with plugged tubes.

The flow resistance uncertainty does not account for geometry changes due to temperature changes, wear, or manufacturing tolerances. The TDHs of each section are added up for a new total TDH. This is statistically conservative because it assumes that all flow resistance uncertainties occur in the conservative direction at the same time, unlike the root sum of squares. Therefore, this conservative statistical approach bounds minor changes in geometry.

The RCP TDH varies with the RCS flow rate. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the RCS flow measurement. The TDF flow measurement uncertainty is accounted for by:
Qₓₑₙ = Qₓₑₙ,ₓₑₙₙₙₙ(1 - Uₑₙₙ)

The uncertainty is added to the TDF case because this will conservatively increase the TDH due to the higher flow. The uncertainty is subtracted from the MDF case because it will conservatively decrease the TDH due to the lower flow.

The new TDHs calculated based on the new flow due to flow measurement uncertainty. The difference between the new TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The RCP TDH varies with the density of the fluid. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the operating conditions (RCS average temperature and pressure). The operating condition uncertainty is accounted by calculating new densities for each section of the RCS loop based on the uncertainty in RCS average temperature and pressure.

Based on these new densities, the head loss in each section will be calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the sum of the new TDHs is the absolute uncertainty due to uncertainty in the operating conditions.

The TDF case will use a higher RCS average temperature and lower RCS pressure because it will decrease the density and increase the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty. The MDF case will use a lower RCS average temperature and higher RCS pressure because that will increase the density and lower the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty.
System curves (TDH vs flow) are developed using:
R = Resistance factor (ft-s2/lb2)
TDH = Total dynamic head (ft)

The resistance factor is calculated for each flow scenario (BEF, TDF, and MDF) based on their respective TDH and flow rate. With the resistance factor known, the TDH at various flow rates can be calculated.
A sample pump curve is developed to show a general representation of how the pump curve can satisfy the acceptance criteria.

entries.text: The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
This report has no acceptance criteria. This report is used for the design basis of the RCP:
The RCP shall generate TDH equal to the calculated TDH for BEF conditions at 100% rated power.
The RCP shall generate TDH greater than the calculated TDH for TDF conditions which include uncertainties.
The RCP shall generate TDH less than the calculated TDH for MDF conditions which include uncertainties.

The SMR-300 consists of two parallel cold legs, each equipped with an RCP. The RCPs move coolant through the cold legs to the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), passing through the downcomer, RPV lower internals, reactor core, and RPV upper internals. The heated RCS coolant exits the RPV hot leg nozzles, flows through the two parallel hot legs up to the Pressurizer (PZR) turn-around region. The RCS coolant then makes a 90 degree turn into the Steam Generator (SGE) tubes and transfers energy to the secondary side of the SGE. The cooler RCS coolant exits the SGE tubes into the SGE lower head, and then flows into two parallel cold legs, which connect to the suction side of their respective RCP. Figure 1-2 shows the general arrangement of the RCS flow loop.
The TDH is calculated using the Bernoulli equation [1]:
TDH = h2 − h1 + P2 − P1 ρ + V2 2 − V1 2 2g + ∑i hfi (1)
h1, h2 = elevation head at points 1 and 2
P1, P2 = pressure at points 1 and 2
g = acceleration due to gravity
V1, V2 = fluid velocity at points 1 and 2
hfi = head loss for section i

entries.text: Using the geometry information in Appendix A, a nominal TDH is calculated based on the TDF flow (95% of BEF). Then as described in Section 3.5, the uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions, are applied individually to calculate a new TDH based on the respective uncertainty. The root sum of squares method is then used to calculate the absolute total uncertainty. This total uncertainty is added to the nominal TDH at TDF conditions. This same process is used for the MDF, except that the uncertainty is subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions.

entries.text: Using the geometry information in Appendix A, a nominal TDH is calculated based on the TDF flow (95% of BEF). Then as described in Section 3.5, the uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions, are applied individually to calculate a new TDH based on the respective uncertainty. The root sum of squares method is then used to calculate the absolute total uncertainty. This total uncertainty is added to the nominal TDH at TDF conditions. This same process is used for the MDF, except that the uncertainty is subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions.

The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
This report has no acceptance criteria. This report is used for the design basis of the RCP:
The RCP shall generate TDH equal to the calculated TDH for BEF conditions at 100% rated power.
The RCP shall generate TDH greater than the calculated TDH for TDF conditions which include uncertainties.
The RCP shall generate TDH less than the calculated TDH for MDF conditions which include uncertainties.

The SMR-300 consists of two parallel cold legs, each equipped with an RCP. The RCPs move coolant through the cold legs to the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), passing through the downcomer, RPV lower internals, reactor core, and RPV upper internals. The heated RCS coolant exits the RPV hot leg nozzles, flows through the two parallel hot legs up to the Pressurizer (PZR) turn-around region. The RCS coolant then makes a 90 degree turn into the Steam Generator (SGE) tubes and transfers energy to the secondary side of the SGE. The cooler RCS coolant exits the SGE tubes into the SGE lower head, and then flows into two parallel cold legs, which connect to the suction side of their respective RCP. Figure 1-2 shows the general arrangement of the RCS flow loop.

entries.text: The TDH is calculated using the Bernoulli equation [1]:
TDH = h2 − h1 + P2 − P1 ρ + V2 2 − V1 2 2g + ∑i hfi (1)
h1, h2 = elevation head at points 1 and 2
P1, P2 = pressure at points 1 and 2
g = acceleration due to gravity
V1, V2 = fluid velocity at points 1 and 2
hfi = head loss for section i

The RCS loop is a closed loop system and points 1 and 2 are at the same location within the loop. Therefore, the elevation head, differential pressure, and velocity differences are zero and Equation (1) reduces to:
From Reference [1], head loss for a specific section i can be written as:
Where, ΔP = pressure drop p = fluid density V = fluid velocity f = friction factor L = length Dh = hydraulic diameter K = minor loss

Most of the major and minor losses within the RCS loop are calculated using equations described in References [1] and [2]. However, the SMR-300 consists of several complex geometries for the RPV (lower head, RPV upper internals, and PZR turn-around region. For these regions, CFD was used to calculate the pressure drop, which is converted to head by Equation (3).

entries.text: Revision 0 Initial Issue.

Complete revision. Change bars are not used. Several corrections were made to the calculation, which include correcting double counting the RPV cold leg nozzle loss, properly accounting for gravitational head in the CFD input data, properly accounting for entrance and exit losses at the boundaries of CFD input data, and using a less conservative roughness for RCS cladding. Additional requirements are added to the RCP design basis to ensure the performance is adequate under thermal design flow and mechanical design flow conditions. The startup analysis of the RCP is removed.
Refined and updated flow resistance uncertainty calculation for thermal and mechanical design flows.

The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later to when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
The RCP shall be designed such that:
The RCP provides 57180 gpm (6000 lb/s) at 220 ft TDH under BEF conditions. This is the guaranteed design point of the RCP.
The RCP shall provide at least 54321 gpm (5700 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or greater than 229 ft under TDF conditions.
The RCP shall provide no more than 60039 gpm (6300 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or less than 214 ft under MDF conditions.
Statement of Limitations:

The calculations and conclusions within this report rely on unverified assumptions. These unverified assumptions are explicitly stated within the report, as well as the responsible engineering groups for dispositioning them.

The BEF is the most likely flow rate to occur in the RCS loop when the plant is operating at normal full-power conditions. This operating state is the design basis point for the RCP. The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions. The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

Uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions are accounted for individually in the TDH calculations at TDF and MDF conditions. These uncertainties are applied to their respective parts of Equation (3) and a new TDH is calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the new TDH based on a specific uncertainty, results in an uncertainty with a dimension (unit) of TDH. These TDH uncertainties are then then combined using the root sum of squares method:

Where: Utotal = Total uncertainty (ft) Ufr = Uncertainty in flow resistance (including SGE tube plugging) (ft) Ufm = Uncertainty in flow measurement (ft) Uoc = Uncertainty in operating conditions (temperature and pressure) (ft)
The uncertainty is then added to the nominal TDH at TDF conditions and subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions:
Where: TDHtotal = TDH at TDF conditions plus uncertainty (ft) TDHnominal = TDH at TDF conditions without uncertainty (ft) UTDHFfr = nominal TDH uncertainty in flow resistance at TDF conditions (ft)

entries.text: The RCP TDH varies with the RCS flow rate. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the RCS flow measurement. The TDF flow measurement uncertainty is accounted for by:
Qₓₑₙ = Qₓₑₙ,ₓₑₙₙₙₙ(1 - Uₑₙₙ)

The uncertainty is added to the TDF case because this will conservatively increase the TDH due to the higher flow. The uncertainty is subtracted from the MDF case because it will conservatively decrease the TDH due to the lower flow.

The new TDHs calculated based on the new flow due to flow measurement uncertainty. The difference between the new TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The RCP TDH varies with the density of the fluid. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the operating conditions (RCS average temperature and pressure). The operating condition uncertainty is accounted by calculating new densities for each section of the RCS loop based on the uncertainty in RCS average temperature and pressure.

Based on these new densities, the head loss in each section will be calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the sum of the new TDHs is the absolute uncertainty due to uncertainty in the operating conditions.

The TDF case will use a higher RCS average temperature and lower RCS pressure because it will decrease the density and increase the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty. The MDF case will use a lower RCS average temperature and higher RCS pressure because that will increase the density and lower the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty.

R = Resistance factor (ft-s2/lb2)
TDH = Total dynamic head (ft)

The resistance factor is calculated for each flow scenario (BEF, TDF, and MDF) based on their respective TDH and flow rate. With the resistance factor known, the TDH at various flow rates can be calculated.

entries.text: The primary objective of this Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection Project Instruction (PI) is to direct the efforts for field data collection and field recordkeeping for hydrogeologic data used in developing the Environmental Report (ER) for the Construction Permit (CP) Application for two new Small Modular Reactor (SMR) units at the Palisades Nuclear Plant site.

The primary objective of this Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection Project Instruction (PI) is to direct the efforts for field data collection and field recordkeeping for hydrogeologic data used in developing the Environmental Report (ER) for the Construction Permit (CP) Application for two new Small Modular Reactor (SMR) units at the Palisades Nuclear Plant site.

The HOLTEC SMR Site is located on the eastern shore of Lake Michigan approximately four and a half miles south of the city of South Haven, Van Buren County, Michigan. The proposed SMR area is located within the boundaries of the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant property. The general location of the proposed hydrogeology investigation is depicted in Figure 1.

Regional geology in Van Buren County consists of 300 to 400 feet of glacial and post-glacial deposits underlying sedimentary bedrock consisting of Mississippian-age Coldwater Shale or Limestone. Groundwater occurs in the shallow dune sand in the glacial drift aquifer, which provides water for domestic supply wells, but is not sufficient for larger non-domestic water supply volumes.

The glacial drift aquifer is isolated from the underlying regional bedrock water-bearing zones by a significant thickness of glacial silts and clays. The bedrock aquifer is not typically used for potable water because of its low permeability and the presence of brackish groundwater. The groundwater flow in both unconsolidated deposits and bedrock units in the region is generally toward the lake.

This PI was developed from a general understanding of site conditions following ENERCON's preliminary review of the limited publicly available hydrogeologic information pertaining to the site. This PI deals specifically with hydrogeologic data collection that will support the development of the ER. Work completed during field operations will be performed in compliance with ENERCON's site-specific Health and Safety Plan.
Specific tasks within the scope of work of the hydrogeologic investigation include the following:
Site reconnaissance and observation of site conditions.
Quarterly collection of groundwater and surface water quality samples for a minimum of 12 months (4 data collection events).
The hydrogeologic investigation approach presented herein is designed to meet the following data collection needs:

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: Collect additional site-specific groundwater data; Validate any findings presented in previous investigations and/or publicly available sources; and Supplement the available groundwater and surface water data to include current hydrogeologic conditions.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: Impediments to the investigations identified in this scope of work should be assessed prior to, or in conjunction with, the commencement of field activities/site reconnaissance. Potential impediments include: Previously identified sensitive habitat for flora/fauna; Sensitive habitat protection zones; Known archeological/historical resources around the site; Restricted access to certain portions of the site; Limited access to portions of the site due to lack of road infrastructure; Buried structures or materials, such as may have been left from historic ranching or similar activities; and Buried utilities – Although the majority of the site is undeveloped land, underground utilities may exist in some areas. Any available documentation of buried hazards is requested from the client. All measures necessary to identify and avoid underground utilities will be utilized. Areas of avoidance to be identified include, but are not limited to: Subsurface utilities, including electric distribution/transmission systems, and fiberoptic lines; Pipelines, including those associated with transportation of oil, natural gas, sewage/wastewater, and drinking water.

Project Manager (PM) – The PM is responsible for technical, administrative, and financial management of the project. The PM is also responsible for assuring compliance with this PI and approving any revisions to the PI.

Hydrology Task Discipline Lead (HTDL) – The HTDL is assigned the responsibility for technical adequacy, oversight of hydrogeologic field activities, compliance with this PI, and field supervision of data collection and record keeping. The HTDL transmits project information to the technical staff and PM submits the Project Field Log and/or field documentation to the PM. The HTDL also provides technical direction based on experience and subject matter knowledge.

entries.text: Appropriate personal protective equipment shall be worn during sampling activities. PPE shall include safety glasses and disposable gloves (nitrile or latex), as a minimum.
Because the HOLTEC SMR site is located in an area with no known source of contamination, purge water from groundwater sampling is

entries.text: not anticipated to be contained for offsite disposal. However, any observation of potential contamination during sampling activities, purging of the well will be immediately terminated and communicated to the HTDL and the client. It is at the discretion of the client to determine whether containment of purged groundwater is necessary.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: When sampling from a boat or riverbank, appropriate flotation equipment and wet gear will be worn. Depending on water flow and safe access, sampling will be conducted using a motorized boat, from a bridge or river overpass, or by wading near the riverbank. If flow is too high to safely collect samples by wading or boat, consult with the HTDL to determine how level proceed with the sampling.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: Prior to using the water level indicator for the sampling event, verify that the water level indicator operational and accuracy checks have been performed, as instructed in Attachment D.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: Calibrate the pH and conductivity sensors of the field multimeter according to the manufacturer's specifications (once per sampling event at a minimum). Complete the Field Multimeter Calibration Form (Attachment B). Record that these activities have been completed in the Project Field Log.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: Duplicate samples may be collected at the discretion of the HTDL as discussed in Section 5.0 of this PI.

entries.section_title: Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection
entries.text: With the exception of dedicated/disposable equipment (such as pump tubing and bailers), sampling equipment will be decontaminated between each usage by washing with phosphate-free detergent and potable water and rinsed with potable water.
Groundwater samples shall be collected as follows:
Open the well cap/seal. Because site wells are constructed with vents, groundwater within wells maintains equilibrium with atmospheric pressure and does not require additional time to stabilize.

Use a water level indicator to measure the depth to water within the well. Grasping the electric tape at the measuring point, read the depth to water to the nearest 0.01-foot below top-of-casing (btc). For consistency, the measuring point is defined as a marked/notched reference point on the top of the well riser/casing. Confirm the reading is stable by slightly raising and lowering the electrode and checking that the indicator depth is the same (repeat the measurement). Record the initial depth to water measurement on the Groundwater Sample Record Form (see Attachment A).

Purge the well using an appropriate sample pump or bailer to evacuate any stagnant groundwater within the well. Purging will be completed by one of the following three methods, as determined by the HTDL:

entries.text: Package the labeled sample containers for shipment, such as with protective bubble wrap. If the requested analytical method requires cold preservation, immediately place the samples on ice. Samples will be transported to a designated laboratory capable of performing the appropriate test method. A chain of custody form and any other paperwork that may be necessary will always accompany the samples.

Groundwater samples will be submitted to the laboratory and analyzed for the parameters listed in Table 1. Samples are not to be filtered in the field unless required by the laboratory or analysis method.

ENERCON staff will maintain sample custody from the time the sample is collected until the sample is released for transportation. A chain of custody form, provided the analytical laboratory, will be completed to document the sample collector, sample transporter(s), and sample recipient (analysis laboratory, to be determined). The sample transporter may include other ENERCON employees or freight companies. The original chain of custody form will accompany the samples throughout transportation.

Samples shall be consumed at the laboratory; no sample material will be returned to ENERCON. The recipient laboratory will be requested to return the completed chain of custody form (or provide a copy) with the completed analytical results. Technical staff will keep a copy of the chain of custody that is included in the sample shipment for submittal to the HTDL (and Site Coordinator, upon request).

Quality control measures will be implemented during field activities to minimize the potential for cross-contamination and ensure usability of the data obtained. Extreme care will be used to ensure all applicable requirements regarding sample collection, labeling, and preservation/storage are followed and adequately documented. Quality control measures will be implemented during field activities to ensure representative sampling in accordance with standard procedures and to minimize the potential for cross-contamination.

Representativeness shall be accomplished by obtaining all samples as outlined in this PI and referenced procedures. Precision and accuracy goals will be consistent with the analytical laboratory's Quality Assurance Plan and Standard Operating Procedures. Acceptable data will be that data which is reviewed and validated by review of sampling information to assure sampling and chain-of-custody procedures have been followed, and reasonableness of analytical results.
All sampling equipment shall be thoroughly decontaminated prior to and between sample collections. A duplicate groundwater sample will be collected as described in Section 4.2.1.
Acceptance criteria for the use of such information shall be limited to published reports or investigations, state and federal databases, and the professional judgment of the PM or HTDL.

Pre-project controls for work to be performed will include a pre-project meeting which will cover the PI and schedule, event sampling plan, project SOPs, equipment training. In addition to these topics, project personnel will be instructed on any site safety issues/site safety plan and emergency contact information in the event of an emergency on site.

The PM or designee may conduct random spot audits throughout the project activities. The auditor has the authority to issue a stop work order upon finding significant conditions that would adversely affect the quality and usability of the data.
Any deviation from the sampling plan will be approved by the HTDL and documented via a CAR IAW QSP-007, Corrective Action.

The HTDL, PM, and/or designee will review all data. The HTDL will be responsible for overall validation and final approval of the data in accordance with project objectives and use of data. Any changes or deviations from the approved PI will be documented via a CAR IAW QSP-007, Corrective Action, and all data will be reviewed and corrected (as necessary) to assure that data are valid and of solid, scientifically defensible quality.

entries.text: Quality control measures will be implemented during field activities to minimize the potential for cross-contamination and ensure usability of the data obtained. Extreme care will be used to ensure all applicable requirements regarding sample collection, labeling, and preservation/storage are followed and adequately documented. Quality control measures will be implemented during field activities to ensure representative sampling in accordance with standard procedures and to minimize the potential for cross-contamination.

Representativeness shall be accomplished by obtaining all samples as outlined in this PI and referenced procedures. Precision and accuracy goals will be consistent with the analytical laboratory's Quality Assurance Plan and Standard Operating Procedures. Acceptable data will be that data which is reviewed and validated by review of sampling information to assure sampling and chain-of-custody procedures have been followed, and reasonableness of analytical results.
All sampling equipment shall be thoroughly decontaminated prior to and between sample collections. A duplicate groundwater sample will be collected as described in Section 4.2.1.
Acceptance criteria for the use of such information shall be limited to published reports or investigations, state and federal databases, and the professional judgment of the PM or HTDL.

Pre-project controls for work to be performed will include a pre-project meeting which will cover the PI and schedule, event sampling plan, project SOPs, equipment training. In addition to these topics, project personnel will be instructed on any site safety issues/site safety plan and emergency contact information in the event of an emergency on site.

The PM or designee may conduct random spot audits throughout the project activities. The auditor has the authority to issue a stop work order upon finding significant conditions that would adversely affect the quality and usability of the data.
Any deviation from the sampling plan will be approved by the HTDL and documented via a CAR IAW QSP-007, Corrective Action.

The HTDL, PM, and/or designee will review all data. The HTDL will be responsible for overall validation and final approval of the data in accordance with project objectives and use of data. Any changes or deviations from the approved PI will be documented via a CAR IAW QSP-007, Corrective Action, and all data will be reviewed and corrected (as necessary) to assure that data are valid and of solid, scientifically defensible quality.

The selected analytical laboratory will be nationally accredited (such as by the National Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Program, NELAP) and recognized by the State of Michigan. Analytical methods used for the various sample parameters will conform to the analyte list presented in Table 1.

Once the data results are compiled, the PM or HTDL will review all data to determine if it is within acceptance limits. While data collected under this PI is not nuclear safety related, reviews will be conducted to ensure that data are high-quality and acceptable for use. If deficiencies are noted, the PM and/or HTDL will determine at his discretion if re-sampling or re-analysis is required.

entries.text: This PI is applicable to all personnel responsible for measuring, recording, or collecting groundwater or surface water data to be used to support the HOLTEC SMR project ER. This PI provides administration controls for data acquisition, data documentation requirements, standard procedures for data collection, and a description of the supplies and equipment needed.
bgs - below ground surface
btbc - below top of casing
CP - Construction Permit
DO - dissolved oxygen
DOE - United States Department of Energy
EGLE - Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy
ER - Environmental Report
HTDL - Hydrology Task Discipline Lead
NELAP - National Environmental Laboratory Accreditation Program
NIST - National Institute of Standards and Technology
NRCS - Natural Resources Conservation Service
PI - Project Instruction
PPE - personal protective equipment
QA - Quality Assurance
SAR - Safety Analysis Report
SR - nuclear safety related
USEPA - United States Environmental Protection Agency
USGS - United States Geological Survey

Groundwater level - The level of the water table surrounding a borehole or well. The groundwater level may be represented as an elevation or as a depth below the ground surface. The depth to the groundwater level is typically manually measured with a water level indicator or electronically measured with a water level transducer system.
Site reconnaissance - The process of conducting a site visit(s) to observe site hydrogeologic and water quality conditions. Non-intrusive, visual, and sensory observations are documented.

Field data may be recorded in a bound field logbook or on an appropriate form/data sheet. All recorded data will be in indelible ink. All original field data sheets in a loose format will be bound and numbered at the project completion to ensure against loss. Each field log will be specific to the fieldwork conducted for the HOLTEC SMR project and labeled with a start and end date (when known). If multiple field logs are necessary, each logbook shall be assigned a unique sequential number or identifier. For hydrology related tasks, field logs will be identified as HOLTEC SMR-HYD-"x", where "x" is a sequential number starting with "01". A digital copy of all Field Logbooks should be kept in a separate location from the logbook itself. At the completion of each day's entry, or as soon as is practicable, a digital copy should be made and added to the electronic files maintained for the project. Digital records should be transferred to the project file at least weekly.
Field data collection activities for the hydrogeologic investigation will include the following tasks:
Site Reconnaissance (refer to Section 4.1);
Water quality analyses based upon quarterly groundwater and surface water sample collection over a 12-month period (refer to Section 4.2).

Prior to conducting the hydrogeologic field data collection activities, a review of historical and publicly-available information will be initiated. This review will also utilize numerous sources such as federal, state, or local government information, university research and publications, published research, and site-specific data collection. The scope of the review is highly dependent upon the availability and quality of existing data at the site. Potentially reviewed information will include, but is not necessarily be limited to:
Site history documents;
Reports of previous investigations;

Reports and maps published by State and Federal agencies such as the USEPA, Michigan EGLE, the U.S. DOE, the U.S. Department of Agriculture NRCS, the Michigan Geological Survey, the USGS, the local county health department, and other resources identified as being relevant;
Interviews with local personnel with knowledge of the use of the site;
Studies of Lake Michigan, such as flow, velocity, bathymetric description (depth, width, bottom contours), and water quality

entries.text: Impediments to the investigations identified in this scope of work should be assessed prior to, or in conjunction with, the commencement of field activities/site reconnaissance. The primary objective of this Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection Project Instruction (PI) is to direct the efforts for field data collection and field recordkeeping for hydrogeologic data used in developing the Environmental Report (ER) for the Construction Permit (CP) Application for two new Small Modular Reactor (SMR) units at the Palisades Nuclear Plant site.

The primary objective of this Groundwater and Surface Water Data Collection Project Instruction (PI) is to direct the efforts for field data collection and field recordkeeping for hydrogeologic data used in developing the Environmental Report (ER) for the Construction Permit (CP) Application for two new Small Modular Reactor (SMR) units at the Palisades Nuclear Plant site.

The HOLTEC SMR Site is located on the eastern shore of Lake Michigan approximately four and a half miles south of the city of South Haven, Van Buren County, Michigan. The proposed SMR area is located within the boundaries of the Palisades Nuclear Power Plant property. The general location of the proposed hydrogeology investigation is depicted in Figure 1.

Regional geology in Van Buren County consists of 300 to 400 feet of glacial and post-glacial deposits underlying sedimentary bedrock consisting of Mississippian-age Coldwater Shale or Limestone. Groundwater occurs in the shallow dune sand in the glacial drift aquifer, which provides water for domestic supply wells, but is not sufficient for larger non-domestic water supply volumes.

The glacial drift aquifer is isolated from the underlying regional bedrock water-bearing zones by a significant thickness of glacial silts and clays. The bedrock aquifer is not typically used for potable water because of its low permeability and the presence of brackish groundwater. The groundwater flow in both unconsolidated deposits and bedrock units in the region is generally toward the lake.

This PI was developed from a general understanding of site conditions following ENERCON's preliminary review of the limited publicly available hydrogeologic information pertaining to the site. This PI deals specifically with hydrogeologic data collection that will support the development of the ER. Work completed during field operations will be performed in compliance with ENERCON's site-specific Health and Safety Plan.
Specific tasks within the scope of work of the hydrogeologic investigation include the following:
Site reconnaissance and observation of site conditions.
Quarterly collection of groundwater and surface water quality samples for a minimum of 12 months (4 data collection events).

If multiple field logs are necessary, each logbook shall be assigned a unique sequential number or identifier. For hydrology related tasks, field logs will be identified as HOLTEC SMR-HYD-"x", where "x" is a sequential number starting with "01". A digital copy of all Field Logbooks should be kept in a separate location from the logbook itself. At the completion of each day's entry, or as soon as is practicable, a digital copy should be made and added to the electronic files maintained for the project. Digital records should be transferred to the project file at least weekly.

Site history documents;
Reports of previous investigations;

Interviews with local personnel with knowledge of the use of the site;
Studies of Lake Michigan, such as flow, velocity, bathymetric description (depth, width, bottom contours), and water quality

entries.text: The BEF is the most likely flow rate to occur in the RCS loop when the plant is operating at normal full-power conditions. This operating state is the design basis point for the RCP.

The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions.

The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

Uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions are accounted for individually in the TDH calculations at TDF and MDF conditions. These uncertainties are applied to their respective parts of Equation (3) and a new TDH is calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the new TDH based on a specific uncertainty, results in an uncertainty with a dimension (unit) of TDH. These TDH uncertainties are then then combined using the root sum of squares method:

Utotal=Ufr2+Ufm2+Uoc2(6)Where:Utotal=Totaluncertainty(ft)Ufr=Uncertaintyinflowresistance(includingSGEtubeplugging)(ft)Ufm=Uncertaintyinflowmeasurement(ft)Uoc=Uncertaintyinoperatingconditions(temperatureandpressure)(ft)
The uncertainty is then added to the nominal TDH at TDF conditions and subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions:

TDHTDF,total=TDHTDF,nominal+U2TDH,fr2+U2TDH,fm2+U2TDH,oc2(7)TDHMDF,total=TDHMDF,nominal−U2MDF,fr2+U2MDF,fm2+U2MDF,oc2(8)Where:TDHTDF,total=TDHatTDFconditionsplusuncertainty(ft)TDHMDF,total=TDHatMDFconditionsminusuncertainty(ft)UTDH,fr=nominalTDHatTDFconditionswithoutuncertainty(ft)UMDF,fr=nominalTDHatMDFconditionswithoutuncertainty(ft)

The RCP TDH is dependent on flow resistance. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainties associated with flow resistance. Uncertainties for flow resistance are taken from Reference [4]. These uncertainties are applied (added for TDF, subtracted for MDF) to each section within the RCS flow loop.
The flow resistance uncertainty can be assumed to have a normal distribution. With a normal distribution, one-sided tolerance limits can be calculated as:

x = Weighted average of the TDH uncertainty. This is calculated by determining the differences between the nominal TDH and TDH with uncertainty at each section with the RCS loop. The weighted average is calculated by summing the squares of the differences in TDH and dividing by the sum of the TDH differences.
k = Coverage factor used to determine the range within which a certain proportion of the flow resistance uncertainty lies within a specific level of confidence.
σ = Standard deviation of the flow resistance uncertainty.
Ufr = Total flow resistance uncertainty

The coverage factor (k) is taken from Table 2.1 of Reference [5]. The k factor is selected such that there is a 99.5% probability that 99.0% of the possible TDH combinations due to flow resistance uncertainty are less than Ufr.
The new TDHs calculated for each section are summed up and the difference between the new total TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The TDF flow resistance uncertainty also accounts for SGE tube plugging, since the tube plugging will increase resistance. The MDF flow resistance uncertainty does not account for tube plugging because largest RCS flow will not occur with plugged tubes.

The flow resistance uncertainty does not account for geometry changes due to temperature changes, wear, or manufacturing tolerances. The TDHs of each section are added up for a new total TDH. This is statistically conservative because it assumes that all flow resistance uncertainties occur in the conservative direction at the same time, unlike the root sum of squares. Therefore, this conservative statistical approach bounds minor changes in geometry.

entries.text: The purpose of this report was to calculate the TDH, NPSHa, and hydraulic power required for each RCP at BEF conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH was also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the TDF conditions and maximum RCP TDH for the MDF conditions.
A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later to when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
Table 9-1 and Table 9-2 summarize the results of the calculations performed.
The RCP shall be designed such that:
The RCP provides 57180 gpm (6000 lb/s) at 220 ft TDH under BEF conditions. This is the guaranteed design point of the RCP.
The RCP shall provide at least 54321 gpm (5700 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or greater than 229 ft under TDF conditions.
The RCP shall provide no more than 60039 gpm (6300 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or less than 214 ft under MDF conditions.

entries.text: The RCP TDH is dependent on flow resistance. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainties associated with flow resistance. Uncertainties for flow resistance are taken from Reference [4]. These uncertainties are applied (added for TDF, subtracted for MDF) to each section within the RCS flow loop.
The flow resistance uncertainty can be assumed to have a normal distribution. With a normal distribution, one-sided tolerance limits can be calculated as:

x = Weighted average of the TDH uncertainty. This is calculated by determining the differences between the nominal TDH and TDH with uncertainty at each section with the RCS loop. The weighted average is calculated by summing the squares of the differences in TDH and dividing by the sum of the TDH differences.
k = Coverage factor used to determine the range within which a certain proportion of the flow resistance uncertainty lies within a specific level of confidence.
σ = Standard deviation of the flow resistance uncertainty.
Ufr = Total flow resistance uncertainty

The coverage factor (k) is taken from Table 2.1 of Reference [5]. The k factor is selected such that there is a 99.5% probability that 99.0% of the possible TDH combinations due to flow resistance uncertainty are less than Ufr.
The new TDHs calculated for each section are summed up and the difference between the new total TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The TDF flow resistance uncertainty also accounts for SGE tube plugging, since the tube plugging will increase resistance. The MDF flow resistance uncertainty does not account for tube plugging because largest RCS flow will not occur with plugged tubes.

The flow resistance uncertainty does not account for geometry changes due to temperature changes, wear, or manufacturing tolerances. The TDHs of each section are added up for a new total TDH. This is statistically conservative because it assumes that all flow resistance uncertainties occur in the conservative direction at the same time, unlike the root sum of squares. Therefore, this conservative statistical approach bounds minor changes in geometry.

The RCP TDH varies with the RCS flow rate. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the RCS flow measurement. The TDF flow measurement uncertainty is accounted for by:
QMDF.U = QMDF.nominal(1 - Ufm)

The uncertainty is added to the TDF case because this will conservatively increase the TDH due to the higher flow. The uncertainty is subtracted from the MDF case because it will conservatively decrease the TDH due to the lower flow.

The new TDHs calculated based on the new flow due to flow measurement uncertainty. The difference between the new TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The RCP TDH varies with the density of the fluid. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the operating conditions (RCS average temperature and pressure). The operating condition uncertainty is accounted by calculating new densities for each section of the RCS loop based on the uncertainty in RCS average temperature and pressure.

Based on these new densities, the head loss in each section will be calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the sum of the new TDHs is the absolute uncertainty due to uncertainty in the operating conditions.

The TDF case will use a higher RCS average temperature and lower RCS pressure because it will decrease the density and increase the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty. The MDF case will use a lower RCS average temperature and higher RCS pressure because that will increase the density and lower the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty.
System curves (TDH vs flow) are developed using:

The resistance factor is calculated for each flow scenario (BEF, TDF, and MDF) based on their respective TDH and flow rate. With the resistance factor known, the TDH at various flow rates can be calculated.
A sample pump curve is developed to show a general representation of how the pump curve can satisfy the acceptance criteria.

entries.text: The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
This report has no acceptance criteria. This report is used for the design basis of the RCP:
The RCP shall generate TDH equal to the calculated TDH for BEF conditions at 100% rated power.
The RCP shall generate TDH greater than the calculated TDH for TDF conditions which include uncertainties.
The RCP shall generate TDH less than the calculated TDH for MDF conditions which include uncertainties.

The SMR-300 consists of two parallel cold legs, each equipped with an RCP. The RCPs move coolant through the cold legs to the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), passing through the downcomer, RPV lower internals, reactor core, and RPV upper internals. The heated RCS coolant exits the RPV hot leg nozzles, flows through the two parallel hot legs up to the Pressurizer (PZR) turn-around region. The RCS coolant then makes a 90 degree turn into the Steam Generator (SGE) tubes and transfers energy to the secondary side of the SGE. The cooler RCS coolant exits the SGE tubes into the SGE lower head, and then flows into two parallel cold legs, which connect to the suction side of their respective RCP. Figure 1-2 shows the general arrangement of the RCS flow loop.
The TDH is calculated using the Bernoulli equation [1]:
TDH=h2−h1+P2−P1ρ+V22−V122g+∑ihi
h1, h2 = elevation head at points 1 and 2
P1, P2 = pressure at points 1 and 2
g = acceleration due to gravity
V1, V2 = fluid velocity at points 1 and 2
hi = head loss for section i

The RCP provides 57180 gpm (6000 lb/s) at 220 ft TDH under BEF conditions. This is the guaranteed design point of the RCP.
The RCP shall provide at least 54321 gpm (5700 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or greater than 229 ft under TDF conditions.

entries.text: Using the geometry information in Appendix A, a nominal TDH is calculated based on the TDF flow (95% of BEF). Then as described in Section 3.5, the uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions, are applied individually to calculate a new TDH based on the respective uncertainty. This same process is used for the MDF, except that the uncertainty is subtracted from the nominal TDH at MDF conditions.
Report No. HI-224200264 Rev. 20

The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
This report has no acceptance criteria. This report is used for the design basis of the RCP:
The RCP shall generate TDH equal to the calculated TDH for BEF conditions at 100% rated power.
The RCP shall generate TDH greater than the calculated TDH for TDF conditions which include uncertainties.
The RCP shall generate TDH less than the calculated TDH for MDF conditions which include uncertainties.

The SMR-300 consists of two parallel cold legs, each equipped with an RCP. The RCPs move coolant through the cold legs to the Reactor Pressure Vessel (RPV), passing through the downcomer, RPV lower internals, reactor core, and RPV upper internals. The heated RCS coolant exits the RPV hot leg nozzles, flows through the two parallel hot legs up to the Pressurizer (PZR) turn-around region. The RCS coolant then makes a 90 degree turn into the Steam Generator (SGE) tubes and transfers energy to the secondary side of the SGE. The cooler RCS coolant exits the SGE tubes into the SGE lower head, and then flows into two parallel cold legs, which connect to the suction side of their respective RCP. Figure 1-2 shows the general arrangement of the RCS flow loop.

entries.text: The TDH is calculated using the Bernoulli equation [1]:
TDH=h2−h1+P2−P1ρ+V22−V122g+∑ihi
h1, h2 = elevation head at points 1 and 2
P1, P2 = pressure at points 1 and 2
g = acceleration due to gravity
V1, V2 = fluid velocity at points 1 and 2
hi = head loss for section i

The RCS loop is a closed loop system and points 1 and 2 are at the same location within the loop. Therefore, the elevation head, differential pressure, and velocity differences are zero and Equation (1) reduces to:
From Reference [1], head loss for a specific section i can be written as:
Where, ΔP = pressure drop p = fluid density V = fluid velocity f = friction factor L = length Dh = hydraulic diameter K = minor loss

Most of the major and minor losses within the RCS loop are calculated using equations described in References [1] and [2]. However, the SMR-300 consists of several complex geometries for the RPV lower head, RPV upper internals, and PZR turn-around region. For these regions, CFD was used to calculate the pressure drop, which is converted to head by Equation (3).

The NPSHa is calculated by considering the pressure and energy of the fluid at the suction side of the pump, as well as the conditions of the fluid in the suction piping. NPSHa is calculated using Equation 5-1 from Reference [1]:
NPSHa = (Pt − Pv) + (Zt − Zs) − hl (4)

The NPSHa varies significantly depending on the operating mode of the plant. The SMR-300 design is not mature enough at the time of this report to analyze all operating modes. An NPSHa is calculated for 100% reactor power at BEF conditions. A more comprehensive assessment will be performed later when the RCP vendor provides NPSHR data.
Hydraulic power is the energy delivered by the pump to the fluid in the form of flowrate and head. Hydraulic power is calculated using the formula from Reference [3]:
Hydraulic Power = Q × TDH × ρg (5)

entries.text: Revision 0 Initial Issue.

1 Complete revision. Change bars are not used. Several corrections were made to the calculation, which include correcting double counting the RPV cold leg nozzle loss, properly accounting for gravitational head in the CFD input data, properly accounting for entrance and exit losses at the boundaries of CFD input data, and using a less conservative roughness for RCS cladding. Additional requirements are added to the RCP design basis to ensure the performance is adequate under thermal design flow and mechanical design flow conditions. The startup analysis of the RCP is removed.
2 Refined and updated flow resistance uncertainty calculation for thermal and mechanical design flows.

The purpose of this report is to calculate the Total Dynamic Head (TDH), Net Positive Suction Head Available (NPSHa), and hydraulic power required for each Reactor Coolant Pump (RCP) with the Reactor Coolant System (RCS) at best-estimate flow (BEF) conditions. The uncertainty associated with RCP TDH is also calculated and used to provide the minimum RCP TDH for the thermal design flow (TDF) and maximum RCP TDH for the mechanical design flow (MDF). A more comprehensive assessment of NPSHa and its margin to NPSHr will be performed later to when the RCP vendor provides NPSHr data.
The RCP shall be designed such that:
The RCP provides 57180 gpm (6000 lb/s) at 220 ft TDH under BEF conditions. This is the guaranteed design point of the RCP.
The RCP shall provide at least 54321 gpm (5700 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or greater than 229 ft under TDF conditions.
The RCP shall provide no more than 60039 gpm (6300 lb/s) at a TDH equal to or less than 214 ft under MDF conditions.
Statement of Limitations:

The calculations and conclusions within this report rely on unverified assumptions. These unverified assumptions are explicitly stated within the report, as well as the responsible engineering groups for dispositioning them.

The BEF is the most likely flow rate to occur in the RCS loop when the plant is operating at normal full-power conditions. This operating state is the design basis point for the RCP.

The TDF is the minimum flow required by the RCPs to ensure that there is margin to the departure from nucleate boiling ratio (DNBR). The TDF accounts for SGE tube plugging, uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH greater than the TDH calculated at TDF conditions.

The MDF is a conservatively high flow rate that is used as the basis for the mechanical design of the components within the RCS. The MDF accounts for uncertainties in the flow resistance, uncertainty in the RCS flow measurement, and uncertainty in the operating conditions. The RCPs shall be designed to have a TDH less than the TDH calculated MDF conditions.

Uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions are accounted for individually in the TDH calculations at TDF and MDF conditions. These uncertainties are applied to their respective parts of Equation (3) and a new TDH is calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the new TDH based on a specific uncertainty, results in an uncertainty with a dimension (unit) of TDH. Using the geometry information in Appendix A, a nominal TDH is calculated based on the TDF flow (95% of BEF). Then as described in Section 3.5, the uncertainties for flow resistance, flow measurement, and operating conditions, are applied individually to calculate a new TDH based on the respective uncertainty. entries.text: The RCP TDH varies with the RCS flow rate. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the RCS flow measurement. The TDF flow measurement uncertainty is accounted for by:
QMDF.U = QMDF.nominal(1 - Ufm)

The uncertainty is added to the TDF case because this will conservatively increase the TDH due to the higher flow. The uncertainty is subtracted from the MDF case because it will conservatively decrease the TDH due to the lower flow.

The new TDHs calculated based on the new flow due to flow measurement uncertainty. The difference between the new TDH and nominal TDH is the absolute TDH uncertainty due to uncertainty in flow resistance.

The RCP TDH varies with the density of the fluid. Therefore, there is an uncertainty in the RCP TDH due to the uncertainty associated with the operating conditions (RCS average temperature and pressure). The operating condition uncertainty is accounted by calculating new densities for each section of the RCS loop based on the uncertainty in RCS average temperature and pressure.

Based on these new densities, the head loss in each section will be calculated. The difference between the nominal TDH and the sum of the new TDHs is the absolute uncertainty due to uncertainty in the operating conditions.

The TDF case will use a higher RCS average temperature and lower RCS pressure because it will decrease the density and increase the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty. The MDF case will use a lower RCS average temperature and higher RCS pressure because that will increase the density and lower the TDH, thus increase the overall uncertainty.

entries.text: This notebook describes the operating conditions of the SMR-300 Reactor Coolant System and designates the design pressure, and temperature for different parts of the system. Design values are selected to provide margin to the most limiting operating conditions associated with that part of the system.

Statement of Limitations: This notebook summarizes preliminary design work. Users of this document are advised that information in this notebook is preliminary and subject to change. Updated information and additional operating conditions will be provided in subsequent revisions of this document.
The loop piping weight of Table 3-3 and control scheme of Table 3-4 are unverified assumptions.

The purpose of this document is to identify the operating conditions of the SMR-300 Reactor Coolant System (RCS) and define design temperatures and pressures for the RCS that bound these operating conditions.
This technical report supports the development of the RCS System Design Description (SDD) [1] and the design of other SMR-300 systems and components which require RCS parameters as inputs.

This report describes RCS conditions in MODE 1: Power Operations where rated power is >5%, the Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCPs) are providing flow through the system at rated speed, RCS pressure is maintained at the normal operating pressure, and average RCS temperature is maintained according to the program band. Additional operating modes, Anticipated Operating Occurrences, and Design Basis Accidents will be addressed in future revisions of this report.

This report identifies RCS pressure, temperature, flow rates, component volumes, and weights based on information available during drafting. The design pressure, and design temperature for different portions of the system are established to provide margin to the most limiting conditions in that part of the system. This document serves as the basis for the design pressures and temperature used in the pipe material class codes shown on the Reactor Coolant System Piping & Instrumentation Diagram [2].

From: Rietz, Christopher <Christopher.Rietz@ksb.com> Sent: Tuesday, July 22, 2025 5:36 AM To: Mark Fleming <M.Fleming@holtec.com>; Aderhold, Martin <Martin.aderhold@ksb.com> Cc: Jim Robin <JRobin@holtec.com> Subject: AW: Preliminary System Flow Curve

CAUTION: This email came from a source OUTSIDE of Holtec!! Do not click any links or open any attachments unless you trust the sender and know the contents to be safe. Clicking links or opening attachments could lead to infecting your computer or Holtec's servers with malicious viruses.

Mark, I've talked with Andreas Baum to this topic We're wondering where the pump curve (Preliminary Single Pump System Curve.png) in the attached picture comes from. The current curve (0452874_0_US_preliminary) we've submitted looks different.
we need to know how it shifts based on temperature, NOP down to 100F

The QH-curve isn't affected by temperature. See attached document, both curves (NOT and T=70°F), which are shown in the diagram, have the same course. Note: K-factor is independent of temperature too.
Also, do you have an estimate for the liquid volume within the new pump? Estimated wet volume within the pump: about 2500 liter (~ 660,4 gallons) - preliminary
Kind regards KSB SE & Co. KGaA Global CM Nuclear Energy CI.2/3 & NC Christopher Rietz E-mail: christopher.rietz@ksb.com Website: https://ksb.com
660.4gal = 88.283ft^3 per pump

entries.text: The purpose of this document is to identify the operating conditions of the SMR-300 Reactor Coolant System (RCS) and define design temperatures and pressures for the RCS that bound these operating conditions.
This technical report supports the development of the RCS System Design Description (SDD) [1] and the design of other SMR-300 systems and components which require RCS parameters as inputs.

This report describes RCS conditions in MODE 1: Power Operations where rated power is >5%, the Reactor Coolant Pumps (RCPs) are providing flow through the system at rated speed, RCS pressure is maintained at the normal operating pressure, and average RCS temperature is maintained according to the program band. Additional operating modes, Anticipated Operating Occurrences, and Design Basis Accidents will be addressed in future revisions of this report.

This report identifies RCS pressure, temperature, flow rates, component volumes, and weights based on information available during drafting. The design pressure, and design temperature for different portions of the system are established to provide margin to the most limiting conditions in that part of the system. This document serves as the basis for the design pressures and temperature used in the pipe material class codes shown on the Reactor Coolant System Piping & Instrumentation Diagram [2].

The design parameters for the RCS are designated in Table 3-1 and Appendix A [2] [3]. RCS volumes shown in Tables 3-2 are used in the current RELAP5-3D modeling. Component dry weights are listed in Table 3-3. Table 3-4 summarizes RCS process conditions at different power levels based on the current assumed control scheme.

entries.text: An initial Civil review between the three (3) base mats at -38’ of the RAB, -21’ of the RAB and 0’ of the RWB compared to the single RAB base mat at -38’ concluded that a single base mat was beneficial for seismic interaction and response, since buildings with separate base mats would result in relative displacements and accelerations, thus amplifying the seismic demand on connections between them. Combined building also provides better stability due to lower center-of-gravity to base aspect ratio. In addition, lowering the base mat elevations reduces the seismic demand on them. This also eliminates the requirement for isolation joints between the RCA and the MCR area of the RAB, and the RAB and the RWB.

The additional space on the lower elevation allows moving the Liquid Radioactive Waste (LRW) Holdup Tanks, currently on -21’ Elevation, to the bottom plant elevation. From an operational benefit, this promotes natural (gravity) drainage from the Radioactive Drain System (RDS) and simplifies water movement from Chemical and Volume Control System (CVC) Holdup Tanks on -38’ Elevation and Spent Resin Waste (SRW) transfer and disposal operations are relocated from the RWB to 0’ Elevation of the RAB, utilizing the open refueling area for these functions. Therefore, evolutions for LRW demineralizer and filter skid and disposal of SRW High Integrity Canisters (HICs) is unchanged.

A construction evaluation [7] shows approximately one-fifth the cost estimated is saved (also refer to Table 1-1, List of Assumptions, Assumption #1 and shortened timeline for the additional excavation of the RAB lower elevation compared to the construction of the RWB. The analysis included estimates for earth work, form work, reinforcement bar, concrete, foundation piling placement, and labor differences only (and none of the commodities).
The potential options mentioned above were further influenced by many other considerations that came out of multiple question and challenge meetings. Table 4-1 lists these other considerations.

The consolidation of the liquid radioactive waste system within the lowest elevation of the RAB enhanced safety as any flooding potential from any system tank rupture was limited once these tanks were all moved to areas far from their previous areas. Additionally, it allowed for other systems to be routed from their previous areas for their consolidation thereby minimizing long piping run. This will lead to better flooding and high energy line breaks (HELB) analysis due to better placement and routing as well as the elimination of transferring both liquid and solid waste between two separate buildings. Next, risks associated with cross-contamination of liquid and solid waste unchanged as the associated systems continue to remain separate. Furthermore, with this change, any liquids associated with severe accident conditions continue to be processed via the LRW filter and demineralization system located on the 0’ Elevation of the RAB instead of the 0’ Elevation of the RWB. This results in the dose impact on the Main Control Room and/or the Remote Shutdown Facility to continue to remain unchanged. entries.text: The purpose of this report is to formally document the decision and basis behind evaluating keeping a separate Radioactive Waste Building (RWB or incorporation of all the functions associated with a separate RWB into the Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) for the SMR-300 project at the Covert, Michigan (Palisades). This Palisades SMR-300 site will serve as a reference project and may serve as a reference design for other future locations.

This design decision is a Category 2 decision in accordance with HPP-8002-0003 [6] because it has been preliminarily determined to affect several engineering disciplines, including configuration of applicable systems and pipe routing in addition to the building design specifications.

The conclusion of this decision paper will inform changes required to the design documentation of the RWB and RAB. As an example, the RAB Drawings [9] are expected to be revised and RWB Drawing [11] obsoleted.

The purpose of this report is to formally document the decision and basis behind evaluating keeping a separate Radioactive Waste Building (RWB or incorporation of all the functions associated with a separate RWB into the Reactor Auxiliary Building (RAB) for the SMR-300 project at the Covert, Michigan (Palisades). This Palisades SMR-300 site will serve as a reference project and may serve as a reference design for other future locations.

This design decision is a Category 2 decision in accordance with HPP-8002-0003 [6] because it has been preliminarily determined to affect several engineering disciplines, including configuration of applicable systems and pipe routing in addition to the building design specifications.

The conclusion of this decision paper will inform changes required to the design documentation of the RWB and RAB. As an example, the RAB Drawings [9] are expected to be revised and RWB Drawing [11] obsoleted.

The draft layout of the RWB [11] was issued by the Civil Structural team once the functional requirements as determined and specified by a Holtec subcontractor, Enercon. Upon reviewal of the building requirements, layout, and functions to be housed, a potential optimization opportunity was identified where the functions of the building could potentially be placed inside the RAB [9] through the expansion of the existing -38' Elevation underneath the non-radiological portion of the Control Building.

A small team of critical stakeholders (Operations, Civil/Structural, and Capital Expenditure) evaluated the RWB structure and functions in accordance with Design Evolution and Freeze Process for SMR-300 [5]. During this process the RWB and RAB were assessed together in a possible design alteration to include the RWB within the RAB. Based on this feedback gathered, the decision was elevated to the Design Decision Register [6] and brought in front of a larger team, to include Nuclear Island Systems, Projects, Balance of Plant, and Construction.

The evaluation team was tasked with preparing and answering internal challenges associated with normal operations, outage operations, construction costs, construction timelines, and RWB absorption without detrimental RAB layout disruption. After this information was assembled and reviewed, it was presented at a meeting with representatives from each of the SM Departments to review and consider any new and/or missing methodology, associated costs, implementation feasibility, any potential unforeseen effects on existing RAB layout or probabilistic risk evaluations, as well as the effect, if any, on the Limited Work Authorization (LWA) [1]. Questions and challenges were posed and answered based on a combination of the best available data, reasonable assumptions, and operational experience [8].

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: 1) Confirm with Hyundai Engineering and Construction (HDEC) the RWB itself, being utilized as a terminal point and collector area for electrical and mechanical utilities (e.g. gas systems, demineralized water, etc.), may be eliminated with minimal impact and/or considerations. HDEC confirmed the elimination of this building will not affect the distribution of electrical and mechanical utilities adversely.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Outcome: HDEC confirmed the elimination of this building will not affect the distribution of electrical and mechanical utilities adversely.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Status: This action item is considered closed.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: 2) Confirm what additional impact on the LWA, if any, will be, if any.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Outcome: The actual impact on the LWA will not be determined for many months until the actual submittal. Nonetheless, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) has already been sent an outline letter that identifies the rad waste systems, structures, and components as non-construction (meaning, not in the scope of construction as defined by 10 CFR 50.10, License Required; Limited Work Authorization). As such, this construction scope could be performed ahead of the construction permit issuance. However, even though the specifics around this approach may change, the RWB absorption into the RAB should have no impact on this. Therefore, this will not adversely affect the LWA submittal or review.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Status: This action item is considered closed.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: 3) Confirm seismic interactions are simplified based on the elimination of the RWB and the consolidation of the RAB base mat [9].

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Outcome: The civil/structural team confirmed a single base mat for the RAB, verses a stepped base mat, combined with a single mat for an entire building, will result in a simplified Soil Structure Interaction (SSI) analysis model, improved seismic response and elimination of seismic isolation joints between Radiological Controlled Area (RCA) and Main Control Room (MCR) area within the Control Building (CB) portion of the RAB, and RAB and RWB themselves.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Status: This action item is considered closed.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: 4) Upon completion of the finalized RAB General Arrangement Drawing [3], it be formally transmitted to HDEC for update of the Site Layout [10] and Terminal Point Process Condition locations [13].

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Outcome: The RAB final general area layout is targeted to be completed before the end of October 2024.

entries.section_title: Several Action Items were identified for follow-up at the conclusion of the meeting:
entries.text: Status: This action item is considered closed.
Table 1-1 lists the major assumptions, their validity, and their justifications used for this decision.

A construction evaluation [7] shows approximately one-fifth the cost estimated is saved (also refer to Table 1-1, List of Assumptions, Assumption #1 and shortened timeline for the additional excavation of the RAB lower elevation compared to the construction of the RWB. The analysis included estimates for earth work, form work, reinforcement bar, concrete, foundation piling placement, and labor differences only (and none of the commodities). The potential options mentioned above were further influenced by many other considerations that came out of multiple question and challenge meetings. Table 4-1 lists these other considerations.
Both the mechanical and electrical Containment penetration areas have been expanded as a result of moving other rooms and equipment.
The risks associated with the Containment Penetrations being located below the flood area (-21' Elevation) have been minimized to the extent practical.
Easier placement of the Motor Control Centers, Power Panels, Distribution Panels, and Lighting Panels will occur as a result of moving other rooms and equipment.
Support design (e.g. cable trays) no longer has to take into consideration different building settling rates over plant life
The new design under the Control Building has allowed additional stairwells which now terminate on -38' Elevation that can be used for emergencies, overall improving egress pathways.
Elimination of the RWB allows for an additional truck bay access to the RAB which will allow one bay to support normal operations and one bay to support outage operations.
The Containment Building HVAC and Pressure Relief Systems can be located on 0' Elevation were they are better suited and maintained instead of located on 0' Elevation on top of the RAB Roof

entries.section_title: 14 Elimination of the Natural Phenomena and Internal/External Man-Induced Hazard Design Criteria for the RWB
entries.text: The RWB is an above ground structure classified as a RW-IIa (High Hazard) structure as per Regulatory Guide 1.143 [2]. Section 6.1 of the Reg Guide mandates the required studies and not having to perform any of these studies will save resources and result in a positive impact on Civil/Structural schedule. More specifically, the analyses eliminated include: wind, tornado, external missile impact, explosion, vehicle related events, and small aircraft impact.

entries.section_title: 15 Higher Elevation for the Volume Control Tank (VCT) [12, 14]
entries.text: The increased elevation of VCT provides for two critical operational considerations, margin for the Charging Pump Suction as well as prevention of inadvertent boric acid solution leakage into the Charging Pump suction during normal Boric Acid Storage Tank (BAST) recirculation and filtration.

The elimination of the separate RWB represents a net reduction of the overall volume of both radiative and non-radiative waste. More specifically, the six (6) sides of the building effectively translate to only four (4) when placed under the control building portion as the ceiling is already the floor above and the south wall is no longer required.
